en: The Lamp of Reasoning (Yuktidīpikā)
The doctrines of the elephant-like Sāṃkhya— whose tusks are both extended and retracted, who frequents the forest of the [Sāṃkhya] school— are as fragile as a thicket of sallakī trees.
Homage to the supreme seer, whose splendor is equal to the rays of the sun, the sun that dispels the thick darkness of the path of saṃsāra; homage to the Guru. // 2 //
To the sage Asuri, a brahmin who desired to know the truth, the [former] sage taught that great system for the cessation of the threefold suffering. (3)
Thinking that its realization cannot be achieved even in hundreds of years due to its vastness, the sages of subtle intellect [concluded this]. (4)
Then, that instruction of the Sage was condensed into a brief treatise and composed by those of stainless wisdom out of a desire for the welfare of their disciples.

Furthermore, the opponents of that proponent of the Lord as the Person (Puruṣeśvara) are the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), the Proponents of Primordial Matter (Prākṛtikas), and likewise those who hold the Person to be a transformation (Vikārapuruṣas).
In order to thwart their desires, teachers of subtle intellect have composed,
within their own tantras, difficult arguments that are like dense thickets.
These [Sāṃkhya texts] are difficult for disciples whose intellects are confused regarding the meaning of reality to fathom;
therefore, this [work] has been composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa with its subject matter condensed. (8)
The treatise known as the *Saptati*, or the entire scripture itself, is that from which the exposition of all categories of entities will be performed here. (9)
The existence of the Pradhāna, its unity, its purposefulness, its distinctness, its subservience to another, as well as its manifoldness, disjunction, and conjunction; // 10 //
The remaining modes of subsistence and non-agency are recorded as the ten topics of the *Cūlikā*;
likewise, the fivefold error and the nine contentments have been stated. (11)
The incapacity of the instruments is considered to be of twenty-eight kinds;
thus, there are sixty categories of objects together with the eight perfections.
It will be explained here in its entirety according to its characteristics in due order;
therefore, this treatise is sufficient for establishing their distinctness. // 13 //
Containing few words but vast meaning, and endowed with all the qualities of a tantra, it is like the reflection of the Great Sage’s tantra appearing in a mirror. (14)
I shall provide its commentary so that it may be established according to reason;
even if it is unrefined, may the wise accept it out of compassion. (15)
He said: "You shall provide an exposition.
However, it was stated at the outset by all [of you] that this tantra is endowed with all the qualities of a tantra.
What, then, are the qualities of a tantra?"
And how many [are they]?
It is said:
the establishment of the components according to the measure of the sūtra, non-deficiency, and the statement of doubt and its resolution.
In this tantra, the excellence consists of the brief statement, the detailed explanation, the sequential order, the designation, and the instruction.
The sūtras, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas),
and the members (avayavas) constitute "sūtra-pramāṇa-avayavas"; the establishment of these is "the establishment of sūtra-pramāṇa-avayavas."
"Arising" (*upapatti*) and "occurrence" (*sambhava*) are not different in meaning; "not another meaning" (*anarthāntara*) means that there is no other meaning.
The word *upapatti* is completed in relation to each [term], as in "scriptural arising" (*sūtropapatti*), and so forth.
He said: "It should be stated that there is the establishment of a sūtra endowed with the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
for otherwise, even a sūtra not endowed with the defining characteristics would possess the status of being a constituent part of the system (*tantrāṅga*).
It is replied: "No, because [the characteristics] are invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*)."
For indeed, without being endowed with the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa), there is no status as a sūtra;
therefore, this [definition] need not be stated.
He asks: "Then why is it called a sūtra?"
It is said: it is called a *sūtra* because it indicates (*sūcana*).
It is a *sūtra* because it indicates various specific meanings.
For example: "The unmanifest cause exists" (ISk 16).
Regarding the [sūtra] "Because of the finite measure of differentiated things" (ISk 15):
here, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) are explicitly stated.

Considering that an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) capable of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) is required for those two, it is understood from this very [reasoning] that the "root-fragments" (*mūlaśakala*) and so forth, though not mentioned here, are nonetheless implied.

Alternatively, the *sūtra* states that for a monk whose external and internal faculties have been withdrawn, the intellect indicates [the presence of] those various objects beyond the senses, such as *pradhāna* and so forth.
Or else, there is the *sūtra*: "Its non-perception is due to subtlety" (ISk 8). For example:
Those who know the sūtras understand a sūtra to be concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in its scope, free from redundancies, and irreproachable.
The meaning is that they are free from filler words (*astobha*) and are not repetitive (*apunarukta*). Likewise,
the wise say that *sūtras* are those which indicate their intended meaning, consist of few syllables and words, and are the essence in every respect.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth; these he will explain later [in ISk 4]: "Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony," and [in ISk 5]: "Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object," and so on.
The members (avayava), moreover, are [both] the desire to know (jijñāsā) and so forth, as well as the thesis (pratijñā) and so forth.
Among these, the desire to know and so forth are the auxiliary factors for exposition.
The thesis and the other members are the means for communicating [the argument] to another;
we shall explain them later. [The opponent] says: there is no statement of the members because they have already been taught.
For the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, are not taught in the same manner as the members [of a syllogism] are taught;
therefore, the argument that "the members are established" is incorrect.
If it should be thought that there is no fault because the author of the Bhāṣya is an authority, [we reply: so be it.
Although the author of the Sūtras did not provide an exposition of the constituent members [of an inference], nevertheless some authors of the Bhāṣyas have compiled them; they are our authority.
Therefore, it is correct that there is the establishment of the constituent members.
And this is incorrect. Why?
Because it deviates from the sūtra.
For commentators who explain in a manner that deviates from the sūtra do not constitute an authoritative source.
And thus it would be contrary to the Sūtra.
It is said: No, because of the indicative mark (liṅga).
This is not tenable, because there is no scriptural instruction; therefore, the desire to know (jijñāsā) and the others do not exist.

Rather, we understand their existence even though it has not been explicitly taught, from an inferential mark (*liṅga*): namely, that this Teacher declares the purpose of the inquiry in the words, "Because of the affliction by the threefold suffering, there is an inquiry into the means for its removal" (ISk 1),
and [states] "The unmanifest cause exists" (ISk 16).
He makes a proposition;
he teaches the reason: "because of the finite measure of distinct things" (ISk 15).
"The mark (liṅga) functions like an actor" (ISk 42) indicates the illustrative example;
"the activity of the primary matter (pradhāna) is just like that of milk" (ISk 57) provides the conclusion.
Therefore, he concludes that the threefold instrument is the door;
moreover, no usage of terms unintended by the teachers is observed in their treatises.

Therefore, we infer from this indicative mark (liṅga) that there exist constituent parts such as inquiry (jijñāsā) and the rest within the treatise (śāstra). He says: "If you think thus—that there exist constituent parts such as inquiry and the rest—then the statement of the purpose (prayojana) is for the sake of instructing those [parts] which already exist.
If you consider it so, then: "There exist constituent parts such as inquiry and the rest."
The purpose for their not being taught in the treatise must be stated—that is, for what reason they are not taught by the Teacher, even though they do exist.
It is said: because they are included within other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
We have taught that these [factors] are included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and the others are members of inference (*anumāna*);
therefore, being included therein, they are not taught separately.
Furthermore, because it is stated in other tantras;

for in other tantras, [the existence of] desire to know and so forth has been taught by masters such as Vindhyavāsin. And since our own masters are authoritative, there is no reason for them not to have taught [these]. Thus, the absence of instruction regarding the desire to know and so forth [in this particular text] is explained.
He said: No, because it would follow that there is no instruction on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, if the members [of the syllogism] were not taught simply because they are taught in other treatises (*tantrāntara*), then perception and the other means of valid cognition would likewise not be taught, since they too are taught in other treatises.
Perception is the functioning of the auditory and other senses.

Inference is the establishment of the remainder from one related part. One who is expert in a matter and unimpaired in that action is an authority (āpta); the instruction of such a person is authoritative testimony (āptavacana). [If this were the case,] there would be the undesirable consequence that even those [other means of knowledge] would not be considered instruction.

Now, if it is argued that when there is instruction from another tantra, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*) are taught and not the [five] members (*avayavas*), is this not merely a matter of personal preference? It is replied: in that case, let the previous refutation stand.
Alternatively, let it be as stated in other tantras; this too is a resolution.
As for what was said regarding the consequence of not teaching the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because there is no fault in teaching that which possesses a purpose.
It is indeed reasonable that an instruction is undertaken for one who possesses a purpose;
however, who would reject the very act of instruction on the grounds that it is faulty?
Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
Furthermore, because when the primary [means] is taught, the inclusion of its subordinate elements is established.
For example, when it is said, "Chaitra, cut [that]," Chaitra employs all those specific instruments without which the act of cutting would not be possible.
Likewise, when the means of knowledge such as perception and the rest are taught, we shall employ all those things by which these [means] are invariably concomitant.
Furthermore, because it is practiced elsewhere as well;
this teacher does not only provide instruction on the primary [subject] here, but also elsewhere.
The members [of the syllogism], however, are understood from that very instruction alone;
for example: "The unmanifest exists as the cause, because there is a finite measure of differentiated entities. (ISk 15–16)
Otherwise, due to the absence of an example, this would not be a valid proof (*asādhana*).

However, the Teacher perceives that a proof lacking an example does not achieve its objective; therefore, when explaining, exponents will include even items such as *mūla* and *śakala*, which are taught in other systems (*tantrāntara*).
Furthermore, [this is so] because in inference there is instruction as if [the object] were already existent.
And for this reason, it is thus that the Teacher says, "He has declared three kinds of inference" (ISk 5). How is this known to be an indicator?
For when there is a restatement of what has been previously declared, the instruction is given by means of a word expressing a state of being (*bhūta*).
Furthermore, he has not previously explained the threefold inference.
If it is argued that he has explained it,
it cannot be demonstrated that it was explained anywhere.

Thus, the fact that he employs a word denoting what actually exists, even though it has not been explicitly mentioned, makes known to us that the Teacher accepts the inclusion here of elements established in other systems (*tantra*). What is the purpose of this indication?

It is that the definition and instruction regarding the sources of ritual action (*karmayoni*) and the various types of vital breaths (*prāṇabheda*), although taught in other systems, become subsumed here. Thus it is established that the non-instruction of certain constituent parts [is due to their] being taught in other systems.

Therefore, it is well said that the "establishment of the members" (*avayavopapatti*) constitutes completeness (*anyūnatā*). Completeness is defined as the totality of the subject matter (*padārtha-kārtsnya*), which is the absence of deficiency (*aśeṣatā*). And the subject matters are the ten topics of the *Cūlikā*.
There are fifty conditions.
Among them, existence and unity are established by five reasons;
purposefulness consists in the relationship between cause and effect.
The state of being for the sake of another belongs to those that act in combination, because they exist for the sake of another; from this very fact follows their distinctness.
The plurality of Puruṣas is established by such [arguments] as: "the birth, death, and instruments [of one] arise from the three guṇas, whereas the power of consciousness [is eternal]," and so forth.
"Union" is for the purpose of the Puruṣa's perception;
"upon obtaining the dissolution of the body" refers to separation;
and "through the attainment of perfect knowledge" refers to the cessation of remaining existence.
And from that misconception follows the non-agency of the Puruṣa; these are the ten topics of the summary.
There are five varieties of misconception, and incapacity arises from the deficiency of the instruments.
Contentment has twenty-eight varieties, while perfection is ninefold and eightfold. (ISk 47)
Thus there are fifty conditions;
this constitutes the sixty categories of entities. Their establishment is such that they are neither more nor less.
The expression "statement of doubt and resolution":
both doubt (*saṃśaya*) and resolution (*nirṇaya*) constitute the pair "doubt and resolution"; the statement of those two is the "statement of doubt and resolution.
Doubt is the mention of a general property.
For example, when it is stated that "the Great One" and so forth are effects, and that these effects are both dissimilar and similar to their primal cause (*prakṛti*),
a doubt arises as to by what property an effect is dissimilar to its primal cause, or by what it is similar. The statement of a specific distinction is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment).
And that [inference] is of two kinds: by way of words and by way of meaning.
As for the words, it is as follows: the effect is dissimilar to its material cause by virtue of having a cause and so forth.

"By means of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth, it is similar in nature to *prakṛti*. In terms of meaning, this is as follows: from those five [tanmātras] arise the five elements; these are known as the "particulars" (*viśeṣa*). (ISk 38)
What is the reason?
Because [the tanmātras] are neither calm, nor terrible, nor deluded;
due to their lack of calmness, terribleness, and delusion, the tanmātras are non-specific (aviśeṣa).
"Enumeration and exposition" (*uddeśanirdeśam*):
enumeration and exposition together constitute "enumeration-and-exposition.
According to the rule that "every copulative compound may optionally be treated as a singular," this is a singular form of a copulative compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*).

A brief statement is an *uddeśa* (enumeration); for example: "This is the creation of conditions, known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment" (ISk 46). An extensive statement is a *nirdeśa* (explanation).
For example, there are five types of misconceptions (*viparyaya-bheda*) (ISk 47),
and the eightfold division of *tamas* (ISk 48), and so forth.
Furthermore, "sequence" (*anukrama*) refers to the instruction on the arrangement of categories (*padārtha*) in their proper order.

For example, from the passage ending with: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-faculty (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen"—this constitutes both the designation and the instruction.
A name (*saṃjñā*) is a word whose purpose is to convey a designation;
and that is of two kinds: that which is based on meaning, and...
And it is based on its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Among these, that which is based on the object depends upon the performance of a purposeful action by virtue of the object.
Since the object's own nature includes universals (*jāti*) and so forth, the term conveys the named object exactly as it is.
For example, [the terms] "cook" or "reaper.
Furthermore, a name based on its own form is merely a means for communicating the designated object;

it assists in conveying the form alone and, by virtue of linguistic convention (*samaya*), communicates the designated object even when that object does not possess the meaning of its constituent parts.
For example, "elephant-ear" (*gajakarṇa*) and "horse-ear" (*aśvakarṇa*).

When the Blessed One, the supreme seer, having perceived the true nature of all principles through his own rishi-like knowledge, applies designations with effort, there is no word based solely on the intrinsic nature [of the object].
For instance, it is called *pradhāna* (the primary cause) because "modifications are deposited (*pradhīyante*) therein."
"One who lies in the city (puri śete) is a person (puruṣa)," and so forth.

Even for those teachers who follow that view, since they conduct their practical affairs by means of those very [conventional terms], there is no concern for establishing a new technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
[This applies to] the instruction (*upadeśa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Instruction is the declaration of the fruit. As it is said:
"Thus, through the non-duality of reality, there arises the knowledge that is pure because free from error—'I am not,' 'nothing is mine,' 'I do not exist'—without remainder; it is absolute. (ISk 64)
These qualities of the tantra, such as being established by the sūtras and so forth, are mentioned;
the particle "iti" is used in the sense of "manner.
Other qualities of this same manner are also to be understood.

Namely: general rule (*utsarga*), exception (*apavāda*), extension (*atideśa*), and so forth. Among these, the general rule is that the manifest (*vyakta*) is dissimilar in form to its primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while [in the case of the exception] it is similar in form.
This is an exception (*apavāda*);
likewise, "the opposite of that" is the general rule (*utsarga*).
And thus, "the person is likewise" (ISk 11) is an exception;
the manifest is insentient, common, and characterized by productivity.
Likewise, "the Pradhāna is [to be understood] in the same way" (ISk 11) is an extension by analogy (atideśa).
In this manner, other principles of systematics (tantrayukti) can also be demonstrated here.
However, since an over-extension of logic obscures the subject at hand, it is here set aside.
Thus, it is established that this is indeed a *tantra* because the connection and validity of the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles) are present;
furthermore, because it does not contradict other *tantras*.
Furthermore, even if this treatise were part of another system (*tantrāntara*), it would be a supplement to one of those such as the *Pātañjala-pañcādhikaraṇa* or the works of Vārṣagaṇya;
we shall demonstrate in various places that there is no contradiction with them.
If it is argued that [this work] is a supplement to a previous system (*pūrvatantra*), the same applies here.
These [treatises] are also supplementary to the earlier tantra;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that they too would constitute independent *prakaraṇas*.
Now, if it is thought that these are distinct tantras because they encompass all categories of topics (*padārtha*), [we reply:]...
Thus, here too, because it encompasses all categories of entities (*padārtha*), its status as a distinct system (*tantrāntara*) must be accepted.
Therefore, it is correct that this is a *tantra*.
This concludes the introduction (*upodghāta*).
Karika 1:
It is asked, "To what kind of disciple, endowed with what qualities, should this tantra be explained?
It is said: The treatise should be explained to a disciple who desires to know, who is intelligent, who investigates, who requests it, and who has been accepted [as a student].
Why?
Because of the authority of the Supreme Sage (paramarṣi).

For the Blessed One, the Supreme Sage who was born before all, having perceived the desire for knowledge of the venerable Āsuri and his possession of the excellence of superior qualities, explained [the system].
Passion (*rajas*) itself is suffering; for one who seeks to dispel that [suffering], this discernment (*viveka*) arises because of the quality of purity (*sattva*).
And this meaning—that purity is distinct from this [passion] and so forth—is taught by such statements as those uttered by the Great Ones.

Therefore, this treatise has been composed for the cessation of the threefold suffering of one who desires to know the means of destroying the affliction of the suffering of passion, and who, through purity, is about to produce the maturation of the roots of merit such as dharma.
"It transforms for the sake of that [student]" means:
this exposition is composed so that the student might indeed be joined with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). He asks:
regarding what was stated—that an exposition should be made for one who desires to know—whence does this desire to know arise, and in respect to what object does it occur?
It is said: as for what was asked—"From where, then, does this desire to know arise?"—to that we reply:
"The desire to know arises from the assault of the threefold suffering.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) and *rajas* are not different things.
It is called "suffering" (duḥkha) because it causes suffering;
the term "three" is a numerical word referring to all substances, and it is qualified by the word "suffering."

And because it is perceived as distinct due to its predominance, it becomes the cause for the genitive case—which is based on difference—since it is related to its substratum; thus, "the triad of sufferings" (*duḥkhatrayam*) [is formed], and that by which [this triad] is struck is "affliction" (*abhighātaḥ*). But what indeed is this so-called "affliction"?

It is said: that connection of the power of consciousness with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) by means of the aforementioned threefold suffering—from that impact of the threefold suffering arises the desire to know (jijñāsā).
Regarding what was asked, "With reference to what object does this occur?", he says:
Regarding "the cause of its destruction":
that which destroys is "destructive" (*apaghātaka*);
that which is destructive of it is "its destroyer" (*tadapaghātaka*).
He said: "In the case of *tadapaghātake*, the formation of the compound is untenable because of a prohibition;
for a genitive case ending is not compounded with the suffixes *tṛc* and *aka* when they denote the agent."
Therefore, it should be stated that he is its destroyer.
It is replied: No, because it is seen in the treatise.
The usage "and the one who prompts that [action] is also the cause" is observed in the treatise.
And the author of the *Padakāra* says: "Because it denotes a genus (*jāti*).

Likewise, the usage of the author of the *Cūrṇi* is that sometimes a quality (*guṇa*) becomes a qualifier of another quality, and sometimes a quality is qualified by its possessor (*guṇin*); therefore, this is faultless.
This, however, is the summarized meaning:
afflicted by the threefold suffering, the brahmin desires to know the cause that can eliminate it, [thinking],
"What indeed might be that cause which would strike down the threefold suffering?"
He said: "The word 'suffering' (duḥkha) is not mentioned at the beginning because it signifies inauspiciousness.

For treatises that begin with auspiciousness become renowned and possess heroic authors; moreover, students, their mental impressions being fortified by such auspiciousness, proceed to master the meanings of the treatise."
Furthermore, this word "duḥkha" has an inauspicious meaning;
therefore, it should not be employed at the beginning of a treatise.

To this it is replied: No, because the word is used for the sake of the sentence's meaning, its lack of independent significance renders it impossible for it to have an inauspicious meaning [in that context].
A sentence is employed for the purpose of communicating meaning, because it expresses a qualified meaning;
a word is not.

For in this way, the sentence-meaning is perceived as being indeed qualified, distinct from the word-meanings; however, an isolated word, not having departed from its general meaning, is incapable of denoting a qualified meaning.
For this very reason, it is not employed as being capable of conveying the intended meaning.
For example, this word "Devadatta" is employed as denoting an agent because it pertains to all actions; for without both the object and the action, a specific meaning is not cognized.
Likewise, "gāmi" is the object (*karman*),
because it is the cause for denoting the agent of all actions;
likewise, "abhyāja" is the action (*kriyā*).
Because it has as its object all possible agents of action:
when it is said, "Devadatta, bring the cow, the white one," then by the word "cow" (go-śabda), Devadatta is distinguished from other potential agents and established within his own domain;
and both the action and the word "cow" are established as the object of Devadatta, distinguishing them from all other agents.
The agent and the object are restricted by their very status as means (*sādhanabhāva*) for the action of bringing near (*abhyājikriyā*).

The word "white" (*śukla*) and the word "cow" (*go*)—having restricted the word "cow," which pertains to all qualities, from other attributes to be superimposed (*ādheya*), and having established it in its own substratum—bring about its status as the object [of that action].
In this sequence, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is qualified.

However, isolated words, having fallen away from their general meaning and failing to express a specific [referent], are purposeless. As it has been said: "Just as the function of the sense organs, which are established separately and directed toward separate objects, cannot be obtained without the body," so too is it with words.
"In the same way, for all words that denote distinct meanings when separated from sentences, no possessive significance (arthavattā) is obtained.

This being the case, how can this certainty be attained— that this word "duḥkha" has an inauspicious meaning— since it is indeed subject to doubt as to whether it is employed to convey its own primary meaning or because it is to be abandoned?
The statement, however, has the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), because it is undertaken for the sake of abandoning suffering.
For it is observed that whatever statement is undertaken for the sake of abandoning suffering has the purpose of auspiciousness.
For example, it is like saying, "May there be the departure of disease" or "May misfortune not occur.
Since this statement is employed for the purpose of abandoning suffering, it is therefore for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
Consequently, what was previously stated—that the word "suffering" should not be uttered at the beginning because it signifies inauspiciousness—is incorrect.
He said: "The mention of the three is purposeless, because the quality is one.
You have understood that *rajas* is suffering."
And that [single cause] alone is taught in the treatise;
therefore, the mention of three is purposeless.
If it is argued that the distinction is merely figurative due to a difference in causes, such might be the thought.
Even though suffering is one, nevertheless, because of the distinction among its causes—characterized as internal, external, and celestial—the designation of its diversity will be applied;
however, that is not so.
Why?
Because it would follow that there is an infinity of qualities due to the infinity of signs.
For the internal [suffering] is of two kinds: physical and mental.
The bodily [suffering] is caused by the imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman).
Likewise, the mental [suffering] is caused by desire, anger, greed, delusion, despondency, fear, envy, malice, attachment, and the perception of distinctions.
And the suffering pertaining to other beings (ādhibhautika) is caused by humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile things.
The *ādhidaivika* [suffering] has its cause in cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, frost, and possession by spirits.
In that case, because there is a distinction of causes, it would follow that there is an infinity of qualities for that which is recognized as being threefold; and that is not desired.
Therefore, the threefold nature does not arise from a distinction of causes.

It is said: as for what was stated—that because *rajas* is a single entity, its threefold nature is untenable, and that this threefold designation is merely figurative due to a difference in causes—that is true.
However, as for the claim that there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinity of qualities (*guṇa*) due to the infinity of causes, that is incorrect.
Why? Because even when there is a distinction, the establishment [of a category] is possible, just as in the case of the number of castes (*varṇa*).

For example, although there is a distinction such as the followers of the *Paippalāda* school and others within the enumeration "there are four castes," since they do not lack the status of being Brāhmaṇas and so forth, this distinction does not serve as a cause for a different number; nor indeed does unity arise simply because they do not deviate from the category of caste.

Thus, regarding this enumeration of "three sufferings," since there is a distinction between the body and so forth, it is impossible for them to be distinct from the internal (ādhyātmika) and other categories; therefore, they cannot serve as the basis for a different enumeration. Nor, indeed, can they be considered one because they are not distinct from suffering.
Furthermore, you yourself have admitted that the designation of difference arises from a difference in causes.
Furthermore, figurative usage is not the ultimate truth; therefore, enough of this effort expended on an inappropriate point.
He says: [if it were argued that] desire to know arises from an impact, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because [impact] is possible for everyone.

Just as it is accepted that the desire to know [the means of liberation] arises for an aspirant (*asura*) due to the affliction by the three types of suffering, it would follow by that same logic that since everyone is afflicted, everyone would possess the desire to know.
If it is thought that while some have the desire to know upon being afflicted by suffering, others do not,
then this is merely a matter of personal whim.
And because of the prior context:
even before Āsuri’s desire to know [the means], there was the affliction by the threefold suffering, yet he did not have a desire to know the ultimate cause.
What follows from this?
Thereafter, it must be explained from what cause this [desire to know] arises for him:

just as in other cases, the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) arises for Brahmā due to the practice [of meditation], the destruction of demerit, and the support of prior merit, so too for others, it arises from the ripening of the cultivation of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
And since this has not been demonstrated, it is stated briefly.
Furthermore, there is no liberation from that [suffering] because it is incomplete;
for liberation is held to consist in [transcending] the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Whether from the three realms of gods, humans, and animals,
or from a single part of cyclic existence, there is the threefold suffering;
therefore, the [proposed] purpose is also untenable.

Furthermore, because other causes exist, the desire to know (vividiṣā) can arise even for one who is indifferent to the pleasures of the divine realms, the desires, and meditative absorption; it does not occur solely for one distressed by suffering.
Therefore, the proposed cause is also untenable.
Furthermore:
"And because it is impossible in either case.
For this inquiry, as it is being conceived, must belong either to the Person (puruṣa) or to the Attributes (guṇas).
What follows from this? That [agency] is not possible for the *puruṣa*.
Why? Because of the acceptance of his being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇya*).
You do not accept that desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, merit, demerit, knowledge, and mental impressions are qualities of the self (*ātman*).
It does not belong to the *guṇas*, because they are insentient;

for insentient things such as jars and the like are never observed to desire the attainment of the beneficial or the avoidance of the harmful. Furthermore, according to you, the *guṇas* are not sentient.
Because it will be stated [later] that "the Pradhāna is the universal, insentient, and characterized by productivity";
furthermore, because the existence of any other principle is untenable.
Furthermore, there exists no other ontological reality (tattvāntara) distinct from the qualities (guṇas) and the person (puruṣa), for which a desire to know (jijñāsā) could be postulated.
Therefore, the desire to know is untenable.
It is replied: as for what was said—that if the desire to know arises from verbal instruction (abhighāta), it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)—[that is not so].
Regarding the statement "because that [sound] arises from all [causes]," we reply:
no, because it is not perceived as such an impact (*abhighāta*).
Even though the impact is indistinguishable, nevertheless, not everyone perceives it as an impact.

For instance, while internal sufferings and others exist—such as acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and violence—these [beings] lack both revulsion and aversion toward sense objects due to their delight and intense attachment;
nor does the renunciation of sense objects occur.
Therefore, the affliction is not undifferentiated.
If it is argued that this is a statement of the cause for the cognition of being struck by affliction despite the absence of a specific distinction?

That is to say: even though there is no specific distinction, why is it that the Blessed One alone possesses the cognition of being struck by the threefold suffering belonging to all living beings, and not others?
In this regard, the cause must be stated.
"For this distinction cannot be established without a cause (nimitta).
This, however, is incorrect.
Why? Because it is unrelated to the question.
The questioner previously asked, "From what does the desire to know (jijñāsā) arise? To this, it was pointed out that its direct cause is "striking" (abhighāta), since no other causes were mentioned.
Now, however, you ask even for the cause of that cause; we do not speak of that for fear of falling into an infinite regress (anavasthā).

If you insist, then we do not deny that the favoring of previous dharmas and the ripening of the cultivation of roots of merit (kuśalamūla) serve as the cause of the cause; so why not accept that very thing?
By this, the previous objection has been answered.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that there would be no liberation upon the destruction of that [body] because it is not complete—that too is incorrect.
Why? Because of a failure to understand the meaning of the scripture.
The divine realm consists of eight types, the animal realm is fivefold,
and the human realm is of one kind;
such is the extent of our saṃsāra.
However, the desire, form, and formless realms are not established anywhere as distinct from that [suffering].
Furthermore, within the fourteenfold cycle of existence, whatever measure of pleasure exists is designated by the term "suffering" because of the preponderance of suffering.
Thus it has been said:
In this regard, the conscious person (puruṣa) undergoes suffering caused by birth, old age, and death;
therefore, in brief, suffering exists as long as the subtle body (liṅga) has not ceased.
Furthermore, in the world, collective apprehension is frequently observed,
such as in the expression "a grove of mango trees."
Therefore, this is a refutation of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

As for the further argument that the presence of a causal sign (*nimitta*) is improper because the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) can arise even in one who is indifferent to the heavenly pleasures of desire and the bliss of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), that too is untenable.
Why? Because it will be refuted later on.
This is indeed accepted as being included [in our position].
Furthermore, the Teacher will refute it in the subsequent sūtra: "The scriptural [means] is like the perceptible, for it is characterized by impurity, perishability, and excess" (ISk 2).
Therefore, even for one who is indifferent to divine pleasure, the desire to know [Brahman] is appropriate.
Even the bliss of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-sukha*) does not transcend deficiency and excess;
that too is included in this very [category].
Therefore, since this position is precisely what is to be refuted, nothing further is stated.
As for what was said—that because it is impossible in either way, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is untenable—let there be a desire to know the qualities (*guṇas*).
As for what was said—that it is impossible because [the intellect] is insentient—we shall demonstrate later that even though the intellect is insentient, desire and so forth do exist.
Therefore, the desire to know is established.

He said: "The word *tat* is redundant because of its connection with every individual term. Indeed, since this word *tat* recited by the Teacher in the Sūtra is not connected with each individual term, we do not perceive even the slightest meaningful purpose for it.
Therefore, we shall not study this [Sūtra] which contains such an incomplete meaning."
It is said: How indeed could it be that a word, due to its dependence on an agent (*prayoktṛpāratantrya*), would lack a connection with another word?
He replies: We do not say that a non-existent connection constitutes "no connection"; rather, a connection that is improper is what truly constitutes "no connection.

For example, regarding the expression "the boy is ill-behaved" (*anācāraḥ māṇavakaḥ*): because a substance possesses the capacity for action, it is impossible for one who is ill-behaved to remain so even for a moment.
One who practices what is improper is called "one of bad conduct" (*anācāra*).
Likewise, a connection of that word (*tat*) with each individual term is not appropriate; therefore, that word is meaningless.
If it is argued that this is because of its proximity to the word *jijñāsā*, such might be the thought.

By the principle that "either an injunction or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes," it might be possible for the word *jijñāsā* (desire to know) to be connected with the pronoun *tat* (that).
However, this is not the case.
Why? Because there is no purpose in its removal.

For there is no purpose whatsoever in the destruction of the desire to know; thus, even though a connection exists, the meaning is not expressed by that word. If it is argued that this refers to "striking" (*abhighāta*), then it might be the case that there is some purpose served by the destruction of the desire to know.
Therefore, its connection with that [word] is not desired.
In that case, then, its connection will be made with the word *abhighāta*;
and in this way, too, that word will be meaningful.
This is untenable.
Why? Because as long as the cause remains, there will be repeated production.
Since this impact is caused by that [cause], and because it possesses a cause, its destruction could not be absolute.
Otherwise, just as a feverish burning subsides through contact with cooling substances yet recurs again and again because the underlying cause remains, this practice would be fruitless.
If it is argued that this refers to the word "three," we say no, because it is dependent [on another].
For number is dependent upon its substratum;
without the destruction of that substratum, its destruction cannot be effected.
And since the pointlessness [of the effort] is the same, there is even less reason for using that word.

If it is argued that the word "suffering" (duḥkha) is the general term— if, upon the connection of these words, the aforementioned fault arises— then we shall connect the word "suffering" with the word "that" (tat). In that case, this negation will apply to it.
And that is not the case.
Why? Because of the intervention of many words.
How could the connection of the word "suffering" (duḥkha), which is separated by many words, be established by a pronoun occurring immediately [before it]?
Therefore, this is nothing at all.
Furthermore,
it is because [the object] is subordinate (*upasarjana*).
Moreover, this word "duḥkha" is a subordinate member within a compound;
and it is not logically possible for a single word to possess both the status of a primary element and a subordinate element at the same time.
Furthermore, it is the primary element that connects with another word.
Therefore, this sūtra is indeed a subject of dispute.
Furthermore:
because it is impossible for eternal things to undergo destruction.
In this world, it is impossible to effect the destruction of things that are eternal,
such as persons;
however, the destruction of things that are impermanent is observed.
For example, as in the case of fever and other such ailments;
and since suffering is constant,
it would be futile to exert effort toward its removal.
If it is argued that "upon the destruction of the function, there is the destruction of that [the eternal entity]," this thought might indeed arise;
it is true that the destruction of eternal things is not possible through reasoning.
But we do not say that there is the destruction of suffering characterized by its qualities; rather, its manifestation is suppressed.
And that is not so.
Why? Because the answer has already been stated.
The answer given here is that [the fault remains] because of repeated arising despite the persistence of the cause.
Therefore, this too is not the path.
Furthermore:

even if one were to assume that the destruction of the function (vṛtti) follows from non-distinction, since the function and the possessor of the function (vṛttimat) are non-different, it would follow that upon the destruction of the function, the possessor of the function is also destroyed; thus, there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Therefore, this rebuttal is weak, and the word "tat" serves no purpose.
It is said: as for what was stated—that the word "that" (tat) is redundant because there is no connection with every single term—let it be connected with the word "suffering" (duḥkha).
If it should be thought that this connection results in the aforementioned fault, [we reply: so be it.
If, then, it is admitted that the word "that" is connected only with the word "suffering," then those faults which were previously stated by us would follow as a consequence.
Therefore, the adoption of this rejected position is mere recklessness.
But this is not so; why?
Because there is a counter-argument.
True, in the absence of a counter-argument, it would be mere rashness;
however, a counter-argument is indeed provided.
"Therefore, this is not a fault.

If it should be thought, "What is that [faultlessness]?"—then let it be stated: what is that counter-argument by the support of which this position is maintained, even though it is struck down by many faults?
For it is not the case that what has not been stated by us can be understood merely through its form.
It is replied: "Certainly.
Regarding what was said—that because of the intervention of many words, the word *duḥkha* cannot be connected with the word *tat*—we say: no.
Because we do not accept that.
For an objection would apply only to one who asserts that the relationship of a word with another word is produced immediately [by the words themselves];
however, we declare that the relationship is produced by the objects [they signify].
And so it has been said:
"Whatever has a connection with something belongs to that thing, even if it is far removed;
however, for things that lack a common purpose, there is no connection even when they are adjacent."
Furthermore, because it is observed in the treatise (*śāstra*).

In the treatise, the connection of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) is seen even when they are separated [from their referents], as in the rule: "When a word is applied to a substance due to the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote that [quality]. In this case, a connection between words based on meaning is accepted.
From a nominal stem ending in a vowel or a consonant;
the plural number is used for the plural [referent];
[the case endings] *sup* are deleted after a verbal root or a nominal stem.

There is an acceptance of the connection between words such as *alug-uttarapade* (in the case of non-elision in a compound ending in a following word), and likewise, the Vārttika provides the example: “O sister carrying water, you who saw an ox running headlong while carrying a jar on its head. For here, even though there is immediate proximity (*anantarya*), the carrying of the ox by the head or the running of the jar is not logically possible.
Just as the connection between separated elements is understood here, so too should it be seen in this case as well.

Furthermore, the claim that there can be no connection with another word because [the member] is subordinate (*upasarjana*) is untenable. Why? Because once it has been extracted from the compound by means of the intellect, its independence is logically established.
It is true that the connection of a subordinate element with another word is not logically possible [within the compound itself];

however, we do not maintain that the connection with the word *tat* occurs only through the operation of the compound formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*). Rather, we desire the connection of that element—which has been extracted from the compound, established by the intellect, and endowed with independence—with another word.

Now, this is undesirable; for it would result in a contradiction with such usages as, "And when that [object] is absent, there would be perception through the means of yoga," and "Now, this is the instruction on words;
of which words? and so forth. And this is undesirable.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that because it is impossible for eternal things to be destroyed, and because if their functioning were destroyed, it would follow that they themselves are destroyed—this too is untenable.
Why? Because it is admitted that when the purpose of the power of the qualities (*guṇa-śakti*) has ceased, they remain established in a state resembling their own essential nature (*ātma-kalpa*).
This is not accepted: that there is a destruction of the *guṇa*, or that its activity is merely suppressed.

Rather, what is intended to be expressed is this: bound by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, once its capacity has fulfilled that purpose, it remains as if identical to the self (*ātman*) because there is no further motive for its activity toward the purpose of the *puruṣa*.
Therefore, it is logical that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) proceeds toward the cause of its removal.
[Objection: If it were seen, this desire would be purposeless, for there exists a perceptible means for the alleviation of suffering.
What is the purpose of transcending that?
It is as follows: for physical [suffering], the cause of its removal is the consumption of various medicinal substances and elixirs;
for mental [suffering] as well, it is the attainment of objects such as attractive women, drinks, ointments, food, clothing, and ornaments.
The means for protection against physical dangers consist of the study of the science of polity, proficiency in weapons and missiles, and not frequenting dangerous places.

If it is argued that even regarding superhuman (ādhidaivika) suffering, since there are visible means— such as timely service consisting of various garments, carpets, inner chambers, palaces, lattice windows, sandalwood fans, necklaces of jewels, and so forth, as well as the performance of various medicinal herbs,
auspicious rites, hymns, and mantras— that inquiry [into the cause of suffering] is useless; we say no,
because these means do not provide absolute or permanent cessation.
And this is not so.
Why? Because of its absolute and ultimate non-existence.
"Absolute" (ekānta) means existence by necessity.
The non-destruction of that which has come to be is absolute (*atyanta*).

"Absolute" (*ekānta*) and "absolute" (*atyanta*)—these two together form the compound *ekāntātyanta*; the absence of those two is *ekāntātyantato 'bhāva*. Therefore, [the word] *abhāvāt* is used in the ablative case in place of the genitive.
Alternatively, the suffix *tasi* is used from the genitive case itself, due to the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) stating "from the genitive [comes *tasi*] when there is a different substratum.
The non-compounding is for the purpose of completing the meter,
and for the purpose of including other faults in the remediation of mental suffering.

For instance, while these two defects exist in women and the like, it is impossible to acquire them because they are not inherent; and even if acquisition were possible, their protection would be impossible because they are common property.
Furthermore, if there is protection, there is exhaustion because it is something produced;
and due to attachment, there is no tranquility, and it is impossible without injury to living beings— these are the defects.
He asks: How is it known that a perceived cause is both inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and non-conclusive (*anātyantika*)?
It is said: This is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself;

namely, when the sequence of medical treatment prescribed in Ayurveda proves futile for a patient who is diligent, self-controlled, and provided with medicine, a physician, and attendants. And it has been said:
The etiology of all disease manifestations is traditionally held to be threefold:
diet, lifestyle, and past actions (karma).
In that regard, substances remove diseases arising from diet and lifestyle;
however, a disease produced by karma is averted only through death.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The physician should avoid that disease which is accompanied by complications, manifests in all its forms, robs one of strength, flesh, and the senses, and is characterized by fatal signs."
Thus, there is uncertainty;
moreover, there is a lack of finality, because we observe that even diseases which have been cured may arise again.
Indeed, diseases that have been eliminated through great effort recur once more.
And so it has been said:
"When a fever recurs, the treatment follows the previous one.
Therefore, just as its status as a cause of remedy for [diseases] such as Ayurveda is established by direct perception, so too is its absolute and ultimate non-existence [established].
The same applies to mental [pleasure].
Just as the means for remedying physical suffering are not definitive, so too are women and the like.
Why? Because even when they are present, one observes a longing for other objects.
For if objects such as women were always capable of counteracting suffering, why would a subject, when those [objects] are present, desire to grasp other objects?
Thus, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
It is also non-absolute,
because even for those whose desire has ceased, further longing is possible.
For if the enjoyment of sense objects were to utterly destroy mental suffering, what would remain by which a seeker of sense objects would have a renewed longing for them?
What is the reason?
Because there is no dependence upon a lamp for Devadatta when darkness is absent.
Furthermore, it is observed that even among those who have ceased their desire, sensualists develop an even greater longing for objects of sense through the very enjoyment of those objects.
Therefore, we consider that this perceived cause does not diminish suffering;
rather, it causes it to increase all the more. And it is said:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures."
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more.
Another says:
Because it is perceptible, because of its heaviness, because it is censured by the virtuous,
and because it is not present everywhere, the [material] cause is not accepted as being seen.
Because they are objects of perception:
among those seekers who lack the means for enjoyment, these [objects] are perceived by the enjoyer as being utilized;
to utilize them without giving anything to them would manifest cruelty.
Since wealth given by a seeker of pleasure to those who desire it would be exhausted due to its limited nature, this is not a means for the wise to eliminate suffering;
moreover, because of the multiplicity [of requirements],
pleasure arises only from the totality of enjoyments— namely, various garments, women, drinks, foods, ointments, ornaments, and so forth.
It does not occur when either one of these is lacking; moreover, their completeness is impossible because it would be inherent in their very nature. And it is said:
"It does not depend on noble birth, nor on consciousness, nor on valor."
And due to the conjunction with the refinement of fortune (lakṣmī-saṃskāra), it remains present only in certain instances.
Thus, because it depends upon manifold objects, the enjoyment of sense-objects is heavy;
furthermore, because it is censured by the virtuous.
Indeed, the enjoyment of sense-objects is censured by the virtuous, for it has been said:
Exertion, frustration, disappointments, fears,
and whatever else is inauspicious in the world— all these proceed from sensual desires.
He spoke again:
"This is a disease accompanied by its field; this is a fever that is absolute. This is the abode of fears; this is the source of evils."
This is a bottomless underworld; this is a mire difficult to cross;
this is a terrifying abyss filled with afflictions, diseases, and fears.
This is the great abode of various anxieties and sorrows;
this is the open field of wretchedness, fatigue, and despondency.
For just as a bird that has escaped from a cage rejoices when it has gone into the forests, so too does he who has withdrawn from the enjoyment of sense objects experience true happiness.
Therefore, the enjoyment of sense objects is unwholesome because it is rejected by the virtuous;
furthermore, because they are not present everywhere—
for even for a lustful person who is deeply attached, there cannot be the presence of sense objects in every place.
Furthermore, it is not possible for them to abide in the same location,
because that would entail the consequence of there being no object of perception;
therefore, they must necessarily be separated.
And since separation [from objects] is inevitable, there is a certain connection with the undesirable; what, then, is the purpose of grasping at sense-objects?
Therefore, the claim that "inquiry is useless because the visible cause exists" is incorrect.
// 1 // Kārikā 2:
He said: "If there is dissatisfaction with the observed cause because it is exclusively and absolutely non-existent, then why is this other cause—which is free from both faults—not accepted?
If you ask what that is, it is said:
it is the ritual procedure of karma taught in the scriptures."
For that is certain.
How so? For it says thus: "By the animal sacrifice, one conquers all worlds";
it does not say that one sometimes conquers and sometimes does not.

"Perhaps not. If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive because the fruit of the action is not perceived through direct perception—meaning, one might think that this fruit of the prescribed action is simply not apprehended by direct perception—then [it is replied]: [The full argument continues: "This is not so, because the non-perception of the fruit is due to its being temporally remote (*kāla-viprakarṣāt*). For example, just as the fruit of sowing seeds in the earth is not perceived immediately, yet it is not the case that there is no fruit from those seeds, so too, although the fruit of the prescribed action is not perceived here and now, it is not the case that there is no fruit from that action. If it is further argued: "Even if the fruit exists, it is not perceived because it is obstructed by something else," [we reply: "That is not so, because there is no evidence for such an obstruction. Furthermore, since the fruit is not perceived even when there is no possibility of obstruction, it follows that it does not exist. Therefore, the action is useless. To this we say: "It is not useless, because it is seen that the action produces a transformation (*saṃskāra*) in the agent. For example, just as the act of bathing produces a transformation in the body, which is inferred from the subsequent perception of pleasure, so too, the performance of the prescribed action produces a transformation in the agent, which is inferred from the subsequent attainment of heaven. Thus, because the action produces a transformation, it is not useless. If it is asked: "What is the nature of this transformation? [we reply: "It is a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) residing in the continuum of the agent, which is inferred from the effect. It is like the capacity produced in seeds by water, heat, and so forth. And it is not the case that this capacity is not perceived, for it is perceived through inference. Moreover, since the capacity is inferred from the effect, it is not the case that the capacity does not exist simply because it is not perceived directly. Therefore, the transformation exists, and because the transformation exists, the action is not useless. If it is asked: "How is it known that this transformation belongs to the agent and not to something else? [we reply: "Because the effect is observed in the agent alone. For example, just as the transformation produced by bathing is observed in the body of the bather and not elsewhere, so too, the attainment of heaven is observed only in the agent of the sacrifice and not in others. Therefore, it is established that the transformation belongs to the agent. If it is asked: "How is it known that the transformation is not destroyed immediately after the action? [we reply: "Because the effect is observed at a later time. For example, just as the transformation produced by study is not destroyed immediately but results in the knowledge of the subject matter at a later time, so too, the transformation produced by the sacrifice is not destroyed immediately but results in the attainment of heaven at a later time. Therefore, it is established that the transformation persists until the fruit is attained. Thus, the objection that the action is useless has been refuted. Furthermore, the scripture (*āgama*) also confirms this. For it is said: "One who performs the Agnihotra sacrifice for a year attains the world of the ancestors; one who performs the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices for a year attains the world of the gods; one who performs the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice attains the world of the Ṛbhus; and one who performs the Viśvajit sacrifice attains all worlds. Since the scripture declares that the fruit arises from the action, it is not the case that the action is useless. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive. Q.E.D. on the first chapter. [End of Chapter 1] [Beginning of Chapter 2] Now, the second chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "Since the fruit is not perceived immediately after the action, it is not reasonable to say that the fruit arises from the action. To address this, the author says: "The fruit arises from the action, because it is seen that the action produces a transformation in the agent, and because the scripture declares it so. This is the meaning. Now, the proof for this is stated: "The fruit arises from the action, because the scripture declares it so. That is to say, the scripture declares that the fruit arises from the action, and since the scripture is authoritative, it is not the case that the fruit does not arise from the action. Furthermore, it is not the case that the scripture is unauthoritative, because it is consistent with perception and inference. Therefore, the scripture is authoritative. And since the scripture declares that the fruit arises from the action, it is established that the fruit arises from the action. Q.E.D. on the second chapter. [End of Chapter 2] [Beginning of Chapter 3] Now, the third chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "If the fruit arises from the action, then why do some people perform the action and still not obtain the fruit, while others do not perform the action and yet obtain the fruit? To address this, the author says: "The non-attainment of the fruit is due to the presence of obstacles (*pratibandha-kāraṇa-sadbhāvāt*). This is the meaning. Now, the proof for this is stated: "The non-attainment of the fruit is due to the presence of obstacles, because it is seen that even when the action is performed, the fruit is not obtained if there is an obstacle, and because it is seen that even when the action is not performed, the fruit is obtained if there is no obstacle. This is the meaning. Now, the proof for the existence of obstacles is stated: "Obstacles exist, because they are declared by the scripture and because they are inferred from the non-attainment of the fruit. This is the meaning. Now, the proof for the non-authoritativeness of the claim that there are no obstacles is stated: "It is not the case that there are no obstacles, because the scripture declares their existence and because they are inferred from the non-attainment of the fruit. This is the meaning. Therefore, it is established that the non-attainment of the fruit is due to the presence of obstacles. Q.E.D. on the third chapter. [End of Chapter 3] [Beginning of Chapter 4] Now, the fourth chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "If the fruit arises from the action, then what is the nature of the action? To address this, the author says: "Action is of two kinds: physical (*kāyika*) and mental (*mānasika*). This is the meaning. Now, the proof for this is stated: "Action is of two kinds, because the scripture declares it so and because it is seen that there are these two types. This is the meaning. Now, the proof for the existence of mental action is stated: "Mental action exists, because it is declared by the scripture and because it is inferred from the subsequent attainment of the fruit. This is the meaning. Therefore, it is established that action is of two kinds. Q.E.D. on the fourth chapter. [End of Chapter 4] [Beginning of Chapter 5] Now, the fifth chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "If action is of two kinds, then what is the definition of each? To address this, the author says: "Physical action is movement (*ceṣṭā*), and mental action is volition (*cetanā*). This is the meaning. Now, the proof for this is stated: "Physical action is movement, because it is seen that movement is the cause of physical action, and because the scripture declares it so. Mental action is volition, because it is seen that volition is the cause of mental action, and because the scripture declares it so. This is the meaning. Therefore, the definitions of the two types of action are established. Q.E.D. on the fifth chapter. [End of Chapter 5] [Beginning of Chapter 6] Now, the sixth chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "If action is of two kinds, then what is the result of each? To address this, the author says: "The result of physical action is the production of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), and the result of mental action is the production of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is the meaning. Now, the proof for this is stated: "The result of physical action is the production of merit and demerit, because it is declared by the scripture and because it is seen that physical action leads to rebirth. The result of mental action is the production of consciousness, because it is declared by the scripture and because it is seen that mental action is the cause of the continuity of consciousness. This is the meaning. Therefore, the results of the two types of action are established. Q.E.D. on the sixth chapter. [End of Chapter 6] [Beginning of Chapter 7] Now, the seventh chapter begins. Herein, the following doubt may arise: "If action produces merit and demerit, then what is the nature of merit and demerit? To address this, the author says: "Merit and demerit are substances (*dr

For instance, one who desires a son may perform a sacrifice and yet not obtain even a daughter; and one who desires wealth may perform a ritual and yet not receive even a single masha. Therefore, this [reason] is not inconclusive.
And this is not so.
Why? Because it is untenable due to the deficiency of means;
for the injunction regarding ritual action is to be accomplished by multiple means.

Where the fruit is not perceived, there the deficiency of the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is to be inferred. Why? Because it is not accepted that an effect does not arise when its cause is present.
Furthermore, there is another point: it would follow that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) does not exist.
For if the fruitfulness of action (*karman*) is not admitted, then it follows that cyclic existence—which has that [action] as its cause—would be non-existent;
and this is an undesirable consequence.
Therefore, its exclusivity is established;
its absoluteness is also established.
For it says: "We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal."
In this context, it is heard in scripture that the attainment of immortality results from the drinking of Soma;
therefore, that alone should be practiced.
What is the use of postulating any other cause? Thus, the inquiry is entirely purposeless.
It is said:
that which is heard traditionally is called *ānuśravika*, for it is "heard" (*anuśrūyate*) thus.
That which exists in oral tradition is "traditionally derived" (*ānuśravika*).
It functions in the same manner as what is seen (*dṛṣṭavat*). The ellipsis of the sentence is: "Is this [tradition] not intended? (i.e., is it not undesirable?).
He asks: "What, then, is this *anuśrava*? It is replied: It is the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* texts, or whatever ancient material is being heard and accepted as authoritative by your honors;
such as the *smṛtis* which are based upon the *śrutis*.
The "limbs" (aṅga) are either the Vedas or the systems of logic (tarka). As it has been said:
"The designation 'Veda' is applied to the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the tarkas.
He asks: Is this scriptural reason (ānuśravika-hetu) undesirable for the same reason as the previous one?
It is said: "No. What then?
For that [means] is indeed endowed with impurity, decay, and excellence.
The word "that" is a reference back to the cause consisting of what is heard from tradition (ānuśravika).
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.
It is endowed with impurity (*aviśuddhi*), destruction (*kṣaya*), and excellence (*atiśaya*).
This is what is meant.
Since this scriptural cause is impure, impermanent, and characterized by gradations, it is as undesirable as the empirically perceived [cause].
In that regard, it is first joined with impurity because of the prescription of violence, as stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "One should sacrifice a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. Likewise—
Six hundred animals are sacrificed on the middle day of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha),
according to the scriptural injunction, being deficient by three animals.
Thus, violence is impurity because it involves the destruction of the desired bodies of living beings.
[The opponent] says: that is untenable.
Because it is enjoined by the scriptures.
If this violence were not enjoined by the scriptures, we would undoubtedly conclude that it is impure; however, it is indeed enjoined by the scriptures.
Therefore, this is not an impurity.
If it should be thought that "it is an impurity because its authority is not accepted," this would indeed be so for those who accept the authority of the Veda; [but it is not so for us].
"We, however, are skilled in the doctrine of reasons (hetuvāda).
Therefore, if there exists some reason established for both parties, let it be studied, so that there may be a cognition free from doubt.
This, too, is incorrect.

Why? Because it contradicts your own tenets. You have accepted that there are three means of valid cognition: perception, inference, and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*). Now, by asserting that the Veda lacks validity while it is in fact authoritative testimony, you contradict your own position.
Therefore, this is incorrect.
If it should be thought that there is no fault because the Veda’s status as the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*) is untenable,
then this criticism could only be rightly stated after first establishing that the Veda is indeed the word of a reliable authority.
This is established by reality;
therefore, this [criticism] is not a valid objection.
This too has already been explained.

Why? Because if it were preceded by human intellect, the word would be subject to investigation as to whether it is the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*) or not, due to its association with passion and other defects. However, the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), being independent and not preceded by human intellect, functions for the sake of the ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) of persons.
Therefore, such a [tradition] does not deserve this kind of undesirable investigation.
Furthermore, [this is so] because it would otherwise follow that impurity could not be established.
If you too were to apply critical inquiry to this matter— namely, how it is determined that the destruction of a living being’s desired body constitutes impure violence—
you must certainly state it on the basis of the authoritative treatise (*śāstra*).
And yet that very same scripture prescribes violence in the context of a sacrifice.

Therefore, what is the reason here? Why is it that while [the scripture] is authoritative elsewhere, it ought to be non-authoritative in this very case regarding the claim that "dharma arises from violence"? If it is argued that the distinction between non-violence and violence is established by perception, based on their respective characteristics of benefit and injury—then it might further be said that from non-violence there arises benefit characterized by the preservation of the desired body.
Furthermore, there is an affliction resulting from violence, characterized by the destruction of the intended body;

and it is logical to infer that the fruit corresponds to the action. Thus, it is established by direct perception that these two are the causes of desirable and undesirable fruits respectively. Therefore, what is the function of the treatise (*śāstra*) in this matter?
And this is untenable.
Why? Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

For if it were conceived in this way, even in the case of approaching the wife of one's teacher, there would be a connection with a desired result due to the capacity to benefit other sentient beings.

Furthermore, one who initiates a young student (*māṇavaka*) and engages him in the instruction of vows, purification, celibacy, the practice of Vedic study, begging for alms, the tending of the sacred fire, service to the teacher, and so forth, would incur a connection with undesirable results.
Therefore, a false argument that contradicts common worldly experience and the scriptures is not acceptable.

If it should be thought that there is the consequence of contradicting the scriptures because both [non-injury and injury] are mentioned therein—namely, that the very same scripture teaches non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), [but also permits violence in certain contexts]—[the response follows].
For that very [act] is violence (*hiṃsā*).
This being so, since two mutually contradictory matters have been enjoined, it would follow that there is a contradiction between the scriptures when it is impossible to favor both;
yet, that is not the case.
Why? Because there is a difference in the scope of the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*).
For the scripture, having established the general rule of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), teaches the exception characterized by the sacrifice (*kratu*) in a specific instance.
And that which is prescribed as a general rule is set aside by that which is prescribed as a specific rule.
For example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; let buttermilk be given to the Kauṇḍinyas.
Therefore, because there is a distinction between the scope of the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*), there is no contradiction with the treatise.
Furthermore:

Because there is no fault in performing the rite again, just as in the case of approaching a maiden; for although approaching a maiden is indeed prohibited by the scripture, one who is handsome does not incur demerit by accepting her and then approaching her.
"A householder should marry a wife of equal status who has not belonged to another [man] before," because of the existence of such a rule in other scriptures;
thus, violence is indeed prohibited by the scriptures.
Now, one who engages in violence during a ritual sacrifice would not be a partaker of undesirable results,
precisely because of the existence of other scriptural authorities as previously mentioned.
Therefore, that which was stated— that violence is impurity because it consists in the destruction of the desired bodies of living beings— is incorrect.
It is said: No, because you have not understood the intended meaning.
Even though this has been stated at length, you do not grasp the underlying intention.
What is the reason?
For we do not deny the authority of the Veda,

nor indeed do we say that one who engages in violence enjoined by the scriptures incurs a connection with undesirable results. Rather, since the performance of a rite prescribed by the Veda— which is a cause for attaining heaven— is not possible without the injury of living beings, it is permitted by those who desire one's welfare.
For it has not been said that one should seek one's own benefit by causing harm to others. It is said:
"One should not do to another what is disagreeable to oneself; this is the Dharma in brief. Anything other than this arises from desire."
He asks: "If this is not accepted, how was it previously stated that violence (*hiṃsā*) is impurity resulting from the destruction of the desired bodies of living beings?
It is replied: "By metaphorically applying the cause to the effect.
That distress which arises in our minds out of compassion, caused by that [destruction], is indeed what is intended by the term 'impurity'."
In that context, the cause is figuratively designated as "impurity," namely violence (*hiṃsā*).
This is like saying, "They are satisfied by mung beans" or "They are happy because of the cows.
[The opponent] asks: How is it understood that the Teacher intends "impurity" to mean merely the suffering that is the effect of violence?
Is it not rather non-violence itself?
It is said: because a comparative suffix is perceived [in the term "more excellent"];
for he will state later that "that which is contrary to what has been taught is better" (ISk 2).
The cognition of excellence arises in dependence upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of the same class;
if the excellence of that which is heard from scripture (ānuśravika) were not intended, it would follow that the cognition of excellence could not occur.
Therefore, this does not contradict the Sūtra.
He said: "The renunciation [of action] is untenable, because of the scriptural teaching that there is no separation [from it].
For you have no power over the non-abandonment or the renunciation of action."
Rather, whatever the scripture says must necessarily be performed;
and that scripture teaches non-separation from ritual actions until death.
Why? Because it says thus: "This lifelong sacrificial session (*satra*) consists of the Agnihotra and the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

"One is indeed released from this obligation by old age and by death. Furthermore, it says: "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live for a hundred years. Therefore, there is no abandonment of ritual actions until death.
If that were so, the actions of other causes would be rendered useless.
It is replied: No, because the means are not inherent in nature;
this injunction for ritual action is accomplished through numerous means, such as union with a wife and so forth.

Furthermore, because those [defilements] lack intrinsic nature (*asvābhāvikatva*), it has been demonstrated that it is impossible to effect their removal through ritual application prior to [the action].
Therefore, actions are impermanent.
If it should be thought that, in a conflict between a treatise on causes and a [revealed] scripture, the scripture possesses greater authority; [End of provided text]
Where there is a conflict between logic (hetuśāstra) and scripture (śāstra), one must necessarily accept that scripture is more authoritative because inference is largely subject to deception;
however, this is untenable.
Why? Because [the means of knowledge] are applied according to their respective capacities.
Depending on capacity, the scripture enjoins rituals such as the *agnihotra* and indicates their non-permanent nature.
How so? For it says thus:
"He who, being capable of performing the *agnihotra*, does not perform the *agnihotra*, him these deities shut out from both this world and the next."
Therefore, actions are impermanent.
Furthermore,
[this is so] because of the capacity for grasping old age.
In your own authoritative source (jñāpaka), there is indeed the mention of "old age" (jarā);
therefore, it is inferred that action is both dependent on capacity and impermanent.
Furthermore, [there would be] the abandonment of the scripture (śāstra).
For both are taught in the scripture:
actions and renunciation.
