If, however, actions are intended to be performed as obligatory duties, then the scripture concerning renunciation is undermined.
Therefore, this is merely a manifestation of your passion for the subject matter.
He says: No, because of the superior strength of what is heard (śruti).

For when two scriptural injunctions of equal strength meet regarding a single object, and it is impossible to favor both simultaneously, there occurs either an option (vikalpa) or a sequence (paryāya).
Furthermore, when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti is more authoritative;
and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is prescribed by Smṛti.
Therefore, there can be no option between these two.
Furthermore, it is certainly not logical to claim that there is no alternative; for it is said: "That [objection] applies equally to the other case.
Just as the scripture teaches the performance of ritual actions, so too does it teach renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
How so? For it is said thus:
"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone did they attain immortality;
that which shines forth, placed beyond the highest heaven in the secret cave, into which the ascetics enter."
Thus:
"The seers who possessed progeny, desiring wealth, were not able to ward off death by means of ritual action;
but other wise seers attained immortality that is beyond all actions."
And on this point there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Those who know this, and those forest-dwellers who worship with faith and austerity, they pass into the light;
from the light into the day, from the day into the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight into the six months during which the sun moves northward, and from those months into the year."
“From the year to the sun, from the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning; there a person who is not of human nature (amānava) dwells, and he leads these people to Brahman.
Again, it says: “Only by knowing this does one become a sage.”
It is for the sake of this very world that renunciants go forth into homelessness.

Indeed, it was thus that the wise of old did not desire offspring, saying: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is not [attained] and this world is not [attained]? They, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lived the life of mendicants.
"Therefore, these are the marks of both renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*sannyāsa*).
He says: 'Even though the scripture is thus, nevertheless there is an injunction regarding their performance;
and what is enjoined must necessarily be carried out.'"
"In the case of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), however, it is merely a commendatory statement (arthavāda)"; this is the distinction between these two.
When that [capacity] exists, the performance [of duties] is superior, not their abandonment.
It is asked: what is this injunction?
What is this *arthavāda*? It is said: An injunction (*vidhi*) is the teaching of something not previously known (*apūrva-upadeśa*) for the sake of that [injunction].

For that which is performed as an instruction of the *apūrva* by means of the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), or the gerundive suffixes (*kṛtya*)—which constitute the meaning of an injunction—is an injunction.
For example: "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice";
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white goat to Vāyu.
These are commendatory statements (arthavāda).
However, the praise that is uttered for the purpose of creating an inclination toward that which has been enjoined is an *arthavāda*.
For example: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; one approaches Vāyu himself with that share; he alone leads him to prosperity."
For having heard such praise, the injunction becomes attractive to the sacrificer who seeks its fruit;
thus, one who desires his welfare engages in it.
To this it is replied: No, for it is precisely because of this that the perfection of renunciation is established.
If you think thus—that the scripture praises that which it considers superior for the sake of creating interest—then the same applies to the perfection of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
Why? Because it has been praised.
The traditional teaching praises renunciation for those who seek much; why, then, does it not please them?
For otherwise, it would be purposeless.

Furthermore, if even while praising, an explanatory passage (arthavāda) were not to incite one to action, then that which was stated by you— that "the explanatory passage is for the purpose of incitement"— would have to be abandoned. For if that were the case, the explanatory passage would be either entirely useless or a statement of some other matter altogether.

If it is not accepted that this [passage] serves the purpose of persuasion, then another meaning must be stated so that a portion of the Veda does not become meaningless. Therefore, we cannot be led away from the true path by such a threat.
Furthermore,
because an undesirable consequence follows from either alternative:
here, this traditional teaching would either praise renunciation as something to be practiced, or it would praise it as something not to be practiced.
What follows from this? If it first praises [renunciation] as something to be enjoined, what else remains to be deliberated?
Renunciation is already established.
Or, if [it is praised] as something to be enjoined...
A purpose must be established for its praise;

for why would the Veda—which is independent, not preceded by human intellect, and which proceeds for the sake of human liberation—seek to provide encouragement for that which is not desired as something to be performed?
Therefore, even having made this assumption, it remains a very weak argument.
Alternatively, this is another meaning of the phrase "the twofold option":
here, does this traditional teaching (āmnāya) recommend renunciation (sannyāsa) by means of what is real, or by means of what is unreal?
What follows from this?

If, first, it encourages by means of what is factual, then since renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the means for attaining immortality, another cause for not adopting it must be stated besides attachment to sense-objects.
Or, if it does so by means of what is not factual, [then it is a falsehood].
A person falls away from the supreme good.

Why? Because it is not logical that the sacred tradition (āmnāya), which is an authoritative means of knowledge, should deceive living beings who seek their welfare by leading them onto a path that is not conducive to the good, according to the maxim of the mother’s sweetmeat.
Therefore, this is unreasonable.
Furthermore, because it is not the case that [the injunction] is non-ambiguous:
it is not an absolute rule that only that which is enjoined must be performed.

And thus the followers of Śabara recite: "In the statement 'Going to the village is good for you,' even in the absence of an injunction, the praise itself encourages Devadatta toward going to the village."
Furthermore, because of the consequence of doubt:
if the Veda were to speak some things as true and some things as false, then, like human speech, doubt would necessarily arise regarding the Vedic statements as well.
And this being the case, the aforementioned undesirable consequence follows.
And this is undesirable. Furthermore, is that [cognition] an inference based on a positive rule (vidhi), since it arises from being a part [of the whole]?
Alternatively, you have conceded that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) constitutes a part of an injunction (*vidhi*).
In that case, having found an explanatory passage regarding renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one must infer that there is also an injunction [for it].
If it is argued that there is no fault because of non-apprehension, this would be so only if that positive entity were apprehended; therefore,
the claim that "because of non-apprehension, he will turn away from this fault" is untenable.
Why? Because there are many divisions.
Let an effort be made toward its apprehension;
for the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is indeed divided into many branches according to each Veda.
In this regard, what was stated—that because of the existence of an injunction, action is primary—is also untenable.

If it is argued that "renunciation is impossible because there is no instruction regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)," then it might be the case that if the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) considered renunciation itself to be something to be enjoined, it would have to instruct upon it just as it instructs, with the recitation of mantras, the procedure for the householder's life, such as the taking of a wife and so forth. Since it does not do so, [the argument fails].
But he did not teach [it];
therefore, renunciation does not exist.
This too is incorrect.
Why? Because of their absence.
For renunciation is the absence of all duties to be performed (*itikartavyatā*). In that case, what scripture will there be to instruct?
The scripture indeed teaches whatever duties constitute the constituent parts of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

How so? For it says thus: "Those who, possessing austerity and faith, dwell in the forest, being peaceful and wise, practicing the life of mendicancy—they, free from passion, depart through the door of the sun to where that immortal Person, the imperishable Self, dwells."
In that context, by the words "those who dwell there with austerity and faith," he describes this dharma characterized by restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), which is endowed with faith.
By "in the forest" (*araṇye*), he means departure from the household. By "tranquil" (*śāntāḥ*), he means the withdrawal of the senses and the internal organ from their longing for sense objects.
"Being wise" refers to the practice of knowledge by the yogi who is undaunted during times such as the first and last watches of the night;
"practicing the life of a mendicant" refers to the regulated intake of limited food for the sake of maintaining the body;
and with the second half [of the verse], he declares the fruit.
Furthermore, the detailed exposition of the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) has been set forth by Manu and others;
and since your position is that the Smṛtis, which contain the etymological explanations of the Śruti, are authoritative,
the claim that "renunciation does not exist because its procedure is not taught" is incorrect.
And thus, the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) are established.
As for what was stated by him—that the scriptural authority (*ānuśravika-hetu*) is inconclusive—that is true;
for the fruit of action must necessarily be admitted.
Otherwise, because the saṃsāra caused by that [ignorance] would be non-existent, there would be the undesirable consequence [of liberation being unattainable].
Therefore, this is indeed undesirable for the Teacher.
He asks: "How is this to be inferred?"
It is said: by virtue of the inclusion of the term "destruction" (kṣaya).
If that which was stated in the preceding sūtra were to carry over here, the inclusion of the term "destruction" would be purposeless.
Why? Because "destruction" is a synonym for absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva).
Thus, the yoga of non-purity is established.
[The opponent] asks: "Now, how is the yoga of exhaustion to be inferred?
It is said: "The yoga of exhaustion is [inferred] from the measurement of the limbs."
Furthermore, the exhaustion of this cause should be understood from the limited number of its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
For those parts of the sacrifice, such as the animal and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), are limited in number.
It is observed that for limited means of accomplishment, such as threads and the like, the resulting effect, such as a cloth and the like, is also limited.
That which is limited is seen to be subject to exhaustion;
it is exactly like that.
Furthermore:
Because cyclic existence is perceived.
Indeed, this cyclic existence is observed to have as its cause the diversity of actions and modes of conduct distinguished by differences in speech, intellect, nature, food, and recreation.

Furthermore, if karma that has been directly performed were to result in non-exhaustion, then cyclic existence would not be perceived among living beings, since there would be no returning [to further rebirth].
If it is argued that permanence [of the Veda] follows from the authority of the word (*śabdasāmarthya*), this might be so: "We take the word as our authority;
whatever the word says is our authority."
And its cause states its immortality: "He crosses over death, he crosses over evil," and so forth.
Therefore, even if one does not wish it, this must necessarily be accepted.
Or, if it is not accepted, there is the fallacy of abandoning one's own thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), namely that "the Veda is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
But this is not so.
Why? Because there is a contradiction with another statement.
The word "impermanence" (anityatva) is accepted as a reason for this [proposition].
This being the case, a contradiction arises.
How so? For it is said: "Now, those who here in the village worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices, meritorious works, and gifts [are our merit],'..."
Then they return again along this very same path:
from the space [they go] to the air;
from the air, they become smoke.
Having become smoke, it becomes a cloud;
having become a cloud, it rains down.
These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans.

"Then indeed, he who eats food and he who sheds semen becomes greater still. In this regard, if it be thought that what was stated—that eternality [of the word] follows from the power of the word itself—is incorrect because it would entail a contradiction with the scripture due to its being expressed in both ways; [we reply: such might be the opinion.
That very same scripture teaches permanence, and that very same one teaches impermanence.
This being so, since two mutually contradictory meanings have been enjoined, and it is impossible to accommodate both, there would follow the contingency of a contradiction within the scripture.
But that is not the case.
Why? Because when there is an impossibility, one postulates another meaning.
For wherever scripture, which is authoritative, enjoins an impossible matter, it then postulates an alternative meaning.
For example, [it is said] in such passages as: "He extracted his own omentum," "The mind is a thief," and "Speech belongs to the speaker of untruth.
Likewise, here too, it is impossible for a single entity to be both eternal and non-eternal.
Therefore, we shall assign a different meaning to the other scripture that expresses its eternality through figurative usage.

If it should be thought that the same applies elsewhere— namely, that just as you have postulated eternity figuratively because eternity and non-eternity cannot coexist in one place, so too will non-eternity be postulated—
this is incorrect.
Why? Because it would entail a contradiction with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For if destruction were postulated figuratively (*bhaktyā*), a contradiction with all *pramāṇas* would follow.
How so? First, there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because saṃsāra is actually perceived.
There is a contradiction with inference, because if the size of the parts were fixed, the eternity of the whole would be untenable.
There is a contradiction with scripture, because of the statement, "They enter into the smoke. However, this fault does not arise if eternity is understood figuratively.
Therefore, this is inconsistent.
He asks: "How, then, should the scripture be interpreted through figurative application (bhakti)?
It is said: by virtue of its preeminent meaning (prakṛṣṭārthatayā).

Just as it is said, "May the vital breaths not abandon your body, whether it be nectar or death," yet the vital breaths of living beings do not depart for eternity; rather, they remain for a long period of time.
Thus, here too it is said that "one crosses over death";
one does not cross over death absolutely, but rather for an extended period of time.
For in common usage, the word "constant" (*nitya*) is applied to that which is preeminent;
as for example, one who laughs constantly or speaks constantly.
Thus, the connection with destruction is established.
He asks: "How is the possession of excellence (atiśaya) to be inferred now for this cause?
It is said: "The possession of excellence arises from the repeated practice of action.
For where an action occurs once and where it recurs many times, excellence is observed there."
For example, in activities such as agriculture,
and in the case of sacrifice, there is a dependence on the capacity to procure materials;
in some cases, however, the engagement occurs all at once.
In some cases, however, there is repeated recurrence;
therefore, there must be a degree of excellence.
Furthermore, this is due to the excellence of the constituent factors (*aṅga*).
In this world, it is observed that through the excellence of the constituent parts, there is also an excellence of the whole, such as a jar;
and here, in every sacrifice, there exists this excellence of the constituent parts, such as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and so forth.
Therefore, in this case as well, there must be excellence [of the result].

If it is argued that "there is no occurrence of diminution or excess because [the deity] enters into the state of being a constituent part (aṅga) of the sacrifice"— that is to say, even if it were the case that for one who accepts the sacrificial material alone as the means of accomplishment, the defects of diminution and excess would indeed be unavoidable;
we, however, know the deity inherent in the material to enter into the state of being a constituent part in the ritual.
"Therefore, this is not a fault"—this is untenable.
Why? Because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).
The infinite number of deities is what is to be established;
and because they enter into the state of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) [of the ritual], there is no fault.
Furthermore, it is our established tenet (*siddhānta*) that [the deities] do not constitute auxiliary members of the self’s action, because [the self] is indifferent (*udāsīna*).
Therefore, this is incorrect;
or even granting it were so,
it would entail the consequence that the performance of sacrifices would become purposeless.
If it is your position that by perceiving a deity inherent in a substance and thereby becoming an auxiliary to that [deity], one attains an inexhaustible and unsurpassed cause,
then any rite whatsoever declared in the Veda could serve to attain that goal.
Why, then, perform sacrifices that have the destruction of living beings as their cause?
How so?
For there is no action whatsoever in which the body does not participate as a constituent part.
Furthermore, the body consists of all the deities; therefore, it is said that "the wise man indeed regards this person as Brahman."
For all deities are indeed concentrated within this body.
Therefore, the claim that "because they attain the status of limbs of the deity, neither decay nor excess is possible" is incorrect.
Thus, this reason is flawed in three ways.
Therefore, it can be inferred that whatever specific result is produced is also of that same nature.

Consequently, this seeker of knowledge has no concentration here [on that path]. He says: "If, considering that this is not superior, this seeker of knowledge has no concentration here, then that specific result which *is* superior must be taught."
It is said: "The opposite of that is better"—
by the word "that," there is a connection with the fruit characterized by the attainment of heaven, which is accomplished through the injunctions for ritual action.
Therefore, the opposite of that is pure, inexhaustible, and unsurpassed—this is the meaning.
What is this? It is said to be liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the highest good (*śreyas*).
This is what is being stated:
Both of these— heaven and liberation— are praiseworthy because they are ordained by the sacred tradition;
however, liberation is more praiseworthy.
Why? Because the aforementioned defects do not apply.
For that [result] is certain because it is necessarily occurring;
and it is imperceptible because it transcends the senses.
Because it is established within one's own self, it is light; because it is present everywhere, it is pervasive;
because it is praised in the sacred scriptures, it is excellent;
and because it is practiced by the virtuous, it is irreproachable.
Being purified through the means of self-restraint (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), [the soul] is pure;
because it is devoid of material substance (*adravyatva*), it is imperishable and unsurpassed.
He asks: "But how, then, is this liberation (*apavarga*) attained?"
It is said: because there is an absence of conjunction, and suffering is the primary [principle].
Thus it is also stated in other treatises: "The power of the effect and the instrument is the cause of suffering."
Therefore, when there is a conjunction with the Puruṣa, then there is impurity for this [Puruṣa].
Due to its connection with specific powers, through the efficacy of causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, it experiences suffering during various transmigrations of birth.
But when the conjunction with Pradhāna ceases, then, on the principle that "in the absence of the cause, the effect also ceases," it no longer experiences the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).
He asks: "But for what purpose is this conjunction of the Pradhāna with the Puruṣa? It is said: "This need not be stated here;
the Teacher will explain it later: 'It is for the sake of the Puruṣa's perception...'"
"Likewise, the purpose of the Pradhāna is for the sake of isolation;
the conjunction of both is like that of the lame and the blind.
[It is asked: "Then, by what cause does their disjunction occur?"
It is said:
"From the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. (ISk 2)
The manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*) constitute "the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower" (*vyaktāvyaktajña*).
The knowledge of these is "the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower" (*vyaktāvyaktajñavijñāna*); [the compound is formed] from that.
Because there is no fixed rule regarding multiple members, the word *jña*, though having fewer syllables, does not necessarily take the prior position [in the compound].
Alternatively, it has been stated that the manifest (vyakta) is the most effective means for the realization of knowledge,
because the comprehension of the unmanifest (avyakta) is preceded by it.
Or else, "the manifest and the unmanifest" refers to those two as the manifest and the unmanifest.
"He who knows them" means one who knows both the manifest and the unmanifest;
through that knowledge, union ceases.
And this he will state later:
"One [the intellect] remains indifferent, thinking 'I have seen'; the other [the ego-sense] ceases, thinking 'I have been seen'" (ISk 66).
In this regard, the manifest is characterized by the fruit of the activity of form.
Furthermore, form consists of the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements.
In general, activity is of two kinds:
that which has the purpose of seeking what is beneficial, and that which has the purpose of avoiding what is harmful.
Specifically, there are five sources of action (karmayoni), namely the five means of livelihood and so forth, as well as the five vital airs (prāṇa) and so forth.
The fruit is of two kinds:
the seen and the unseen.
In this regard, the "seen" is characterized by success, contentment, incapacity, and their opposites;

the "unseen" is the acquisition of a body within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. This is the manifest (vyakta). The apprehension of specific distinctions among these qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—occurs through their entering into the relationship of primary and subordinate factors.
When they remain with their specific distinctions erased, not assuming the status of being limbs [of a whole], they are then called the "Unmanifest" (avyakta).
Because its nature is the power of consciousness, it knows the manifold activity of the qualities (guṇa); thus, it is the "Knower" (jña).
Having discerned both the difference and non-difference of these three, one attains the cessation of conjunction.
Why? Because the cause of *yoga* (union) is the opposite of the cause of *saṃyoga* (conjunction).
Here, since the conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* has non-perception as its cause, it must be brought to an end by knowledge, which is its opposite and the cause of disjunction (*viyoga*).
What is the illustration?
It is like darkness and light.
Just as objects such as jars, when concealed by darkness, are not perceived,
but their perception occurs once they are illuminated by a lamp, which is the antithesis of that darkness.
The same should be understood here as well; thus it is established that liberation comes from knowledge. And it has been said:

"Just as a man whose foot has slipped from the top of a tree falls inevitably even if he does not wish to, so too one who knows the distinction between the qualities (*guṇas*) and the person (*puruṣa*) becomes isolated (*kevalin*), even if he does not desire it."
Furthermore: because it is declared in the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
For this matter—that liberation results from knowledge—is based upon the sacred tradition;
it is not accidental.
How so? For it is said thus: "He who knows Brahman—truth, knowledge, infinite, hidden in the cave of the heart within the supreme heaven—he attains all desires together with the wise Brahman.
And: "From which words turn back, along with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere."
“Only by knowing that very [Self] does one attain immortality; no other path for going exists.
Likewise, it is said in the Brāhmaṇa:
“The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.”
‘“One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.

Therefore, on the authority of this sacred tradition (āmnāya) as well, we maintain that liberation results from knowledge. [The opponent] says: Since [the scripture] accepts that the word for knowledge is the cause of immortality, another extensive sacred tradition would be rendered purposeless.’

If it is admitted that immortality is obtained from a fragment of the scripture (*āmnāya*) that denotes knowledge, then it follows that the great other scripture denoting ritual action (*kriyā*) would be rendered purposeless.
What is the reason?
For when the desired goal is attained without effort, one who engages in an action involving great exertion is not acting skillfully. As it is said:
"If one should find honey on the threshold, why would one go to the mountain?
When the desired object is obtained, what wise person would exert effort?"
It is said: if, on the other hand, ritual actions are intended to be performed absolutely, how can the meaningfulness of the Vedic scripture (āmnāya) which expresses knowledge be established?
He replies: in the case of their combination, however, both [scriptures] possess meaningfulness.

But when the combination of knowledge and action is accepted, the meaningfulness of both scriptural injunctions is established, because of such statements as "the learned man should sacrifice" and "the learned man should officiate at a sacrifice. Likewise, all persons possess the qualification for ritual action, according to the principle that "everyone is qualified except those who are not learned in the Vedas, eunuchs, and Śūdras."
Therefore, it is argued that the attainment of the desired goal results from the combination of knowledge and action.
To this it is replied: No, because the previous fault has not been avoided.
If it is accepted that actions must necessarily be performed by the knower alone, then the previously mentioned fault—the consequence of the non-existence of saṃsāra—remains.
That [objection] is not a valid refutation.
Furthermore, there is the abandonment of the scripture;
for that which is taught in the scripture—namely, "Those who perform sacrifices and works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta) attain the smoke"—would be contradicted by this interpretation.
Furthermore: because their fruits are distinct.
In this context, substances that have non-distinct fruits are combined, just as the various components of a meal, such as soup and so forth.
Their fruit, characterized by satisfaction, is non-distinct;
yet this fruit of knowledge and action is not itself non-distinct,
because they are the causes of heaven and liberation respectively.
If it is argued that liberation is the inseparable fruit resulting from the power of knowledge, then there is no distinction from the previous [position].
Furthermore, the consequence already stated—that there would be an absence of saṃsāra—remains unrefuted.
Moreover, there is a contradiction with the fruits as they are heard in scripture.

Furthermore, this contradicts what is heard regarding the fruit of an action, such as "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" and "One conquers a kingdom by means of the Agniṣṭoma," as well as the fact that ritual action possesses the status of being a subordinate element.
Because, while making its own purpose subordinate,

it brings about another purpose— just as actions such as "threshing" and the like, by subordinating their own fruit, assist the sacrifice through that medium and thus become subsidiary to it— in the same way, action, being the fruit of knowledge, would likewise be subsidiary to it.
If it is argued that action is primary because of the existence of an injunction (*vidhi*), we say no—because this has already been stated.
How so?
There is no distinction produced by an injunction.
Or, having approached [the teacher];
for even in that case, it arises from him.
Indeed, there exists a scripture that prescribes knowledge as well.

How so? For it is said thus: "That Self which is free from evil, free from hunger and thirst, free from old age and death, free from sorrow, with all its desires cast away—that is what must be sought, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found the Self, understands it, obtains all desires"—such are the words of Prajāpati heard [in scripture].
Furthermore, it says: "Two sciences are to be known: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā). Which [is the higher]...?
Therefore, the claim that action is primary because of the existence of injunctions is merely an attachment to one's own position.
Some say it is because [knowledge] has a visible purpose.
However, other teachers consider that the very visible fruit of knowledge—characterized by the cessation of ignorance—is not enjoined by the scripture.
What is the reason?
For regarding an action whose purpose is directly perceived, scripture is not the motivator;
since the engagement in it occurs spontaneously due to the desire for the result, as in the case of eating and so forth.
The statements that prescribe those [actions] are relied upon as restatements for the purpose of prescribing the qualities of the means;
for example: "He offers with curd," and "He offers with milk."

As for what is indeed said— that "the learned man should sacrifice," "the learned man should officiate at a sacrifice," and "the Śrotriya has the right to perform rituals"— its meaning is this: having studied the Veda and understood the sequence of the ritual acts, one should proceed to engage in the performance of the rites.
And this being the case, there is no fault whatsoever.
If, however, the entitlement to perform ritual action were restricted by necessity to those who know the Self, it would follow that saṃsāra would cease to exist,
because [the knowledge of the Self] is innate.
This contradicts all the injunctions regarding consciousness and scripture;
therefore, there is no synthesis of knowledge and action.
Another says: "True."
There is no combination of these two; rather, action serves every purpose while knowledge is for the sake of negating [the results of] prohibited acts.
For those such as eunuchs, the blind, and the deaf, who are utterly excluded from ritual action (*karman*), the attainment of immortality occurs through knowledge in another stage of life (*āśrama*).
But for others, it occurs through action alone in the fundamental stage of life. Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal for the proponent.
It is said: No, because it contradicts one's own tenets (*svasamaya*).
For this proponent who speaks thus, his very own tenet is contradicted.
As it has been stated: "The wise did not desire offspring."
"What shall we do with offspring?
And as for what was said— that having risen above the desire for sons and the desire for wealth, they live the life of mendicants—
it is not possible for eunuchs to rise above the desire for sons.
Because it was created by the gods;
and for another reason, because it is a secret:
for the knowledge of the Vedas is indeed a secret.
For it says: "Indeed, Āruṇi Auddālaki taught this to his eldest son;
a father should declare this Brahman to his eldest son, or to a worthy pupil, but to no one else whatsoever."
"Whoever should give this earth, surrounded by waters, rich in wealth and full of treasures—this [gift of the Dharma] is even greater than that.
And there is a verse on this point: "The supreme secret of the Vedas is recited at their conclusions."
If it is claimed that this [Veda] is intended for the sake of eunuchs and the like, then by good fortune, the Veda has achieved its fruitfulness!
It is indeed stated in the Śruti that "the wise man should perform actions"; yet he alone would be truly wise who has completely desisted from action.
Let that very path be pursued by the wise: is it what is right, or is it a delusion of the mind? Is it attachment to the objects of the senses, or is it aversion toward the path to liberation?
Because it is the cause for attaining liberation, the praise ordained by the Vedas is commended by distinguished masters such as Yājñavalkya, due to their certainty regarding reality.
This science, being offered like a maiden to a eunuch by those blinded by passion for sense-objects and who propound perverted meanings, does not shine.
Therefore, having dispelled this army of fallacious arguments uttered by those who follow passion, a wise man should indeed proceed from one stage of life to the next upon reaching womanhood.
Thus ends the first daily lesson in the *Yuktidīpikā*, a commentary on the *Sāṃkhyasaptati* composed by the venerable teacher Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
[The opponent] says: You have correctly taught that liberation is attained through the thorough knowledge of the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*).
Now it must be taught how these three are to be practiced.
It is said: the practice of these three is traditionally handed down in two ways:
in brief and in detail.

That same triad is divided by five subject matters (*adhikaraṇa*). What, then, are these subject matters? It is said: the occurrence of the primary nature and its modifications (*prakṛtivikāravṛtta*),...
The operation of cause and effect, the operation of excellence and non-excellence,
and the operation of the sign and the signified.
Regarding the phrase "the functioning of the object and the subject":
since the other categories (adhikaraṇas) are preceded by the functioning of the material cause (prakṛti) and its modification (vikāra), we shall explain their distinctions.
Furthermore, that [functioning] is divided into four kinds.
Some things are causes only and not effects;
some things are both causes and effects;
and some things are effects only and not causes.
"Is it that there is neither cause nor effect at all?
He replied: "This has been taught in terms of extreme generality; it does not remain fixed in our understanding.
Therefore, let it be explained in detail: what is the function of which category of entity?"
It is said: "Certainly;
it is taught that primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification."
Root (*mūla*), support (*ādhāra*), and foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) are synonymous. It is called *prakṛti* because it produces (*prakurute*).
And this root is the primordial nature (prakṛti); thus it is the "root-nature" (mūlaprakṛti).
Of what is the root-nature the root?
It is the root of the great principle (mahat) and the others.
This designation "pradhāna" (the primary cause) refers to the *mūlaprakṛti* (root-nature).
And its meaning is that it is unmodified (*avikṛti*), non-transformed (*avikāra*), and unproduced (*anutpādya*).
[The opponent] says: "The formation of the compound is untenable because of the inclusion of another qualifier."
The word *mūlam* (root), being employed here as a qualifier for *prakṛti* (primordial nature), takes on another qualification, namely *mahadādi* (the Great One and so forth).
In that case, the rule prohibiting compound formation for words with qualifiers—stating that "there is no [compound] for those having qualifiers"—would apply.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because another type of compound is prescribed, the thought might be: "If this fault arises in this particular compound, another compound will be prescribed here; namely, *mūla-prakṛtiḥ*, meaning the root of the primordial natures."
And this is untenable. Why? Because another fault arises.
Even so, since that which is expressed by the genitive case is subordinate (*upasarjana*) according to the rule "the subordinate is placed first," it would have to be placed first.
In this regard, it must be understood that the root is the primary nature (*prakṛti*) of all things, and that the primary nature is the root.
Therefore, this [objection] is also without substance.
It is said in reply: let the compound be exactly as previously stated.
A relative term is always compounded in a derivative formation (vṛtti) when it is dependent [on another].

As for what was said—that the formation of the compound is untenable because of the introduction of another qualifier—we reply: since relative terms do not attain their own essential nature without depending on another related term, they must necessarily enter into a formation while still possessing expectancy.

For example, in the expression "Devadatta’s teacher's house" (*devadattasya gurukulam*), although the word *guru* (teacher) depends upon the word *devadatta* because it is a relative term, it nevertheless enters into a compound with the word *kula* (house).
In the same way here as well, the word *mūla* (root), being a relative term, enters into a compound with the word *prakṛti* (nature), even though it depends upon *mahat* and the other [evolutes].
Furthermore:
Because the meaning conveyed by the sentence is perceived within the compound (*vṛtti*).

For it is established in the treatise that where the meaning conveyed by the sentence is not obtained through the compound—as in the case of "the king's man who is wealthy" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*)—there is no compounding of words accompanied by qualifiers;
yet here, the meaning conveyed by the sentence is indeed understood even when the compound exists.
Therefore, this is not a fault.

Furthermore, it is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Indeed, the indicator is the rule: "That which has an action equal to [the action of] an object is treated like an object" (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*).
Likewise, [it is said] "the letter *a* is taught as being open," and so forth.
Therefore, one should not feel resentment in this matter.
He says: "The reflection upon a constituent part is untenable because it is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*)."

For in the case of compound words based on names, there is no reference to the individual parts; for example, in the cases of *gajakarṇa* ("elephant-ear") and *aśvakarṇa* ("horse-ear"), one does not ask "of which elephant? or "of which horse? [as if they were separate entities].
It is said: no, because the meaning is applicable.
For wherever a meaning is applicable, there indeed occurs a reference to the constituent parts within words that are proper names;
for example, "he has seven leaves on each joint."
"Eight steps of this [tree] in each row [make it] a seven-leafed tree; thus it is called 'eight-stepped' (aṣṭāpada). And this meaning is applicable here; therefore, there is no fault in this.

He said: "The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; it should be called 'nature' (prakṛti). As it is said: 'The seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and modifications.'"
It is said: there is no statement regarding the state of being a primal nature (*prakṛtitva*).
And the state of being a primal nature need not be stated of the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
For what reason?
This follows from the implication of the context;
thus, it is established that the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unevolved (avikṛti). For if it were explicitly stated, it would be redundant.
He said: "The definition of *prakṛti* is untenable because of the acceptance of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
For *prakṛti* is that which acts (*prakaroti*)."
Its state is being the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*). And that [state] is not possible when the effect already exists.
Why? Because for things that already exist, such as the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, a cause is not logically tenable.
It is said: that is equally applicable elsewhere as well.
For just as a cause for existing things such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth is not tenable, so too it is for non-existent things such as a hare’s horn; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The third alternative, however, is merely a state of despair and weakness.

If it is argued that the establishment of one's own position results from the rejection of both alternatives, it might further be said: you have demonstrated that there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent regarding their connection with action;
therefore, the rejection of both positions has been accomplished.
Yet, the establishment of one's own position does not follow merely from the rejection of both positions.
And this is incorrect. Why? Because it will be refuted later on.
Indeed, this proponent rejects the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda); therefore, we shall turn him back to his own specific position.
He said: "The statement that [Prakṛti] is not a modification is meaningless, because its establishment follows from its being the root-prakṛti.
If it is the root of all prakṛtis, it must exist as a non-modification itself."
Otherwise, its status as the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) would be untenable.
For if even the Pradhāna were to have another primal nature, its status as the root-primal nature could not be established.
Therefore, since that [status] is proven simply by the statement of its being the root-primal nature, the inclusion of the term "unmodified" (avikṛti) is redundant.
It is said: No, because it is for the purpose of avoiding the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For just as the seed is the primary cause (*prakṛti*) of roots and so forth, and there would likewise be an infinite regress if one were to say that there is another cause for that [seed] and yet another for that [other], so too, since the Pradhāna is the root-cause of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, there would result an infinite regress if one were to say that there is another cause for that [Pradhāna].
Lest this occur, that [Pradhāna] is designated [as the ultimate cause] in order to avoid that [regress].
He said: No; because no reason has been stated.
This might indeed be so beyond doubt, but no reason for this has been provided by you here.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the wise to accept that which lacks an assigned cause;
therefore, this [position] is untenable.
It is replied: because other causes are negated.

Because the Puruṣa is not an agent, and because it is impossible for the constituents (guṇas) called Pradhāna to exist in any other state [than their own], its unchangeability is established. Here, the Primordial Nature (prakṛti) which is being commenced must be produced either by other causes such as Īśvara,
or by the Puruṣa, or by the constituents (guṇas).
What follows from this? That [world] is not, first of all, produced by other causes such as Īśvara and so forth.
Why? Because of its negation.
How those other causes do not exist will be demonstrated through a refutation later on.
Now, having proposed the four categories— sattva, rajas, tamas, and puruṣa—
it is further maintained therein that the agency of the puruṣa is denied.
Once that is denied, the relationship of cause and effect pertains solely to the various states of the guṇas.
The acquisition of form by subtle elements is the effect;
their abiding in a state of non-distinction, wherein specific qualities have ceased, is the cause—this is the established doctrine.

In that state, the specific qualities have set, the activity of transformation has ceased, they no longer enter into the relationship of primary and secondary constituents, and their powers have been withdrawn.

For those who have attained that other state which is the equilibrium of all modifications, the dissolution of all powers, devoid of both existence and non-existence, and characterized as unmanifest— neither being nor non-being— there exists no other subtler state than this,
of which this state characterized as *pradhāna* could be the effect.
Therefore, it is rightly said that the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification.
The seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and modifications.
"Beginning with the Great One" means those of which the Great One is the first.
The analysis is by means of the individual members,
while the collective whole is the meaning of the compound;
otherwise, "great" itself would remain unaccounted for here.
"Prakṛtis and vikṛtis" means those which are both causes and effects;
that is to say, causes and their effects.
Among these, the Great Principle (mahat) is the *prakṛti* (cause) of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the *vikṛti* (effect) of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

Egoism (ahaṃkāra) is both the cause and the effect of the two stages, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the sense organs (indriya). Furthermore, the subtle elements are the cause of the stage of the gross elements (bhūta) and the effect of egoism.
He asks: for what purpose is the mention of "seven" [in the verse]?
It is said: the mention of "seven" is for the purpose of delimiting the boundary.
For if the mention of "seven" were not made, it would not be known which group of primary elements (*prakṛti*) is designated as both "primary" (*prakṛti*) and "modified" (*vikṛti*).
In that case, even the categories of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) would undesirably result in being considered primary.
He said: This purpose does not exist, because it is established by elimination. Here, according to you Pañcaśikhas, there are twenty-five principles (tattvas).

In this regard, it has been stated that the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; furthermore, he will state that the group of sixteen is a modification, while the person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification.
By process of elimination, only seven remain.
Therefore, there is no purpose in including that [ego] by means of the mention of the seven.
It is said: "It is for the sake of encompassing the ego.
To this, Patañjali replies: "In that case, the ego does not exist at all."
Because it is accepted that [the self] has the nature of the notion "I am" (asmimāna), this [objection] will serve as its refutation. He says:
No, because it is taken up later.
There is no purpose [in stating this here], for the Teacher will later state with great emphasis: “From Prakṛti comes Mahat, and from that, Ahaṅkāra” (Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṃkhyakārikā 22);
by that alone, this is established.
There is no purpose served by the inclusion of the word "seven" even for that reason.
It is said: it is for the sake of making known the non-difference in essence despite the difference in form.
If that is so, then there are eight forms of cognition to be described, beginning with dharma and so forth.
And the ego (ahaṃkāra), being of the nature of the *vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *bhūtādi*, is said to have three characteristics as will be explained hereafter.
In this context, the mention of "seven" is made so that there may be no confusion regarding the distinction between categories (*tattva*) due to the difference in their forms.
[The opponent] says: This cannot be understood without a logical reason (*hetu*).
Even when stated explicitly, those who rely on reasoning do not accept it without logical justification; how much less so that which is produced by the afflictions?
Therefore, the resolution to this must be stated: how can cognition, though appearing in many forms, be one and the same?
It is said: no, for this will be examined later.
We shall examine this further on: even when multiple forms manifest, does that very same thing remain that entity, or does a difference in nature arise from the difference in form?
Therefore, let it be observed here for now that it is established that the seven beginning with Mahat are both prakṛtis and vikṛtis;
whereas the group of sixteen is only a vikāra (modification).
This is the Saṃgha of sixteen because its measure is sixteen;
the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "the measure of that [number] is used as a designation for a collection, a sūtra, or a recitation.
He asks: "But what is this 'of sixteen'?"
It is said: the five great elements and the eleven faculties;
the word "tu" (but/however) serves the purpose of restriction.
He said: "Furthermore, this meaning can be obtained even without the word 'tu'.
How so? For it was taught previously that 'the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolutes.

Therefore, once it is established that [the sequence] is preceded solely by the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), the restriction regarding the stages of the sense organs and the gross elements will follow from their being mentioned again."

For example, regarding the rule "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," although by the very fact of the matter all substances capable of counteracting hunger would naturally be subject to eating, this further scriptural statement serves as a restriction;
this should be understood in the same way.
If it should be thought that [the repetition] is for the purpose of definitive determination according to one's preference:
In that case, the word "but" (tu) will serve the purpose of restriction according to our intention;
that is, so that it may be understood that "the group of sixteen is indeed a modification," and not that "the group of sixteen is [merely] a modification."
If this is so, then the word "tu" has been placed in the wrong position;
it should have been stated as "the sixteenfold transformation, however" (*ṣoḍaśako vikārastu*).
Now, if it is thought that this word "tu" was placed in this spot for the sake of completing the meter, then it should be understood that it belongs only where it is not defective.
This is untenable.
Why? Because there is no doubt.
When it is stated that "the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolutes," why should we be uncertain?
Therefore, we do not see any purpose for its inclusion in the recitation.
Now, it might be argued that although this is established by the sense of the matter, this teacher nevertheless takes care to provide a restriction for the sake of clear comprehension.
What is the reason?
For the intentions and methods of the authors of grammatical sūtras are diverse.

For example, the Blessed Pāṇini— in rules such as *na kye* and *rātsasya*, where restriction according to his preference is established even without explicit effort— exerts effort in other instances, such as *ajādī guṇavacanādeva*, *stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇyabhāsāt*, and so forth.
"The same should be understood here as well"—this is untenable. Why? Because it is impossible.
Furthermore, even if the word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), how can a restriction be understood here?
For the effects characterized by the body and so forth are also observed to belong to the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Regarding this, some state the following resolution:
Because the body and so forth are not entities distinct [from their causes], earth and the other elements lack the status of being primary material causes (*aprakṛtitva*).
For it is said that the effect of earth and the others is merely a particular arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣamātra*), like a fist, a knot, or an earring, and is not a separate entity.
Therefore, these [elements] do not possess the status of being primary material causes.
And this is untenable.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
For according to the Sāṃkhyas, every effect is indeed non-different from its cause.
In this regard, according to this conception, it would follow that all principles (tattvas) lack an original nature (aprakṛtitva);
and if this is undesirable, [then...]
This results in a contradiction with the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkārya*).
Others, however, say: "Because the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not undergo transformation, their state of being manifold cannot be determined.
That too is untenable.

Why? Because it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, the transformation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—such as a mass [of matter] into a sprout or milk—is perceived through direct perception itself; however, the transformation of other principles (*tattva*) is graspable through inference (*anumāna*).
Thus, this results in a contradiction between what precedes and what follows;
therefore, this is untenable.
[The opponent] says: "In that case, should it not be understood that there are exactly sixteen transformations?"
It is said: it must be understood.
What is the reason? Because no other reality is possible.

In this system, because they have fallen away from their state of equilibrium due to the cause that is human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), this transformation of the *guṇas*—beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*)—is established by the rule of the production of successive principles (*tattva*).
However, there is no production of a principle distinct from those such as earth;
therefore, these [elements] possess only the nature of modifications (*vikāra*).
Furthermore,
because there would be no other perceiver:

just as when earth and the other elements are produced from those subtle elements (tanmātra), another perceiver characterized as a sense organ arises from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) as something appropriate for them.
There is no other perceiver of transformations such as jars and the like that exists apart from earth and so forth;
therefore, they are not a different reality.
Consequently, earth and the others are merely transformations.
Furthermore:

as there is the disappearance of the state of being the primal cause (*prakṛti*) in the Primal Substance (*pradhāna*) because no further subtler state exists beyond it, so too is there the disappearance of the state of being a modification (*vikāra*) in those [evolutes], because no further subtler state exists beyond them.
Just as the state of being the primal cause ceases in the Primal Substance since there is no other state more subtle than it, so the state of being a modification ceases in those [evolutes].
Therefore, it is rightly said that this [group] of sixteen is indeed a transformation (vikāra). He asks: "In that case, what is the status of the Puruṣa? It is replied:
The Puruṣa is neither primordial nature nor its transformation.
For this person does not undergo a transition to another state, nor indeed does one state become another state.
He said: "This is not to be believed without logical reasoning."

Therefore, explain how its status as neither a primal cause (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*) can be established. It is said: its status as a primal cause is untenable, because it will be refuted later on.
And regarding the phrase "from that perversion" (ISk 19),
we shall set forth the reasoning;
therefore, for now, it follows that this [perversion] is not the fundamental nature.
The state of being unchanging is like that of *pradhāna*.
Just as *pradhāna* is, so too this *puruṣa*, even when acted upon by other causes such as Īśvara and the like, is not produced.
Why? Because of its prohibition.
Just as there are no other causes [for this], so a refutation will be made later;
because of the equality with other persons.
All persons are equal.
Furthermore, a causal relationship between identical things has never been observed.
Moreover, because these [entities] are inactive and pure, any action characterized by transformation or characterized by motion is untenable due to their omnipresence.
Why? Because they do not originate one another.
It is not [produced] by the qualities (guṇas), because they belong to a different genus;
for we shall demonstrate here that the qualities are insentient.
Furthermore, whatever is produced by something must consist of that very thing.
If the commencement of persons were by means of the *guṇas*, then they too would be insentient; however, they are indeed sentient.
Therefore, it is established that they are not originated by the *guṇas*.
Some causes are not effects;
some are both causes and effects;
and some are effects alone.
"Neither cause nor effect exists at all"—thus has the fourfold operation of causality been established. This is the summary aphorism of the proposition.
Herein, that which has been set forth by you should be understood as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in this treatise. // 3 //
Kārikā 4:
It is asked—now, from what is this object of cognition established?
It is said:
For the establishment of the objects of cognition proceeds indeed from the means of valid cognition.
That which is measured is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
The establishment of the object of cognition is "the establishment of the *prameya*.
Establishment means comprehension or understanding; such is the meaning.
That by which something is correctly cognized is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The suffix *lyuṭ* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
That [means of valid cognition] is indeed one alone.
Because the unity of cognition (*buddhi*) is admitted;
however, due to the influence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), it is treated as differentiated, such as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and "inference" (*anumāna*).

Disregarding that differentiation produced by limiting conditions and accepting the commonality of being a determiner of the object of knowledge (*prameya-paricchedakatva-sāmānya*), the singular designation "from the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāt*) is employed.
From this, it should be understood that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is established.
How so? Like rice and other grains.

Just as the object of cognition such as rice is delimited by a measure such as a *prastha*, so too here the object of cognition such as the manifest (*vyakta*) is delimited by means of cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In this context, for what purpose would the word "hi" (for/indeed) be used now?
[If you say] it is for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), he replies: If that is so, then the word "hi" should not have been uttered.
Because restriction is untenable;
for in this sūtra, restriction of any kind is not possible.
Therefore, it is logical that the word "hi" (for/indeed) is simply not to be uttered.
If it is argued that [the determination] belongs to the object of cognition itself—no, because nothing else is possible.
For when the possibility of deviation exists, a thing is determined as such—for example: "This is indeed a cow, not a horse."
"This is Devadatta and not Yajñadatta.

Nor is there any logical consequence that both the cognizable and the non-cognizable must be delimited by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such that the restriction "of the cognizable alone" would be required for the sake of excluding [the latter].
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] arise "from the pramāṇas themselves," this is not so, because it would entail a contradiction with the knowledge of the sages (ārṣajñāna).
For it is your position that the knowledge of the Blessed One, the Supreme Sage, is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) and not preceded by any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇapūrvaka*);
for there is the statement: "Innate states are qualities such as *dharma* and so forth, whether natural (*prākṛtika*) or modified (*vaikṛta*). (ISk 43)
If both [terms] are restricted, then the faults belonging to both positions follow as a consequence;
therefore, this is untenable.
If it is argued that "it is indeed established," we say no, because of the lack of certainty (*anekāntāt*).
Sometimes this cognizer is obstructed from determining objects such as directions, even when a probans (liṅga) like the sun is present.
Therefore, because [the reason] is inconclusive, the restrictive determination that "success [of cognition] arises only [from the means of knowledge]" is incorrect.

It is replied: as for what was said—that the word *hi* should not be stated because a restrictive determination is untenable—let there be the restriction: "only from the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇebhya eva*).
As for what was stated regarding the consequence of contradicting the knowledge of the Sages (*ārṣajñāna*), this is not a fault.
Why? Because [the entities in question] are of an established nature (*siddharūpa*).

For things that are in the process of being produced (*sādhyamānarūpa*) possess a requirement for a connection with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the sake of the production of their own form, due to their necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*). However, [established things do not].
The knowledge of the Blessed One, the supreme seer, is indeed established in its perfected form;
therefore, it is not logical for him to have any expectation regarding the connection with a means of proof (*sādhana*).
Alternatively, let there be the emphatic determination that it is simply established (*siddhi*).
As for what was stated—that [the argument] is inconclusive—that is untenable.
Why? Because there is no fixed rule regarding the relationship of primary and subordinate among the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
for it is possible that a deficiency in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from the predominance of *tamas*.
In this case, the relationship of primary and secondary among sattva and the other guṇas is not fixed;
for, by the power of place, time, and causal conditions, sometimes sattva predominates,
and sometimes rajas.
Sometimes there is darkness (*tamas*).
And because *sattva* is luminous by nature, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, when *tamas* prevails, then because *sattva* is overwhelmed by it, its effect—inference (*anumāna*), which has the three times as its constituent part—arises.
Therefore, even though the operation of the indicative marks such as the sun persists, it is obstructed with respect to objects such as the determination of direction;
otherwise, however, there would be no loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

But for one who does not accept an obstruction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to a deficiency in its production, it follows that there must be a loss of the essential nature of the means of valid cognition themselves.

How so? For their essential nature consists solely in the determination of the object of cognition (*prameya-pariccheda*). Therefore, it is appropriate that the word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to emphasize this point.
He asks: "Many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are accepted by the teachers; do you assent to all of them?"
It is said:
threefold means of valid cognition are accepted.
Rather, "vidhā" means a mode;
"tisro vidhā asya" means it has three modes, which signifies that it is of three kinds.

By this, he explains the following: the single reality characterized by intellect (*buddhi*), through the distinctions of forms delimited by specific effects produced by the assistance of other causal factors, [appears in various ways].
That which is denoted by terms such as "perception" (dṛṣṭa) appears as if distinct from the powers (śakti) due to their auxiliary function; however,

it is not as the proponents of other systems maintain— that there exist here cognitions produced by sense organs encountering objects, which, when postulated, would constitute three independent means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It might be asked: "How can there be distinctions among the powers that constitute the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if they reside in a single entity?
It is said: like *sattva* and the other [guṇas].

Just as, although the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* reside in a single entity such as sound, there is no confusion of their forms because of the distinction in their effects—such as illumination and so forth—[so too is it here].
Or, just as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, though residing in a single substance, are apprehended by different types of cognizers;

or just as the powers characterized as agent, instrument, locus, recipient, point of departure, and object—though residing in a single substance—do not have their essential natures confused because they are delimited by their respective specific effects;
so too should this be understood.
If it is argued that the production of another capacity constitutes the arising of a different entity, we say no, because this is not accepted.
Indeed, we do not accept the audacious doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) even out of fear of punishment, let alone on the basis of reasoning.
But since this is not the appropriate occasion for that, let us pause for now.
He asks: "How, then, is it understood that there are exactly three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not many more?
It is said in reply:
Because it is established by all means of valid cognition.
And all those means of valid cognition are "all means of valid cognition" (*sarvapramāṇa*).
The state of being established is "establishedness" (*siddhatva*).
The establishedness of all means of valid cognition is "the establishment by all means of valid cognition" (*sarvapramāṇasiddhatva*).
The meaning is that "establishment" (*siddhatva*) implies inclusion.
Therefore, because it is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
the ellipsis of the sentence is "in those very three kinds of valid cognition."

This is stated as "because it is established by all means of valid cognition" (*sarvapramāṇasiddhatvāt*) in order to show that all means of valid cognition imagined by others are included within these very three types of means of valid cognition.

Alternatively, *sarvapramāṇasiddha* means "established in all means of valid cognition"; the compound is formed according to the rule for the locative case with words such as *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*, as in the examples "one established in Sāṃkāśya" (*sāṃkāśyasiddhaḥ*) or "one established in Pāṭaliputra" (*pāṭaliputrasiddhaḥ*).

Its state is being established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it is because it is established by all three types of valid cognition. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "Of what [threefold thing]?"—namely, of the threefold valid cognition.
But in what manner is the threefold valid cognition established?
It is said: because of their mutual distinction.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate how these other [means of knowledge] are distinct from this triad.
He asks: what, then, are those three kinds of valid cognition?
It is said:
perception, inference, and authoritative testimony. (IS 4a)
Thus it is said. Among these, "perception" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to that determination which arises from the functioning of the sense organs toward their respective objects as they are grasped.
"Inference" (*anumāna*) is the subsequent cognition regarding another related thing, preceded by the direct perception of one of two things that are invariably concomitant.
"Valid testimony" (*āptavacana*), however, is the ascertainment of an object that is entirely beyond the senses, mediated by a source who has become a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*).
This is merely a brief enumeration;
however, the teacher himself will state the fundamental definition [of perception] as "perception is the determination of each respective object," and so forth.
[The opponent] says: "The threefold knowledge is untenable."
Because of the hearing of [different numbers] both less and more;
some belonging to other tantras assert four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), based on the statement: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition."
Likewise, others say there are six:
perception, inference, verbal testimony along with comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-existence; these are the means of proof that establish what is to be proven.

Because of this statement [in the *Abhidharma*], others maintain that there are nine [means of knowledge] when these are combined with probability (*sambhava*), tradition (*aitihya*), and gesture (*ceṣṭā*).
The Vaiśeṣikas and Buddhists, however, maintain that there are only two: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
In this regard, how is it determined that there are exactly three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and neither fewer nor more? It is said: what, then, is this so-called analogy (*upamāna*)?
He said: "Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be established through similarity with something well-known.
'Well-known' means recognized; [comparison functions] by virtue of that similarity."
The means of establishing that which is not yet established is comparison (*upamāna*).
As for the method of cognition: one who has not perceived a *gavaya* asks someone who has already perceived one, "What is the form of a *gavaya*?
He explains to him: "Just as a cow is, so is a *gavaya*."

In that regard, one who has not previously perceived the actual nature of the gavaya through direct experience, but whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has been instilled by the knowledge of its similarity to a well-known object as explained by an authority, cognizes it thus: "Surely, such is the form of the gavaya.
Another says: for one in whom a mental impression has been instilled by the knowledge of similarity to a well-known object produced by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), at a later time—
The comprehension of the relationship with a name, which occurs after perceiving that [object] through direct perception— namely, "this is the object, and this is the name of this word"—
is called analogy (*upamāna*). If this is so, then analogy is not mentioned separately from tradition (*aitihya*).
Because it is established through authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*).
Just as one understands that "a gavaya is like a cow" by the power of authoritative instruction, the cognizer perceives the previously unknown gavaya, and not merely through similarity.
Therefore, comparison (*upamā*) is not distinct from verbal testimony (*śabda*).

As for what is indeed called "thus it was said" (*iti ha uvāca*)—this so-called *aitihya* (tradition) which is postulated as a distinct means of valid cognition—it too is not something other than verbal testimony (*śabda*), because it depends upon a specific speaker.

[The opponent] says: No, because it depends upon similarity (*sādharmya*). For if tradition were merely the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta-upadeśa*), then [the inference] such as "as there are Apsarases in heaven,"...
In cases such as "the Northern Kurus," understanding arises even without the explicit mention of a common property (*sādharmya*); the same would apply here as well.
However, when a speaker intends to convey a *gavaya*, he employs a term that contains within it a well-known similarity, and not merely the word alone.
Furthermore, the hearer understands from that very [term] and not from the word alone.
Therefore, its instruction must be given separately.

If it is argued that it is included therein because of the operation of the word—that is, if it be thought: "This object, characterized by well-known similarity, is accompanied by the operation of the word in the cognition of the *gavaya*, and not alone;
therefore, it is included therein"—that too is untenable.
Why? Because that [fault] would follow for the *vīta* and *avīta* as well.
Even when the *vīta* and *avīta* reasons are employed for the purpose of instructing another, they depend upon the operation of words;
thus, there is the consequence that these two also would be authoritative statements (*āptavacana*).
And this is undesirable;
therefore, authoritative instruction is not analogy.
It is said: [it is] because of the non-exclusion of similarity.
Because it serves as a means [to the goal],

the cognizer's knowledge of the gavaya arises precisely from the authority of the speaker; however, considering that this matter is difficult to accomplish due to a lack of skill, he employs a well-known similarity [as a means].
Therefore, for the one who employs similarity as a means for the sake of conveying the meaning of the word "gavaya" from the speaker, a distinct object arises from the word.
Now, if it is maintained that even such [cognitions] constitute a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then it is far too little to say that there are only four means of valid cognition.
Rather, one would have to include gestures of the hand, winks of the eye, and so forth as well.
Furthermore, because it depends on the specific speaker:

for where comprehension arises by virtue of the meaning itself, the comprehender does not depend on the specific speaker, thinking, "This has a perceptible object" or "This has an imperceptible object," as is the case with inference.
Furthermore, there is a dependence upon a specific speaker regarding the object of comparison;
therefore, that [comparison] is not a distinct entity from the word.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way.

For if one were to think that the cognition of a gavaya arises solely from a well-known similarity— such as [the statement] "as is a horse, so is a gavaya"— then from this too there would be a correct understanding of it; yet this cannot be the case,
because it would be a false cognition.

As for the claim that "that from which the understanding of the relationship between a name and its referent arises is analogy (upamāna)," this is untenable. Why? Because it would lead to an infinite regress.
For example, when many people are seated together and someone asks, "Who here is Devadatta?", one might reply, "He who wears a crown, has earrings, a broad chest, and copper-colored, long eyes.

From this, there would follow the realization of a relationship based on verbal designation (*samākhyā-sambandha-pratipatti*), which entails the consequence that this is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). In this way, there would be an infinite regress of means of valid cognition, and this is undesirable.
Thus, analogy is not a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) separate from others.

When one has personally perceived both a cow and a gavaya and then forms the conceptual judgment, "As this [cow] is, so is that [gavaya]," that [analogy] is not a valid cognition at all, because its object has already been apprehended by another means of valid cognition.

Therefore, it was well said: "This [analogy] is established under the category of authoritative instruction (āptopadeśa), since it is included within tradition (aitihya) and the word of a reliable person (āptavacana)."

Furthermore: [the term] "is not mentioned" is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Among these, *arthāpatti* (presumption) is that wherein, having previously observed the non-deviation between two things, one subsequently attains cognition of the other upon seeing or hearing one of them. *Saṃbhava* (possibility) and *abhāva* (non-existence) are established through inference (*anumāna*), as is *ceṣṭā* (action). Thus, [they are not mentioned separately].

In this regard, what is called *arthāpatti* is as follows: when one has first perceived the invariable concomitance between two objects, and later, from either seeing or hearing one of them, there arises a comprehension of the other.
For example, upon perceiving the molasses through sight and so forth, one understands its sweetness, which is an object of another sense-faculty;
or as when, having heard the word "molasses," one understands the sweetness that is not itself audible. This, indeed, is another form of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Where, having observed the non-deviation between two properties, one postulates a concomitance even for their opposites,
that [concomitance] is of two kinds:
deviant and non-deviant.

In that regard, an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāriṇī*) is as follows: when it is stated that "that which has parts is impermanent," it is implied by the sense that "that which is partless is permanent. Since this is not observed in the case of action (*karman*) and so forth, such [an inference] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all due to its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
However, that which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvinī*) and non-deviant (*avyabhicāriṇī*) is as follows: having observed the meeting of a lion and a boar in a thicket, at a later time...
Upon perceiving only a lion whose body is marked by the wounds of a boar as it departs, one concludes, "The boar has been conquered"; this is inference (*anumāna*).
How so? Because there is an invariable relationship (*avyabhicāri-sambandha*) between the victory and defeat of the lion and the boar respectively.
In that case, when one perceives the lion's victory—which is invariably concomitant with the other's defeat—one understands the defeat of the latter; what else could this be but inference?

For inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of one related member by a cognizer who has already apprehended the whole consisting of both related members and has directly perceived one of those related members.
And since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) functions in this same manner, it ought not to be distinct from that [inference].
As for probability (*sambhava*), when it is said "a *droṇa* is a *prastha*," the presence of half-*droṇas* and so forth is understood.
Thus, this too is merely an *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on the postulation of concomitance (*sāhacarya*).
How so? Because the word "droṇa" applies to a substance of the stated measure, neither to one less nor to one more.
In that context, when "Droṇa" is mentioned, the presence of those parts which are absolutely co-existent with it—even if they are denotable by other words—is simply *arthāpatti* (presumption).
And that has been stated to be inference (*anumāna*).
