As for what is called non-existence (*abhāva*): just as the existence of fire is cognized from the existence of smoke, so too the non-existence of fire is [cognized] from the non-existence of smoke; this is described as *arthāpatti* based on the conceptualization of a concomitance between opposites.
In that regard, when there is the assumption of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) despite concomitance (*sāhacarya*), there is simply an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).
For example, the absence of smoke in iron, embers, and the like does not imply the absence of fire.
However, where there is an absolute certainty—as in the case of "that which is produced is impermanent"—therein lies inference (*anumāna*).
How so? Because of the logical possibility of concomitance (*sāhacarya*), just like the relationship between being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*).
Others, however, describe non-existence (*abhāva*) in another way.
For example, when it is said, "Caitra is not in the house," the understanding arises that he is outside;

in this case, the absence from the house is the cause for the comprehension of his presence outside, which is indeed an *arthāntarāpatti* (presumption) based on the conceptualization of a concomitance with its opposite.

How so? Just as in the statement, "Devadatta, though fat, does not eat during the day," because fatness—which is the counter-correlative of eating—is perceived, [one infers] at the time opposite to the day [i.e., at night].
Just as at night a meal is inferred from the fact that one is not present [to eat], so too here, by the force of the statement regarding the absence of the house, its opposite is inferred.
Otherwise, if mere non-existence were intended, he would simply have said, "Caitra does not exist.
And presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a form of inference (*anumāna*).
Gestures (*ceṣṭā*) refer to certain bodily activities, such as slapping one's belly or joining the palms, which indicate an internal intention.
For they establish hunger and other states that are not otherwise perceived; thus, they are called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And this is indeed nothing but inference (*anumāna*).

Why? Because if an activity performed as concomitant with a desire for food and so forth were to indicate that concomitant [desire], then it could not be asserted as something distinct from inference.
He says: "In that case, intuition (*pratibhā*) will be another means of valid cognition. It is replied: What is this so-called intuition?

He said: That cognition which arises—dependent on the latencies of prior habituation—regarding external objects such as women and so forth, which are indistinguishable in their objective reality for gods, humans, and animals throughout beginningless saṃsāra, and which is differentiated by various forms such as a corpse, a beloved woman, or food, and which serves as a factor in one's course of action—that indeed is *pratibhā*.
And thus it has been said:
For, according to habit, comprehension arises from sentences in various ways— even in the absence of an object—
conforming to one's own internal cognition.
For when a certain object has been habitually associated with pleasure and so forth, a cognition arises from the mere word even without that object;
just as, for example, when it is said, "A tiger dwells here," sweating, trembling, and the like occur by the force of habit alone, even without an external object.
Therefore, intuition (*pratibhā*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is a factor in determining what ought to be done by gods, humans, and animals. And it is said:
All the world follows it as a valid means of knowledge;
even the worldly transactions of animals proceed by its power.

It is said [in response]: because no other form of cognition is possible apart from perception (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth, [the term] "non-utterance" (*avacana*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

If it is accepted that *pratibhā* (intuition) is a cognition dependent upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior practice, then it follows that this [intuition] is included within these: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*).
Why? Because we never perceive anything in the form of direct perception apart from seeing and so forth.
Therefore, intuition (*pratibhā*) is not a distinct entity from those [mental states].
If it is argued that this is incorrect because of the possibility of the intuitive cognition of the seers (*ārṣapratyaya*), it might be as follows:
For there exists, among all objects, an innate cognition distinct from perception and the other means of knowledge, which belongs to the sages;
that will be the intuitive (prātibha) [cognition].
But this too is incorrect.
Why? Because it has already been stated.
It has been stated that the knowledge of the Blessed One, the Supreme Seer, is of an established nature;
therefore, it does not depend upon means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that this applies to yogins, we say no,
because we do not accept it; for we shall explain later how the knowledge of yogins is indeed preceded by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that it is worldly, no;
because it is not certain.
This might be the case: there exists a worldly cognition distinct from seeing and so forth.
For example, as one walking in deep darkness, a cognition arises instantly: "There is a solid object obstructing me standing before me and above me.
But that is not so;
why? Because it is indeterminate.
For in that case, no certainty arises that "this is that substance" or "it exists manifestly before me.
Nor is it accepted that uncertain knowledge is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, [if it were so], there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And if a cognition of this kind is also accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results.
For what reason?
Because there would be no end to the process of verification.

Since manifold conceptualization— whether correct or false— arises through the gateways of desire, anger, greed, and dejection, it follows that such worldly cognition is not *pratibhā* (intuitive flash).
As for what is indeed said— that a cognition arises even regarding non-existent things like tigers by depending on the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of repeated practice— that is not so.
This is true;
however, because it is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), it is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thus there is no fault.
Therefore, it is established that since no other form [of cognition] is possible apart from perception (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth, intuition (*pratibhā*) is not mentioned separately.
And therefore, since it is established by all means of valid cognition, it is settled that the threefold means of valid cognition is accepted. // 4 // [The opponent] says:
Let this be so.
Because their definitions have not been stated, they are not understood;
therefore, those definitions must be stated.
For the definitions of the seen and so forth are indeed unstable.
Due to the diversity of views:
some maintain that perception is knowledge produced from the contact of the sense-faculties and their objects, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature;
others hold that it is something else, produced from the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the object.
Others maintain that perception is the arising of cognition when a person’s sense organs are in contact with existing objects;
the Vārṣagaṇas say it is the functioning of the ear and other senses;
while others say it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
In this way, the definition is unstable;
thus, there is no comprehension of [the objects] such as the seen and so forth.
Therefore, the definition must be stated.
It is said:
"Perception (dṛṣṭa) is the ascertainment of each respective object"; objects (viṣaya) are sound and so forth, because they bind (viṣiṇvanti).
Alternatively, the meaning is that they are "perceived" or "apprehended.
And these are of two kinds:
distinguished and undistinguished.

The specific [elements], characterized by earth and so forth, are perceivable by those such as ourselves; the non-specific [elements], characterized by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), are perceivable by yogins and those whose stream flows upward.
This will be stated further below: "Of these, the five sense organs have both the specific and the non-specific as their objects" (YS 3.44).
And it will be stated that "determination is intellect" (ISk 23).
"Toward each object" means with respect to an object.
What is that? It is the sense organ (*indriya*).
The determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding it is "determination with respect to each object.

This means that when the sense organs have taken up their objects, there arises a luminous form—devoid of *rajas* and *tamas* due to the predominance of *sattva*—which coincides with the functioning of the senses; this is what is meant by "perception" (*dṛṣṭa*).
That which is seen is what is meant by "perception" (pratyakṣa);
this is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The fruit of this is the assistance rendered to the power of consciousness (cetanā-śakti) by means of it.
The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are sound and so forth.
In this same manner, the relationship between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is to be understood in what follows as well.
He asks: "Furthermore, is this result of the means of valid cognition something distinct from it, or is it not distinct?"
How, then, can it be that [knowledge] is not something other than [the object]?
He says: Why? Because it has the nature of realization (*adhigama*).
For knowledge has the nature of realization.
Since the object is realized by the very arising of that [cognition], how can there be a distinction in the result?
It is said: How, then, could it have the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*)?
He replies: Its status as an instrument, however, is due to conventional consensus (*prasiddhi*).

The arising of cognition, which manifests as an object, is indeed of the nature of apprehension; yet, because it is perceived in the world as if it possessed an operation (*vyāpāra*), its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is accepted through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
It is said: the result is a distinct entity, because of the difference in their loci (*adhikaraṇabheda*).
For the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which is termed "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya), has the intellect (buddhi) as its locus,
whereas the result (phala), characterized by benefit, has the person (puruṣa) as its locus.
And it is not possible for two things with distinct loci to be one and the same.
As for the claim that knowledge alone is the fruit because it consists of realization (*adhigama*), that is untenable.
Why? Because it is unproven.
For just as objects such as jars cannot be understood—either as being of the nature of knowledge or not being of that nature—without knowledge, [so too is the case here].

In this way, knowledge (*jñāna*) as well, in the absence of the principle of the Person (*puruṣapratyaya*), is neither of the nature of an object nor of the nature of a non-object. Thus says the scripture: "Through union with that [the Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 20). Therefore, for the Sāṃkhya, the claim that knowledge is of the nature of apprehension in the absence of the principle of the Person is unestablished (*asiddha*).
And linguistic convention proceeds by means of what is established for both parties.
If it is argued that this is improper because of the non-existence of the Person (puruṣa), we say no, because it will be demonstrated later.
We shall establish the existence of the Person in the [sūtra] beginning with "Because composite objects exist for the sake of another."

Therefore, it is established that for one who maintains that determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the fruit (*phala*) is something distinct from the means of valid cognition.
He asks: "If determination is indeed the means of valid cognition, how does the worldly usage ‘the object is perceived by direct perception’ (*pratyakṣaṃ vastu*) become meaningful?
It is replied: The word ‘direct perception’ (*pratyakṣa*) applies to the object because it is cognized by that [means] and because it is caused by that [means].
Just as a heap of rice measured by a *prastha* becomes denotable by the word "prastha," so too an object cognized through perception (*pratyakṣa*) should be denotable by the word "perception.
[The opponent] says: No; because that consequence would apply elsewhere as well.

If the word "perception" is applied to the object because it is cognized through perception, then an object cognized through inference (*anumāna*) would likewise have to be called "inference" (*anumāna*).
An object cognized through verbal testimony is [the object of] verbal testimony.
However, fire, heaven, and so forth are not denotable by the word "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa).
Therefore, [verbal testimony] is preceded by a dissimilar mark and its possessor.

Furthermore, for yogins dwelling in the stages of meditative concentration (*dhyānabhūmi*), there arises an intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*) that transcends inference and scripture; this too should be included [among the objects of perception].
Why? Because pleasure and the like are not graspable by the functioning of the ear and other senses, and the knowledge of yogins is suprasensory (*atīndriya*).

If it were performed according to the original formulation, those objects would also [be included]; who could then prevent the perceptuality of the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) regarding them?
It is said in reply: because that [object] is absent, there is no application [of the definition] to other cases.
In the case of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, there is no common basis (*nimitta*). Why? Because "inference" (*anumāna*) is that by which something is inferred;
and since nothing is inferred by fire and the like, they do not share the same verbal designation.
He asks: For what purpose is the inclusion of the term "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*)? It is said: For the purpose of avoiding an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it were stated merely that "that which is seen with respect to each object," it would follow that whatever exists with respect to each object—whether as a benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) or as a harmer (*upaghātaka*)—all of that would be considered "seen."
However, if the inclusion of "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya) is indeed made, no fault arises.
[The opponent] says: No, because this is within the context of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
there is no purpose for the word "ascertainment."
Why? Because this is the section concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And nothing whatsoever is cognized as an object apart from determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*);
therefore, by implication, we understand that it is determinative cognition itself that is intended here.
For example, in the context of Vedic study, when it is said, "Let the Brahmins be brought," only those who are actually engaged in study are brought.
It is replied: [the specific mention] is for the purpose of removing doubt regarding other instruments.

If that is so, then this quartet—consisting of any one of the senses such as hearing and the internal organ (manas)—operates toward the object by way of the relationship between the door and the one who uses the door.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya) is made so that there may be no doubt.
He says: Let there be this doubt;
however, no single object is apprehended by any one [of these means] alone.
"By that, we shall establish the perceptibility of all [objects].
It is replied: "If everything were accepted, there would be a loss of the treatise (*śāstra*).

For if the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all [means of knowledge] were accepted, then that treatise which asserts that there is only one vision—that vision is indeed manifestation (*khyāti*)—would be abandoned."

Furthermore, the Teacher will state: "These [faculties] are like lamps" (ISk 36), and "Because it is the intellect that accomplishes everything for the sake of the person's experience" (ISk 37); [if your view were correct], that would be contradicted.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya) must be made so that doubt does not arise.
He replies: No, this merely results in doubt.
In all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific determination [of meaning] comes from the explanation; for there is no lack of definition due to doubt.
In that regard, we shall explain that "perception" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to the ascertainment [of an object].
It is said: and [this is] free from doubt because it is the apprehension of the functioning of the sense organs.
This might be so if there were doubt here; however,
no doubt at all arises in this matter, for what occurs is simply the apprehension of that which has already passed beyond the range of hearing.

He asks: What, then, is the reason that, despite there being no distinction in their being causal signs (*nimitta*), it follows that only the functioning of the ear and other [senses] is grasped here, and not the direct perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone?
It is said in reply: In that case, the functioning of the ear and other [senses] is primary (*mukhya*).
Why? Because [the senses] possess the capacity to grasp objects directly;
the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) does not, since cognition occurs through it as a medium.
And between the secondary and the primary, preference is given to the primary;
for example, in the injunctions "A cow is to be sacrificed" and "A goat dedicated to Agni and Soma," the Vāhīka [ox] is not sacrificed.
He asks: if it is accepted that perception is simply the functioning of the auditory and other senses, what fault would there be in this case?

It is said: that cognition which has passion and so forth as its object and is preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), as well as that intuitive (prātibha) cognition which arises for yogins dwelling in the stages of meditation (dhyānabhūmikā) and transcends inference and scripture—these should be included [as types of perception].
Why? Because pleasure and the like are not external to the functions of the ear and the other senses.

And as for the claim that the knowledge of yogins is beyond the senses: if it were arranged otherwise, those [objects] would also be objects [of perception]; who then could prevent the perceptual status of their determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*)?
He asks: "In that case, what is the purpose of the phrase 'with respect to each object' (*prativiṣayagrahaṇa*)?
It is said: "The phrase 'with respect to each object' is for the purpose of excluding what is non-existent (*asad*).

If it were stated merely as 'perception (*dṛṣṭa*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*),' then even that determination which occurs with respect to a mirage, a circle of fire, a city of Gandharvas, and so forth, would be [considered] perception."
However, by specifying "the grasping of each respective object" (*prativiṣayagrahaṇa*), their exclusion is accomplished.
He asks: "If this is so, let it simply be called 'ascertainment of the object' (*viṣayādhyavasāya*); what is the purpose of the term 'each respective' (*prati*)?"
It is said: the inclusion of the prefix *prati* is for the sake of indicating proximity (*sannikarṣa*).
If it were stated merely as "the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object is perception" (*dṛṣṭam*), the understanding would apply to the mere object.
But when the prefix *prati* is employed, it functions in the sense of being directed toward (*abhimukhya*).
Therefore, that determination which arises from the operation of the sense-faculties in close proximity [to their objects] is understood as "perception" (*dṛṣṭa*).
He asks: "But in the case of what [object] does perceptuality occur when there is contact with something beyond the senses?
It is said: "In the case of inference (*anumāna*)."
Why? Because that [cognition] arises regarding an object not present to the senses through the observation of a mark (*liṅga*).
He says: there is no over-extension of inference, because what is prescribed in a general way is sublated by what is prescribed for a specific case.

For, having established that perception consists in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the object in its general aspect alone, [the treatise] teaches that inference is preceded by the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) regarding the specific aspect.
And what is prescribed in a general way is sublated by what is prescribed in a specific way, just as in the case: "Let this be given to the Brahmins; but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya."
It is said: In that case, it follows that memory would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
To this, the following exception is not applied.
He says: No, [it does not apply] to memory.
Because this is the section concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is the section concerning the means of valid cognition;
and nothing at all is cognized by means of memory (*smṛti*).
Because memory arises regarding an object already cognized, it is said:
"In that case, [memory] would result in doubt.
It does not result in doubt.
Because of the inclusion of the term "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). For ascertainment is said to be what is seen; and doubt is not ascertainment, because it is indeterminate.
It is said: [If that were so], there would be an over-extension to the objects intended by other sense-faculties.
If that is the case, then the fault does not arise because [the cognition] occurs through the engagement of the sense-faculty's activity when it is in contact with its object.
He says: [One must] add "passion and so forth" to the enumeration.

If it is accepted that "perception" (dṛṣṭa) is that determination which occurs through the operation of the senses in proximity [to their objects], then cognition whose object is passion and so forth would not qualify as perception because it transcends the senses; therefore,
an addition must be made to that definition.
It is said: In that case, this term "prati-grahaṇa" (the act of grasping toward) is not a qualifier of the sense-faculty (*indriya*), meaning "that which functions toward each respective object.
What then? It is a qualifier of the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), meaning "the determinative cognition that occurs toward each respective object.
He asks: If it is a qualifier of the determinative cognition, [what follows]?
There must be an addition [to the definition] for sound and so forth;
by that [definition], it follows that only sound and the rest would possess the nature of being perceived,
and thus an addition for them must be made.
What is the reason?
Because contact with those [objects] is impossible for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
You have previously conceded that the prefix *prati* is intended to signify contact.
Now, if that [contact] were a qualification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
contact of the internal organ with sound and so forth would not be possible,
because it would entail the consequence of the auditory organs and others being useless.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the very nature of door and doorway.
Therefore, even if one goes as far as possible, one is not released from grasping by means of its rejection;
or rather, [it is not released] because of the inclusion of passion and so forth.
It is said: Let it be then that for the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the specific characteristic is their respective grasping of objects.
As for what was stated—that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for passion (*rāga*) and so forth—to that we reply:
it is established by means of the grammatical rule of "elision of one" (*ekaśeṣa*).

In that case, the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of similar forms will be applied as follows: "perceptual determination with respect to each object" (*prativiṣayādhyavasāyaśca prativiṣayādhyavasāyaśca prativiṣayādhyavasāyaḥ*).

Among these, by the first [term], there is the inclusion of external-sense perception (*aindriyaka-pratyakṣa*); by the second, there is the inclusion of internal-sense intuition (*prātibhasa*). Thus, the cognition of yogins regarding objects such as passion and so forth is also included. In this way, perception has been explained.
He said: "Inference must now be explained.
It is replied:
"Inference is declared to be threefold."
Inference has been described by the Teachers as being of three kinds: that which possesses a prior [cause], that which possesses a remainder, and that which is observed through general correlation.
In this context, "preceded by" (*pūrva*) refers to a cause;
for whatever is the cause of something is said in the world to be "preceded by" that thing. For example, a cloth is preceded by threads.
"Yajñadatta has Devadatta as his predecessor. That which possesses something before it is "preceded by" (pūrvavat).
"Remainder" (śeṣa) is a term for a modification.
This is because [the word] is derived from the sense of "to be taught.
And so it has been said: "There is no remainder of fire that is produced by another";
the meaning is that it is impossible for offspring to be produced by someone other than its progenitor.

That which has a remainder is "the remainder-possessing" (*śeṣavat*). Among these, the "prior-like" (*pūrvavat*) is when one perceives the future existence of an effect based on the appearance of its cause; for example, when clouds arise, one perceives the future existence of rain.
He said: This is not a valid example because it is inconclusive.
For the rising of clouds is not necessarily the cause of rain, since there is the possibility of obstruction by other factors such as wind.
It is said: If, then, one perceives the causal power—supported by other auxiliary powers and unopposed—and thereby attains the manifestation of the effect;
for example, when one perceives the clay being presided over by an active potter equipped with tools such as an iron rod, then [the manifestation occurs], just as before.
The *śeṣavat* [inference] is when one perceives the existence of a cause after seeing the completion of its effect;
for example, perceiving sexual union upon seeing a young child.
He said: "This is not a valid example."
Because it is not the case that the emergence of living beings is preceded solely by the union of a couple;
for we hear of the particular mode of birth of Droṇa and others as being otherwise.
It is said: "In that case, when one perceives the rising of the moon or the sun after seeing the sky colored by its radiance, then it is an inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*).
He replies: "Even this is not a valid example, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntāt*)."
For the reddening of the light in the sky is not caused solely by the moon and sun;
rather, it is also caused by such things as a conflagration on the horizon.
It is said: when one perceives rain after seeing the swelling of a river, that is an inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*).
This too is not a valid example, because it is inconclusive. For the cause of a river's swelling is manifold, such as the melting of snow, the breaking of a dam, or the sporting of elephants.
Therefore, this is incorrect.
It is replied: when one perceives a lotus leaf and infers the lotus root, or perceives a sprout and infers the seed, then it is an inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*).
Alternatively, let the previous example stand.
As for what was said—that [the reason] is inconclusive—we reply: because of the efficacy of the *vīta* and *avīta* [reasons].
We shall explain that the intended object is established by means of the *vīta* and *avīta*, which serve as the reasons.
And the *avīta* syllogism functions by way of the exclusion of other related properties (*prasaṅgidharmāntara*).

In that regard, when there is a negation of the related properties—such as the melting of snow and so forth—by means of place, time, and indicative marks (*liṅga*), then comprehension occurs free from doubt.
First, regarding place: for example, "In the Deccan, the possibility of snow melting does not exist."

Regarding time, it is as in the rainy season. Regarding indicative signs (*liṅga*) as well, because there is a non-perception of things such as mung beans, *gavedhukā* grass, *śyāmāka* millet, wooden sticks, threads, and dung, whereas there is a perception of heat, turbidity, and so forth, therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), water is indeed pure.
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness.
By establishing it in this way, even the previous examples become logically consistent,
by virtue of the power of the investigation into place and so forth.

The *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is that wherein, having perceived the non-deviation between two things in one instance, one realizes the non-deviation between members of those same classes in another place or at another time.
For example, having seen the connection between smoke and fire in one case, one realizes the existence of another fire through another smoke elsewhere.
An opponent says: "This is not a valid example."
Because it would lead to the consequence of there being no distinction.
For in every inference, having observed the non-deviation between two things in one instance, one understands the non-deviation between other things of that same class in another instance.

For example, having observed the production of a jar from a lump of clay possessing the necessary means in one case, one understands the production of another jar from another lump of clay possessing those same means in another case.
Likewise, when rain is perceived at one place due to the swelling of a river, and another rain is inferred from a different river swelling elsewhere;
and this being so, there would follow the consequence that the three types of inference are indistinguishable.

It is replied: when, upon perceiving a specific quality in one of several co-existent things, the possession of that same quality by the remaining ones is inferred, then it is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).

For example, having observed the ripening of one fruit on a tree, the ripening of the remaining fruits on other trees is inferred. He said: "This too is not a valid illustration, because it involves multiple threads [of causal continuity]."
For it is not the case that the maturation of all fruits occurs at the same time,
because they are accomplished at earlier and later times and because their causes differ.

It is said: In that case, when one has tasted a single drop of water from the ocean and infers the saltiness of the remainder, or when one perceives a single grain of rice in a cooking pot and infers the cooking of the rest, that is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation). [The opponent] says: This is not a valid example.
Because it does not encompass everything.
This teacher will state later on: "But from what is perceived through general observation, the cognition of supersensible things arises through inference" (ISk 6).

When the means of valid cognition is conceived in this manner, there would be the comprehension of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*), because the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is observed in both causes and effects, as well as in their aggregates.
It does not belong to a person, because objects of that same class are not perceived.

It is said in reply: when, having observed the non-deviation of one property from another property in some instance, there arises—upon the perception of that single property—the cognition of another property which belongs to a different class and has been absolutely unperceived, then...
This is inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

For example: having observed that Devadatta reaches another location by means of movement, one infers that the movement of the celestial bodies—which are never directly perceived—also involves reaching another location.
Likewise, having observed that palaces and such things possess length preceded by growth, one infers growth in medicinal herbs and trees upon seeing their length.
He said: "This too is not a valid example, because it is no different from the previous one.
You have previously conceded that the apprehension of a cause from its effect is 'the remainder' (śeṣavat)."
And here too, there is the apprehension of the cause characterized by motion from the effect characterized by reaching another location.
Therefore, it follows that there is no distinction between the *śeṣavat* and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* types of inference.
It is replied: No, because of the lack of necessity.
For our intention is this: that inference by which a cause is necessarily understood through its effect is called *śeṣavat*.
But such [necessity] does not exist in the case of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
Why? Because it proceeds from the generality of being a composite (*saṃghātatva*).
A proof for the commonality of being for the sake of another is also observed;
as it has been said: "But because they are non-deviant, the particulars, when cognized, are the means of communication.
This is also observed in the case of the commonalities of the probandum and the probans.
For example, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced.
In that case, for one who asserts a restrictive rule (*niyamavādin*), there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
By this, fallacious proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*)—namely, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—are refuted.
For it has been explained that inference is non-conclusive because it is caused by doubt, error, and ignorance.
He asks: "What is the definition of authoritative testimony (āptavacana)?
It is said:
But authoritative scripture is the word of a reliable person.
"Reliable" (āpta) refers to one who is free from passion and the like, whose speech is for the sake of others and is not based on any perceptible motive.
"Hearing" (śravaṇa) is "scripture" (śruti). That which is both reliable and scripture is "reliable scripture" (āpta-śruti).
Alternatively, an "āpta" is one who possesses what is authoritative (*āpta*);
the suffix *-a* here has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*),
just as in the case of "tunda" (one who has a belly) or "ghaṭa" (one who has a pot).
"Āptaśruti" means "hearing from authorities" (āptebhyaḥ śrutiḥ). The form "āptaśrutiścāptaśrutiḥ" is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) based on the rule for identical forms (*sarūpāṇām*).
Therein, by the first [statement], "the acquisition of authoritative scripture," he establishes that the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is not preceded by human intellect;
being independent and proceeding for the sake of human liberation, it is undoubtedly a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By the second [statement], it is established that the words of Manu and others regarding the *smṛtis*, as well as the Vedāṅgas, logic (*tarka*), epics (*itihāsa*), and Purāṇas, and the speech of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and those devoted to various arts who possess uncorrupted minds—all that is a means of valid cognition.
It is so; the word "tu" (but/however) serves to emphasize.
Only that which is the speech of a trustworthy person (āptavacana) is [authoritative], not mere sound (śabdamātra).

This being the case, that which was stated by the proponents of other systems—that words such as "śiṃśapā" are included within inference because they possess the three characteristics (trilakṣaṇatva) of a logical mark—is refuted without effort. Thus, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) have been explained.
By means of these, the objects of cognition (prameyas) previously mentioned should be understood according to their respective natures. // 5 //
Kārikās 6–7:
It is said: Let it be granted, for now, that objects in close proximity to the senses are apprehended through perception;
and that even those not in close proximity are apprehended through inference when their relationship [to a mark] has been perceived.

As for those entities that transcend the senses, because they possess characteristics distinct from both [the perceptible and the inferable], there is no apprehension of them through either perception or inference.
If their existence were established solely by scripture (*āgama*), it would follow that all doctrines would be proven;
therefore, it follows that they are absolutely ungraspable.
In this regard, the claim that all objects of knowledge are understood through these many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is incorrect.
It is replied: This would be so if inference were studied as having only a single form;
what then? It is threefold.

In that regard, since *satya* (perception) and *śeṣavat* (inference based on remainder) have as their result objects whose relations were previously experienced—as stated before—it is not accepted that the comprehension of all things arises from those two. Rather, the establishment of supersensible things occurs through inference based on what is perceived in a general sense (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
However, it should be understood that the comprehension of supersensuous objects (*atīndriya-artha*) is achieved through this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

How so? Just as, having observed the coexistence of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) in a jar, one infers impermanence in another case, such as sound, upon seeing its state of being produced;
likewise, since pieces of wood and the like are established as belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatā*) by virtue of being preceded by sandalwood and so forth, [the supersensuous is known].
Since the cause-and-effect relationship is established as being preceded by that [Puruṣa] due to its belonging to the same genus as pleasure and so forth,
and since beds and the like— being composite entities— are established as existing for the sake of another,
it follows that the cause-and-effect itself, being a composite entity, is established as existing for the sake of another; thus, everything desired is comprehended.

However, for those who hold that *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference is exactly like *śeṣavat*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-apprehension of the *puruṣa* (Spirit), because that [inference] has as its cause the apprehension of [an object] by means of its effect.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the term "effect" (*kārya*) is used figuratively (*upacāra*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the thought might be: although there is an absence of effects belonging to the *puruṣa*, nevertheless, at the present time, the apprehension of the *puruṣa*, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), and ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*)—along with the specific elements (*viśeṣas*)—is said to occur through their own respective functions (*vṛtti*).
Why? Because it is claimed that their power of functioning (*vṛtti-śakti*), treated as an effect, joins itself with its own self;
and that is incorrect. Why? Because another reason has been stated.
If the apprehension of the Puruṣa through its manifestation (*vṛtti*) were easily established, the Teacher would not have stated "being for the sake of another" as a reason for its being composite.
And since that [manifestation] is itself devoid of manifestation, one must necessarily admit that there is a distinct object for both the *śeṣavat* and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* types of inference.
Therefore, it is established that the comprehension of supersensuous objects proceeds from *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
Its twofold nature arises solely from the difference in its application:
it is *vīta* and *avīta*.
They state the definition of these two as follows:

When a reason is employed in its own form for the establishment of the probandum, it is *vīta*; the other is *pariśeṣita* (the remainder), because it implies the exclusion of other [possible] objects.
Indeed, the nature of a probans (*sādhana*) is twofold: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).

Among these, the common is the objective essence (*arthātmā*) which coexists with the probandum (*sādhya*) and is properly relied upon as the cause for its cognition. The uncommon, however, consists of such factors as magnitude (*parimāṇa*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and being for the sake of another through aggregation (*saṃghātaparārthatva*).

In that regard, when a reason is presented for the establishment of a probandum by means of its own essential nature in accordance with the actual state of affairs, having regard for the opposing position, it is then called *vīta*.

However, when it is presented for the establishment of a probandum through elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*), having performed the exclusion or rejection (*kṣepa-apoha*) of other possible factors related to the subject that are distinct from the probandum itself, it is then called *avīta*. For example: "If the origin of the world is not possible from atoms, the primal spirit (*puruṣa*), God (*īśvara*), karma, fate (*daiva*), time, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), or chance (*yadṛcchā*), then by elimination, it must be from primordial matter (*pradhāna*). This, then, is again called *avīta*.
It occurs as follows:

when the speaker, having removed the cause [of doubt], presents a statement to the listener by means of another cognition that imparts a form similar to the cognition [he himself] has attended to in his own mind—
for it is impossible to transfer an object into another's intellect without a sentence— then [the meaning is established].
Then the statement consisting of members (*avayava-vākya*) is postulated.

Furthermore, its members—characterized as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), feasibility (*śakyaprāpti*), and the removal of doubt (*saṃśayavyudāsa*)—are the auxiliary elements of exposition (*vyākhyāṅga*).

The proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), application (*upasaṃhāra*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) are the auxiliary elements for the instruction of others (*parapratipādanāṅga*).
In this context, *jijñāsā* is the desire to know. Someone, having approached another, says: "I wish to know about the person;
does it exist or not?"
Being questioned as to "whence the doubt," he replies: "Because that which is not perceived is seen in two ways.
Here, that which is not perceived is seen in two ways—as existing and as non-existing.
And that which exists is, for example, the far side of the orbs of the sun and the moon.
And things such as a rabbit's horn are non-existent;
yet this self is also not perceived.
Therefore, there is doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist.
Being asked what the purpose of this inquiry is, he explains: it is the comprehension of the true nature of the treatise, and from that, the attainment of liberation.

How so? If indeed this self exists, then through the knowledge of its non-materiality, neutrality, omnipresence, and other such qualities—which serve as the antidote to the delusion of non-self (nairātmya)—the attainment of apavarga (liberation) becomes inevitable.
As it has been said, "Liberation is attained through the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower"—thus that scripture becomes meaningful.

Now, if it is determined that [the Knower] does not exist, then by means of that inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*), one might conclude that other categories of reality likewise do not exist.

Abandoning such a vision of the Sages (*ārṣadarśana*) which is full of deception, one should instead take hold of the supramundane state through the disappearance of the view of self-grasping (*ātmagrahadṛṣṭi*).
Having attained the meditative object that is empty, characterized by the cessation of the afflictions of the three realms, one will obtain ultimate nirvāṇa;
and this matter can be ascertained because it is established through the inclusion of the three means of valid cognition.
The thesis (*pratijñā*) is the determination of the probandum after having set aside doubt;
that which is the determination of the probandum, such as "it is a person," is the thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is the statement summarizing the means of proof.
That by which something is established is the *sādhana*, namely the logical mark (*liṅga*).
A compound (*samāsa*) is a concise expression. The concise statement of the means of proof is "the concise statement of the means of proof" (*sādhanasamāsavacana*).
The mention of "proof" (sādhana) is for the purpose of excluding what merely appears to be a proof;
for those [pseudo-proofs] are not actual proofs, because they are causes of doubt and error.
The mention of the "composite" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of providing space for the other members [of the syllogism].
The mere indication of the "mark" (*liṅga*) constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
As for its elaboration, characterized by its coexistence with the probandum (*sādhyasahabhāvitva*), it is said that these are the other members.

In this context, an "example" (udāharaṇa) is an illustration or a corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta). That which demonstrates the concomitance of that probans (sādhana) with the probandum (sādhya) is the example.
For instance, it is observed that things acting in combination exist for the sake of another.
Just as in the case of beds, seats, chariots, and shelters;

however, since the negative (avīta) [reason] consists in the exclusion of other concomitant properties, it is included therein, and for that purpose an example by dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is stated.
The application (upanaya) is the subsumption of the subject and the example under a single operation.
Regarding the probandum, characterized as the eyes and so forth being for the sake of another,
and the example, such as a bed and so forth, there is an attribution of a single function.
In that case, because they are distinct entities, a single function cannot logically apply directly to both the probandum and the example.
Because that [self] cannot be demonstrated by that [body] itself, it is metaphorically attributed a single function based on the commonality of its properties, such as saying "this is like that.
Just as beds and so forth, being composite, exist solely for the sake of another, so too must the eyes and other faculties exist for the sake of another;
and that "other" is the *puruṣa*.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the repetition of the proposition (*pratijñā*) by virtue of that [reason].

Furthermore, the conclusion is that repetition which depends upon the restatement of the reason and the example. For example: "Therefore, the person exists. Thus, a collection of these members, which possesses a specific meaning through their mutual connection, is taught as a "sentence" (*vākya*).

When even a single sentence, though its own primary meaning is subordinate, is joined with another because it assists that other meaning, then even an entire treatise (*śāstra*) is determined to be a single sentence.
An objection is raised: "There is no mention of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth;
for the meaning is understood by itself even without those."
And because one demonstrates [the object] to another just as one has determined it for oneself;
for it is logical that just as the cognition of the determiner arises within oneself, so too does it arise in the other who is being informed.
Furthermore, for one who is personally apprehending the object, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and other such factors have no operative function therein.
Therefore, it is not even conceivable that their apprehension is for the sake of another;
furthermore, the statement would be purposeless because its meaning is already understood.
For when the proponent and the opponent have already reached certainty regarding their respective positions, there is no purpose in their mutual questioning based on doubt.
Furthermore, there is the statement that the purpose and the feasibility [of the inquiry] must be stated.
Because that [intention] is understood precisely from the acceptance of the means of accomplishment;
for the activity of great beings is not possible without a purpose,
nor does it occur toward an impossible object, such as leveling the Himalayas.
Therefore, that statement is purposeless.

If it is argued that "because [the result] exists when those exist," this might be so: when there is a desire to know and so forth, there is engagement toward the realization of reality; when they are absent, there is none.
Therefore, these too will be means of proof;
however, this is untenable.
Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Since activity is observed even when the self, the internal organ, the sense organs, light, and objects are present, these too would have to be considered means [to knowledge].
This is undesirable.
Therefore, the desire to know and so forth are useless.
The thesis and the other members are ill-defined.
How so? Because the determination of the probandum (sādhya) occurs even in other members [of the syllogism].

If it is said that the thesis is the determination of the probandum, then by that definition, whatever determination there is of the probans (hetu), the example (dṛṣṭānta), or anything else, would also result in being the thesis.
Because there is no distinction in the sign (nimitta).
For this word "probandum" (sādhya) functions as a general term;
it cannot be restricted to a specific instance without further effort.
Furthermore, there is the non-occurrence of the definition of a reason (*hetu*), because no proof (*sādhana*) has been taught.
For he who declares that the definition of a reason is "the statement consisting of a concise formulation of the proof" must first state what the proof is.
Then it should be stated that "the concise statement of such-and-such is the reason," but this has not been said;
therefore, this is not a valid definition.
Furthermore, the concise statement would entail the undesirable consequence of precluding a detailed exposition.

For if the inclusion of the compound term (*samāsagrahaṇa*) were made, then this elaborate proof— beginning with "this observed uniformity of a single genus among internal divisions consisting of cause and effect"—
would be stated as being without a logical reason (*ahetu*).
Therefore, the inclusion of the compound term is undesirable.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the logical reason (*liṅga*) is being stated— namely, that for us the logical reason is the means of proof (*sādhana*),
and its indication has been made here— then [we respond as follows].
"Therefore, this undesirable [consequence] is superimposed due to the dullness of your own intellect,
and not due to our negligence"—
this too is incorrect.
Why? Because that [reason], though divided into two types, functions as a means of proof in five ways.
For that logical mark (liṅga) is intended to be both positive (vīta) and negative (avīta);
thus it is divided into two.

In that case as well, since the *vīta* has five divisions, it is impossible to state that a single member extracted from that aggregate constitutes the probans (*liṅga*). Furthermore, there is an incompatibility with the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because it would lead to an undesirable consequence regarding the definition of the meaning of words.
Regarding the statement "that illustration is the example" (*dṛṣṭānta*):
here, would the word by which the probandum and the probans are illustrated be the example,
or would it be the object in which they are illustrated?
What follows from this? If, first of all, the word [“as”] is not included, then the definition of the application (upanaya) is contradicted.
Why? Because it is not logical for there to be a single function such that “the probandum is exactly as it is stated.”

Furthermore, if the meaning [of the probans] is what is being grasped, then because the denotable object is not a constituent part of the sentence, there is a contradiction with the [required] five-membered structure.

Moreover, there would be no distinction between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*), since they would merely express the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*).

For it is precisely the status of being a means of proof—characterized by the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum—that is communicated through the example and the application.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the meaning of the conclusion (*nigamana*) to be a separate member [of the syllogism] from the proposition (*pratijñā*). It is argued: "Since they become members by means of one's own certainty, there is no mention of curiosity (*jijñāsā*) and so forth for the sake of informing another. To this we reply: No, because it has already been stated.
This was stated previously: curiosity and the rest are members of the exposition (*vyākhyā*).
The exposition of the scriptures is undertaken by the wise for the purpose of benefiting everyone;
it is not for their own sake, nor for the sake of a sense of self-importance.
Since this is the case, there is no pointlessness in these [expositions] with respect to those who are to be instructed.

Now, this is undesirable: it contradicts the statement that "the determination of the wise, which is the discourse of the treatise, is for the sake of favoring those whose intellects are doubtful, perverted, or untrained.
Furthermore, because no such restriction is accepted;
for we do not claim that their expression is mandatory.
Rather, when the opponent questions—"What do you wish to know?"—one must necessarily state "the word.
[The opponent asks: "By what property? Is it eternal or non-eternal?"
Whence arises this doubt? From the fact of having form (*mūrtatva*).
These [objections] need not be addressed to one who does not raise such inquiries.

If it is argued that because there is futility in some cases, it would follow [as a fault] everywhere, we say no; for that same consequence would apply to the other [members of the syllogism] as well.
In that case, since there are instances where even the thesis and other members are not explicitly stated, it would follow that they too need not be mentioned in all cases.

And thus, as you yourself have stated: "For someone, however, something may already be well-known; therefore, the statement of only one [of the two parties] also constitutes a proof (*sādhana*), because both meanings are understood, just as in the case of the word [which conveys both]. Consequently, there would be no mention of either [the thesis or the reason].
As for what was said—that there is no statement of doubt because [the matter] is certain—that is incorrect.
Why? Because it has already been stated:
that such a statement occurs when there is an inquiry.
By this, the [necessity of] purpose and feasibility have been answered.
For if someone were to inquire, "What is the purpose of this, or is this matter even feasible?", one should say this to him.
As for what was also stated—that [the relationship is established] because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists—that is not so.
Because we do not accept that [thesis].
We do not say that these [members] are constituent parts because the realization of reality exists when there is inquiry and so forth;
rather, they are the means of proof (*sādhana*) for that person with respect to whom they function as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) in the process of comprehension.

As for what was said—that because the thesis (pratijñā) is admitted as expressing the probandum (sādhya), the same consequence would apply to the reason (hetu) and the example (dṛṣṭānta) as well—this is incorrect. Why? Because [the designation "probandum"] is understood only when there exists a desire to know (jijñāsā) and so forth.

Although this word *sādhya* expresses another object in a general sense because it is already established, nevertheless, for one toward whom there exist desire to know, doubt, purpose, and feasibility, it serves to eliminate that doubt.
The determination of the probandum is the thesis (*pratijñā*); it is incorrect to say that this [determination] does not exist in the case of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, because there is no contradiction in its presence [in those two].

But when desire to know and so forth occur with respect to the reason or the example, then the determination—such as "is sound produced or not produced? or "is cognition eternal or momentary?"—is indeed the thesis (*pratijñā*).
As for what was said—that because no means of proof (*sādhana*) is taught, it lacks the definition of a reason (*hetu*)—that is incorrect.
Why? Because it is well-established in common worldly usage (*lokaprasiddha*).

For example, when you state the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) as "the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*"), you do not thereby state the definition of the "probandum" (*sādhya*). Why?
Because in the world, it is established that "that which is to be proven is the probandum."
Thus, by stating the definition of the reason (*hetu*) as a summary of the means of proof (*sādhana*), we do not state the means of proof itself.

Why? Because in common worldly usage, that by which something is proven is established as the "means of proof" (*sādhana*). Alternatively, it is because we are merely pointing out inference (*anumāna*) while provisionally accepting [the conventional term].

For the *liṅga* (logical mark) is our means of proof (*sādhana*), and that has already been specified. As for what was said— that because there is a distinction between *vīta* and *avīta*, there is a fivefold nature of the means of proof— [that is not so].
To this we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because of the force of the inclusion of the term "compound" (samāsa).

For this very reason, the mention of the compound is made so that it may be understood that a "reason" (hetu) is merely the expression of the essential nature of the means of accomplishment (sādhana),
whereas the "elaboration" (prapañca) consists of the other constituent parts.
By this, the consequence of a refutation by over-extension (*vistarapratiṣedhaprasaṅga*) has been applied.
How so? Because it is not the case that this is the meaning of the word "compound" (*samāsa*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—that because of the undesirable consequence in the conceptualization of the word's meaning, the definition of an example (*dṛṣṭāntalakṣaṇa*) is untenable—[that too is refuted].
Let it be that the word (*śabda*) serves as the example for now.
As for what was said—that the definition of the application (*upanaya*) is contradicted—that is untenable.
Why? Because when [the primary connection] is impossible, the cognition of the effect arises through another related factor.
Since [the five-membered structure] is impossible in the case of the word, we shall understand its application to the meaning. Alternatively, let the meaning itself serve as the illustrative example.

As for what was said—that because the denotable object is not a constituent part of the sentence, there is a contradiction with the five-membered structure—we reply that since it is impossible in the case of the meaning, we shall understand its application to the word.

As for what was said—that because it expresses the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) are not separate members—this is not a fault. Why? Because we do not assert this. Indeed, this is not asserted by us.
Rather, the statement of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*);
the statement of the mere form of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the reason (*hetu*);
and the illustration of its coexistence with that object of cognition is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption under a single operation based on the commonality of properties between the subject to be proven (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement of the function of the entire collection for the sake of establishing the probandum.
Therefore, this [objection] is incorrect.
Furthermore,
because there is no fault in conceiving that [the sentence] as such, just as one might conceive of a single thing as having the nature of a means of proof;
for both the sentence and its meaning are primary word and meaning.
Because it is accepted that these two have an identical meaning, one establishes a single object—undivided and non-sequential—in the intellect;

then, by means of the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of capacities characterized as audibility, impermanence, being produced, knowability, and so forth, speakers describe them as distinct, having assumed the forms of the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and doubt (*saṃśaya*).
However, because they are properties of a single object, the identity of the designations for the probandum, the probans, and doubt does not follow.

Likewise, since a single means of proof (*sādhana*) would have to express the various capacities characterized by being the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and its coexistence with that [property], there would be no other members such as the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth.

In that case, what was stated—that because they express the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), the example, application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) are not separate members—is incorrect.
Therefore, it is well said that the *vīta* [inference] consists of ten members.
The teachers consider it logical that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) should occur prior to that;
for what reason?
Because there is no contradiction with the characteristic of non-cessation (*avītalakṣaṇa*).
For the definition of *avīta* is the support of the probandum by means of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*).

In that case, when the conclusion is made merely by the negation of the opponent’s position regarding the subject (*dharmin*)—the primary characteristic of which has been understood through its own nature via positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—the definition of elimination is violated.
Why? Because here, at the outset, mere negation is stated.

Therefore, just as it can be inferred that the manifest does not arise from atoms and the like due to a contradiction with the cause, so too it can be inferred that it does not arise from the *pradhāna* either due to the absence of a cause.
Thus, its exclusion is also understood through the *avīta* [reasoning].
This being the case, what could remain as a possibility?
However, when the subject (*dharmin*) is delimited by its own nature, the application [of the reason] is appropriately conceived.

If the manifest world does not arise from atoms and so forth, then by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*), it follows that the manifest arises from Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) alone; this is what is meant by "from the aforementioned [reasons] such as positive concomitance" (*anvaya*).
Therefore, it is established that prior to the use of the *vīta* argument, there is the comprehension of supersensible objects through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
He said: No, because things that are not perceived due to other causes would not be apprehended.

If it is accepted that everything imperceptible is understood through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), then it follows that even those objects which are not perceived due to other causes would likewise be apprehended by that very same means. For example:
Due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and merging with similar objects. // ISk_7 //
In that regard, first, [non-perception occurs] due to extreme distance, as in the case of a bird that has flown away; due to extreme proximity, as in the case of collyrium and the like;
and due to the impairment of the sense faculties, as in the case of sounds and so forth.
Because of the instability of chariots and the like;
because of the subtlety of atoms and the like;
and because of the obstruction by gold and the like.

[The non-perception of objects occurs] due to being overwhelmed, as in the case of planets and so forth by the light of the sun; due to the blending of similar [objects], as in the case of the lights of many lamps;
and, because of the word "and" (ca), due to the possession of sovereign power, as in the case of gods and so forth.
And it cannot be so, because the commonality of properties (dharmasāmānya) is not established.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that everything beyond the senses is graspable by inference.
It is replied: it is indeed possible to comprehend, through inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa), certain things that are not perceived due to other causes.
For example, a bird situated nearby is perceived by the eye without effort;
however, as it moves further away, it is perceived by directing the gaze, until finally it reaches a state of invisibility through a gradual process.
In that case, as the distance increases, one perceives that invisibility is increasing; subsequently, even absolute invisibility is inferred to have that [distance] as its cause.

Likewise, just as inferential cognizers— having first perceived the indistinct form of a substance situated not too near, and subsequently perceiving it with increasing degrees of clarity as they approach it from afar— infer that the non-perception of black antelope skins, collyrium, and so forth is due to extreme proximity; similarly,

having previously perceived a sound near a mountain, river, or ocean that obstructs hearing, and later failing to perceive a sound in that very same place, they infer an impairment of the sense of hearing.
Therefore, even that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is to be proven by means of authoritative scripture.
Furthermore, by the phrase "and therefore it is unestablished," he declares that the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [type of inference] has no application regarding the domain of scripture (*āgama*).
By the word "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*), he indicates the object;
by the phrase "the probandum from the scripture of a reliable person" (*āptāgamāt sādhyam*), he states the subject.

This is what is meant: therefore, even by means of that inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), that which is not established— namely, that which is perceptible yet unperceived by oneself, whose status as an object is obstructed by other causes, or that which is entirely beyond the senses, such as heaven, liberation, and the deities, being devoid of the common characteristics of *dharma*— is to be proven through the scripture of a reliable authority (*āptāgama*).
If it is argued that [scripture] lacks authority because it would entail the establishment of all doctrines, this might be so:
if scripture were indeed accepted as authoritative, then one would necessarily have to admit the authority of those who are experts in each respective treatise.

This being the case, since the activity of reasoning (*tarkavṛtti*) is diverse due to the manifold conceptual constructions arising from the authority of all these teachers, it would follow that [scripture] is erroneous because of its lack of definitive certainty.
And this being the case, there would be an obstruction to those seeking knowledge from attaining liberation.
Therefore, like a physician, your instruction of others does not please us;
yet this is improper.
Why? Because the definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) has not been determined.

We declare that the status of an authoritative person belongs to the Great Sages (*maharṣi*), such as Īśvara, who have eliminated defects such as passion, whose intellects are free from doubt, and who perceive objects beyond the senses;
it does not belong to everyone.
Furthermore, if there exists another such phenomenon, let it be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Moreover,
its validity regarding its own object is free from defect.

Furthermore, regarding whatever object belongs to a particular person, one must necessarily admit that concerning that object, his word is a means of valid cognition even without a formal proof (*sādhana*).
Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of the rules of conduct and established customs within various treatises whose purposes are unperceived (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
By this, scripture (*āgama*) is shown to be a distinct category from all inferential marks (*liṅga*).
Since reasoning is sought through extensive exposition, scripture (*āgama*) is therefore a distinct category from the mark (*liṅga*) because it depends upon reasoning.

[The opponent] says: No, because it is a cause of comprehension through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Just as a property such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), when observed in relation to an object such as impermanence and not observed in its absence, brings about certainty regarding the object of impermanence; likewise, a word is also not observed in its own referent or in anything of that same class—[and thus it too functions through concomitance].
It becomes the cause for comprehension;
therefore, this [perception] is indeed non-different from inference.
It is said in reply: "In that case, what would be the comprehension regarding the moon and other such objects, which are unique [particulars]?"
He said: Because it depends upon its constituent parts, the word "candra" (moon) indeed applies to many utterances— namely to universals, substances, qualities, and actions—
and likewise does the word "Ḍittha" and others.
Therefore, there is no difference [between these] and inference even for such types [of objects].
It is asked: "In that case, how can heaven and so forth be objects of inference?
He replies: "Because of the capacity of the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) to be non-deceptive."
Just as the speech of authoritative persons such as Hairaṇyaka and others is non-deviant, so too are the great ṛṣis, including Īśvara, authoritative.
Therefore, their speech is also non-deviant; thus, it is possible here as well to conceive of it as having a general object.
In this way, scripture is indeed inference.

It is said: regarding the claim that "word is inference because it is a cause of cognition through positive and negative concomitance," we reply: no, because this is not our position. For we do not assert that things such as trees, which follow conventional usage, possess the nature of scripture (*āgama*).
Rather, it concerns [objects] such as heaven, which are absolutely beyond the senses.
Therefore, since this was not asserted, this is not a valid objection. Or, even granting it for the sake of argument, it is because [the cognition] depends upon the speaker.
Alternatively, even granting that all words are scripture, we maintain that inference is a distinct means of knowledge from them.
For instance, the logical mark "because it is produced," when employed even by Caṇḍālas or Kāpālikas, produces certainty by depending on concomitance;
it does not depend on the particularity of the speaker.
But sound depends upon a particular speaker;
therefore, it is not a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, it is because of the contrary.
For a gender-sign does not change in another region,
whereas a change is observed in the case of words;
for that very same word [is used differently] in another region.
If it is argued that [the word] does not convey its own meaning at another time but rather praises another meaning because no connection [between them] is perceived— this might be so,
[but only] if another connection were unobserved in another place.
Therefore, the claim that there is a reversal of word and meaning is untenable,
because of the dissimilarity of their logical marks (*liṅga*).
For when the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), such as a cow and so forth, which is intended to be perceived directly, is apprehended, its mark is not [thereby] apprehended;
whereas the word, while being apprehended, is not apprehended in relation to the cow and so forth.
Therefore, it is not a mark.
Furthermore:
because of the restriction of location.
For no restriction of location is observed for a logical mark (liṅga).
However, there is a restriction of words to specific regions;
for example, the root *śavati*, meaning "to go," is used only among the Kambojas,
while *raṃhati* is used among the Easterners.
Likewise, the root *dā* has the meaning of cutting;
the word *dātra* [meaning "sickle"] is used among the people of the North, but not elsewhere.
Therefore, the word is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, because it is employed according to its suitability,
the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is intrinsic.
For smoke cannot be extracted from fire and placed in water, wind, space, or anywhere else.
A word, however, is applied wherever the speaker’s intention lies;
for example, words such as *vṛddhi* and so forth, which are well-known in their own senses of increase and the like, are applied to sugarcane and other things [by the speaker's will].
Therefore, they are not an inferential mark (*liṅga*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because a word possesses the capacity to denote everything, the following might be thought: a word has the capacity to denote all things, and an object has the capacity to be denoted by all things; through human activity, the restriction of these capacities is effected.
How so? "Let this very word be the signifier of this specific object."
Let this very same meaning be expressed by this word;
the human function extends only this far.
Therefore, the natural relationship of the word is manifested through its dependence upon the speaker.
This too is untenable.
Why? Because it would entail that the word is even more distinct from inference than its object.
Even by assuming this much, it follows that the word is even more distinct from inference than its meaning.

Why? Because it is not the case that, just as a word—which, though applicable to all objects, has its power delimited with respect to a speaker—has its application restricted from other meanings by the speaker; likewise, a logical mark (*liṅga*), which is applicable to all objects, is not restricted from other meanings by the speaker. And just as a single word, when uttered in the world, is capable of denoting every object depending on the speaker’s intention, so too a single logical mark might be capable of conveying every object through some particular reasoning.
Therefore, a word is not a logical mark.
Furthermore, as for this statement that a generality (sāmānya) dependent upon the parts of the moon and so forth is accepted, that is incorrect,
because it is not common [to all].
In the absence of inference, the claim that "an object is established by verbal convention" is a contradiction.
Furthermore,
because [the object] is to be proven through genus and so forth, there is a mutual difference between genus, quality, substance, and action.
Furthermore, it is the aggregate that is the object to be proven;
therefore, it is incorrect to say that these [cognitions] have a universal as their object in relation to that [probandum].

As for what was also stated—that words such as "heaven" and so forth are forms of inference because they share the common property of being non-contradictory with the speech of a reliable person (āpta)—[that too is not tenable].
To this we reply: this too is untenable.
Why? Because it is an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is true that there exists this conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*) of a universal (*sāmānya*) for these [particulars].
That [cognition], however, has the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its object, not the object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
Yet, your own position is that inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object of valid cognition;
and that is refuted because universals are not applicable to things such as heaven (*svarga*), which are unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Therefore, let this suspicion—that inference itself is scripture—be abandoned.
Another, however, who maintains the non-difference between inference and scripture, says this:
words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why? Because its object is not apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For that word whose object is not apprehended through perception or inference is not a means of valid cognition;
however, the other [word] is a means of valid cognition.
For example, [the words] "a grove of ripe mangoes on the bank of a river" or "a cart of molasses overturned on the road"—
and the referents of words such as "heaven" and so forth are not perceived by any other means of valid cognition.

Therefore, just as arguments such as "the self is omnipresent because pleasure and so forth arise everywhere" are invalid against the Buddhist—due to reasons such as the unestablished nature of the subject (*dharmyasiddhi*)—so too are the words of the Veda for the most part;
however, this is not a sound position.
Why? Because it involves the unjustified repudiation of all words.

For what logic is there here that the words of those who are authoritative (pramāṇabhūta), even regarding a matter not perceived by people such as ourselves, should be contrary to reality? Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that there exists some authoritative person (āpta) and that his word concerns an unseen object;
therefore, this same consequence applies equally to you in this case as well.
Furthermore, a means of valid cognition does not require another means of valid cognition for the establishment of its own object.

In that regard, if it is maintained that the truthfulness of a verbal statement depends upon another means of valid cognition, then it follows that not only [objects such as] heaven and so forth, but the words themselves would be invalid.

Moreover, since it is accepted that inference functions as a means of knowledge independently of other means of valid cognition, it follows all the more clearly that scripture (āgama) is a distinct category from that [inference].

Therefore, it is established that such nihilistic doctrines, which contradict both reason and scripture, must be avoided from afar by those seeking the highest good. Thus it is said: "A reality not established through inference is to be proven through authoritative scripture.

In this way, the objects of cognition (prameya)—both those perceived by the senses and those not perceived due to other causes—have been explained in relation to these three types of means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
