This too is incorrect. Why? Because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).

Even if there were the existence of a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhāva*), the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and inherence (*samavāya*) would both remain to be proven, just as in the case of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) that is a distinct entity.
Therefore, this pervasion would [have to] exist;
yet since that is unestablished, this is not correct.

If it be argued: "Like the shuttle and so forth," meaning that just as the shuttle and other tools are the causes of the whole (avayavin) even though they are distinct entities, so too are the threads.
This is untenable.
Why? Because it is not accepted [as such].
Looms and so forth are the instruments (karaṇa) of the cloth.
"It is not the cause"—this is our position;
therefore, this example is incongruous.
Furthermore:
Because that would lead to the consequence of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*).
For one who asserts that "the threads are a different entity from the cloth, just like a shuttle (*vema*) and so forth," there follows the consequence of non-pervasion as in that case.
Furthermore, what else?
Because there is resistance toward that which possesses touch, action, form, and weight,
as in the case of [the resistance] of one possessing a different touch against another possessing a different touch;
for instance, as a jar [is resisted] by a stone.
Furthermore, since that cloth possesses a different tactile sensation from its threads, it is illogical for it to pervade them.
The same must be said for [its] action and other properties.
Therefore, it is correct that because distinct parts are perceived, the "whole" (avayavin) is not a separate substance.
For this reason as well, the whole is not a distinct substance:
because its subsistence either in its entirety or in part is untenable.
For when that [whole] exists in its parts, does it exist in all of them together, or in each individual part?
And what follows from this? First of all, it does not subsist in its entirety [in each part].
Why? Because if only one part were grasped, it would follow that there is no apprehension [of the whole].
It is observed that when something exists in many locations, its apprehension occurs only when its entire substratum is apprehended;
as, for example, in the case of duality and so forth.
And this being the case, it would follow that upon the apprehension of the horns and other parts, there must be an apprehension of the cow.
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of there being no parts.
For if that [whole] were to pervade its parts, what else would it pervade, since there is no other part apart from those?
And if one were to admit further parts, it would result in the consequence of an infinite regress.
Furthermore, the dilemma of whether [the whole] subsists in its entirety or in part applies equally here.
Therefore, it does not subsist in all [atoms] collectively, nor does it subsist in each one individually, because that would entail the consequence of [the whole] being manifold.
For it is observed that multiple things, such as color-form and so forth, are completed within multiple substrates.
Furthermore, there would be the abandonment of the treatise;
for one who maintains that the whole is completed in each individual part, that whole would occupy the same location as its corporeal parts.
Furthermore, that treatise which states that corporeal entities do not occupy the same location would be contradicted, and it would follow that [the whole] possesses the dimension of its parts.
Moreover, because [the qualities] such as magnitude are fully contained [within it], it would follow that it consists of only a single substance.

Consequently, there would be a loss of the treatise's definition that a substance is either composed of multiple substances or devoid of constituent substances; and by this much, its [logical] consistency would be undermined.
In every respect, there is a logical flaw.

Therefore, the composite (avayavin) is not a distinct substance. If it is argued that "distinctness [is established] because one observes the arising and destruction of one thing while another thing remains," then this might be so: while the threads exist, the cloth does not yet exist, because the other cause characterized by conjunction has not arisen.
However, it occurs at a time subsequent to the conjunction;
and while the threads themselves are still present through the completeness of their causes, [the cloth] undergoes destruction.
Furthermore, when there is the persistence of a distinct entity following disjunction, the arising and destruction of another distinct entity are observed.
For example, it is like a forest fire situated on the Himavat mountains.
Therefore, the cloth is a different entity from the threads;
this too is incorrect.
Why? Because it is yet to be proven (*sādhya*).

This must first be established: does something else arise or perish here, or rather do the application and cessation of the designation "cloth"—which depends upon a particular state of arrangement within the very threads—occur, as is the case with the terms "army" or "forest"?
Therefore, this too is not a proof for the existence of the composite as a distinct substance.

If it should be thought that [the word "other"] is justified by its occurrence in *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva* compounds—namely, that a *tatpuruṣa* compound is observed here when there is a different referent—then [we reply]: no.

For example: "the king's man" is *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, which is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; "one who has brindled cows" is *citraguḥ* or *śabalaguḥ*, which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; and "the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees" is *plakṣanyagrodhau*, which is a *dvandva* compound.
And here too, there exists a *tatpuruṣa* compound, as in "the cloth of threads" (*tantūnāṃ paṭaḥ*);
a *bahuvrīhi*, as in "having firm threads" (*dṛḍhatantuḥ*) or "having white threads" (*śuklatantuḥ*); and a *dvandva*, as in "threads and cloth" (*tantupaṭau*).
And therefore, the composite is a different entity [from its parts];
but this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is inconclusive.
For even when there is non-difference, a *tatpuruṣa* compound is observed;

for example, "an elephant of the army" (*senāgaja*) or "a tree of the forest" (*kānanavṛkṣa*). And a *bahuvrīhi* compound is also observed; for example, "an army with brave men" (*vīrapuruṣā senā*) or "an army with rutting elephants" (*mattagajā senā*).
If it were a copulative compound (*dvandva*), then the whole (*avayavin*) would indeed be a distinct entity;
however, no one ever employs such an expression as "bring the threads and the cloth" at the stage when the cloth exists.
Therefore, this is merely a product of imagination.
By this, the distinctions based on the capacity of designations are employed;
and these are also observed in cases such as an "army" when there is no actual external object [corresponding to the whole].
Therefore, the composite (avayavin) is not a distinct substance.

Since it is asserted that the composite whole (*avayavin*) is produced as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), it is incorrect to say that the effect exists [prior to its production] merely because it is a particular arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*).
Furthermore, as for the statement that the effect is non-existent because it is not perceived:
To this we reply: even this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is a cause of doubt.
And that is the non-perception of the six objects;
for this very reason, we are in doubt. But one who relies on that [non-perception] alone for the sake of certainty does not follow the path of reasoning.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that [the effect exists in the cause] because no other cause [for its non-perception] has been stated—this too is untenable.
Why? Because of a failure to understand the intended meaning.
For this censure would apply only to one who asserts that the effect exists in the cause in the same way that jujube fruits are placed in a bowl as distinct entities.

We, however, maintain that the cause itself is the effect, as multiple powers residing in a single substratum bring about the disappearance of the preceding power and the manifestation of the succeeding one upon being assisted by other auxiliary powers;
yet these two powers are not perceived simultaneously because they are mutually obstructive.
It should be viewed as being like the length and breadth of a cloth, or like the limbs of a tortoise;
just as the length and breadth of a cloth do not become objects of perception due to the obstruction of its contraction.
Or, just as a tortoise does not withdraw its limbs from existence,

so too for entities such as threads and the like, whether their states regarded as causes or effects occur sequentially or remain stable, the conceptual distinction between the apprehension and non-apprehension of those [states] is based upon that [existence].
By this, the apprehension of a "cause" is refuted.
As for what was said—that it would follow that other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be precluded—that is true.
However, as for what was said—that there is an absence of inference because action, quality, and designation are impossible—that is untenable.
Why? Because separateness (pṛthaktva) is not admitted.

For those who maintain that cause and effect are distinct, it would be logical to infer a distinctness in their actions and qualities; therefore, the objection—that because the cloth's action and qualities are perceived while the threads remain in place, there is no such inference [of a distinct entity]—would have some validity. However, for us, who assert that it is simply through the aggregation of the causes alone, or by assuming a different configuration, that there occurs an accumulation of actions and qualities constituting a specific manifestation, there is no such fault.
But the designation [of cause and effect] is a synonym for the relationship between cause and effect;
that is untenable.
Why? Because it is not invariably certain.
If it is accepted that there is a relationship of action, quality, effect, and cause among substance, quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth— and this is indeed the meaning of the term "liṅga"—
then we are not to be questioned as to why the effect is non-existent [prior to its production], since there is no such designation. What is the reason?
This follows from the context.

For it was precisely this that was under discussion: "Since there is a disagreement, we shall establish the comprehension of the effect prior to its production by means of the inferential mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, the lack of exclusivity (anaikāntikatva) is the same [in both cases].
Since you admit the existence of a substance immediately after its production, it follows that qualities originate in a substance that already possesses them.
However, according to your own tenet—that "action and quality are themselves devoid of qualities"—a substance, as soon as it is produced, remains inactive and devoid of qualities.
Yet, for such a substance, there exists no indicative mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, you assert that existence [is established] because it is apprehended through proof; if this is your claim, it is not so,
for it would entail the absurd consequence that all disputes are thereby proven.

Having proposed a thesis whose meaning is contradicted by an example, one who is refuting it must remember that [the object] is an established domain of cognition; if such a conceptualization were accepted, it would follow that all disputes would be resolved. Furthermore, this is because the same [objection] applies equally to the opposing position.
In that case, even according to our own position, the pre-existence of the effect must be accepted, because [the existence of] the Blessed Pañcaśikha and others is directly perceived.
Therefore, the effect is not non-existent simply because of the impossibility of [its prior] action, qualities, or designation.
As for what was further stated—that the effect is non-existent because the effort of the agent would otherwise be fruitless—[that too is incorrect].
To this we reply: this too is incorrect. Why?
Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced (*asadakaraṇāt*).

If there were a connection with action for that which is non-existent and established according to both parties, then it would be appropriate to say that "if the effect already exists, the effort of the agent is useless. [But since the effect is not yet existent, such a claim is untenable.]
The production of what already exists in reality is untenable;
therefore, this is incorrect.

If it is argued that there is no proof because a reason has been stated—namely, that just as honey and other such things are capable of being held [in a vessel] because they are already produced—then [the following applies]:
"The statement 'the pot is not being produced' is the reason we have put forward; you have not stated that in this way the cause of a non-existent effect is untenable.
Therefore, [your objection] is unestablished.
This too is untenable.
Why? Because of the consequence of a fault whether a relation exists or not.

For when that [action] is being performed, is it performed by the causal factors (kārakas) while a relation exists, or while it does not exist? And this relation of theirs would have to occur either at the time of their engagement [in the action], or...
Or at the time of its completion?
What follows from this? First of all, a relationship [between word and meaning] is not tenable at the time of its operation.
Why? Because it lacks substantiality (*adravyatva*).
At the time of its production, since the agent and other factors lack the designation of action or quality, your "effect" is a non-entity, comparable to a hare's horn.
And there can be no relation between such a thing and that which possesses substantial reality.
Now, if it is connected at the time of completion, then there is a contradiction with what was stated—that because [the effect] already exists, its production through action is impossible.
Alternatively, if it is thought that completion occurs even in the absence of a connection, then it follows that the operation of the causal factors (kārakas) would be futile;
furthermore, it would follow that the effect is completed even prior to the employment of the causal factors. And it has been said:
Because it is non-existent, there is no connection with the causal factors that are associated with existence;
and for one who desires the arising of that which lacks a connection, there is no established order.
Thus [it is asked]. He replies: "But surely, in the middle time (*madhyama-kāla*), the effect is produced by the agent and so forth.
[The questioner asks: "What, then, is this middle time? He replies:
"When agents have set out toward an undertaking,
but because the task has not yet been accomplished, they consider that to be the intermediate time.
When the causes have begun their operation directed toward an effect, yet the manifestation of the resulting entity has not yet occurred, that is the intermediate time.
It is said that "the effect is produced by the causal factors (kārakas) in that [locus].
To this it is replied: No, because no other state [of the effect] arises;
prior to its production, there is non-existence (asattā).
For that which has been produced, there are two states:
existence and non-existence; there is no intermediate state that would possess both existent and non-existent forms.
Therefore, this [position] is not tenable.
Furthermore:
since the previous fault has not been avoided, does one perform an action directed toward oneself with the aim of attaining personal gain?
Even in this case, this line of inquiry does not cease.
Therefore, even by expanding upon this elaborate argument, you have not avoided anything at all.

Consequently, it is correct that [an effect] which does not exist is not produced, because of the consequence of faults whether a relation exists or does not exist. However, for one for whom the effect pre-exists (satkāryavādin), there is no such fault. Why?
Because of the inclusion of the term "appropriation" (upādāna),
we explain "appropriation" as the cause, such as the threads and so forth;
for that [cause] is grasped— that is, connected— by its agents.
And because the effect is not a different entity from that [cause], there is no fault in the fact that the causal factors, being connected to the cause, are connected with the effect itself.
He says: "But surely, even for one for whom the effect exists [in the cause], that effect would be a different entity from its material cause.
Why? Because one takes up the material cause for the sake of the effect."

Whatever is produced for the sake of something else is distinct from that thing, just as a cloth is distinct from the loom and other such factors; and since threads are produced for the sake of a cloth and so forth,
therefore the cloth is also distinct from them.
By this, existence is established:
whatever is produced for a certain purpose does not exist therein [prior to its production],
just as a cloth does not exist in the shuttle and other tools.
It is said: No, because the composite whole has been refuted.
Since the composite whole as a distinct substance has already been refuted, this [argument] is therefore untenable. Furthermore, because everything would then be possible.

For one who asserts that the cloth is a distinct entity from the threads because their material cause (*upādāna*) is common—just as in the case of a jar and other objects—it would follow that, due to the commonality of being a distinct entity, the effect could arise from any cause whatsoever, just as it does from threads.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, because there is no possibility of everything arising from everything, this [argument] is incorrect.

Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of a difference in genus (*jātibheda*) and the consequence of the commencement of a distinct entity (*arthāntarārambha*), for one who asserts that "the cloth is a distinct entity from the threads due to its material cause being common [to other things]," just as the shuttle and so forth are of a different genus from the cloth, so too would the cloth be of a different genus from the threads; and just as when a cloth is already present, the shuttle and so forth produce another cloth, so too would the threads, while that cloth remains present, commence yet another cloth.
And this is not accepted.
In that case, the cloth is not a different entity from the threads simply because they are the material cause, as in the case of a chariot and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding what was said—that whatever is employed for a certain purpose does not exist therein—we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because we do not admit the relationship of container and contained.
We have stated more than once that there is no such thing as a "cloth" existing in the threads;
rather, the threads themselves are the cloth.
But that [truth] is not accepted by you because of your hatred for the true path;
furthermore,
because it is non-absolute (anekānta).
Or, having approached the matter, we say: how is it that sesame seeds are taken up for the sake of oil, yet oil exists therein;
and the grape is taken up for the sake of its juice?
And there is flavor in this [cow]:
the milker takes the cow for the sake of milk,
and there is milk in her.
Furthermore, a bundle of rice stalks is gathered for the purpose of obtaining rice, yet rice grains already exist therein; thus, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive.
He says: this is untenable because an obstruction is perceived.
An obstruction in the case of sesame seeds and the like is perceived through direct observation;
because of that [obstruction], there is no grasping of the oil and so forth.
Furthermore, the agent's activity is for the purpose of removing that [obstruction], but there is no obstruction of the effect itself.
Therefore, the example is dissimilar.
It is replied: No, because it is a different path.
"Whatever exists here is employed for that purpose"—this was previously granted by you.

Now, for one who says that there is an apprehension [of the object] even when it exists for the sake of its subsequent disappearance, there is a shift to another position, an abandonment of the previous thesis, and a failure to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
As for what was said—that there is no fault because transformation and so forth are possible—let it be so.
However, regarding what was said—that another path is impossible—we reply: this too is incorrect.
Why? Because of a failure to understand the nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
This criticism would be manifestly applicable to one who asserts that transformation is the cessation of an existing property and the arising of a non-existent one;
however, we do not establish ourselves by following such a course.
Rather, transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the manifestation of another property and the concealment of a previous one in a substrate (*dharmin*) assisted by causal factors.
Furthermore, manifestation and concealment are not [identical to] arising and cessation.

It must be investigated whether arrangement (*vyūha*), conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and accumulation (*pracaya*) are properties that do not exist [in the substrate], or whether they are non-existent in themselves.

What follows from this? If, first of all, phenomena belong to something that is non-existent, then it must be stated to what they belong. Alternatively, if they themselves are non-existent and only later come into being, that too is illogical.
Why? Because they are not different entities.
If there were the state of being a different entity, then things that were previously non-existent but later perceived would refute the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Yet, this state of being a different entity for them is not established.
Therefore, what is appropriate here?
And the refutation has already been stated regarding the dilemma of apprehension and non-apprehension.
Furthermore:

Because it would contradict the production of a distinct substance. Even granting their production for the sake of argument, we say: if the effect is held to be merely transformation (*pariṇāma*), aggregation (*vyūha*), conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), manifestation (*vyakti*), or accumulation (*pracaya*), then there is a contradiction of the statement that "substances originate another substance."
Why? Because these states are not distinct substances.
Therefore, your understanding leads only to regret, like the fault of approaching a forest fire when one is already fainting from the heat of the sun's rays.
By this, the objection regarding the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between beginning, ceasing, and arising—based on the term "birth" (janman)—is refuted.

How so? For when the causal agents, by means of their respective operations, manifest that specific configuration of the threads— which constitutes the cloth itself and stands in the place of an arrangement— then worldly usage proceeds with such expressions as "it is being made," "it arises," or "it is born."

But when the causal factors, through the manifestation of another power, bring about a state characterized by eagerness by means of another configuration, then the previously perceived configuration comes to be designated by the term "destruction.
However, in the ultimate sense, there is neither the arising nor the destruction of anything whatsoever.
Furthermore, as for that which was said—that the word "birth" (janman) expresses the commencement of the existence of an object that previously did not exist—that too is a mere assertion.
Why? Because of the dispute.

Since the dispute regarding whether birth has an existent or non-existent object persists, for one who claims that the word "birth" expresses the existence of something previously non-existent, it is equivalent to saying what has already been said [and thus redundant].

If it is argued that [the reason] is unestablished because [origination] is not observed in the case of the *puruṣa* and so forth, then this might be so; for if the meaning of "is made," "arises," or "is born" is conceived as having an existent (*sat*) as its object,
then that [consequence] would apply to both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* as well, since there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent (*asat*).
And for this reason, it is argued that this section concerns only a state of dispute;
however, this is incorrect.
Why? Because its object is configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
It has been stated that when an entity assumes a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is not distinct from itself, these words are applied.
And this is observed in the world; for example, one says "he makes," "he produces," or "he generates" a fist, a knot, or an earring;
and in the case of roots, water, and so forth, once their own nature has become manifest, one says "it has arisen" or "it has been born."
However, regarding things such as the horns of a hare, which are established for both parties, these words do not apply;
therefore, the undesirable consequence falls upon you alone. And it has been said:
"If non-existence is held to be the cause for the production of jars and the like..."
Since the case would be identical even for a rabbit's horn, it follows that you must admit its production as well.
Thus, the pre-existence of the effect is established.
For this reason as well, the effect exists [prior to its production]: because a capable agent produces that which is possible for him to produce.
"This belongs to him" and "he is capable of this"— this rule is observed among the virtuous,
just as, for example, the relationship between the eye and visible form.
Furthermore, there is this restriction regarding the cloth and the shuttle and other such implements;
therefore, the effect exists [in the cause].
If it should be thought that this restriction is like that of auxiliary causes—just as water is capable of producing a sprout from a seed, whereas wood or fire is not—[then we reply:]
And both [fire and water] exist within those [gems],
yet due to the separation from the seed [of their respective causes],
it is as follows: just as the sun is capable of producing fire from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) but not water from a moon-crystal (candrakānta).
Neither of these two [alternatives] exists there;
and thus, there would be a restriction of the capacity for reality and so forth to the cloth alone,
yet the existence of the cloth in the threads would not be possible.
And this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is yet to be proven.
Even sprouts and the like are effects of earth and the other elements.
Therefore, the point to be proven is this:
does the sprout exist, or does it not exist at all?
Likewise, [does] fire [exist] in the sun-gem?
It is for that very purpose that this dispute has ensued.

As for what was said—that because water is distinct [from the seed], the sprout does not exist within it—even there, it must be established that the sprout is non-different from those waters which, through entering the seed, undergo transformation into the state of a sprout.
Therefore, this argument amounts to nothing.
Furthermore: because of the established definition of form (*rūpa*).

For example, although it is a cause for the arising of consciousness, the fact that "form is not seen" does not mean that form, by virtue of its similarity [to what is not seen], becomes non-form (*arūpa*) now.
In this way, because they are the causes of the cloth, the shuttle and other such tools are not the cloth; yet for that very reason, the threads are also not non-cloth.
Therefore, it is logical that the effect exists [in the cause], because that which is capable produces what is possible;
and because the effect exists as the nature of the cause, the effect is existent.
In this case, where there is no effect, the state of being a cause does not exist, as for example in the case of a barren woman.
But here, the state of being a cause exists between the threads and the cloth; therefore, the effect pre-exists.

If it is argued that "the notion of a cause [arises] elsewhere because one observes the production of an effect from another cause," and if the thought were that "having previously perceived the production of a different, non-existent effect from a different cause, one subsequently forms the notion of causality regarding that other cause"—this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is not accepted.
The very production of a non-existent effect is not established, because it is unestablished in the case of things such as a rabbit’s horn;
how, then, could there be a cognition of its cause or its form?
If it is argued that this is so "because of the existence of the cause"—this might be the case.
Even though there is no difference in their non-existence, the cloth has causes characterized as inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental;
therefore, it is called "cloth," but not so the horn of a hare.
And this is incorrect. Why? Because there is no reason (*hetu*).
For even though there is no difference in their non-existence, the reason has not been stated for why the cloth has a cause while the rabbit's horn does not.
If it is argued that this is like the case of a person, [we reply: it might be so;

just as when existence is equal, there is a cause for a cloth but not for a person, so too, when non-existence is equal, there is a configuration for a cloth but not for a hare's horn—this also is incorrect.
Why? Because it has already been stated. It was previously stated that the configuration is the effect of the cloth, but the configuration is not [the effect] of the person.

If it be thought that there is a distinction based on configuration (*saṃsthāna*), such that—just as there is no distinction in their existence [between a cloth and a person] yet a cloth has configuration and not a person, so too, despite no distinction in their non-existence, a cloth is an effect and not a hare's horn—that too is incorrect. Why? Because of the relationship between the universal and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*).

For configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the grasping of particulars by a universal; however, no such conceptual differentiation exists within the capacity of consciousness. Therefore, the person (*puruṣa*) is not a configuration.

But for that which is non-existent, because it lacks self-nature (*nirātmaka*), a distinction is difficult to establish; or, if such a distinction were established, it would follow that it possesses existence (*sattva*). And it has been said:
"Because they lack self-nature, all non-existent things are indistinguishable."
If the qualifier is distinct [from the qualified], then existence must be admitted for it.
Therefore, it is logical that the effect exists because of the existence of its cause.
Thus, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) cannot withstand scrutiny according to the Vaiśeṣika school.
However, there are even more faults in the Buddhist position.
How, then, is a cloth not accepted as a distinct substance?

Because the existence of the whole is refuted by such reasoning as, "The notions of 'cloth' and so forth arise only with respect to the threads arranged in that particular way," conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also not accepted as an entity distinct from the conjuncts (*saṃyogin*).
In this regard, the following conceptualization might occur: namely, that the cloth is either the conjunction of the threads, or...
Is it conjunction that is the cause, or a different substance?
And for you, neither of these is a distinct entity from them.
Furthermore, to claim that production and destruction belong to anything at all is merely the behavior of a magician.
Even so, this presentation is most remarkable;
however, because the followers of Kaṇāda admit the production and destruction of distinct substances, their investigation does not resemble that of a true logician.
Therefore, the position of the Great Sage alone is superior.
Just as the non-existent effect is not possible, so too—by virtue of the word "and"—the existent-nonexistent effect is also not possible.
Some say that because of mutual contradiction, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
this also is untenable.
Why? Because the existence of the effect prior to its production has been ascertained through the statement of the reason [in the preceding verse]. // 9 // We shall now discuss the subject at hand.

And what is the subject under discussion? It is the Great One (mahat) and the rest; and that effect possesses both dissimilarity and similarity to its material cause (*prakṛti*), according to the statement. [The opponent] says: "The mention of similarity was made previously."
Because it is the cause for easy comprehension:
for one who has already grasped the similarity, the comprehension of the dissimilarity occurs easily; therefore, the mention of similarity must come first.

This is just as, according to other systems (tantrāntarīya), after stating the general characteristics common to substance, quality, and action—namely, that "it exists," "it is impermanent," "it possesses substance," "it is an effect," "it is a cause," and "it possesses generality and particularity"—[the specific differences are then established].
It is stated that substances originate another substance and qualities originate another quality; such distinctions are asserted. It is replied: that is untenable, because there is no distinction.

Just as for one who has already apprehended similarity, the apprehension of dissimilarity is easier, so too for one who has already apprehended dissimilarity, the apprehension of similarity is easier.
Why? Because they are mutually dependent;
for similarity is dependent upon dissimilarity.
And since dissimilarity (vairūpya) depends upon similarity (sārūpya), he says:
even so, the statement of the purpose for mentioning dissimilarity first must be given;
for when there is no distinction between two things, a restrictive reason must be stated for mentioning one of them first.

It is said: No, because dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is not an integral part of the context. Since dissimilarity is disconnected [from the main topic], the Teacher acts in this manner so that, having first stated it, he may easily state similarity (*sārūpya*), which is an integral part of the context. If it is asked how similarity is an integral part of the context, it is because the definition of the qualities (*guṇa*) is taught by means of the exposition of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).

And when that [Pradhāna] is established, non-discrimination and the other qualities are established as manifest; furthermore, because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the triadic nature (traiguṇya) and so forth are understood to exist in the Pradhāna;
and since the existence of the Pradhāna is proven by the teaching on the non-doubtful relationship between cause and effect, when that is established, the object of enjoyment [is also established].

Because the existence of the Puruṣa is established through its dependence on an enjoyer, and because the conjunction between that enjoyer and the object of enjoyment—once the enjoyer and the enjoyed have been understood—is easy to comprehend; and because the creation of the principles, the elements, and the states of existence exists for the sake of that [conjunction];
therefore, it is logical that this similarity is taught later, as it serves as a subordinate member of the present section.

"Because that is not connected, the other [is] prior. He says: "If you then consider it logical to state a dissimilarity prior [to the similarity], then it must be explained: what, moreover, is this dissimilarity?
It is replied:
The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.
In this context, "cause" (*hetu*) and "reason" (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous. That which possesses such a cause is "caused" (*hetumat*).
It is eternal and constant.
It is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Because it pervades, it is all-pervading;
it is neither non-pervasive nor pervasive.
The meaning is that it is not omnipresent (*asarvagata*). "With action" means possessing action (*sakriya*). "Many" means diverse (*aneka*).
The supported is that which is to be contained;
the mark is that which possesses its defining characteristics;
and "parts" (avayava) are so called because they are separated (avayūyante).
The meaning is that they are perceived separately. "With parts" means possessing parts; "dependent" means reliant on another.

These qualities, beginning with "having a cause" (*hetumat*) and ending with "dependent" (*paratantra*), are without exception the specific attributes of the Manifest (*vyakta*), as distinguished from Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*).
An objection is raised: the term "having a cause" is non-distinctive because it exists everywhere;
for since all things—the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Spirit—possess a cause, this [quality] should be recited as being without distinction.
It is said: No, because of the inclusion of a specific causal agent (*kāraka*).

Although the state of having a cause (*hetumattva*) is indistinguishable for the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the person (*puruṣa*), nevertheless, we shall adopt a specific causal agent as the cause.
And since that [agent] belongs only to the manifest and not to anything else, this lack of distinction will not apply.
He said: That is untenable, because no specific [reason] is provided. This term "reason" (hetu) is a general term.
Furthermore, general terms do not settle upon a specific meaning without a connection to context, purpose, or other words; therefore, a specification would have to be provided.
Yet, no such specification is provided.
Consequently, these terms remain entirely non-specific.
It is said: No, because a designation that applies to all possible cases implies excellence.
In this context, when a property applicable to all possible instances is attributed to a single object, excellence is understood from that.
For example, when it is said, "The boy is an eater," since the quality of being an eater is possible for everyone, it is understood that he is an eater in a preeminent sense.
Likewise here too, the Teacher has stated that "everything is possible" and "the manifest is caused.
From this, we shall understand its excellence.
And what is this excellence?
When both the producer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*) are possible, only the producer is to be understood;
or else, because of its connection with the word "non-eternal" (*anitya*).
Alternatively, this Teacher, having stated "that which possesses a cause" (*hetumat*), recites the word "non-eternal" (*anitya*).

Because of the connection with another word, it is understood here that the reason (hetu) which is concomitant with impermanence is what is being grasped. And what is the reason concomitant with impermanence? It is the agent (kāraka).
He said: Even so, this is untenable.
Why? Because it is possible in both cases.
For the proponents of other systems (tantrāntarīya) maintain that destruction is invariably present in both produced and manifested things, since it is observed in the case of cloth and the like.
Either a rebuttal to that must be stated, or it must not be stated that there is a fixed position regarding the specific distinction. It is said:
no, because that would entail the fallacy of an extremist doctrine.
For every proponent must necessarily admit that something is eternal;
even regarding destruction, there is no object whatsoever that is not manifested by sound and cognition.
Were it otherwise, this would be an extremist doctrine.
And that [position] is not accepted by those who employ reasoning;
for if it were so conceived, even a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) would be subject to destruction.
Therefore, it is an act of extreme audacity to assert the destruction of both that which is produced and that which is manifested.
He said: "The impossibility of impermanence follows from the acceptance of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
For just as there is no arising of what is non-existent, so too there ought not to be destruction of what is existent.

If, however, the destruction of even the existent is accepted, then the subsequent arising of principles (*tattva*) and so forth—which had been destroyed at the time of dissolution and were thus non-existent—would refute the theory that the effect pre-exists."
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the manifest is impermanent. It is replied: No, because we assert the disappearance of manifestation; for we always declare that what exists is indestructible.
We shall refute the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*).

Rather, what is intended by the term "destruction" is this: when causes undergo a particular configuration through their mutual conjunction, that [configuration] becomes concealed due to the manifestation of another opposing power.
Thus, the followers of Vārṣagaṇya recite: "This very triple world departs from manifestation..."
"Even when separated from its manifest state (*sattva*), it does not cease to exist, because destruction is denied.
Furthermore, its subtlety arises from its non-conjunction [with the senses], and from that subtlety there is non-perception; therefore, destruction is the departure from manifestation.

That [destruction] is of two kinds: the persistence of the principles (*tattva*) for some period of time until the end of the cosmic cycle (*pralaya*), and for others [the duration] until the end of creation (*sarga*)."
He said: "This is incorrect. Why? Because it contradicts [our position].
The followers of the son of Śākya have maintained that everything—excluding space and cessation—is momentary and cognizable by the intellect."
Their refutation must be stated, or it must be asked whether the impermanent is of two kinds.
It is replied: No, because no reason (hetu) is accepted.
Regarding the claim that "the three worlds perish at every moment," even those who are learned do not perceive any logical mark (liṅga) for this.
Therefore, this does not remain in our minds.
He says: because destruction is observed at the end;
for here, that which undergoes destruction at its end is seen to be momentary.
For example, like the flame of a lamp, cognition, and sound;
since conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) undergo destruction at their end, they are said to be momentary (kṣaṇika).
That [argument] is untenable.
Because it is that which is yet to be proven;
whereas here, extension occurs by means of what is already established,
as for example, [the knowledge] of a gavaya by means of a cow.
But the momentariness of the lamp-flame, cognition, and sound is not established;
therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
He says: This is not unestablished.
Why? Because no increase is observed.
For if another flame were to arise within the interval between fuel-pieces while the preceding flame has not perished, there would indeed be an increase; however, no such increase is seen.
Therefore, the flame of a lamp is not stable;
furthermore, because it lacks a basis:
since the flame arises depending on a basis, it ceases at the very moment it is arising, and thus it is not logical for it to persist without a basis.
For it would follow that [the flame] would persist even when its fuel has been consumed;
furthermore, it would follow that the light would be divided by the falling of an obstruction upon it.
For one who maintains that flames persist, the light would be split in two—like a thread—by the impact of an obstruction from above.
And this is undesirable;
therefore, there is no persistence of flames in a lamp.
By this, sound as well is refuted.

How so? If even that [sound] were not subject to destruction, there would be an increase [in its magnitude] due to the striking of swift winds and torrents of water, because new sounds would manifest at every moment while the preceding sounds would perish;
yet such an increase is never observed.
Furthermore, because it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For it is established by direct perception that sound produced by the striking of a hand does not exist after its initial arising.
If it is argued that this is merely "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*), [we reply: no.
Because no such restriction is observed.
A restriction regarding the causes of words is seen in the case of those words that are distinguished by differences in their referents and speakers;
however, this is not the case for words perceived by the same sense organ.
Furthermore, because it is heard separately:
sound is heard at a location distinct from the cause of its manifestation;
and this is not observed in the case of manifested objects such as jars and the like.
The causes for the destruction of momentary cognitions have already been stated.

Regarding that which was said—that because the momentariness of lamps, flames, cognitions, sounds, and so forth is yet to be proven, conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) are not momentary—that is incorrect.
It is replied: as for what was said regarding "the non-perception of increase,"...
To this we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because of the apprehension of a distinction.
This temporal designation "momentary" (kṣaṇika) is understood to refer to a specific measure of time that has been previously stated.
Furthermore, due to the absence of growth and other such factors, one sometimes perceives mere destruction;

however, that destruction occurs for flames that persist for only a single moment, and not for two moments—this [claim] is without proof and is merely a dogmatic assertion. Who who has received training would venture to accept it?
As for what was said—that there would be the consequence of a division in the light due to the impact of an obstruction—[that too is untenable].
This too is untenable. Why? Because it is inadmissible in either case.
First of all, is that which is observed to undergo division non-momentary, or is that which is not so observed momentary?
What follows from this? If it is first accepted that whatever undergoes bifurcation is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), then it would follow that the thread (*tantu*) is non-momentary.

Alternatively, if the view is held that whatever is not seen to undergo bifurcation is momentary, what is the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*) for this? Why? Because a discourse (*vāda*) cannot stand without an illustrative example.
By this, the increase of sound is refuted.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that sound produced by the striking of the hand does not persist—
therein you yourself have stated that it is because [the sound] is manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
As for the claim that sound is not manifested because of the observation of a fixed rule (*niyama*), that is incorrect, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For example, white and black are invariably conveyed by the words "white" and "black," yet they are not unmanifested by those words.
In this way, there would also be a restriction regarding the speaker of the word,
and it could not be non-manifested (*avyaṅgya*).
As for what was also stated— that because a spatial separation between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is untenable, the word is not manifested— [that too is incorrect].
That too is incorrect.
Why? Because it is established in the same way as the eye.
For example, even though there is a difference in location between the eye and visible form, they stand in the relationship of the manifestor and the manifested.
The same would apply to sound as well;
therefore, sound too is not momentary.
As for cognition, however, its own specific function alone is the reason for its momentariness, which we shall explain under the section on causes (*kāraṇa*).

Regarding that which was stated earlier—that because their destruction is seen at the end, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary, like the flame of a lamp, a cognition, or a sound—that is incorrect.
He says: "In that case, the momentariness of lamps and other entities follows from this. Why? Because there is no cause for their non-abiding."

If it is admitted that an object is destroyed, then surely it follows that there is no obstacle to its destruction as soon as it has arisen; thus, the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of all entities would result.
To this it is replied: No, because of the occurrence of causes.
For the arising and the persistence of all beings occur by virtue of their formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
These [conditions] are sufficient for their persistence;

however, since there is perishability, when the causal efficiency (*saṃskāra*) is exhausted, there is the cessation of persistence. Therefore, entities remain for some time, and yet there is no consequence of eternal immutability (*kauṭasthya*).
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of the destruction of the continuum (*santati*).
If it is maintained that the destroyer perishes immediately after its arising, then the continuum itself must also be a destroyer, since its exhaustion is observed at the end.
Its destruction would likewise follow in that very same manner;
consequently, since the three worlds would vanish as soon as they are seen—like a flash of lightning—there would be the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of saṃsāra.
Therefore, it is illogical to claim that destruction occurs at the very same time as the arising of the destroyer.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the persistence of the cause—it might be thought:
there exists a cause, namely a previously arisen entity, for the arising of the subsequent one; and that [subsequent one] is likewise [the cause] for the next.
Thus, there is no interruption of the continuum; however, due to contact with another contradictory state, there is a cessation because of its arising in that manner from both sides.
This too is incorrect.
Why? Because of the abandonment of the prior cause.

It was previously stated that that which ought to perish does not remain even for a moment beyond [its arising], even through the application of mantras and medicines; however, now it is claimed that the continuum of the perishing entity remains precisely due to the force of its causes. This is a rejection of the previous reason.
If it is argued that momentariness follows from the absence of a cause of destruction:
It might be argued that no cause for the destruction of entities is perceived;
therefore, destruction is inherent.
Consequently, why should it not occur at the very same time as their arising?
This too is incorrect. Why? Because it is not accepted.
For who would deprecate this [view]: that destruction is without cause?

What then? It has already been stated that the persistence of entities occurs by the force of their nature... [namely] through connection with another substance, whether internal or otherwise, which is not contradictory [to them].
If it is argued that this is untenable because it would entail the consequence of destruction being destroyed, then if even non-existence (*abhāva*) is postulated as having a cause;
It follows that this [destruction] is also subject to destruction, just like a jar;
and this is undesirable.
Therefore, the claim that destruction is causeless is incorrect.
Why? Because we maintain the thesis that it is the disappearance of manifestation.
This objection would indeed be true against one who holds that existence itself is subject to destruction;
however, for us, destruction is not the disappearance of existence.
But how could that which possesses a cause be contradictory [to momentariness]?
Therefore, it is not the case that the conditioned is momentary simply because of the absence of a cause for its destruction.
For this reason as well, it is not momentary.
Why? Because it would follow that there is no apprehension [of it]. In this world, the non-apprehension of what is non-existent is observed, such as, for example, a second head.
And since those jars and other objects do not exist even for a moment thereafter,
it follows that they too would never be perceived.
If it is argued that there is no fault because something similar arises— namely, that even though the jar ceases at the very moment of its arising, another [jar] of a similar kind arises— then...
Upon the cessation of that, there is the apprehension of another in such a way that there is no interruption, like the continuous connection of a flame, a river, or a stream.
This too is incorrect. Why? Because of the absence of a cause.
This might be so if there were a cause for the production of something similar at that time.
But that does not exist even prior to cessation;
therefore, this is incorrect.

If it is argued that its establishment [as the cause] follows from its being the causal state of what has already arisen, we say no; for its production is well-known to proceed from a material cause (*upādāna*).
In this world, the production of a jar from a material cause known as a lump of clay is well-established.
Furthermore, at that time, the lump of clay does not exist;
moreover, because the sequence is not perceived—
here, the production of a jar from palanquins and other materials is observed to occur in a gradual sequence.
Furthermore, there is no sequential order;
moreover, it is because of the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
In this world, the production of a jar is well-known to result from the causal complex of the potter, the staff, the wheel, the string, and the clay.
Furthermore, their occurrence therein is impossible;
moreover, because that which is produced by what is itself produced cannot be established. In this world, the production of a jar from a jar is not recognized in common experience.
Nor is there an unestablished example.

If it be argued that "it is like cognition and sound," meaning that just as cognition produces a similar subsequent cognition and sound produces another sound, so too does the production of a jar arise from a [prior] jar.
This too is incorrect.
Why? Because it is established that one cognition arises from another cognition and one word from another word; this is also well-known to us.
Therefore, this [objection] is mere idle chatter.

In this regard, that which was stated— that because of the arising of something similar, there is an uninterrupted perception of "this is that" even though entities are momentary— is incorrect. Furthermore, at the time of the production of the effect, the cause has already ceased.
When the cause does not exist, the effect is not produced, because it would follow that two pots could be perceived simultaneously.
But when the effect is produced, the cause has already ceased; thus, the manifestation would occur without a seed.
And this is undesirable.

Because it would follow that [the effect] arises constantly. If it is argued that there is no fault because the cause possesses efficacy while the effect is as yet unarisen, then there would be a purpose for the cause while the effect is unarisen; once the effect has arisen, the operation of the cause is redundant.
Furthermore, it is argued that the cause exists while the effect has not yet arisen;
therefore, manifestation is not without a seed.
This too is incorrect.
Why? Because it would follow that they could arise even in the absence [of their causes].
Come now; let them be divided into atoms, or let them be cast into fire—even then, it is possible to point out that those threads have indeed undergone destruction as established by experience.
If a cloth arises from those [threads],
then this is an error.

If it is argued that the simultaneous arising and ceasing of cause and effect is like the depression and elevation of the ends of a scale— just as when one end of a scale goes down, the other goes up— this may be so.
That simultaneous arising and perishing of cause and effect occurs in this manner is also untenable.
Why? Because the relationship of cause and effect is not observed [to exist simultaneously].
What is this clinging to foam by those sinking in the water?
For the downward displacement of that one is equal to its state [of being submerged], and it becomes the cause for the upward rise of the second;
thus, for you, the destruction of the cause and the production of the effect occur simultaneously.
Nor can a causal relationship between those two be postulated;
therefore, this is untenable.

If it should be thought: "The establishment of momentariness follows from the perception of specific differences"—that is, if there were no cessation of entities immediately upon their arising—then [the following would hold].

What is the cause of the difference between bodies and the like—produced by the exertion of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, or by form and so forth—and that of lotuses, stones, and the like—produced by cold and hot touch?
Furthermore, the perception of bells and other objects which were previously soundless as subsequently possessing sound [is explained by the presence of a cause].
Therefore, the claim that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is not refuted is incorrect.
Why? Because it has already been stated.
The answer to this has been stated: because it would follow that there is no production in the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, because no other configuration is perceived.
For we do not perceive here any other configuration that is contrary to the previously perceived configuration;

therefore, let it be understood that they are indistinguishable. Any perception of difference, however, arises from the manifestation of another capacity when there is an association with a different object.
And it has been said: "The disappearance of the manifestation is accepted because of the loss of the previous configuration;
due to the absence of that [manifestation], its distinction... [is not established].
*Note: In this manuscript, a considerable portion is left blank, and it is evident that the discussion regarding verses 11 and 12 was omitted.*
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile.
Heaviness alone is darkness (*tamas*);
the word "alone" (*eva*) is applied to each [quality].
Lightness alone is intended as goodness (*sattva*), and it is illuminating alone.
Whatever is light and illuminating in the performance of its function should be understood as having the nature of *sattva*.
In that regard, lightness (*laghutva*) is the quality that is the cause for the emergence of the effect,
while it is the cause for the clarity of the operation of the instrument.
Luminosity (*prakāśa*), however, is the illumination of other substances through the removal of darkness (*tamas*), which is characterized by shadow and is a property of earth.
Instrumentality (*karaṇa*) is also included; it consists in the respective engagement with objects of volition, self-identification, and determination.
Rajas is indeed stimulating and mobile.
Whatever support and mobility are perceived should be understood as having the nature of *rajas*.
In this context, "support" is effort (*prayatna*),
and "mobility" is action (*kriyā*).
And that [change] is of two kinds:
characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*) and characterized by motion (*praspanda*).
Among these, change characterized by transformation is the displacement of a substratum (*dharmin*), which is assisted by other auxiliary factors, from its previous state.
The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, characterized by pulsation, as well as the functions of the organs of action such as speaking;
the rising, falling, and rotating of external objects;
and *tamas*, which is heavy and solely obstructive.
Whatever heaviness and obstruction are perceived should be understood as having the nature of *tamas*.
In this context, heaviness is a property that causes the downward movement of an effect, while in the case of an instrument, it is the dullness of its function.
Obstruction, moreover, consists in the concealment of one substance by another within the effect.
Furthermore, impurity residing in the instruments (the sense organs) is the direct opposite of luminosity.

Thus, this perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of *sattva* and the other qualities as being unmixed is the basis from which their distinctness is determined. As for what was stated—that because a confusion of intrinsic natures is observed among women, Kṣatriyas, and clouds, a single quality possesses three forms—[this is not so].
Regarding the claim that either all [effects] are of all forms, or that there is the production of something possessing a different form [from its cause], we reply: no;
for since that which is subordinate [to the primary cause] assists through its own nature, the form of the principal [effect] is thereby established.

In this case, when that which has become subordinate (guṇabhūta) assists the primary factor through its own nature (bhakti), it is observed that it attains a form corresponding to that [primary factor] by virtue of such nature.
For example, milk and the like:

indeed, having acquired an activity directed toward the mouth and other [organs], it enters into a state of being a constituent part of bile in its own form; yet, through the assistance of that [bile], it becomes bitter.
Nor is it always the case that it is exactly so;

for even *sattva*, when it has become subordinate to the qualities of the female (*straiṇa*), undergoes subordination as a constituent part of its own form through the *rajas* of the rival wife, and from that, suffering arises as its consequence;
likewise, from *tamas* comes delusion (*moha*).

Thus, the *rajas* of the warrior (*kṣatra*) belongs to a being characterized by noble wifehood, while the *tamas* belongs to one characterized by banditry. Likewise, the pure *tamas* belongs to a farmer, while the *rajas* belongs to a woman whose beloved is away.
Therefore, there is no inherent transmutation of the qualities (*guṇas*).
Furthermore:
because they grasp the intrinsic nature of those things that have not become qualities;
and when these, having ceased to function as constituent parts, become neutral and possess equal formative forces, they exist by their very own nature.
Therefore, the nature of the qualities is unmixed.
He says: No, because of doubt;
for in the case of milk and so forth, the perception of another form is observed in both ways.
Because they possess that same nature and because they have been transformed by those [qualities], as well as due to their subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*).

As it was stated there: "How is this determined with absolute certainty—that the perception of other forms belongs to *sattva* and the others due to their subordinate status, and not simply because they possess that same nature?
It is replied: Because of the observation of variations in perception.

If a being were feminine by virtue of its very nature, it would be perceived as such even by a rival wife; consequently, it would follow that the husband, as well as neutral observers and those with similar mental impressions, would likewise perceive it so. But this is undesirable.
Therefore, this perception of the variation in qualities is merely figurative.
Furthermore,

at a later time, one observes the apprehension of a being characterized by feminine nature (*straiṇa*) by means of its own form, through rival wives who have ceased their resentment after perceiving that form and have attained a state of common purpose with it;
and likewise, the apprehension of Kṣatriyas by means of their noble wives residing in their own homes.
And because farmers [rejoice] at clouds when the crops have ripened,
this perception of the conceptual construction of "grasping" is therefore figurative.
Therefore, it is correct that the qualities function through mutual production.
Nor are they of a mixed nature.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that the mutual coupling [of the qualities] is untenable because *sattva* is opposed to the others— [that is not so].
To this we reply: this contradiction among the qualities does exist, yet their functioning is for the sake of the object, like that of a lamp. (ISk 13)
"What arises? is the completion of the sentence.

For example, although the wick, the flame, and the oil are mutually contradictory, when they have entered into a state of accomplishing the single effect of producing a lamp, their functions coalesce in one place; thus, their coexistence persists even for an extended period of time. It is the same with *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

If there is a contradiction, [one might object that] the functions (*vṛtti*) of those [factors] such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), which have attained the state of being means for a single effect, occur together in a unified manner in one place.

If it is thought that this is unestablished due to a lack of reasoning—asking what the reasoning is by which contradictory things come to have a single effect—it is said: because of the relationship of subordinate and predominant (*guṇapradhānabhāva*).
For a counter-entity that has become subordinate does not conflict with that which is primary, because it serves to assist it; thus, it is able to exist in association.
However, between two things of equal strength, there is indeed no connection for coexistence.
And so the venerable Vārṣagaṇya declares: "Excesses of form and excesses of function are mutually contradictory."
Universals, however, coexist with their specific excellences;
for example, water and fire in the effects of cooking and sweating,
and shadow and sunlight in the illumination of subtle forms.
Cold and heat are established as existing within living beings.
Thus, it is proven that there is a coexistence of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* despite their mutual opposition, just like a lamp [which possesses light, heat, and color].
He says: regarding what was stated—that the plurality of the *guṇas* arises from the difference in the intrinsic natures of qualities such as lightness (*laghu*)—we reply:
If the qualities, such as existence (*sattva*) and the rest, are distinct from one another due to differences in their characteristics,
then they would each possess six qualities, because they are endowed with those very characteristics.

If the mutual plurality of *sattva* and the other qualities is accepted on the basis of the distinction between their characteristics—such as lightness and so forth—then there must also be a distinction between lightness (*laghutva*) and illumination (*prakāśatva*), which would result in two separate qualities.
Similarly, from support (*upastambha*) and mobility (*calatā*), and from heaviness (*gaurava*) and obstruction (*varaṇa*), there would likewise be two each; thus, six qualities would follow.
If, however, it is thought that lightness and illumination are non-different, then it follows that they should not be mentioned separately.

Or, if one does not accept a difference in apprehension despite that difference [in the substrates], then it follows that there would be no difference in the quality even when there is a difference in lightness and so forth; thus, it follows that "the quality is one.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that because of the assistance rendered figuratively by that which has become subordinate, it attains the form of the principal—if the *sattva*, while entering into a state of subordination, were to become suffering, [then...]
Because of the introduction of dissimilarity, the previous fault is not avoided.

For if *sattva* assumes the state of being a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) to *rajas* due to its assistance, it would thereby take on that [rajasic] form; thus, because of the introduction of a different form than what was previously asserted, each of the *guṇas* would result in having three forms, or else there would be the production of a form that already exists.
Therefore, since the previous fault has not been avoided, this "solution" is merely a restatement of the original thesis.

As for what was also said—that [the qualities] are perceived because they are not subordinate (*aguṇabhūta*) to their own nature—even for a seer (*ṛṣi*), there is no perception that is independent of their being constituent parts (*aṅgabhāva*).

Even for the Supreme Seer (*paramarṣi*), it is only the effect (*kārya*) of the qualities that is directly perceived; they do not exist as mere potentiality (*śaktimātra*), because such a state is imperceptible.
And in that case, it is unavoidable that they enter into a relationship of subordinate and principal;
therefore, one who does not wish for this fault must abandon the virtues.
Or rather, even if one goes very far, there is no avoidance of the fault of their commingling.

It is said in reply: As for what was stated—that because of the difference in characteristics, for one who asserts a plurality of qualities, there would follow six qualities for each [element] due to the conjunction of two characteristics—that is not so.
Why? Because the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) between two [distinct entities] is untenable.
In this world, the relationship of subordinate and principal occurs between one distinct entity and another distinct entity.
As has been explained regarding women, kṣatriyas, and clouds,
there is no mutual relationship of subordinate and primary between lightness and manifestation, support and motion, or heaviness and obstruction; therefore,
since these qualities are not distinct entities from the dharmas themselves, there is no consequence of there being six [categories].
Furthermore, because it is unestablished;
for this is not established anywhere— that as many properties as there are, so many substrata (dharmin) there are—
and there can be no linguistic convention based on what is unestablished.
Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of absolute distinctness (*pṛthaktvaikānta*).

For one who asserts plurality based on the difference of characteristics, since all objects possess both their own specific and general characteristics, each object would be distinct from itself; thus, there is the consequence of absolute distinctness.
If this is not desired, then one should not say that "the qualities are six because of the difference of their characteristics."
Furthermore, as for the claim that the previous fault is not avoided because that which is a subordinate member (aṅga) assumes the form of the principal (pradhāna), that too is incorrect.
Why? Because it is stated figuratively (bhakti).
We have repeatedly studied that this alternative apprehension of the qualities is merely figurative.
Furthermore, devotion is not the ultimate reality; thus, effort [directed toward it] is misplaced.

As for what was said—that the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, being non-substantial (*aguṇabhūta*), are not even within the range of the Sage’s perception—that is true. However, as for the statement that because the effect is an object of cognition, the relationship of subordinate and principal among the qualities depends upon the entire existent effect (*satkārya*), [that is also true].
Likewise, it is understood that women, Kṣatriyas, and clouds, being mentioned in the context (*prakṛta*), attained the status of being subordinate members (*aṅgabhāva*) [of the sacrifice].
For general terms are established in a specific sense through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Just as when it is said at mealtime, "Bring the *saindhava*," the understanding refers to salt and not to horses or other things.

Therefore, to point out faults in the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) while disregarding its specific context is like the speech of a child. Thus, the existence of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is established through the instruction on the characteristics of the qualities. // 13 // Kārikā 14: The three qualities are not perceived as distinct from one another, nor are they perceived as non-distinct; they are not perceived as separate, nor are they perceived as a single entity. He asks: "How is the group beginning with non-discrimination (aviveki) now to be understood?
It is replied:
"The group beginning with non-discrimination is established by virtue of consisting of the three guṇas."
"That which consists of the three guṇas is non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive" (ISk 11).
If it is asked how this is known,
it is because there is no absence of its opposite.
Since the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is the opposite of these qualities,
we shall demonstrate later that it does not possess the state of being an object, lack of consciousness, or the nature of productivity;
therefore, by process of elimination, there is no contradiction of these attributes in the manifest (*vyakta*).
He said: "Previously you stated that the Pradhāna is likewise [constituted].
How, then, is this now to be understood—that the Pradhāna also possesses the three qualities (guṇas) and so forth? It is replied:
Because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the unmanifest is also established.
In this world, it is observed that an effect possesses the qualities inherent in its cause, as in the case of cloth and the like.
Since the presence of the three gunas and other such qualities is perceived in the manifest (vyakta),
it can be inferred that its cause must likewise be of the same nature.

The Master provides this mere presentation of the established conclusion (siddhānta); however, we shall establish the logical reasoning (nyāya) in the passages as they have been stated. // 14 // Kārikā 15:

He said: If the properties of the effect are admitted to exist in the cause upon the perception of the effect, then there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the cause] would possess properties such as having a cause (*hetumat*), because there is no distinction. If it is accepted that a property seen in the effect exists in the cause, then since properties such as having a cause are also observed in the effect, they would necessarily follow in the *pradhāna* as well.

Alternatively, if, despite the perception of the effect being equal, properties such as having a cause are not admitted [in the cause], then other properties would likewise not have a presence in the cause.
It is said: no, because there is a cognition that sublates it due to its contradiction with its own nature.
By the mark that "the effect consists of the qualities of the cause," properties such as having a cause and so forth would also follow for the cause;
however, because those [properties] contradict the nature of cause and effect, they are known to be sublated.

How so? If, first of all, properties such as having a cause—which are observed in the manifest—are manifested in the Pradhāna, then it follows that it is merely an effect because it is produced, and not a cause.

Furthermore, because it is impermanent, it would perish of its own accord; because it lacks supporting factors, and due to its non-pervasiveness and other such qualities, it would be devoid of the power to produce infinite transformations.

Because [the Sāṃkhya] accepts [these qualities] in the *pradhāna*, such properties as "being causeless" (*ahetumat*) and so forth would also apply to the manifestation (*vyakti*); since a cause is impossible, it follows that it would not even be an effect.
However, properties such as "non-discriminative" (*aviveki*) and so forth, which exist in both [the *pradhāna* and the *vyakti*], do not contradict each other's essential nature.
Therefore, because the relationship between cause and effect is accepted, there is a refutation of [the claim that the *vyakti* is] "causeless" and so forth.
Furthermore, the existence of causes for other things is established.
As for the statement that "because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the unmanifest is also established," that is incorrect.
Why? Because the causal relationship between the manifest and the unmanifest is not established.
For this would only be the case if the causality of the manifest and the unmanifest were established; however, that is not established. Therefore, this is untenable.
If it should be thought that there is equality between both sides because no specific distinction has been stated—

just as you have said that the relationship of cause and effect between the manifest and the unmanifest is unestablished, we shall say this: the unestablishment of their relationship of cause and effect is itself unestablished.
Nor is there any distinction anywhere, for it will result in the equality of both;
and that is incorrect. Why? Because its existence is not established.
True; if no distinction were stated, there would indeed be equality between the two positions.
However, this is the distinction: the very existence of the unmanifest (avyakta) is unestablished.
Therefore, this [objection] is also untenable.
If it is argued that because an effect is preceded by a cause, and because the manifest is an effect, there is a cognition of the existence of the unmanifest—this might be so:
an effect is seen to be preceded by a cause;
since the manifest, such as a jar and so forth, is established as an effect, therefore this [manifest] must also be preceded by a cause.
And that which is its cause is the unmanifest (avyakta);
but this is untenable. Why? Because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, the spontaneous arising of an effect is observed here,
such as that of a rainbow,
and [the arising] of what is non-existent from mere illusion.
It is, for example, like an illusion, a dream, a magical display, a mirage, a firebrand-circle, or a city of the gandharvas;
and because of the existence of a cause,
as, for example, from clay and so forth [arise] jars and so forth.

If the effect is unmanifest, then there is a doubt: does its manifestation occur suddenly like a rainbow, or from what is non-existent like an illusion, or from what is existent as its cause like a jar?
It is said in reply: the manifest is not accidental nor previously non-existent. Why?
Because of the finite measure of distinct entities (*bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt*).
The arising of that which is finite is observed,
such as in the case of the root, sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, husk, chaff, awn, flower, milk, grain, and kernel; likewise,
the distinctions characterized by the limited ego-consciousness, the sense organs, the subtle elements, and the gross elements are finite.
Therefore, they are preceded by a cause;
that which is their cause is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Thus ends the third lesson and the first chapter in the *Yuktidīpikā*, a commentary on the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*.
He said: Why does the unmanifest exist?
Because even for non-existent particulars, a limited magnitude is observed.
If it be thought that this is inconclusive (anaikāntika), [the response follows].
For there is indeed a finite measure even to those distinctions that conform to illusions, dreams, and magical conjurations;
therefore, the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive.
But that is not so.
Why? Because there is no fixed rule for them that they must arise from these alone and not from others;
rather, those elements such as the Great One (mahat) and the rest, which were latent at the time of dissolution, arise again as exactly that many.
