He said: "The non-ascertainment of magnitude [is due] to the non-perception of two points of time.
True; in the present time, things such as the 'Great' (mahat) possess a determinable magnitude because they are perceived through direct perception and inference.
However, regarding the past and future times, there is no established proof."
Therefore, this is incorrect.
It is replied: No, because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is perceived for the contrary case.
While it is possible to infer that there are only this many varieties at present, there is no established proof regarding the past and future times.

Therefore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress of differences. He says: because of the infinite regress of difference and non-difference, it is impossible to determine the limit of those differences of mahat and the rest—namely, gods, humans, animals, jars, and so forth.
If it should be thought that this is incorrect because they are included within the general category (*sāmānya*), the argument might be:
there is a commonality of the great elements (*mahābhūta-sāmānya*) among bodies, and a commonality of earth (*pṛthivī-sāmānya*) among jars and so forth;
since these [bodies] are limited by that [commonality], they too are limited.
That is incorrect.
Why? Because of non-existence.
For you, a universal does not exist as a distinct entity from the substance.
It is not said [that there is a universal] based merely on similarity, because a distinct reality (tattvāntara) is untenable.
What is intended by us is that "differences are limited by a distinction in reality"; as we have stated, and as it has been said: "If such a distinct reality exists, let it be explained."

Furthermore, as for what was said—that on your position, a universal existing as a distinct entity is untenable—that is true. Nevertheless, we shall explain that even such a [universal] does not preclude conventional usage.
Therefore, it is established that because there is a limitation of differences, the Unmanifest exists.
Furthermore:
because of concomitance;
for here, the existence of that by which the various particulars are followed is observed.
For example, as clay is the material cause of jars and the like;
and this concomitance of sound and other objects with pleasure, pain, and delusion exists.
Therefore, those [qualities] which are pleasure and so forth, when their specific distinctions have subsided, constitute the unmanifest (avyakta).
Therefore, the unmanifest exists.
[The opponent] says: No, because it is unproven.
On what grounds is it to be understood that sound and the other objects are followed by pleasure and the rest? This is not established.
It is said: because it is the cause of that cognition.

Here, when sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are present, cognitions in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion arise in living beings due to their connection with specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
And whatever [object] produces a particular kind of cognition, it is endowed with that [quality].
For example, [fragrant] chips and so forth [are produced] from sandalwood and the like.
Therefore, the concomitance is not unestablished.
He replies: this concomitance is indeed unestablished.
Why? Because we observe the production of effects that are dissimilar [to their causes].
For there is no such rule that an effect must be produced as being exactly similar to its cause;
rather, it is dissimilar, as in the cases of fire and smoke, or sound and so forth.
How so? For fire does not have the nature of grass and the like, nor does smoke have the nature of fire; nor does sound have the nature of a drum or a drumstick.
Therefore, the claim that sounds and other phenomena are permeated by pleasure and the rest is merely a matter of wishful thinking.
It is said: No, because [the nature] has been specified.

We have specified from the very beginning that sound and the other objects possess the intrinsic nature of pleasure and so forth, and that it is due to their proximity that cognitions arise in the form of pleasure and so forth.
Therefore, they are not of different classes.

As for the objection raised—that because fire and other such diverse things are seen to arise, it would follow that the various modifications of the Pradhāna are not of its own class—that is incorrect.
Why? Because the intended meaning has not been understood.

We do not say that whatever is a modification of something belongs to the same genus as that thing; rather, we say that whatever belongs to a certain genus is a modification of that [genus]. Therefore, this [position] is incorrect.
Furthermore, because the example is not established:
this example—that fire and so forth do not conform to the nature of their own causes—is not established.
Why? Because they conform to [their specific] power and intensity (*balavīrya*).
For example, it is like the smoke of fire, which follows upon the oiliness of substances such as sandalwood or bamboo, and follows upon its sharpness and so forth.
Sound is a modification of the drum, but it does not remain fixed in the same manner as the form of the drum;
rather, it is manifested by the striking of the stick, just as [color is manifested] by a lamp—this is what is to be established.
Furthermore, each individual among form and the other [sensory objects] does not constitute the substantial form [of sound], because they possess the nature of a collection.
Therefore, sound is not a modification of the drum.
Consequently, the statement that "the positive concomitance (anvaya) is unestablished because the production of an effect with different characteristics is observed" is incorrect.
Therefore, it is logical that the unmanifest exists because of its pervasive presence.
Furthermore:
"And because of activity from potency."
Whatever activity whatsoever is observed here in the world, all of it proceeds from power (*śakti*).
For example, a potter has the activity of making a jar due to the presence of power characterized by the arrangement of instruments such as the rod;
and since this manifest world is an effect, its activity occurs when that [power] exists.
Therefore, that [Unmanifest] must also possess power;
that which is this power is the Unmanifest.
Consequently, the Unmanifest exists.
He said: "Prior to the activity, there is an absence of power, because no activity is perceived.
If you consider that activity is preceded by power, then it follows that as long as activity is not perceived, power does not exist."
Why? Because if the effect were absent despite the presence of power, it would follow that the power itself lacks its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, if an existing power were not to produce an effect due to some obstruction, it would result in the conclusion that this is merely a "power" in name only.
Therefore, powers arise for objects at the very same moment as their activity, through the proximity of other auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-bhāva-antara*).
And they perish at that very moment.
In this regard, what was stated previously—that because power is observed prior to manifestation, there exists a power that brings about the manifest—is incorrect.
Furthermore, it is untenable because the conceptualization of either difference or non-difference is impossible.
In this case, would power (*śakti*) be identical to the primal matter (*pradhāna*), or would it be distinct from the primal matter? What follows from this?

If, first of all, power were identical to the primal matter, then since diversity is observed in the effects, a diversity of powers must be inferred; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the multiplicity of the primal matter due to the diversity of its powers.

Alternatively, because the *pradhāna* is one, it follows that its powers (*śakti*), being non-different from it, must also be one; consequently, there would be an absence of diversity in effects. Now, if this fault is to be avoided, and the powers are admitted to be entities distinct from the *pradhāna*, then since the powers are established as diverse through their activity, it follows that the *pradhāna* is not established at all.
Furthermore,
there is the designation of its own nature (*svarūpa*):
having accepted that the Pradhāna is a distinct entity even from its mere potentiality (*śaktimātra*), one asserts that "the form of this Pradhāna in its own state is such-and-such."
And that [power] is impossible to describe;
therefore, since the conceptualization of difference or non-difference is untenable, power (śakti) is not to be conceptualized.
To this it is replied: as for what was stated previously—that there is an absence of power before activity because activity is not perceived—[that is incorrect].
To this we reply: no, because [the reason] is unestablished.
Potency is the cause and activity is the effect;
and it is not established in the world that the absence of an effect follows from the non-perception of the effect.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that upon the accomplishment of an effect, there is a loss of the power’s own nature—we reply: no, because of the example of a lamp.
Just as a lamp possesses the power to illuminate objects such as jars and so forth.
And yet, due to the obstructive power of walls and other such barriers, it is unable to illuminate jars and the like;
nor can it be said that the lamp’s power of illumination has become powerless.
In the same way, other entities as well would possess their power even prior to their actual operation.
Nor would its own nature be lost simply because its activity is not observed.

As for what was said—that the manifestation of the potencies of objects occurs at the very same time as their activity due to the proximity of other auxiliary factors—we reply: that is unproven, because [activity] depends upon potency.
In this world, every agent, depending upon a potency inherent in himself, takes up another auxiliary factor according to his own suitability.
If that [capacity] did not exist prior to the engagement [of the means], there would be the consequence of non-undertaking because the nature of the objects of the means could not be determined;
and this is undesirable.
Therefore, the capacity exists prior to the engagement.
As for what was said—that it perishes at that very moment—we say: no, because we observe the completion of the effect.
If it were the case that destruction occurs simultaneously with the activity, we say: no.
Because the completion of the effect is observed.
If destruction were to occur at the very same time as the activity, there would be no completion of the effect;
for the effect has that [activity] as its cause, and yet this completion does indeed exist.
Therefore, the destruction of the capacity does not occur at the very same time as the activity.

If it is argued that the completion of the effect occurs through the arising of a similar succession, we say no; for it is impossible for [the effect] to arise at the same time as its own destruction.

Furthermore, it might be argued that within a single capacity, having completed the portion of the task to be accomplished in a moment, that capacity perishes; then another similar capacity arises, and when that perishes, yet another arises.
In this way, the completion of the effect occurs through a continuum of capacities.
This too is incorrect. Why? Because the arising [of an effect] at the same time as destruction is impossible.

For what reason here could one determine that another effect exists in the form of a potentiality simultaneously with destruction, rather than [determining that] the very prior [effect] remains? Furthermore:

This is because the fault of immutability (*kauṭasthya*) has been avoided. Furthermore, the objection that was raised—that if entities were to persist beyond the moment [of their production], it would entail the consequence of immutability—has now been answered.
Therefore, there is no destruction of the potencies at the time of their activity.
It does not exist even after the time of activity. Why?
Because activity is observed again.
If it is argued that this is because another capacity arises even after the time of activity, we say no.
Because there is no reason for it.
For what compulsion is there here that, once that [volition] has perished, another volition becomes the cause for the subsequent activity, and not that very same one?
If you say it is because its purpose has been fulfilled, we say no, because that is not admitted.
For it is not accepted that a capacity exists solely for the purpose of a single jar;
rather, by the very same cause through which one does not perish after determining a single jar, by that same [cause] all that is to be done is accomplished.
Therefore, capacities persist throughout the three times.
Furthermore, regarding what was said—that the conceptualization of difference and non-difference is untenable—we reply: let it be that power is non-different from the Pradhāna;
yet this does not entail either its manifoldness or the oneness of the power.

Why? Because the conventional usage of number depends upon cognition, and since its cause—cognition—is absent due to the nature of the primary causal power (*pradhāna-śakti-svabhāva*), this conventional usage of number here depends upon cognition.
How so? That which produces a non-differentiated cognition is "one."
And in the state of primordial matter (pradhāna), the powers (śaktayaḥ), because their specific distinctions have subsided, produce a non-differentiated cognition.

Therefore, that [power] is one; yet at the time of its manifestation, when specific distinctions are apprehended, it attains differentiation, such as "the power of a god" or "the power of a human," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no oneness of these [powers], and thus the conceptualization of difference or non-difference is not untenable.
If it is argued that because powers are observed in the manifest, they are understood to exist in the unmanifest—this might be so;
for the operation of powers is seen in the manifest, but not in the unmanifest.
It is incorrect to claim that in some cases the manifest alone is established from this reason and not the unmanifest.
Why? Because [the unmanifest] is established through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
For just as, by observing Devadatta’s arrival at another location through his activity, one infers [his movement] even though it was entirely imperceptible;

Just as the motion of luminous bodies is inferred from their arrival at another location, so too, because activity is regulated by a capacity (*śakti*) and because activity is the manifestation of that which is unmanifest, one must necessarily admit a capacity that is entirely imperceptible; thus it is established that the unmanifest exists through its capacity for activity.
Furthermore:
"Because of the distinction between cause and effect" (*kāraṇakāryavibhāgāt*).
Cause and effect are "cause-and-effect" (*kāraṇakārye*); their distinction is the "distinction between cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇavibhāga*).
The separation (*vibhāga*) which consists of the dual classification by means of the intellect that "this is the cause" and "this is the effect" is the separation of cause and effect.
This is observed to be preceded by entities established in that state,
such as beds, seats, chariots, wheels, and so forth.

Furthermore, this distinction between cause and effect exists for the manifest; therefore, this [manifest] also must have an abiding entity as its antecedent, and that which is the abiding entity is the unmanifest.
[The opponent] says: This is incorrect because it is not perceived.
For no distinction whatsoever between cause and effect is perceived in the case of things such as beds and so forth;
therefore, this [objection] is untenable.

It is replied: since "cause" and "effect" are synonymous with "benefactor" and "beneficiary," what is intended here is the relationship of producer and produced, not merely the distinction of cause and effect.
Rather, it is a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary;
and this exists between the bedding and so forth and the manifest [consciousness].
Therefore, this is not a designation of negligence.
He asks: "What, then, is the relationship of cause and effect between one manifest and another?

It is said: First, regarding the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—their activity occurs through mutual assistance by means of their respective characteristics of illumination, motivation, and restraint; this is as stated in the sūtra: "They consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion" (YS 1.12).
This has been explained.
Likewise, sound and the other [objects] have mutual purpose and a common substratum within earth and the other [elements];
and the ear and the other [senses] have the functions of acquiring, preserving, and refining one another.

From the effect, there is for the instrument [the elements] the maintenance, injury, destruction, healing, drying, and preservation resulting from its own activity; and from the instrument [the elements], there is for earth and the others the state of being "cows" and so forth through the gathering of their functions, the supporting of the paths, and the providing of space. For gods, humans, and animals, there is mutual study, the engagement in their respective duties, and the state of being objects of sensory experience, through seasonal rites, nourishment, feeding, and social interaction. As for the castes (varṇas), there is the engagement in their own specific duties and the state of being objects of perception.
Furthermore, other worlds should be understood according to what is possible.
An objection is raised: that is untenable, because neither succession nor simultaneity is possible.
This mutual assistance among the qualities (guṇas) through their manifestation, activity, and restraint—which is indeed accepted—is it to occur successively or simultaneously?
What follows from this? First of all, it is not possible for it to occur successively.
Why? Because if one [quality] were to function independently, the same would necessarily follow for the other two as well.

If it is maintained that *sattva* first manifests by its own power alone, independent of the other qualities, and thereby assists them, then just as *sattva* does so, the other two would likewise perform their own functions independently of any assistance; thus, the concept of mutual assistance becomes purposeless.
Now, if it is thought that this fault must not occur and therefore simultaneity is resorted to, that too is untenable. Why? Because things that exist simultaneously cannot be mutually beneficial.
Like a cow's horn;
and furthermore,
because the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is untenable.
In this case, does the manifesting *sattva* reveal the luminosity of *rajas* and *tamas* as something already existing, or as something non-existent? What follows from this?
If it first reveals what is already existing, then because all [the guṇas] would possess a single nature, the consequence would be that they are all merely *guṇas*.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of independence for the other two [qualities] as well, just as for *sattva*.
Just as *sattva* possesses the power of illumination and therefore manifests independently of other qualities, so too would the other two; thus, there is no fault.
Alternatively, the power of illumination, though non-existent [in them], arises in *rajas* and *tamas* through their connection with *sattva*.
Therefore, what was stated previously—that "the potencies remain even before the activity [begins]"—is deficient;
consequently, there is a contradiction with the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda). Furthermore, this [argument] is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For it is not an absolute rule that those things which mutually assist one another must be preceded by a permanent state of being.
Indeed, [the qualities] such as *sattva* and the others mutually assist one another, yet they are not preceded by a permanent state of being.
Therefore, what was stated—that the unmanifest exists because of the distinction between cause and effect among the manifest entities—is incorrect.
It is said: as for what was stated— that there is an absence of assistance because of the impossibility of succession or simultaneity—
let there be simultaneous assistance.
As for what was said— that coexistent things cannot be mutually beneficial, like the horns of a cow— we reply: no,
because it is otherwise inexplicable.
For it is not because of their coexistence that the production of the sound "au" is impossible;
rather, it is because they lack a single common effect.
However, for those things which have a single effect, their mutual assistance in coexistence is not prohibited.
For example, earth and the other elements [function] through their powers of supporting, cohesion, maturation, and providing space.
However, even though the hooves and horns of a body exist simultaneously, there is no mutual assistance between them.
Therefore, coexistence and non-coexistence are not the causes of assistance and non-assistance.
Furthermore, because it is observed.

Indeed, it is observed that when air moves upward with great velocity, there is a simultaneous benefit to water-wheels and other such things; thus, there is no fault, and the same would apply to the qualities as well.
If it is argued that conjunction is the cause, we must ask: is "conjunction" something that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), or is it merely contact (*prāptimātra*)?
Furthermore, regarding what was said—that the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is untenable—we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because, as in the case of the lame man and the blind man, no fault arises in their mutual assistance.
For example, due to the reciprocal connection between the lame man and the blind man, there is no obstruction to the existing capacities for seeing and moving within each other's respective domains.

Furthermore, there is no manifestation of two things that do not exist, yet the accomplishment of a single effect occurs; just as the mutual assistance of earth and the other elements is manifested through their own powers and not by the power of another, so it is with the *guṇas*.
As for the argument previously stated—that [the reason] is inconclusive—that is incorrect.
Why? Because of a lack of understanding of the treatise (*śāstra*).

Here, for us, since the objects of cause and effect are not admitted [as external entities], it is simply a different state of the *guṇas*—independent of any other state—that receives the designation of "cause" and "effect.

In that regard, as for those *guṇas* which exist in the state of the *pradhāna*, because they consist of mere potentiality and possess an indefinable nature such as luminosity (*prakāśa*) and so forth, there is no assistance (*upakāra*) based upon them.
When they reach a state of imbalance, then, possessing forms such as light that are unimpeded, they provide assistance caused by that [imbalance].

Therefore, since it is accepted that manifested things (*vyakta*) receive assistance, it is not contradictory for them to be preceded by an eternally abiding entity; thus, this statement is made without having understood the treatise.

If it should be thought: "Because assistance is not accepted in the state of the *pradhāna*, the same consequence would follow for the subsequent time as well, making this reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
If, during the initial provocation of the qualities (*guṇas*), there were a falling away from the previous state solely by their own power, then it would likewise occur at a later time as well.
Or, if there is assistance even in the state of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), then the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
But that is not so.
Why? Because it is caused by its own lack of power, like fire.
For example, a subtle fire produces its own subtle light spontaneously, but for the illumination of objects such as jars, it depends upon oil, a wick, and so forth.
In the same way, the initial agitation of the guṇas occurs through their own inherent power;
however, it depends upon the mahat and the other principles by way of mutual assistance.
Therefore, it is logical that the unmanifest exists because of the distinction between cause and effect.
And what more?
Because of the non-differentiation of the manifold forms. (ISk 15)
In this world, the non-differentiation of that which possesses manifold forms is observed,
just as in the case of water and other elements;
for water, earth, and the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat) possess manifold forms.
Therefore, these too must exist in a state of non-distinction;
that which is this non-distinction is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Consequently, the Unmanifest exists.
He asks: "What, then, is this 'multiformity' (vaiśvarūpya), and who is the 'one of all forms' (viśvarūpa)? It is said in reply: by "multiformity," we mean a specific state of being.
"Non-differentiation" means the state of having subsided distinctions.
Since a particular must be preceded by a universal, what is meant by the statement "from the non-differentiation of the multiform" is this very point.
Thus, by these five *vīta* arguments, it is established that there exists an unmanifest cause of the manifest.
He said: There follows the consequence of contradiction, because you have not stated the negation of other causes.
For instance, as you have asserted: "Pradhāna exists as the cause capable of producing the world."

In this way, those belonging to other systems assert that atoms, the person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), karma, fate (daiva), inherent nature (svabhāva), time (kāla), chance (yadṛcchā), and existence (bhāva) are the causes;
and since their refutation is not stated [here],
a contradiction arises.
Is the Pradhāna alone the cause, or rather these [elements] themselves, or both?

If it is argued that this [position] is untenable because we observe the principle of "concomitance" (anvaya), it might be thought: "In earth and the other elements, the characteristics of pleasure and so forth are indeed perceived as being concomitant with the Pradhāna;
and it has already been established that whatever is pervaded by something is a modification (vikāra) of that thing."
Therefore, [the opponent claims] that the manifest is merely a modification of the Pradhāna;
but this is untenable.
Why? Because it would entail the consequence of multiple lineages of descent.

For the continuity of atoms is indeed manifestly perceived due to the existence of form and other qualities; the continuity of the person (puruṣa) is perceived because the instrument possesses consciousness;
and the continuity of the Lord (īśvara) is perceived because those endowed with specific powers are observed.
The succession of karma is established because of the observation of the diversity in the world;
the succession of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is established because entities do not deviate from it even when in contact with other substances;
and the succession of time is established because of conformity to the [succession of] ages and so forth.
A connection by chance is impossible due to the lack of any restrictive rule.
A connection through non-existence is seen in the case of cows and other such things, where they are mutually applied because they do not perceive each other's essential nature.
Furthermore, even if the manifest were preceded by another cause, the dimensions and other qualities of its potentiality would have had to be postulated beforehand.

Therefore, it is incorrect [to claim] that "the unmanifest exists as a cause because of positive concomitance and so forth. To this we reply: as for what was said—that there would be the consequence of contradiction because atoms have not been refuted—we say that this is untenable because their existence is not admitted.
For if the existence of atoms were admitted, then indeed this doubt might arise:
"Is this universe preceded by atoms, or is it preceded by *pradhāna*?
But their existence is not established with certainty.
Therefore, this is incorrect.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the existence of atoms must be postulated—just like that of *pradhāna*—because of the perception of color and other qualities in earth and the rest, and because of the observation of their persistence (*anvaya*), this too is untenable.
Why? Because that [perception] can be accounted for in another way.

For even if it were assumed that earth and the other elements are preceded by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), [the objection remains] because color and the other qualities exist [in them]; therefore, this is not tenable.

If it is argued that since pleasure and the others are accepted as qualities of the self (*ātman*), they would consequently also exist in the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), we reply: even so, just as the possession of color and the other qualities is assumed for the subtle elements, and the fact that earth and the others are preceded by them—though visible—is distinguished from the atoms by the mark (*liṅga*) of the existence of color and the rest in them; [so too should it be here].

Thus, since we accept that pleasure and the like are qualities of the self (*ātman*), it will be argued that if these are the causes of cognition, then earth and the other elements must be preceded by *pradhāna*.
But this is untenable.
Why? Because the status of pleasure and the like as qualities of the self is denied.

And regarding the phrase "from that misconception" (ISk 19), we shall establish the refutation of the view that pleasure and the like are qualities of the self; therefore, that [position] is incorrect.
He says: "But if, on the other hand, it is admitted that the atoms themselves are the tanmātras, what fault would there be in that case?"
It is said: it cannot be so.
Why?
Because we accept that the primary causes (*prakṛti*) are characterized by those [subtle] elements (*tanmātra*) which possess growth.
Why? Because it is our established tenet that the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is greater than its own effects;
and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as earth and the rest, are indeed great. Therefore, they must exist as something distinct from that [primordial nature], namely as earth.
Furthermore, atoms have delimited spatial dimensions;

therefore, their acceptance does not follow from the acceptance of the *tanmātras*. Or, even granting [the existence of the *tanmātras*], their [existence as atoms] is impossible because they would be produced (*kṛtakatvāt*).
Or, even if the existence of atoms were granted, we still maintain that the production of the world from them is impossible.
Why?
Because they are produced [effects].
For the cause of the world ought to be uncreated, yet atoms are created;
therefore, even though they exist, they are not accepted as the cause of the world. Is this not so?
It is said: because that [very thing] would necessarily follow as the cause.
For it would be more logical to postulate that which is the cause of those atoms as the cause of the world, rather than the atoms themselves, which possess a beginning.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because their "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is unestablished, the thought might be: if the fact that atoms are produced were well-established, then it would be appropriate to say, "For this reason, atoms are not the cause."
This is established by reality;
therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
It is said: because it occupies a delimited space.
In this world, whatever has a delimited location is seen to be produced,
just like a jar; and [sound] has a delimited location.
Therefore, atoms are produced.
Furthermore, because they possess form and other qualities;
for in this world, whatever possesses form and other qualities is seen to be produced.
For example, pots and atoms possessing form and so forth;
therefore, they are produced.
Furthermore, because of its association with heat:
whatever is associated with heat is produced,
just like a lamp.
And the atoms of fire possess that [quality]; therefore, they are produced. Furthermore, because they possess velocity.
In this context, whatever possesses velocity is produced;
for example, an arrow possesses velocity, and likewise the atoms of wind possess it.
Therefore, they are produced.
Furthermore, because of their association with viscidity and fluidity:
whatever in this world is associated with viscidity and fluidity is produced.
Just as water in fields and the like,
so too are the atoms of water;
therefore, they are produced.
Furthermore, because it is something to be placed:
whatever is placed upon another thing here is produced,
just as, for example, a jar.
Furthermore, atoms are supported upon the earth; therefore, they are produced.
Moreover, because they serve as the substratum for other entities.
In this context, whatever functions as the substratum for another entity is produced;
for example, a jar.
And since atoms function as the substrata for other entities such as dyads (dvyaṇuka), they are therefore produced.
Furthermore, because of the intervention of contact:
here, those two things between which another substance stands as an intervening factor for the contact are produced.
For example, two fingers;
likewise, when two atoms are situated with an interval between them, whatever acts as an obstruction to their reaching one another is produced, and therefore those two [atoms] are also produced.
Furthermore, because it initiates another substance:
in this world, whatever initiates another substance is, according to you, produced;
for example, a thread.
Furthermore, atoms are the originators of substances;
therefore, they are produced.
Moreover, because they are perceptible.
In this world, whatever is perceived is seen to be produced,
such as a jar;
and atoms are perceived by yogins.
If it is argued that they are produced because of this very fact—
that is, because atoms are directly perceived by yogins, for that very reason they are produced—
what is the reason?
"Because we observe that jars and such things, which are perceptible to us and others, are indeed produced"—this too is untenable.
Why? Because it would entail the consequence that the body is also produced.
For even the bodies of yogins are perceptible;
let them, if you wish, also be uncreated.
If this is not so, then atoms are certainly not uncreated.
If it is argued that this [fault] would apply to the *pradhāna* and so forth, we say no, because we do not accept it.
Even for the venerable Brahmin Kapila, our scripture states that both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* are imperceptible.
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

If it be thought that "it is like existence and so forth"— that is, just as existence (*sattā*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), form-ness (*rūpatva*), and the like, despite being perceptible, are indeed uncreated, so too will it be for atoms— that too is incorrect.
Why? Because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).
Just as the non-produced nature (*akṛtakatva*) of atoms, the existence of [properties] such as "being" (*sattā*) is unestablished.
Therefore, this is ungraspable, like the establishment of a human horn from a hare's horn.
If it should be thought that "because of the subtlety of atoms, there is no possibility of their being produced," [the response is:
indeed, there is no other entity more subtle than atoms that could serve as their constituent cause;
for atoms represent the ultimate limit of subtlety.
Therefore, it is argued that their being produced (kṛtakatva) is untenable;
however, this is incorrect.
Why? Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the case of things produced by baking (pākaja).
Because of their subtlety, there is the consequence that they would be uncreated.
Those atoms are indeed subtle;
however, it is observed that the Pradhāna and Puruṣa are uncreated precisely because of their extreme subtlety, provided that they possess omnipresence.
Furthermore, atoms do not pervade the universe in the same manner as the Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
therefore,
given their subtlety, their being produced is unavoidable, just like things born of maturation (pākaja).

However, for those who hold the position that the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) is what is cooked, this objection does not apply; therefore, action inhering in the atoms (*paramāṇusamavetaṃ karma*) should be cited as the example. For that [action] is subtle, supersensible, and produced; thus, it is established that atoms are produced. And because they are produced, their impermanence is inescapable. Consequently, during the intermediate dissolution (*antarālapralaya*), the periodic dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), and so forth, due to the destruction [of the atoms], there would be an absence of effects because of the absence of causes. Thus, based on the inference established in our own school, the fault of the total cessation of the world (*jagaducchitti*) would follow.
Likewise, for those who possess enjoyments, there would be the destruction of their performed karma through its non-enjoyment after it has been accumulated;
and this is undesirable. Therefore, atoms are not the cause of the world.
Furthermore, this doubt that the world might arise from a person is also untenable.
Why? Because of the refutation [in the verse]:
"And because of that misconception" (ISk 19).
We shall establish that the person (puruṣa) is not an agent.
Because there is no distinction in his sentience, this same rule regarding the negation of causality should be understood to apply to God (īśvara) as well.
An opponent says: "Indeed, God exists," so say the Pāśupatas and Vaiśeṣikas.
Why? Because a specific effect is preceded by a superior intellect (*atiśayabuddhi*).
Here, a specific effect such as a palace or a celestial mansion is observed to be preceded by a superior intellect;
and this specific effect, characterized by the arrangement of the great elements, the sense organs, and the worlds, exists [as well].
Therefore, this [creation] must also have been preceded by an intellect characterized by excellence;
that which precedes it is Īśvara. Thus, Īśvara exists.
Furthermore, because the connection between the conscious and the unconscious is produced by the conscious;
for here, the connection between the conscious and the unconscious is seen to be produced by the conscious,
just as, for example, that between a cow and a cart.
Moreover, this relationship exists between the conscious and the unconscious, between the body and the embodied;
therefore, it must also be produced by a conscious agent.
He by whom this was made is the Lord (Īśvara).
Therefore, God exists as the cause.

To this it is replied: regarding what was first stated—that the existence of God is established because specific effects are preceded by an intellect characterized by excellence—we say: no, because [the existence of God] is yet to be proven.
The point to be proven is that things such as palaces are preceded by the intellect of someone like us, or else they are preceded by an intellect of superior capacity;
therefore, [your objection] is no answer.

Furthermore, since the intellect (*buddhi*) does not exist prior to the activity of the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and because other causes have been ruled out, this [Primal Matter] would have to produce specific effects intentionally.
And it is logically consistent that the intellect itself does not exist prior to the transformation of the Primal Matter.
If it is argued that [the Primal Matter acts] spontaneously due to its possession of power, it might be replied: "The Lord (*īśvara*) is endowed with all powers."
"The existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) in him is not denied, because even prior to the transformation of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), it is connected to desire by its own nature.
This too is untenable.
Why? Because there is no supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
When one is questioned regarding the claim that "cognition [is known] by itself," what example do you have?
Therefore, this is untenable.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*), [the response is:
even so, other intelligent beings do not possess a capacity equal to that of Īśvara.
Therefore, their cognitions arise either from the *pradhāna* at the same time as the manifestation of bodies, or from the contact of the self (*ātman*) and other factors.
"But [the claim] that God [acts] by Himself" is also untenable.
Why? Because it would entail the consequence of establishing all doctrines.

If one were to maintain that a specific capacity must be remembered by someone who is obstructed while taking up a matter contradicted by an example, then the consequence would be the establishment of every possible doctrine.
Therefore, this is merely a grasping at straws.

Thus, if the possibility of consciousness in God *per se* does not exist, it is rightly said: "Because consciousness is impossible prior to the activity of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), this particular effect is not preceded by an intelligent being."
Furthermore, because a result would be impossible:
it is observed that intelligent persons undertake specific tasks, such as palaces or celestial mansions, with a view toward a result, whether seen or unseen;
and this [creator], by virtue of his sovereignty, is unimpaired [by any lack of means].
Furthermore, because an instigator is untenable;
furthermore, because of inconclusiveness.
Not every particular effect is preceded by intelligence.
Because trees and such things arise independently of that [intention];
if one accepts that everything is preceded by the intellect of God, there would be no example [to support it]. And there is no argument that has not been cited as an example.
Therefore, the manifest world is not preceded by an intelligent agent.
Furthermore, because it is characterized by an abundance of suffering:
if this particular effect were preceded by an intelligent agent, there would be no purpose for the creator in ordaining such a state of excessive suffering.
If he were capable [of creating], he would produce that which results in happiness;
yet this world results in suffering;
therefore, this particular effect was not produced with prior intelligence.
Furthermore, because it is a means to suffering:
if this particular effect were produced intentionally, then the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa would be means to happiness,
yet they are means to suffering.
Therefore, it is not preceded by [human] intelligence.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is caused by *dharma* and *adharma*, the following might be thought:

even though this particular variety of effects is preceded by Īśvara, nevertheless, at the initial creation, for those living beings produced by us who possess a preponderance of happiness, there occurs—due to their appropriation of *dharma* and *adharma*—an association with inferior, middling, or superior age, caste, nature, and so forth.
"Therefore, this is not the fault of Īśvara.
This too is incorrect.
Why? Because there is no cause for the arising of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

If God were desired as the cause for the arising of both righteousness and unrighteousness, He would produce only righteousness for living beings, since that is the cause of happiness, and not unrighteousness, because there would be no purpose for it.
Now, if it is thought that the production of dharma and adharma from their own causes is inherent,
then the statement that "everything manifested is preceded by the intellect of Īśvara" is contradicted.
Therefore, Īśvara is not the cause.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the existence of God follows because the connection between the conscious and the unconscious is produced by a conscious being—we reply: this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).
By what conscious being was this connection between these two, the conscious cow and the unconscious cart, made?
If it were by Caitra,
he too would be insentient because he is a mere aggregate of causes and effects.
Furthermore, if it is maintained that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the witness of the body denoted by the word "Caitra" and that [the creation] was performed by him, that is incorrect,
because it is something yet to be proven;
for the agency of the Puruṣa is not established in our position.
Conventional discourse proceeds by means of what is established for both parties.
Furthermore, there is the consequence of infinite regress:

for one who asserts that the connection between the conscious and the unconscious is produced by a conscious being, it follows that the connection between the cause and effect of God must also be produced by a conscious being.
And thus, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
Now, if it is maintained that this fault shall not occur and that the relationship between cause and effect for the Lord is inherent (svābhāvika),
then the reason [adduced] is not conclusive.
If it is argued that there is no fault because those two are insentient,

it might further be said: since both the effect and the cause of the Lord are sentient, and the Lord himself is also sentient, the counter-example based on their relationship is therefore appropriate.
This is incorrect.
Why? Because it would entail the consequence of a lack of connection.
Due to the non-distinction of consciousness, there is no mutual connection between one self and another self.
In this way, it would also not be possible for Īśvara and his effects to stand in the relation of cause and effect;
and this is undesirable.
Furthermore, it would lead to the consequence of non-inversion.

For one who maintains the thesis that both possess consciousness, just as the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties are instruments for the Lord (*īśvara*), so too would the Lord be an instrument for the intellect and other faculties.
Why? Because there is no distinction.

Now, if this is undesirable, then there is no consciousness in both [the cause and the effect]. If it is argued that there is no fault because the relationship of cause and effect is not admitted, [we reply: [the Self] is all-pervading, partless, and possesses infinite power, [being subtler] than the subtlest things.

Those who know the reality declare that the category of the Lord (īśvara) has the characteristic of being infinite: it is subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest, the substratum of all attributes, and beginningless.
How could this [world] be superposed upon it by depending on any cause or effect?
This too is untenable. Why? Because it contradicts inference.

For if God exists in this way, then that inference—namely, that a specific effect is preceded by an intellect characterized by excellence, and that the connection between the sentient and the insentient is produced by a sentient being—is thereby subverted.
Why? Because this [scripture] has never been seen to have such a meaning as that. Or, even granting it for the sake of argument, it would contradict the acceptance of [the Lord's] corporeality;
for if the Lord were exclusively of such a nature [as being formless], [the scripture could not describe Him as having a body].
The assumption of forms such as the earth and so forth would be contradicted.
Furthermore, there is the testimony of scripture (*śruti*);
for scripture also describes his form, saying: "Clad in animal skins, holding the Pināka bow, with a drawn bow, having a blue crest," and so on.
If it is argued that by accepting this [scriptural statement] one's own position is abandoned,
the thought might be: "If, then, the Lord is accepted as possessing a physical form on the basis of the words of the Śruti,
then His existence is established."
Why? Because it is held that the possession of form is not possible for that which is non-existent.
This too is incorrect, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning.
For we do not absolutely deny the Blessed One’s specific power, since he possesses a body of majesty and so forth;
however, our intention is this: that there is no agent of those two [pradhāna and puruṣa] distinct from them, as you have stated.
Therefore, this [argument] is a refutation [of that position].
Consequently, the connection between Pradhāna and Puruṣa is not produced by another.
Furthermore, it is because [such a production] is impossible.
Furthermore, when this [agent] establishes a connection, would he do so with the body alone, or with the embodied self?
And what follows from this?
Therefore, it does not act by means of the body alone;
why? Because for that which is independent, there is no cause for the production of a body.
Nor does it act by means of the cause of the body, because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
The connection between a delimited cow and a cart is produced by another [agent], and likewise,
Pradhāna and Puruṣa are all-pervading (vibhu).
Furthermore, [Pradhāna is non-sentient] because it exists for the sake of another.
The connection between two ox-carts is seen to be for the sake of another;
however, the connection between primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) is not for the sake of another.
If it is argued that it is for the sake of God (īśvara), no, because that has already been refuted.
It has already been stated at the very beginning that a purpose consisting of both seen and unseen results is untenable for Īśvara;
thus, first of all, there is this fault in the Pāśupatas’ acceptance of Īśvara. And this same fault applies to the Vaiśeṣikas as well.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of whether or not there exists a distinct category of reality such as substance and so forth is untenable.

When they conceive of Īśvara, is he conceived as being composed of the categories of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence, or is he conceived as a distinct category of reality?
And what follows from this? That [entity] is not, first of all, a substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
Why? Because substance is of two kinds: that which consists of multiple substances and that which does not consist of substances.
In this regard, the Lord is not composed of multiple substances,
because that would entail defects such as being produced;
nor is he substanceless, because [substances] have been exhaustively enumerated.
In your system, there are exactly nine substances, beginning with earth and ending with mind;
this is because the particle "iti" serves to indicate completion,
and furthermore, because of the mention of qualities and actions.
If it were a substance (*dravya*), the Teacher would have provided a definition of its specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*),
and he would have specified an action capable of employing other causes;
however, he did not do so.
Therefore, it is not substance, quality, and so forth;
for qualities and the like are dependent upon a substratum and exist for the sake of another.
Thus, it is neither constituted by substance and the rest, nor is it a separate category of entity.
For if it were indeed a category (padārtha), its definition would have been stated, just as those for substance (dravya) and the others were;
however, it was not stated by the Teacher. Therefore, according to the view of the author of the Sūtras, God does not exist.
If it is argued that this is due to an inferential mark (*liṅga*), the following might be thought: "The act of assigning names is a mark of those superior to us;
or, because the act of naming is preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), from this inferential mark the Master’s acceptance of God (*īśvara*) is established."
That too is incorrect. Why? Because the intended [conclusion] is not established.
It is true that by means of this mark there might be a cognition of someone possessing superior power compared to ourselves—whether it be one who has a body of majesty or something else.
However, just as you maintain that there is only a mere designation (saṃjñāmātra) for a single independent cause that is the motive for the creation, withdrawal, and activity of all things,
so too is our understanding derived from this inferential mark (liṅga).
Furthermore:
Because if he had not taught it previously, it would follow that he was unskilled;
furthermore, if the activity and cessation of atoms were dependent upon Īśvara, he should have taught him first.
Alternatively, it follows that the author of the Sūtras was unskilled because he did not first teach the category of *pradhāna*, which is like *dharma*.
Moreover, neither of these two [positions] is accepted.
Furthermore, because he is not mentioned:
in the section of the treatise dealing with this, this Īśvara is not mentioned by the Teacher anywhere at all.
Nor would there be any occurrence of fault for him in pronouncing the name of his father-in-law, as there might be for a daughter-in-law;
this undesirable consequence is imputed to the Teacher merely for the sake of sharing out the blame, but it is not his actual view.
Thus, the claim that "God exists" among the followers of Kaṇāda is an innovation of the Pāśupatas;
therefore, God also is not the cause.
[The role of] karma has been explained by means of atoms.
How so? Just as atoms are not the cause of the world because they are created, so too karma is not the cause of the body;
therefore, that [karma] also is not the cause.
If it be argued that there is no fault because they are mutual causes, the thought might be:

"Just as it is observed that action does not arise without a body, so too it is impossible to imagine another cause for the body without action; thus, because they are mutual causes, no prior limit of this cycle is discerned."
Therefore, there is no other cause for these two;
however, this is incorrect.
Why? Because we observe that non-abiding is preceded by abiding.
For example, just as the body arises from semen and blood, and semen and blood arise from the body, the prior limit of this cycle is not perceived;
yet it is asserted that the bodies of the Lord (Īśvara) are not born from a womb during the initial creation.
Likewise, seeds arise from sprouts and so forth, and seeds [in turn] arise from sprouts and so forth, resulting in an infinite regress.
And here, at the initial creation, it appears that even from a mere atom there is the manifestation of a seed, and likewise there is an infinite regress regarding bodies and karma.
Furthermore, both now and at the initial creation, the production of a body would occur solely by virtue of one's specific qualification (*adhikāra*).
If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of all bodies having a common form, it might be so.

If it is admitted that the production of a body is caused by [karmic] qualification (*adhikāra*) at the beginning of creation, it follows that all persons would be connected with a single body, because there is no cause for restriction.
Consequently, other bodies would be useless,
since the capacity for experience would belong to all through that very one.
This is untenable.
Why? Because it contradicts direct perception.
This is true from the standpoint of inference.
However, since bodies are perceived as distinct for each individual,
this consequence does not apply.

If it should be thought that there is the consequence of a restriction regarding liberation— that is, if the production of the body were solely due to the force of [karmic] qualification, then the body produced by the Supreme Sage alone would result in the means for liberation.
It is said: it does not belong to that one alone;
rather, because of the predominance of all the *guṇas*, bodies caused by them arise spontaneously at the beginning of creation.
Among these, he whose body and instruments are dominated by *sattva* is the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*).
That being whose *sattva* is abundant with *rajas* possesses a body of majesty (*māhātmya*).

Thus, through the contact of the *guṇas*, by way of their predominance or non-predominance, there occurs the manifestation of bodies even down to those of stationary beings; therefore, there is no partiality on the part of the *guṇas* toward any particular body.
Consequently, it is logical that action (*karman*) is not the cause of the world, because it is something produced (*kṛtaka*).
And by this, it is explained as follows:

if it is argued that even that [notion of a self] is merely a designation for those very karmas whose maturation has been reached, and that it is indeed a different entity [from the karmas themselves], then that must be proven.
Therefore, it too should not be postulated.
As for what was also stated—that the world will arise from time—that is untenable. Why? Because that [designation] is applied solely to the movement of causes.
For us, there is no such thing as "time" at all.

What then? It is because only those things currently undergoing action—such as the movement of the sun, the milking of cows, the potting of jars, or the thundering of clouds—serve as the cause for the cognition of specific limits [of time], since the marks (liṅga) such as "prior" and "posterior" exist therein.
If it is argued that this is not so because such marks are not applicable to uncreated things, we say no;
for they are indeed applicable to uncreated things.
In whatever is produced, the cognition "this is superior" or "this is inferior," and so forth, is observed.
If that [cognition] were caused by something other than action (*kriyā*), it would occur without distinction among both permanent and impermanent things.

If it is argued that there is no fault because of the capacity [of the cause] in certain cases—just as the contact with fire is the cause of qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*), and thus, despite the lack of distinction, it becomes the cause for the production of baked qualities only in earth—it might be thought thus.
It does not exist in space and so forth.
Likewise, time too would be the cause of priority, posteriority, and so on, only in respect to impermanent things and not in respect to permanent ones;
and that is incorrect.
Why? Because a distinction is logically established.

Fire is the cause of the transformation of color and other qualities; it is therefore appropriate that it should produce qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*) in a substance possessing those [qualities], but not in things like space which do not possess them.
Time, however, merely assists in the relation [between causes and effects] and is not the cause of transformation;
therefore, this [position] is untenable.

Thus, if time is held to be something other than actions, then either the vibration of the primary cause (*kāraṇa-parispanda*) must be the cause of the world, or else something else must be established as such.
Even chance (*yadṛcchā*) is not the cause, because there exists a relationship of cause and effect, just as with karma.
For it has been explained previously that this manifest world is constituted by the relationship of cause and effect.

Furthermore, since that relationship of cause and effect is observed in the case of things like beds made with deliberation, but is not observed in the case of accidental things, it cannot be asserted that [chance] is its mark (*liṅga*).
Non-existence (abhāva) is also not the cause, because [qualities] such as dimension (parimāṇa) are observed;
for it is not possible for dimension to belong to things produced from that [non-existence], and therefore there is no positive concomitance (anvaya).
Because there is an absolute difference in genus between that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self;
nor is there causal capacity, because such capacity is absent; nor is there assistance, because it would lead to an infinite regress.
There is no differentiation because of the absence of a self (nirātmakatva).
Therefore, the manifest world does not arise from atoms, the person (puruṣa), the Lord (īśvara), karma, fate (daiva), time, inherent nature (svabhāva), chance, or non-existence (abhāva).
If it does not arise from these, [then what is the cause?]

By process of elimination, this is a mark for the very existence of the Pradhāna. Therefore, it is logical that there exists an unmanifest cause of the differentiated effects, on account of their finite magnitude and other such reasons. // 15 // Kārikā 16: [The Manifest is not produced from non-existence; for what is non-existent cannot be produced, nor can that which is existent be destroyed. The manifestation of the world proceeds from the Unmanifest. This is because the effect pre-exists in the cause, because there is a necessary relation between cause and effect, because everything does not arise from everything, because things proceed from their own specific causes, because there is a distinction between cause and effect, and because the efficient cause acts upon what already exists. Furthermore, because the Unmanifest is imperceptible while the Manifest is perceptible, and because they possess different qualities, the Manifest must have the Unmanifest as its cause. Thus, the existence of the Unmanifest is established. // 16 //
He said: Even so, its being the manifest cause is untenable because it is a unity;
for it is observed that many things, such as threads and the like, initiate an effect, whereas Pradhāna is one.
Therefore, it is argued that [the Pradhāna] does not possess the power to initiate that [evolution].

To this it is replied: although the Pradhāna, characterized by the gunas, is a single state because it is the cause of a non-differentiated cognition, nevertheless, at the time of its effectuation, it possesses powers (*śakti*) that—though designated as distinct due to the emergence of some degree of inequality—are mutually supportive.
It attains the state of a composite aggregate;
therefore,
it now proceeds from the three qualities (guṇas) and from their aggregation.
By the phrase "it proceeds," he expresses its origination.

By the phrase "from the three qualities" (*triguṇataḥ*), he describes another definable state resulting from the imbalance of the powers of the qualities—which are themselves indefinable in form—due to their being either primary or secondary.
That state wherein it can be said that "there are the three, [namely] *sattva* and the others," is the state that initiates the effect.
By the term "from the collection" (*samudayāt*), he illuminates the productive power of those [qualities] which are mutually dependent.
This is what is meant: at the time of the effect, the qualities, having abandoned their previous state and attained differentiation, combine through mutual assistance;
and being combined, they produce the manifest.

Therefore, there is no fault of the Pradhāna being a single entity because the different states are the cause of a non-differentiated cognition; nor is it the case that a single [Pradhāna] cannot initiate an effect due to the difference between the Guṇas.
[The opponent] says: In that case, since Prakṛti is devoid of activity, the initiation of an effect is untenable.
Or, if activity is not admitted, there is a contradiction with the [Pradhāna's] dissimilarity to the Manifested (vyakta).
It is said: No, because of the difference due to the dissimilarity of activity.

For activity is of two kinds: characterized by vibration (*praspanda*) and characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*). Among these, vibration is denied in the case of *pradhāna* because of its subtlety (*saukṣmya*).
"But it initiates that effect through transformation.
He says: "But surely even transformation is not possible for the Pradhāna because of its subtlety."
Why? Because no transformation of subtle things such as space is observed on account of their subtlety. It is replied:
even though a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is subtle, its transformation must nevertheless be admitted.
Therefore, it is logical that [the mind] undergoes subtle transformation.
He asked: "What, then, is this so-called transformation (pariṇāma)?
It is said:
"When [a substance], abandoning one property, assumes another..."
"The substrate (dharmī) that does not deviate from its essential nature (tattva) is called transformation (pariṇāma).

When, through the assistance of another power (śakti), the substrate—without deviating from its own nature—manifests by means of another attribute (dharma) after having caused previous attributes to disappear, that state is what we call "transformation.
[The opponent] says: We do not accept this mere assertion without an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
Therefore, how it is to be explained must be stated.

It is said: just as a *pālāśa* leaf, due to the favor of another cause such as heat (*ātapa*) that has not yet departed from the leaf, causes its blackness to disappear and attains yellowness—so too should this be understood.
[The opponent] says: No, because the arising of something different is not prohibited.
How, then, is this understood—that the *pālāśa* wood, without deviating from its own nature, effects the abandonment and acquisition of other attributes, and not otherwise, nor in a different manner?
It is said: because the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has already been established, there is no cause for the re-arising of entities that have perished.
And since arising is untenable in the absence of that [dharma], he says:
because you admit the non-difference of the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), it follows that when a property arises or perishes, the substratum itself must arise or perish;
for for you, the substratum is not other than its properties.

In that case, if the cessation of the property (*dharma*) is admitted, the cessation of the substratum (*dharmin*) would also necessarily follow because of their non-difference. Furthermore, when the property arises, the substratum arises as well.
Therefore, what was stated—that the essential nature of the substratum remains even when there is a contradiction regarding the arising of the property—is incorrect.
It is said: no, because its establishment is possible in the manner of an army and so forth.
For example, an army is not something other than its constituent parts;
yet, when the constituent parts of the army perish, the army itself does not perish.
For example, it is not like another cloth,
because for Buddhists there is a negation of the composite whole (*avayavin*) resulting from conjunction;
furthermore, the destruction of the cloth does not entail the destruction of the threads.
In that regard, what was stated—that with the destruction of the substratum (dharmin), there is the destruction of the property (dharma)—is incorrect.
He says: even so, it is incorrect.
Why? Because the conceptualization of the essential nature of the substratum as being either a universal (sāmānya) or a particular (viśeṣa) is untenable.

In this case, would that which is being conceptualized as the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) be the generality (*sāmānya*) of form and so forth, or rather the particularity (*viśeṣa*) of form and so forth? And what follows from this?
First of all, it is not possible to conceive of the generality of form and so forth as the essential nature of the substratum.
Why? Because it is impossible.

If, first of all, earth is the universal and the jar and so forth are the particulars, then earth itself is a particular in relation to those [subtle elements]. This continues up to the Pradhāna; thus, there is no universal at all.
Due to the absence of that [universal], there is an absence of the very nature of the substratum (dharmin).
Now, if the particulars such as pots are [the subject], they cannot coexist with other particulars because the nature of the substratum (dharmin) would not remain stable;
consequently, what was stated— that "the substratum, without deviating from its own nature, abandons one attribute and acquires another"— is contradicted.

It is replied: As for what was said—that the conceptualization of the nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) is untenable regarding the universal and the particular of form and so forth—let the universal exist.

As for what was further stated—that a universal becomes a particular in dependence upon another universal, and that when cognition ceases, the universal does not persist, and therefore the nature of the substratum is established [as non-existent]—[we respond as follows].
As long as this cognition "earth" does not cease, the pot and so forth are the particular (viśeṣa) and the universal (sāmānya);

and since that [earth] is substantiality (dravyatva), and because its own nature is established through the arising of cognitions in that form despite the transformation of other attributes, the pot and so forth are the attributes (dharma).

But when the cognition of "earth" ceases, then the state of being a mere substrate (*tanmātra*), its commonality, and its substantiality are its specific qualities; that is to say, this continues up to the *pradhāna*. However, because no further commonality can be established for it, it possesses absolute immutability (*kauṭasthya*). That in which all specific qualities are absent is the *pradhāna*.
If, however, earth and the other elements were eternally unchanging, they would necessarily possess immutability (*kauṭasthya*).
Therefore, there is no absence of the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*),
because it is admitted that power (*śakti*) exists as a universal (*sāmānya*).

Alternatively, it is the powers of pleasure, pain, and delusion themselves that undergo transformation through the causal signs beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements;

and because these powers constantly serve as the cause for the cognition of the general [principle], their state as a substance persists even when they do not deviate from their own nature—this is the "property-likeness" (dharmatva) of the sign.
If it is argued that this is untenable due to a lack of established proof, we say no, for it has already been explained.
It has been stated previously that the universe is preceded by pleasure and so forth.
[The opponent] says: Even so, the manifold variety of forms (vaiśvarūpya) is untenable, because of the specific nature of the cause.

If only the powers such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth were subject to transformation, then this manifold diversity (*vaiśvarūpya*)—beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary world—would not be possible.
Why? Because an effect that is non-different [from its cause] cannot arise.
It is said in response: "And because of the power, [the cause] is subject to transformation."
By that, indeed, there is manifoldness. How?
Like water, due to the specific distinctions of the substrata of the respective qualities. 16.
Just as water, though indistinguishable from the atmosphere, undergoes a transformation upon falling into different substrates— such as cows, serpents, camels, and so forth—

and thereby attains a manifold diversity (vaiśvarūpya) such as milk, urine, or poison; in the same way, the powers of the qualities (guṇa-śaktayaḥ), being differentiated by their mutual dependence on specific substrates, attain a manifold diversity ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, consisting of various species, forms, speech, intellects, natures, diets, and modes of life.
Therefore, it is established that primordial nature alone is the progenitor of all manifestations, and there is no fault whatsoever. // 16 //
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Yuktidīpikā*, the commentary on the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*. Karika 17:
[The opponent] says: The *pradhāna* has been understood.
Now, it must be established that the Puruṣa exists as distinct from cause and effect.
If it is asked, "From where does this doubt arise?", it has been stated: "Because that which is not perceived is seen in both ways.
Furthermore:
This is due to the teacher’s misconception.
The followers of Śākyamuni maintain that there is no object whatsoever distinct from the aggregate of consciousness.
Why? Because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this context, whatever exists is apprehended through means of valid cognition such as direct perception,
as for example, visible form and so forth;
however, this self is not apprehended by direct perception.
Why? Because it is characterized by the absence of sound and other such qualities.
It is not perceived internally through direct perception.
Why? Because that which is the opposite of the three *guṇas* and so forth is not an object of such perception.
It is not [established] by means of *pūrvavat* or *śeṣavat*,
because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable;
nor is it established by means of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
Because there is no commonality among phenomena;
because it is not the word of a reliable authority;
and because it is not accepted [as such].
For the Buddhists, the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas are not authoritative.
And as for their own scripture, it says this:
"The self itself does not exist for the self; it is imagined through error."
Herein there is no sentient being or self; these are merely phenomena arising with their causes.
There are only twelve members—aggregates, sense-bases, and elements;
having reflected upon all these, no person (pudgala) is found.
Know the internal to be empty; see the external as empty.
Even that person who meditates upon emptiness is not to be perceived at all.
Furthermore, it says: "Karma exists and its maturation exists,
but an agent is not found who projects these present dharmas and reconnects with others."
Except for the conventional designation of "dharma," therefore, because the self is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it does not exist.

To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that the self is not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor through the methods of "prior" (*pūrvavat*) or "residual" (*śeṣavat* [inference])—[that is incorrect].
This is true;
however, as for what was stated— that non-perception [proves] the impossibility of a general self because it is based on inference from common observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)— that is incorrect.
Why?
Because they are aggregates for the sake of another;
here, aggregates are observed to exist for the sake of another.
For example, beds, seats, chariots, wheels, and so forth;
and this collection characterized as a body exists.
Therefore, it too must exist for the sake of another.
That which is the "other" is the Puruṣa;
therefore, the Puruṣa exists. It is said: because of the perception that composite objects exist for the sake of another.
For beds and the like, even though they exist for the sake of another, are for the purpose of a composite whole.
If, by means of these, an extension [of the principle] is made regarding the composite whole of cause and effect, it follows that this [composite] must likewise have the purpose of a composite whole.
In this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of establishing a meaning contrary to the Puruṣa.
Now, if this is undesirable, then the eyes and so forth would not be for the sake of another.
It is replied: it is not possible to establish this.
Why? Because the debate proceeds on the basis of the establishment of non-compositionality. This debate concerning the Person (puruṣa) has proceeded once non-compositionality has been established;
therefore, its purposefulness for another (pārārthya) is not negated by it.
If it is asked how this is understood,
it is because [the self] is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For if it were a composite entity, this person would be perceived directly, just like Devadatta and others.
And this being the case, because there would be no doubt, there would be no engagement at all with this doctrine.
Therefore, it is incorrect [to claim] that the eyes and so forth have a collective purpose, like a bed and such things.
[The opponent] says: "Their subservience to another is established because they provide mutual assistance."
In this world, the field, water, the sun, and so forth, are the benefactors of crops and the like;
likewise, because they stand in a relationship of cause and effect, there is also a composite whole.
As it has been said: "Therefore, it is illogical for these to possess dependence upon another."
It is said: No, because they possess purpose through something other than that, unlike the case of a bed and so forth.

For example, although the parts of a bed and such things provide mutual assistance to one another, they possess purpose through something other than themselves; in their absence, they would lack purpose.
Likewise, although the eye and the other faculties provide mutual assistance to one another, they must possess purpose through something other than themselves.
"And in the absence of that [the self], there would be a lack of purpose for objects.
To this he replies: Since things such as beds exist for the sake of Devadatta, and since he is distinct from them and external to them, it follows that they must exist for one another's sake.
Thus, beds and so forth exist for the sake of Devadatta.

Furthermore, the aggregate of causes and effects is what is denoted by the word "Devadatta"; since it is the distinctions [within that aggregate] alone that constitute the meaning of the term "distinction," the accomplishment of the human goal [occurs there].
Alternatively, there is an absence of an illustrative example.
Now, if it is thought that sleeping and so forth are not for the sake of Devadatta, [then...]
Rather, they are for the sake of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
If that were so, the example would be equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*).
To this it is replied: No, because [the argument] conforms to what is already established (*prasiddhi*).
It is true that the aggregate of causes and effects exists for the sake of another;
however, the status of being an enjoyer is not established [for that other].
In the world, it is well known that beds and such things exist for the sake of Devadatta.
Therefore, following that [line of reasoning], we also say this.
Why? Because of what is well-established (*prasiddhi*).

For by means of what is established, that which is not yet established attains the status of being its property (*taddharmatā*). As you yourselves have stated: "For that which does not undergo alteration at every moment, there is no distinction between external conditions."
There is no subsequent apprehension of a difference,
just as there is none for the qualities produced by baking in the case of earth that is not being baked.
Nor is it the case that there is no change at every moment in the earth.
Because it would otherwise follow that [the self] is non-momentary,
the example was employed [in the Sāṃkhya Kārikā] stating that "the distinction [between the self and the body] is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety.
Therefore, it is established that because composite objects exist for the sake of another, the Puruṣa exists.

Furthermore: because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth, that which possesses the three qualities, is non-discriminative, is an object, is common, is insentient, and is productive— whether external or internal— is likewise the Pradhāna.
In this regard, if this were all [that was intended], then what would be the point of saying "because of the three qualities (triguṇya) of both the manifest and the unmanifest" in relation to what?
