Furthermore, there is another [reason]: because of superintendence (adhiṣṭhāna).
In this case, if the primary activity were to occur spontaneously, there would be no necessity for the determination of arrangement according to purpose.
That [arrangement]—the hearing-organ and so forth among earth and the other elements—is for the sake of providing benefit and non-obstruction among gods, humans, and animals.
Therefore, there exists something distinct from those [elements], presided over by which the qualities (guṇas) undergo this manifold transformation.
If it is argued that the superintendence [of the Puruṣa] is untenable because it would entail the consequence of his being an agent,
the following might be thought: if it is admitted that the activity of the guṇas occurs when they are superintended by the Puruṣa, then agency would accrue to him.
If, on the other hand, it is not an agent, then there can be no status as a controller;
however, this is incorrect. Why? Because that term is applied metaphorically to the object.

In such a way that the purpose of the Puruṣa is accomplished, the Guṇas are arrayed in the relationship of cause and effect; therefore, because they are dependent upon him, their state of being presided over is established, as is the Puruṣa’s status as the presider.
Consequently, there is no consequence of his being an agent.
Therefore, this is logical: the person exists because of [the need for] a substratum.
Furthermore:
the person exists because there must be an experiencer.
In this world, both the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta) are insentient because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion;
therefore, experience by these two in relation to one another is not possible,
and thus there must necessarily be an experiencer.
That which is the enjoyer is the *puruṣa*. He asks: "What, then, is this so-called enjoyment?
It is said: enjoyment consists in the existence of perception.
Since consciousness alone is capable of apprehending objects, let there be only that much; what is the use of postulating a *puruṣa*?
It is replied: But what indeed is this so-called "consciousness"?
He says: it is *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*.
And that consciousness is of six kinds: visual consciousness,
auditory consciousness,
and olfactory consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
In that regard, conditioned by form, the eye gives rise to visual consciousness.
Likewise, the ear, sound, nose, odor, tongue, taste, mind, and mental objects give rise to the mind.
Its factors are feeling, [perception, volition, contact, attention, and so forth].
Perception, contact,
and mind.
Formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are such; therefore, because the capacity for experience belongs only to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), there is no self (*ātman*).
It is replied: No, because consciousness cannot arise from that which is an insentient transformation.
For it is indeed accepted that, depending on form and the eye, visual consciousness arises, and so forth.
Therefore, because it is a modification of that which is insentient, it follows that it is itself insentient, like a jar or similar objects.
Thus, the claim that "consciousness is a property of the mind" is merely a wishful thought.
If it is argued that its existence is established by the observation of the production of an effect with distinct characteristics, [we reply:]...
It might be thought: "This is not a fixed rule, namely, that an effect must be of the same nature as its cause;
rather, it is observed that entities arise from causes of a different character.
For example, an arrow is produced from horn."
From the hair of the head and the hair of the tail, *dūrvā* grass [is produced];
from a young calf and the moonstone in conjunction with the moon, water;
from a sunstone, cow dung, and contact with the sun, fire; and from the friction of the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*), fire [is produced].
Thus, it is claimed that consciousness arises from non-conscious entities such as form and so forth;
however, this is incorrect,
because there is a fixed rule for the arising of consciousness from non-consciousness, just as there is a fixed rule for its [the latter's] own production.

Just as, given this manifestation of a dissimilar effect, there is for you the rule that a non-conscious object such as a jar does not arise from a conscious mind, so too, given this manifestation of a dissimilar effect, our rule is that a conscious mind does not arise from non-conscious forms and the like.
Therefore, although these [examples] are numerous, they are inferior because, like the construction of a city by a magician, they are objects of knowledge that do not correspond to reality.

If it is argued that its establishment is like that of a lamp, it might be as follows: just as from insentient [factors] such as *sattva* and so forth, an insentient object like a jar is produced, and therefore a sentient Great Principle (*mahat*) is not now produced;
likewise, since from insentient [elements] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, an insentient jar and the like are produced, a sentient mind (*citta*) is not now produced.
This too is untenable.
Why? Because of the distinction in their potencies.
Sattva is of the nature of determination because its inherent quality is luminosity.
That is appropriate if, when that [object] is perceived, a great resolve (*vyavasāya*) of a determinative nature arises;
for jars and other objects, due to the predominance of *tamas*, possess a determinative character.
But for you, form and the other [sensory objects] would appear in a single uniform manner; therefore, this concentration (*samādhi*) of yours is inconsistent.

He asks: "Is there any difference in nature between determination (*vyavasāya*) and consciousness (*caitanya*), or not? It is replied: What then? Since it possesses the nature of cognition due to the three *guṇas*, the intellect (*buddhi*) is an object of experience; however, insofar as its form is that of determination, so too is its form that of consciousness. And thus the Vārṣagaṇyas recite: "For the *puruṣa*, being permeated by the modification of the intellect, follows after it as it persists in the form of cognition. And he [the author] says:
Just as the intellect appears in the form of an object, so does the person;
appearing through the intellect, it is therefore called the "knower," like a gem.
In whatever manner the mental activity of a person exists, in that very manner he assumes the form of the intellect; because it is conscious, it depends upon another.
He said: Since there is no difference in form between the person (*puruṣa*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the conceptualization of either one is redundant.
If, then, the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*) is just like the nature of determination (*vyavasāya*), this being the case, should one postulate merely determination or merely consciousness?
Why?
Because there is no capacity for two things that produce exclusively distinct results to be conceived as simultaneous,
nor is there the designation of them as having different natures.

Now, if it is argued that there is indeed a distinction between volition (*vyavasāya*) and consciousness (*caitanya*), and that they are eternally distinguished as separate categories, then it must be stated which belongs to this [volition] and which does not belong to that [consciousness].
It is replied: First, he who says that there is no difference in objects because there is no difference in their forms (*rūpa*) should be asked this: What then?
Is there for you a difference in form between consciousness and its object, or not?
He says: no. Why?
Because if there were a different form, the determination of the object would be impossible.
For it is not possible to determine the intrinsic nature of an object without its manifestation in consciousness.
In that regard, if a cow were of one form while the cognition of the cow were of another form, then— just as a cow of one form is not determined by a cognition of a horse of another form—
likewise, a cow of one form would not be determined by a cognition of a cow of another form.
Therefore, there is no difference in form between the object and its cognition.
To this it is replied: Now, regarding these two—the object and the cognition of that object—is there duality or non-difference?
He asks: Why? Because of their relationship as the known and the knower.
It is said:
Just as there is a distinction between knowledge and its object despite the non-difference of their form,
so too is there a distinction between the self and its manifestation by way of the relationship of grasped and grasper.

"In that case, just as for you there is indeed a distinction between cognition and the object of cognition due to the conceptualization of the relationship of grasped and grasper despite the difference in their forms, so too would it be for the person (*puruṣa*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
If it is argued that this is incorrect because the relationship of grasped and grasper is not established [between them], it might be as follows:
just as the relationship of grasped and grasper between a cow and the cognition thereof is certain, it is not so between the person and the internal organ."
"Therefore, there is an inequality"—this is untenable. Why? Because it involves proceeding by way of another path.
It was stated previously that those things which lack a distinction of form possess unity;
however, now, even though there is no difference in form, this is a different path because one speaks thus on the basis of the very relationship between the grasped and the grasper.
If it should be thought that [this view] is non-Buddhist because it accepts mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), [we respond as follows]:
Cognition itself, colored by unreal objects that exist within it, manifests in the form of both object and subject;
however, there exists no external thing whatsoever that has assumed the nature of an apprehended object.
Therefore, the claim that cognition and the cognizable are distinct because of a distinction between the apprehender and the apprehended is un-Śākya (i.e., not the doctrine of the Buddhists).
That too is incorrect.
Why? Because of the difference in philosophical tenets.
This fault applies only to the position of those who maintain that external objects exist.
"But as for the others, we shall refute the relationship of object and subject regarding mere cognition.
He replies: "Even so, there follows the consequence of an infinite regress of objects, because you assert that the subject itself becomes an object."

If it is asserted that even the subject (*viṣayin*), which is the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*), possesses the status of an object (*viṣaya*), then it follows that for the person (*puruṣa*), who is also a subject, there must be another subject, and for that one as well another; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if it is argued that this fault must not arise, and therefore the person (*puruṣa*), because he is of the nature of certainty, is not an object [of cognition], then one should not postulate a distinct entity from the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) as the certifier.
To this it is replied: such a [separate] entity is untenable in the case of the person because of his sentience (*cetanātva*).
Since the sense organs, being of the nature of mere apprehension, are non-cognitive, an internal instrument possessing cognition is first postulated.

The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), although it assumes the form of the object through the contact with the functioning of the sense organs directed toward their respective objects, is itself incapable of perceiving that object because it is insentient; therefore, it depends upon the conscious person as its enjoyer. However, since the person is sentient, it is impossible to postulate another seer for the person.
Therefore, there is no consequence of infinite regress.
[The opponent] says: It follows that the person (puruṣa) must be the agent of determination (adhyavasāya), because of his sentience (caitanya).
If the intellect (buddhi) were insentient, then, like a jar or other such objects, it could not possess determination as its function.
Therefore, it follows that determination belongs to the person (puruṣa), and consequently, there would be an absence of intellect (buddhi).
To this it is replied: No, because [if that were so] there would follow the consequence of the lack of obstruction [of the self] even in isolation (kaivalya).
We shall explain later that the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) is of an unmixed nature.

If it were of the nature of determination (*vyavasāyātmaka*), then there would be determination without obstruction regarding the ascertainment of directions and so forth, even for those who are asleep, intoxicated, or unconscious.
Thus, an obstruction to determination is observed in one who is in such a state;
therefore, determination does not belong to the *puruṣa*. However, for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) performs the determination, this fault does not exist.
Why? Because of the three qualities (traiguṇya).
For the intellect (buddhi) is a specific configuration of sattva and the other [qualities], since other instruments have been ruled out.

In that regard, when *sattva*, which is characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*), has its power obscured by *tamas*—which predominates due to the absence of the other qualities (*guṇa*)—then there is an obstruction to determination.
[The opponent] asks: "But how is it known that all this is insentient (*acetana*)?
It is said: Because it consists of the primary nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*).
In this world, whatever exists as a relationship between material cause and its modification is insentient;
for example, threads and cloth and so forth. Since [the body] exists as a relationship between material cause and its modification, it is therefore insentient.
If it is argued that this is not necessarily so because [insentience] is observed in space (*ākāśa*), we say no.
Because it is unestablished;
for the absence of the relationship between material cause and modification is not established in the case of space being included within the category of the self.
Therefore, it is correct that everything is insentient because it exists as a modification of a material cause.

For this very reason, consciousness (cetanā) does not constitute either the primordial nature (prakṛti) or its modification (vikāra), due to its mutual dissimilarity [with them]. Therefore, it is not possible for anything else that is ultimate (paramārtha) to be an enjoyer, because of its insentience (acetanya); thus, it is well said: "The Puruṣa exists because of the state of being an enjoyer."
And because activity proceeds for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
In this world, for those things that possess activity, cessation without a cause is not possible;
and the Pradhāna, too, possesses activity, as is observed from its manifestations.

Therefore, that person (puruṣa) for whom isolation (kaivalya) is the cause of the activity of primordial matter (pradhāna) [is the self]. If it is argued that "because primordial matter is not accepted, neither [of the two] is established," this might be so; for us, primordial matter is as unestablished as a conscious being.

As for the argument that your presentation of activity as a mark for the existence of the *puruṣa*—intended to establish its isolation (*kaivalya*)—is being demonstrated as unproven, this is incorrect. Why? Because that has already been established previously.
If one were to speak thus without first establishing the Pradhāna, one would indeed deserve such a challenge;
however, since the Pradhāna has already been established through [the reasons of] dimension and so forth, this objection amounts to nothing.
If it be thought that the accomplishment of the human goal results from the disagreement among all the teachers: [End of excerpt]
If the person were indeed a real entity (sattva), then there would be no disagreement among teachers regarding its nature;
yet such a disagreement does exist.
For instance, for some it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
For some, it is dependent on others;
therefore, for all [others], it is all-pervading,
whereas for others, it is limited.
Likewise, [the claim that] "it is one" or "it is not one"—
therefore, the conceptualization of a person is mere delusion—
is untenable.
Why? Because it would entail the non-existence of all categories of entities,
and because there is disagreement even regarding form and the other [sensory objects],
some of which are held by certain [schools] to be momentary.
For some, they abide for a period of time; likewise, they are either dependent or independent, and so forth.
Likewise, there is a dispute regarding whether the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest, are material (bhautika), derived from ego-consciousness (āhaṃkārika), or belong to the Puruṣa (pauruṣa).
In this way, there would be an absence of all entities.
Therefore, the Self exists.
In that regard, it is incorrect to say "the Self does not exist" because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this [objection] is untenable.
As for what was said, "Behold the internal as empty," we shall later state the refutation of that.
Furthermore, as for this which was said, "Karma exists and its maturation exists, but an agent is not perceived," this is true.
For our position is that there is no agent in the casting off, the re-linking, or elsewhere of the aggregates of a person.

Therefore, those seeking the highest good should set aside the irrational delusion of the conceptualization of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), which contradicts all scriptures and reasoning; rather, by means of the thorough knowledge of the existence of the Person (*puruṣa*), they must attain the supreme, immortal, and eternal state, which serves as the antidote to all calamities such as birth and death. // 17 //
[Kārikā 18] He says: For now, we accept that this self exists;
however, it must now be investigated whether it is manifold or one.
If it is asked, "Whence comes this doubt?",
it is because related things are observed in both ways.
In this world, the relation of a single thing with many is perceived.
For example, as the body [is related] to the ear and so forth; or as one thing may be related to many,
such as space [is related] to jars and so forth.
Furthermore, since this self is related to cause and effect, there arises the doubt: is it manifold like the auditory organ and so forth, or is it one like space? Moreover, there is another reason:
because of the disagreement among teachers.
Indeed, the followers of the Upaniṣads maintain that the Self is one,
whereas the followers of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, the Arhats, and others maintain that it is many.

Just as there is this disagreement regarding the oneness or plurality of the Self, so too is there disagreement concerning its being a witness, its neutrality, its being a seer, and its being a non-agent.
Therefore, it must be explained how these factors (dharmas) abide in the person (puruṣa).

It is said: as for what was stated—that because of its being a related entity, there is doubt regarding the category of the self (ātman) as to whether it is many or one—here we reply: the proposition is that there are many persons. Why?

Birth is the connection, according to one's latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), of the subtle body—the *liṅga* consisting of the great elements (*mahat*) and so forth—to an external body; this occurs due to the specific determination of the instruments of birth and death.

Death is the abandonment by the *liṅga* of its previous body, occurring upon the completion of the experience of the fruits of previously performed karma and the presentation of the experience of the fruits of present karma.
He will state that the instruments (*karaṇa*) are of thirteen kinds (ISk 32). Birth, death, and the instruments are "birth-death-instruments";
there is a fixed allotment (*niyama*) of these for each individual soul (*puruṣa*).
From this indicative mark, the plurality of the self is determined.
This is what is meant: birth as a characteristic and death as a characteristic are two different states of the cause-and-effect complex;
they are mutually contradictory, like darkness and light.
In that regard, if there were a single self, then just as a single substance cannot simultaneously experience darkness and light occurring in the same location because it is impossible,
so too this [self] would be unable to experience both birth and death.
Yet, this experience of birth occurs through one set of causes and instruments, while the experience of death occurs through another.
Therefore, we consider that selves are manifold,
since they possess the capacity for the experience of contradictory attributes.

Likewise, the instruments [of perception] possess an excellence of illumination and an excellence of impurity characterized by the apprehension of objects, consisting of twenty-eight kinds of incapacity (*aśakti*).
Because these two are mutually contradictory, simultaneous enjoyment by a single self is not possible.

Indeed, it is impossible for a single self to simultaneously experience an excellence of illumination, characterized by the apprehension of objects, and an excellence of impurity, characterized by incapacity, due to their opposition.
Yet, this restriction—determined by the instruments [of perception]—exists for each individual self.
Therefore we conclude that the selves are manifold. Furthermore: because their activities do not occur simultaneously.
The plurality of Puruṣas is established;
why? Because of the non-simultaneity of activity—this refers to the Pradhāna, for whose activity [this plurality] is logically justified.
Of what does activity arise?
Of the Pradhāna. How so?
It is said: if there were only one self (*ātman*), then the primary cause (*pradhāna*) would be bound to the authority of that single person;

and since he would be capable of simultaneously experiencing many bodies, it would follow that for as many bodies as are required to exhaust the measure of time within this cycle of existence (*bhavaparivarta*), the *pradhāna* would operate simultaneously toward the production of all of them.

However, it is observed that the activity of the primary cause (pradhāna) does not occur simultaneously in the form of bodies; therefore, because of this non-simultaneous activity, there must be multiple selves (ātman).
Others, however, say: [it is so] because of the non-simultaneous activity of the external organs alone.

How so? If there were a single self, then all the instruments (karaṇas) would be bound by the impressions (saṃskāra) of that [single self]; consequently, one would perceive objects simultaneously through the instruments residing in every individual body.
Or, in the event of an impairment such as deafness, the perception of sound and other objects by means of the instruments belonging to another body would be unimpeded for this person.
But such is not the case.
"Therefore, because the instruments do not function simultaneously, there must be multiple selves.
This is incorrect.
Why? Because it is no different from the previous [argument].
This point is already included by the statement "due to the specific determination of the instruments";
therefore, let it remain exactly as stated.
Furthermore, what else?
And also because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth.
In this world, the properties of being composed of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive are perceived in every individual object (*piṇḍa*).
And just as these [properties] exist, so too do their opposites—such as being devoid of the *guṇas* (*nirguṇya*) and so forth—which are the properties of the *puruṣa*.

In that regard, just as the existence of a single *puruṣa* is established from a single object due to the perception of a nature contrary to the nature of the *guṇas*, so too the plurality of *puruṣas* is to be understood from the perception, in every object, of a nature contrary to the nature of the *guṇas*.
Therefore, it is established that there are not multiple selves. [Objection: It has been proven that the self is manifold.
For what reason is the status of being a witness, isolation, neutrality, the state of being a seer, and the state of being a non-agent now established?
It is said:
"And from that very [state of] inversion, the witness-status of this Puruṣa is established."
Isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the state of non-agency.
By the word "therefore" (tasmāt), he expresses the general reason;
the word "and" (ca) serves for emphasis;
and by the phrase "from error" (viparyāsāt), he situates the generally stated reason within its specific context.
By the statement, "The witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established," and so forth, he indicates the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
In that context, by the term "witnesshood," he makes known the independence of the qualities (guṇas) in their activity,
because the activity of Pradhāna is dependent upon that [Puruṣa] as its purpose.
How is it that there is a presiding agency?
It is said: Just as when some witness of action is present, the agent—who conforms to that witness's will—accomplishes the effect, and is not independent; [so too is the case here].

In the same way, primordial matter (pradhāna) also manifests itself through the forms of the great principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, the gross elements, gods, humans, animals, and immobile beings, so that the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣa) may be accomplished through both activity and cessation;
it does not do so by chance.
Therefore, because the activity and cessation of the *pradhāna* are dependent upon that [Purusha], the Purusha is their witness.
By the term "isolation" (*kaivalya*), he negates the quality of association for the Self;
it is not like the mutual association of *sattva* and the other qualities, which depend upon one another for qualities such as illumination.
In this way, neutrality arises for the Puruṣa through those [qualities].

By the term "neutrality" (mādhyasthya), he demonstrates that because neither increase nor decrease is possible, it is impossible for the Puruṣa to experience either affliction or favor from the Guṇas, and that there is no partiality toward them in their engagement in their own effects.

By the term "the state of being a seer" (draṣṭṛtva), he shows that although the capacity for consciousness exists in the indifferent one simultaneously with the manifestation of the aggregate of cause and effect, [the Puruṣa remains distinct] from those things whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
He asserts that there is merely the perception [of objects] through the mere proximity of the qualities (*guṇa*) and the activities whose objects have not ceased.
By the phrase "and the state of being a non-agent," he relies upon a sevenfold non-agency:
for this [Puruṣa] does not perform the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding objects, even when the external and internal organs are in proximity.

Furthermore, while the qualities of *sattva* and the others function through mutual assistance by means of their respective characteristics of illumination, activity, and restraint, the Spirit does not assume the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) through its own characteristic of consciousness,
nor does it assume the status of the principal member (*aṅgin*).
Thus, together with the qualities, it does not produce an effect, like a woman or a young boy.
It does not perform a stationary activity like one who propels a chariot, a cart, or a machine; nor does it act from itself like a lump of clay;
nor does it act from another like a potter.
Nor [is it born] from non-space, like a magician;
nor from both [space and non-space], like a mother and father.

Thus, by means of this Sūtra, the Teacher establishes that the Person possesses the qualities of being a presiding controller, being devoid of attributes (nirguṇya), being indifferent (audāsīnya), being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva), and being a non-agent (akartṛtva); having thus established these, he presents the opposite of the three attributes and so forth as the means of proof.

By means of those five types of actions—which are the opposites of the three qualities (guṇas) and so forth—the activity of these five [elements] is to be understood according to their respective possibilities.
Since this [Self] is an entity distinct from pleasure and the rest, it is therefore the witness of their activity.
In that regard, its status as a witness arises from its being devoid of the qualities (nairguṇya).
He said: Because that is unestablished;
because the absence of qualities (nairguṇya) is unestablished.
If the nature of the self as possessing qualities such as pleasure were established, then it would be appropriate to say this.
This is established by the very nature of reality;
therefore, this [position] is incorrect.
If it should be thought that "because no distinction is stated, establishment from the other [alternative] also follows," [that is not so].
In the case of the claim that pleasure and so forth are qualities of the self and not qualities of sound, you likewise do not state any distinction;
therefore, this too is unestablished.
This also is incorrect.
Why? Because if they were syntactically unified with the ego (ahaṃkāra), there would be a difference of locus [between the self and the experience].
However, it is observed that "I am happy" and "I am suffering.
Therefore, it is not logical that pleasure and pain have sound and other objects as their essential nature.
It is said: No, because [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to "fair-complexioned" and so forth.

For example, just as in the case of "I am fair" or "I am dark," the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) establishes that the self has a different locus from the attributes of the body; likewise, it would be the same for pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, they would not be qualities of the self.
He said: This is untenable because of their separate perception.

Even though the apprehension of [qualities] such as "fairness" occurs as undivided from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), nevertheless, one who first apprehends these separately prior to the self and subsequently apprehends them as undivided is able to establish the determination: "this belongs to this person," and not "to that person."
But pleasure and pain are not perceived separately in this manner;
therefore, this [objection] is incorrect.
It is said in reply: it does not arise in that way.
Why? Because it involves shifting to another line of reasoning (*mārgāntaragamanāt*).
Previously, it was established that [sound] is a quality of the self because it is perceived as inseparable from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*);

but now, by asserting its non-existence despite that [perception] still occurring because it is perceived separately, you have shifted to another line of reasoning and have failed to avoid the fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, because there is no distinction from doubt:
it is precisely for this reason that while the white [color] and so forth are perceived separately, pleasure and so forth are not; thus, this is merely doubt.
Moreover, it is not logical that certainty should arise from the very same source as doubt.

Therefore, it is logical that pleasure and so forth are identical in nature with sound and the rest, because they are apprehended as non-different from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), just like [the qualities of] "white" and so forth. Furthermore,
[otherwise] there would follow the consequence of non-appropriation, due to the failure to determine their own-nature (svabhāva).

If it should be thought that sound and the other [objects] consist of pleasure and so forth— just as fire is taken up as the cause of cooking and yet remains essentially earthen, so too sound and the others might be taken up as the causes of pleasure and so forth, and yet remain essentially qualities of the self—
that too is untenable.
Why? Because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For example, fire, as the instrumental cause of cooking, does not have coreferentiality with the results of the cooking, such that one would say "the cooked fire" or "fire is being cooked. Likewise, since sound and the other [objects] are merely instrumental causes, there would be no coreferentiality [between them and pleasure].
However, it is observed that the word "pleasure" is used for "pain."
Therefore, they are not apprehended for the sake of their objective signs (*nimitta*).
He says: even so, it is not logical that pleasure and the rest have sound and the rest as their essential nature (*ātmabhāva*).
Why? Because of contradiction (*vipratipatti*).
For just as sounds, being of the nature of sound, are perceived by all in the form of sound, so too this [pleasure], being of the nature of pleasure, would be perceived by all in that form;
yet, a disagreement is observed.
Therefore, [it might be argued that these] are qualities of the self.
It is said in reply: No, because they are caused by specific conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*).
For example, there is a misconception regarding sweetness and so forth due to the influence of bile and other [humors].

Nor is there any disagreement regarding pleasure and so forth on the grounds that these [objects] lack qualities such as sound, or because of their connection with specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Nor is it the case that these lack qualities such as sound.
Furthermore, what else?
Because that same consequence would follow even if [the world] were caused;
for this is equally true for one who maintains the existence of causes,
since there is no disagreement regarding the relationship between cause and effect.
It is just like the case of a lamp and its light.
Consequently, even the status of sound and other [factors] as causes for misconception would have to be considered untenable.
Furthermore, one should not attribute a fault that applies to both parties to only one of them.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the Self] desires its own qualities, it might be thought: "Because the primary cause (pradhāna) is characterized by its causal efficiency, it produces pleasure and pain for the Self through the power of the ripening of other [factors]. However, since the primary cause is devoid of desire when it consists of those [qualities], a distinction in its functional arrangement is not tenable.
But this is not so.
Why? Because it has already been stated.
It was stated right at the beginning that even when [a quality] consists of that [substance], there is a disagreement regarding sweetness and so forth because of its subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*).
Therefore, the claim that "consisting of that" implies predominance (*prādhānya*) is an uncertain statement.
He said: Even so, this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is observed even in the past and future.
Therefore, it is not logical that pleasure and the other [feelings] have the nature of sound and the other [objects].
It is said: No, because cognition has memory as its cause.
This connection with remembered pleasure and pain occurs even regarding sounds and other objects that are past or future;
however, through contact with those [objects], it is experienced by the person in that way.

If, however, pleasure and the like were qualities of the person (*puruṣa*), then—just as in the case of things produced by cooking (*pākaja*)—their intensity or mildness would be untenable due to the absence of any specific cause for their production.
Therefore, it is not logical that pleasure and pain have the nature of sound and the other sense objects.
Furthermore:
Because it would follow that there is no liberation;
since a substance is never dissociated from its qualities, if pleasure and pain were qualities of the self, it would follow that the self could never be liberated from them.
Therefore, it is incorrect for those two to be qualities of the self.

If it should be thought that there is a cessation of those [qualities] just as in the case of the dark color and so forth— just as when the atom possesses the quality of darkness, that [quality] ceases through contact with fire, and when space possesses the quality of sound, it remains in a state of being soundless, so too it would be for the self.
This is incorrect.
Why? Because it would entail the consequence of having to specify a distinction, and because it remains a thesis to be proven.

For just as an atom, having abandoned its blackness, takes on a specific color characterized by redness without abandoning its possession of color, so too the self might take on another pleasure from pain, or another pain [from that], through the power of external causes.
It would not abandon them entirely.
Likewise, for us, this point remains to be proven: that space, which has sound as its characteristic, becomes devoid of sound in some state.
We shall demonstrate, however, that sounds such as those of a drum are indeed qualities of that [space]. Therefore, it is illogical for pleasure and pain to have the nature of sound and so forth.
Thus, the self is of an unmixed nature.
Consequently, it is untenable for desire, aversion, effort, merit, knowledge, and mental formations—which possess diverse intrinsic natures and are mutually contradictory—to be its qualities.
Therefore, it is logical that the self is devoid of qualities; and because it is devoid of qualities, it is a mere witness, solitary due to its state of being distinct.
Therefore, this [Self] is distinct from the qualities; consequently, it is solitary and does not exist in association with them.
[The opponent] asks: "What, then, is intended by this distinction of the Self from the qualities?
It is said: it is the distinction of the capacities of the qualities, such as *sattva* and the others, for their own respective effects, independent of any assistance from that [Self].

For the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, while functioning through mutual assistance by means of properties such as illumination (*prakāśa*), do not depend on any assistance rendered by a *puruṣa*.
Rather, they proceed from the mere presence of the properties such as illumination.
Thus the followers of Vārṣagaṇya recite: "The activity of *pradhāna* is independent; even without being appropriated by a *puruṣa*, it proceeds at the beginning of creation."

Since the qualities function independently of any assistance from that [substance], therefore it too does not experience association with them. However, even in the world, there is observed the conceptualization of distinctness despite having a single effect;
for example, "these brothers are separate."
Among these, there is not a single effect;
nor are these distinct things of which one might say "this is one.
That which stands in the middle is neutral because it is an object.
Since this person is the subject (viṣayin), he is therefore neutral.
What is the reason?
Because objects (viṣayas) possess unequal powers.
Furthermore, since deficiency and excellence are logically possible, mutual sublation and assistance would arise;
yet this [perception] is the subject [of cognition].
Therefore, there is no possibility of deficiency and so forth.
Consequently, there would be an absence of consciousness;
furthermore, since attachment and aversion do not have the *guṇas* as their objects because they are of unmixed nature,
would one therefore be neutral?
The state of being a seer arises from consciousness (*caitanya*).

Since consciousness must be extracted from *sattva* and the other constituents—which are modifications of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—and established as residing in the Puruṣa, and since the state of being a seer is not possible for those that are insentient, the Puruṣa alone, by virtue of its consciousness, is the seer; no other distinct principle is so.

The state of being a non-agent [is established], because of the absence of the nature of production. "Production-nature" (*prasavadharma*) means a property whose purpose is production; that which possesses such a property is "one having the nature of production" (*prasavadharmī*).
What, then, is this phenomenon whose meaning is "procreation"?
It is said: it consists of vibration and transformation;
that is to say, because it is devoid of action, it is a non-agent.
Therefore, because it lacks the capacity for procreation, it is a non-agent.
If it is asked how it is devoid of action, the answer is: because of its sentience.
For it is observed that insentient things such as milk possess activity.
Because no one possesses volition (cetanā), the person (puruṣa) is inactive (niṣkriya).
Furthermore, it is because its nature is unmixed;
for things such as milk, which possess activity and the like, have a mixed nature.
And this [Self] is of an unmixed nature;
therefore, it is inactive.
If it be argued that this is so because of its omnipresence (vibhutva), then:
Just as the Pradhāna possesses activity due to its omnipresence, so too must the Puruṣa possess activity due to his omnipresence;
however, that is not the case.
Why? Because [activity] is observed only in association with the two [other] attributes (dharma).
That sovereignty, accompanied by insentience and multiplicity of form, is observed in that which possesses activity, but not in isolation;
however, it is not so in the case of the Puruṣa.
Therefore, this [comparison] is unequal.
Thus, the Puruṣa is inactive; and because of this inactivity, he does not perform the function of cause and effect in relation to Pradhāna.
Why? Because it is observed that only an active potter possesses the capacity to produce an effect from a lump of clay.
This might be so.

It effects the maintenance of that which has been produced by another, like a nurse for a young boy; or it provides the impetus for that which is already established, like one who propels a chariot, a cart, or a machine.

This too is untenable for the very same reason as before. Furthermore, if it were argued that the Person (puruṣa) himself performs the activity of producing effects and instruments, that too is incorrect;
because of the absolute difference between the conscious and the unconscious, the relationship of material cause and its modification (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva) is impossible.
Now, if it is thought that [the self] exists in both ways, that too is not possible, because it would entail the faults of both positions.

It might further be argued that a person creates an effect and an instrument even without specifying a source (yoni) through mere volition (abhidhyāna); this is incorrect. Why? Because volition is impossible in the absence of birth.
It was stated previously, in the refutation of God as the cause, that prior to the transformation of primordial matter (pradhāna), there is no intellect (buddhi) belonging to an intelligent being.
Furthermore, intention is not possible without intelligence,
because it is a function of that [intelligence]; thus, the refutation of a creation preceded by an intelligent agent made there [in the previous argument] should be applied here as well.
Furthermore, the agency of determination has already been refuted.
Thus, by virtue of these seven kinds of non-agency, the *puruṣa* is a non-agent. And it has been said:
"The *puruṣa* does not perform determination, nor does he [perform] maintenance or activity."
Not from itself, not from another, not from both, nor from no cause at all.
This is logical;

therefore, from this very inversion, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation (kaivalya), neutrality (mādhyasthya), state of being a seer (draṣṭṛtva), and non-agency (akartṛbhāva). (Sūtra 19)
Kārikā 20:
Since it is through its connection with the power of consciousness that the Puruṣa alone is the seer, and not any other principle;
and since the Guṇas are the agents, and not the Puruṣa.
Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient;
and likewise, although the Guṇas are the actual agents, the indifferent Puruṣa appears as if he were the agent.

For, through contact with the *puruṣa*, there occurs the activity of grasping, retaining, discerning, speaking, reasoning, and deliberation; this is because of the perception of the instruments (*karaṇa*)—which possess the nature of functioning and are like forms of cognition—as they conform to the operation of the power of consciousness (*cetanāśakti*).

Due to the connection with the active qualities of *sattva* and the others, which are situated within that state [of consciousness], there arises a perception as if the [power of consciousness] itself were permeated by activity.

For in that regard, there appears to living beings this particular kind of knowledge—which is the cause of the seed of existence and depends upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the repeated practice of false cognitions occurring over many periods of time—such as:
"the ear is perceived," "the skin, eye, tongue, and nose," and so forth;
likewise, "the person (*puruṣa*) is the agent of actions."
"The person [is the experiencer] of pleasure and pain.

Therefore, the nature of the instrument as "grasping" and the nature of the person as "agent" are to be understood metaphorically (*bhaktyā*), since they are perceived in one place while actually belonging to another due to contact with a different correlate.
Not from the perspective of ultimate truth. And it has been said:
"Intellect, though presided over by consciousness, is perceived as if it were itself conscious;
and the self, though residing in the agents, appears as if it were the agent and the enjoyer."
He said: If [the self] assumes the form of another through conjunction, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because there is no distinction.

If, due to conjunction with consciousness (*cetanā*), the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth are metaphorically designated as having cognition (*pratyaya-vad-upacāra*), then since this [self] is all-pervading (*vyāpin*), its conjunction with jars and other objects is not precluded; therefore, the metaphorical designation of those [jars] as having cognition would also follow. Alternatively, if—despite the lack of distinction in conjunction—it is only the instruments (*karaṇa*) that are metaphorically designated as having cognition and not jars and the like, [then...]
"In that case, a distinction must be stated. It is replied: "That consequence does not arise, because [the cognition] depends upon capacity, as in the case of crystal and the like."

Just as when there is a particular conjunction with a substrate, between space and a crystal, it is the crystal alone—and not space—that appears in the likeness of the substrate due to its inherent capacity (*śakti*), so too, despite the lack of distinction in the conjunction with the person (*puruṣa*), it is the intellect (*buddhi*) alone that is perceived as having assumed the form of consciousness due to its capacity, and not the jar.
[The opponent] says: This entails the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the person is subject to modification (*vikāryatva*).
Because it assumes another form.

If, then, the person (puruṣa) undergoes the metaphorical attribution of agency and the assumption of a form similar to the object due to its connection with the instruments, it follows that this [person] is also subject to modification (vikāryatva), because it assumes another form like a crystal.
Now, if it is argued that there is no assumption of the form of the object for this [Puruṣa], then the Puruṣa would not have the nature of an instrument.
It is replied: No, because this is accepted figuratively.
The intellect (*buddhi*) attains a form corresponding [to its object] through the occurrence of the activity of the senses directed toward their respective objects.

However, the Person (*puruṣa*) is metaphorically designated as having the form of the intellect—due to mere proximity, due to being endowed with a specific capacity, and due to being the enjoyer of the fruit—just as victory or defeat belonging to a servant is metaphorically attributed to the king.
Yet, he does not actually become of that same form through contact with the intellect.
For this very reason, when the power of volition is present, its agency in regard to purposeful action is denied;
let there not be the undesirable consequence of it possessing multiple natures and so forth upon the assumption that it undergoes transformation into the form of the object.
Therefore, even through contact with an object, the Puruṣa remains unchangeable.

For because it is eternal, nothing can either benefit or harm it. And it has been said: "Just as mustard seeds and the like, when scattered upon the point of a needle, do not remain there because of its extreme subtlety, so too do the pairs of opposites [of afflictions] not remain in the Omniscient One."
Thus [it is said]. However, its status as a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) is innate due to its connection with the power of volition (*cetanā-śakti*).
If this is so, then what [use] are rain and sun to the sky? For the fruit of those two exists only in the skin.
If it is like a hide, it is impermanent; if it is like space, it is equivalent to a non-entity.
Thus, that is incorrect.
Why?

Because, due to the mere proximity of space—which is unchangeable in nature—to clouds, water, dust, smoke, and so forth, its location becomes non-distinct from them; consequently, even though it is absolutely pure, its form appears as if stained.
Nor is there any state of being subject to modification;
thus, this would also apply to the non-Self.
Therefore, it is correct that the metaphorical designation of cognition belongs to the instrument due to its conjunction with the Puruṣa.
And [it is argued that] the Puruṣa’s designation as an agent is merely figurative, due to its conjunction with the guṇas.
To this it is replied: this is incorrect. Why? Because conjunction is impossible.
For when the conjunction between the person and the qualities is postulated, it must be conceived as either produced by the action of one of the two— such as that between a post and a hawk—
or produced by the action of both— such as that between two rams— or produced by a prior conjunction— such as that between two fingers and space.

Is it by way of intrinsic nature, as in the case of fire and heat; or by way of a causal capacity, as in the case of the eye and visible form; or characterized by functional suitability, as in the case of a fish and water?
Therefore, among these, neither conjunction born of the action of one nor that born of the action of both is possible.
Why? Because of their omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
Nor is it natural, because that would entail the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*).

Just as there is no liberation from the inherent heat of fire, so too, because of the inherent nature of the self, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation from the conjunction with the guṇas.
And [if it were argued that this is due to] a causal capacity, what [would follow]? Precisely the same undesirable consequence of no liberation.
The phrase "it does not exist" carries over [from the previous context].
For if conjunction were postulated as being caused by the powers of owner and owned, then because those powers would exist eternally, the consequence of no liberation at all would follow.
Furthermore, that which is characterized as "fitness" (yogyatā) is imperceptible because it consists merely of power; therefore, its existence is unestablished.
Furthermore, because no other purpose is possible:
for that which is conducive to activity is called "suitable" (*yogya*).
Yet, once that very activity has occurred, it is impossible to postulate another cause by setting aside the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Furthermore, if it were accidental, the two-fold restriction would be untenable.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the relationship between the Person (puruṣa) and the qualities (guṇas) is characterized by mere fitness;
it is not arbitrary.
Because it would be impossible to establish a rule for the cause of liberation.

The cause of isolation (*kaivalya*) is that which is the opposite of the cause of conjunction. If the conjunction of the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* were accidental, there could be no cessation of it through knowledge; consequently, the exertion undertaken for that purpose would result in futility. Furthermore, because no distinction [between states] would be possible, another cause [for the conjunction] must be admitted.
It is impossible to conceive [of it as such]; therefore, this too is untenable.
It is not [a cognition] based on an object (*vaiṣayika*).
Because it would follow that there is no liberation.
For if the subject-nature of the Puruṣa were eternal and unceasing, and the object-nature of the Guṇas likewise, it would indeed follow that there is no liberation.
And this much alone would have to be postulated as the conjunction [of the two], were it to be postulated at all.
In every respect, [the claim] is not tenable;

therefore, it is improper to state "due to conjunction with that. It is replied: there is no fault here because conjunction is impermanent and because [the relationship] is conceived as being merely instrumental (*aupakārika*).

In this context, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is of many kinds. For example, there is conjunction preceded by [another] conjunction, as illustrated by such statements as "conjunction is produced by one [action], produced by both actions," and so forth.

Where that [substance] does not exist, it is metaphorically postulated through devotion based on the mere commonality of proximity, just as space is [postulated] in relation to cows and the like by means of their locations. If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence [of such a substance], [we reply: no.
For those [directions] are also metaphorically conceptualized as parts of space because space is partless, so that the fault of being produced and impermanent does not follow.
Therefore, due to the metaphorical application of "parts," the effect is also metaphorically applied.
But the scriptural conjunction is for the purpose of an object.

Since multiple conjunctions are possible there, whereas here [in this case] the person and the internal organ occupy the same location, we say this by metaphorically postulating a conjunction based on the commonality of mere proximity; thus, there is no fault. // 20 //
[The opponent] says: The two types of conjunction have been understood.
However, this other technical (śāstrīya) conjunction based on meaning (*arthanimitta*) is being defined by you.
In this regard, it must be asked: for what purpose does he exist?
It is said:
for the purpose of the Puruṣa’s perception.
"View" (dṛṣṭi) means seeing (darśana). The word "object" (artha) signifies a cause (nimitta). That which has seeing as its object is "that which has seeing as its object" (darśanārtha).
"Caused by perception" (darśana-nimitta) means having perception as its cause, having perception as its reason; such is the meaning.

This is what is being said: although there is no difference in terms of proximity between the self (ātman) and space (ākāśa) and so forth, because the person (puruṣa) is endowed with the power of vision, he [the self] possesses the status of an enjoyer along with the primary matter (pradhāna), which has entered into the state of cause and effect; whereas space and the other elements do not [possess this status], due to their lack of consciousness.
Alternatively, the word *artha* denotes a result (*phala*).

Just as the act of eating ceases when satisfaction is achieved, and the act of going ceases when the destination is reached, so too the conjunction of the Puruṣa with Pradhāna has the purpose of seeing (*darśana*); once that seeing has occurred, the conjunction ceases.
And so he will say: "One [nature] is indifferent, thinking 'it has been seen by me'; the other ceases, thinking 'I have been seen'" (ISk 66).
He says: Even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of cessation occurring at the very same time as the perception of sound and the other objects.
What is the reason?
Even in that state, it can be said that the primordial nature (prakṛti) has been seen.

It is replied: although this is so, nevertheless, just as the conjunction of the Spirit (puruṣa) is for the purpose of seeing and for the purpose of liberation (kaivalya), so too is it for the primordial nature.
Kaivalya (isolation) is the state of the Self characterized by non-association with *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, as delimited by discriminative discernment (*viveka*).
That is its object; thus, this is the "object of isolation.
For even though there is no difference in the act of perception, the *pradhāna* proceeds for the sake of the isolation of the *puruṣa*.
When his intellect perceives those qualities which, due to the predominance of tamas, have assumed the form of effects— namely, the internal [organs] such as the head and hands,

the external [objects] such as cows and so forth, and those that have assumed the form of causes characterized by perception, volition, egoism, and determination— [then it is said to be under the influence of tamas].

When one forms the synthesis of the cognition "I am that" [with the Self], then [the notion of agency] indeed proceeds. But when there is the synthesis of a distinct cognition— namely, that other qualities are primordial (prakṛti), modifications (vikāra), effects (kārya), or causes (kāraṇa), being insentient (acetana) and for the sake of another (parārtha),
whereas "I am other than these— not primordial, not a modification, not an effect, not a cause, not insentient, but for my own sake"— [then the notion of agency ceases].
When that [purpose] is accomplished, it ceases.
This purpose of the Puruṣa— which has the power of vision as its cause and which is delimited by the limit of isolation (kaivalya) for the Pradhāna—
is established even though it is technical in nature.
The union of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man;
this is what is meant:
even prior to the relationship between cause and effect, consciousness (caitanya) is already established in the Puruṣa.
For example, the burning of fire or the cutting by an axe is not manifested when there is no object to be burned or cut;
however, it is manifested at the very moment that [the object] is present.
Therefore, it depends upon a primary cause (*pradhāna*).

Likewise, even primordial matter (*pradhāna*), without the assistance of the Spirit (*puruṣa*), would be incapable of its own activity, equivalent to one whose task remains unaccomplished, and thus it would be purposeless; therefore, it depends upon the Spirit.
In this regard, the teachers call that mutual dependence of the two the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) which constitutes the bond of worldly engagement (*adhikārabandha*).
As for the analogy of the lame man and the blind man, it is intended merely to illustrate their necessary concomitance.

Just as a cripple cannot become possessed of a specific purpose through the power of sight without an eye, and an eye cannot [attain its purpose] without a cripple for a specific purpose, so too the *pradhāna*—though capable of producing effects—is not able to perceive them without the *puruṣa*; and though it proceeds without limit, it does not cease because there is no distinction [to prompt such cessation].
Likewise, although the *puruṣa* possesses consciousness, he cannot be a perceiver in the absence of something to be perceived without the *pradhāna*; thus, he depends upon the *pradhāna*.
Therefore, when conjunction is conceived as being mutually dependent, it is said: "Indeed, bondage for the Puruṣa is not possible without creation;
creation is for the sake of his liberation—oh, how well-spoken is the Sāṃkhya!"
Thus, that is incorrect.
Why? Because it is not the case that this [liberation] is not possible without creation. And it has been said:
"Through the relationship of the seen and the seer, there is the connection between Prakṛti and Puruṣa."
Dependence is designated as bondage by those who know the truth of the scriptures.
Since the person is thus bound by the qualities even without creation,
let this desire of desires go to futility.
Thus, conjunction is established;
from that, creation is produced.

For this creation of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the Great One (mahat), as well as the creation of dispositions (bhāva) such as merit (dharma) and the creation of elements (bhūta) such as Brahmā, proceed based on the causal condition of the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed between primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa).

And that dependence does not cease because of the infinity of Puruṣas; therefore, since those primary principles (prakṛtis) are purposeful, there is no cessation as long as they have not completed their task. // 21 //
Thus ends the fifth lesson and the second chapter in the *Yuktidīpikā*, the commentary on the *Sāṃkhyakārikās*.
Kārikā 22:
In this way, because other causes have been refuted, it is established that this transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) into the manifest state occurs for the sake of the Puruṣa.
In this regard, there is currently a disagreement among the teachers.
Some say that from the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) another reality (*tattva*) arises whose nature cannot be specifically designated; from that, the "Great One" (*mahat*) arises.
According to Patañjali, the Pañcādhikaraṇas, and the Vārṣagaṇyas, however, the Great Principle (mahat) arises from primordial matter (pradhāna).

For others, the authors of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, the position is that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises from the Great Principle, because they admit that the Great Principle is the agent of the notion "I am.
All [schools] agree that the five subtle elements (tanmātra) arise from the ego-sense.
From the *mahat* (the Great One), six non-specific principles (*aviśeṣa*) are produced: the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the *ahaṃkāra* (ego); this is the opinion of Vindhyavāsin.
Likewise, all [schools] agree that the sense organs arise from the *ahaṃkāra*.
However, the opinion of Pañcādhikaraṇa is that the sense organs are elemental (*bhautika*).
Others hold that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) have a single form;
Vārṣagaṇya maintains that they increase by one [attribute] each;
and some say that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) possess forms assumed through their connection with specific formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Others say that they have limited dimensions; Vindhyavāsī’s view is that they are all-pervading (vibhu). Some also state that the substrata (adhikaraṇa) are of thirteen kinds.
"Elevenfold," says Vindhyavāsin;
likewise, for others [the sense-faculties], there is the apprehension of all objects in the great [intellect],
while for Vindhyavāsin it is in the mind (manas).
For others, there is a plurality consisting of volition, self-identification, and determination;
for Vindhyavāsin, however, there is unity.
Likewise, the instrument (karaṇa) has its own nature effaced, being like a deserted village or a riverbed.

However, others hold that the fivefold group [of organs] consists of both natural (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛtika*) cognitions which, being comprised within the impelling members, proceed from the Pradhāna; but it is not so, they say.
For there is a great transgression of the nature of the causes by the Pradhāna.
Vārṣagaṇya maintains that [knowledge] is both very slight and self-originated;
Patañjali maintains that all [knowledge] is self-originated; and Pañcādhikaraṇa maintains that all [knowledge] is originated by another.
Some maintain that the intellect (*buddhi*) is momentary, while others hold that it persists through intervals of time.

Thus, among teachers who hold various such determinations, the Teacher sets forth his own view in order to refute those who assert a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the Great One (*mahat*). [He states: "From primordial matter, the Great One..."
From primordial nature (prakṛti), the Great One (mahān) arises.
"The Great One," "Intellect" (buddhi), "Mind" (mati), "Brahmā," "Fulfillment" (apūrti), "Renown" (khyāti), "Lord" (īśvara), and "Vikhara"—these are synonyms.
It is called "the Great One" because of its greatness in space and its greatness in time.
It is called "great" because it possesses a vast magnitude compared to all things that are produced;
however, according to the position of others, ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) does not exist at all, and thus he says this with the intention of negating that [other view]:
"From that, ego-consciousness [arises]."
From that Mahat, the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises.
Furthermore, in order to refute the claim that "from Mahat the six non-specific principles are produced— namely, the five subtle elements (tanmātra) and the ego," he says:
Therefore, the group of sixteen arises from that.
From that ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), the group of sixteen is produced:
the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the eleven sense organs.
By this very [argument], it should be understood that the proponent of material sense-faculties is refuted.
Therefore, from those sixteen [elements], the five primary elements arise from the five [subtle elements].
From that group of sixteen, the first group of five arises; from that, the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are produced.

Here, although one should say "the great elements," the term "elements" (*bhūta*) is used by eliding the first member of the compound. For the designation "element" applies to the subtle potentials (*tanmātra*), not to earth and the others; however, there is no disagreement among the Sāṃkhya teachers on this point. But the Mīmāṃsakas and Ārhats maintain that the elements are eternal.
In order to refute that [position], this is stated: // 22 // [Kārikā 23] It is said: "From *pradhāna*, *buddhi* arises."
In this regard, it must be stated: what is the characteristic of intellect (*buddhi*)? It is said that intellect is determination (*adhyavasāya*). What is this determination?
The cognition or certainty that "this is indeed a cow" or "this is indeed a person," which is the apprehension of an object, is *adhyavasāya*.
On this point, the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) says: if cognition is the apprehension of an object, it is impermanent.
Why? Because it depends upon causes.
For the apprehension of an object depends upon the proximity of the sense organs and other factors, as well as the absence of obstructions and so forth;
and dependence upon causes is not possible for that which is eternal.
Therefore, cognition is impermanent.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [cognition] is manifested, one might think: "The apprehension of an object is not produced by the proximity of the sense organs and other factors, but rather is manifested.
But that is not so.
Because there are two kinds of defects.
For that manifestation must be either the acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*) or the removal of an obstruction to its apprehension (*grahaṇapratibandhavyudāsa*).
What follows from this? If it were the case that its own nature is produced, then it follows that the apprehension of the object is [itself] produced.
The claim that darkness is the obstruction to the apprehension of objects, and that its removal [is what constitutes perception], is also incorrect; because it is a contradiction.
For it is contradictory to say that there is both an apprehension and an obstruction of it.
Furthermore, because of difference:
for while the manifested objects such as jars do not differ based on differences in the moon, sun, medicinal herbs, gems, jewels, or lamps,
there is indeed a difference among cognitions due to the difference in their objects.
If it should be thought that there is no fault because of the difference in modes (*vṛtti*), just as in the case of clay—
just as the substance of clay remains non-different even when there is a difference in its modes such as the form of a jar and so forth, so too it is with cognition—
that too is incorrect.
Because of their non-difference:
when the intellect is distinct from its modifications, it follows that there must be a distinction in the intellect corresponding to the distinction in those modifications.
Furthermore, the example is unestablished;

for this is yet to be proven: does that very same clay-substance undergo various states of existence such as a jar and so forth, or rather, does something else and something else arise due to the influence of different conditions?
Moreover, there is a difference in the constituent parts.
Or, having approached [the matter], we state the following rebuttal: for that is not a single substance of clay;
rather, it consists of many atoms of clay whose existence is delimited by multiple locations.
Furthermore:
Because of the mention of "distinction from cessation" (*nivṛtti-vibhakti*).
For that clay-substance is indeed perceived even in dependence upon its configuration (*saṃsthāna*),
but there is no perception of the cognition itself without depending on the perception of the object.
Therefore, the example is dissimilar.

If it should be thought that there is no fault because of measurement— namely, that since there is a fixed relationship of primary and subordinate among the constituents such as *sattva* and the rest, their "functioning" (*vṛtti*) consists in their transformation into the respective forms of apprehending objects—
this too is incorrect.
Because both assumptions lead to logical faults:
if manifestation and non-manifestation were the acquisition and abandonment of distinct attributes (*dharmāntara*),
this position has already been answered.

Now, since destruction and origination [belong to the properties], because the property and the substratum are non-different, it follows that from the destruction and origination of the properties, there would also be the undesirable consequence of the destruction and origination of the cognition itself.
Or, if this is not accepted, the fault is that they must be different. And it has been said:
"Because of non-difference, that which is destroyed and that which is originated would be either impermanent or indeed permanent."
For those that have perished, those that have arisen, and those that have not perished, there is never at any one time [a simultaneous existence].
As for what was also stated— that there is a fixed relationship of primary and subordinate members among existence and the other factors— that is incorrect;
for it is precisely from this that impermanence is established.
Because it is impossible for things that are equal to stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal,
and because you admit that sattva and the other qualities stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal, their increase and decrease must necessarily be admitted.
Consequently, it follows that the intellect (buddhi) is impermanent.
Because it is not other than them.
Now, if it is thought that even in that state it remains eternal,
then it follows that cognition is not of the nature of existence (*sat*) and so forth.
Furthermore, this would contradict the principle that there is no distinction between cause and effect.
Therefore, [the claim] that "cognition is impermanent" is stated.
To this, it is replied: as for what was first said—that cognition is impermanent because it depends on causes—that is incorrect.
Why? Because it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
Who here has a misconception as to whether cognition (*buddhi*) might be non-eternal or eternal?
Rather, because of the statement that "the manifest (*vyakta*) is caused and non-eternal," it is certainly non-eternal.

Therefore, this very point is included [in our position]. If it is argued that for this reason alone momentariness [is established], then it might further be said that conditionedness (*saṃskṛtatva*) indeed consists in dependence upon causes.
The conditioned, however, is momentary,
just like a lamp. Therefore, even though impermanence has not been specified as a particular quality, it is precisely momentariness that is established for cognition by this reason.
Why? Because it would entail a contradiction with the subsequent statement.

Even so, the subsequent argument stated for the purpose of establishing momentariness—namely, that "it is impermanent because the apprehension of each object is distinct," and so forth—would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, because the preceding and succeeding parts are contradictory, this entire treatise is not worthy of study.
It does not deserve rejection;

for even if one disregards the fault of refuting an irrelevant answer— on the grounds that others' intellects are fixed upon this [position]— this [argument] is nonetheless not a proof for each [individual case],
because it pertains to the scope of a derivative function (*vṛtti*).

If it is argued that the objection is avoided because the activity known as the apprehension of an object belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*)— which is perfected by its own causes— and depends upon the proximity of the sense organs and so forth,
rather than belonging to the intellect itself, since the two are non-different;

even if one imagines it thus on the grounds that the modification (*vṛtti*) and the possessor of the modification (*vṛttimat*) are non-different, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not cease.

And so it has been said: "The specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) is the function (*vṛtti*) of the triad" (ISk 29). That too is not a contradiction. Why? Because it is a figurative designation (*upacāra*).
It is true that they are non-different, because the activity and the possessor of activity are not perceived as distinct;

nevertheless, even when the function of an axe or similar instrument has ceased, its essential nature does not cease. Thus, by metaphorically attributing distinction, linguistic usage proceeds with reference to various different effects.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that there would also be otherness [between the whole and its parts], because of their absolute identity.

For example, when an army, a line, or a bracelet ceases to exist, there is no cessation of those things arranged therein, nor is there a difference in their causal function, yet there is no otherness.
In this way, it would also apply to the relationship between the occurrence and that which occurs.

Therefore, it is correct that the intellect is not impermanent because the dependence on a cause pertains to the occurrence [of its manifestation]. By this, the dilemma regarding the individual instance (*vyakti*) is also refuted.
Since that [object] is also the domain of the function (*vṛtti*), it has likewise been stated: "Because there is a difference [in cognition] due to the difference in the sense-faculties and so forth.
This too has been stated by this very [argument]:
"In this case, the difference [in cognition] is not due to a difference [in the object]."
Furthermore, [the argument fails] because of inconclusiveness (*anekāntāt*).

Just as there is a difference in reflections due to differences in water and so forth, yet this does not imply that [the reflection] is unmanifested (*avyaṅgyatva*), so it would be in other cases as well.
If it should be thought that there is no fault because another substance (*dravyāntara*) arises, [we reply:]...
The claim that, due to the contact of water with the face, a distinct substance characterized as a reflection arises, and that the face itself is not divided, is incorrect.
Why? Because it is logically untenable to conceive of both [the face and the water] as causes. For it cannot be said that the face is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).

Because of their remoteness, there would be the undesirable consequence that the nose and other organs would still perceive [objects] even when removed from the mouth, just as in the case of things produced by heating (*pākaja*).
As for what was said—that there is no fault because of the difference in the mode of functioning (*vṛtti*), as in the case of clay—let it be so.

However, regarding what was stated—that [the example is invalid] because of non-difference and because the example is unestablished—the non-difference of the mode of functioning has just now been refuted.
And it has been stated in the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that there is no production of earth and the other elements in one way and then another way.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the substance of clay is not a single [entity]," in this case, cognition (*buddhi*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*):
that which is the cause of a single cognition is a single [entity].
In this regard, if the cognition "we" is perceived as having the clay as its manifold object,
then as for what was stated—

that the intrinsic nature of the substance clay is determined apart from its configuration, whereas the nature of cognition cannot be apprehended without the apprehension of an object— [that is not so].
That is incorrect, because non-existence lacks form (*arūpa*). Or, even granting [the point],
just as the mental continuum (*cittasantati*) manifests in various external states and so forth, [so it would be here].
Just as the mere seed exists therein, so too should the intellect be understood.

Just as it is accepted that the continuum of consciousness possesses the form of external objects, yet for those who are asleep, unconscious, or have entered a state of meditative obstruction, there exists only the seed [of consciousness] even in the absence of the form of an object—on account of the statement that "that is some kind of state of consciousness"—why is it not likewise postulated that the intellect (*buddhi*) is also such? Furthermore, as for what was said—that if manifestation and non-manifestation consist in the acquisition and abandonment of other attributes, this position has already been answered—it is as follows: *Note: The provided text contains a reference to a prior argument regarding the nature of manifestation and non-manifestation.*
That is equally true for the other case as well.
Furthermore, since we have already provided an answer to the rejection of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), this position is not being refuted by us in detail.
As for destruction and arising, however, they are simply undesirable [consequences], so no effort is made to offer a rebuttal.

As for what was said— that there exists nothing else that is neither destroyed nor produced, other than that which has been destroyed and that which has been produced— that is incorrect, because it is not accepted.
Who asserts destruction and production such that this [statement] would have meaning in relation to them?
Furthermore, because this would entail your own position:
for you, the continuum is not other than the aggregates that have perished and arisen, and yet there is no fault;
