thus, by some reasoning, it might be argued that "this [continuum] is indeed other," and consequently, the claim that "it is a single continuum" is abandoned.
As for what was said—that there is impermanence due to the increase and decrease of the qualities (guṇas)—that is untenable.
Why? Because of the nourishment by another form.
For when *sattva* attains excellence, it nourishes *rajas* and *tamas*, which undergo diminution in the form of *dharma* and so forth, within the intellect (*buddhi*).

They do not produce a different object, nor indeed do they produce a non-existence; likewise, when sattva experiences an intensity of rajas or tamas, they nourish the intellect in the form of qualities such as deficiency,
but they do not produce a different object, nor do they produce a non-existence.
Thus, even when there is an increase or decrease in its qualities (*guṇa*), because the form (*rūpa*) is replenished, there is no destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, that which was stated—that the intellect is impermanent because it depends upon causes—is incorrect.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that it is momentary because the perceptions are distinct, like the oil-drops in a lamp and so forth, and because there is a difference in sound—[that too is refuted].

To this we reply: it has already been stated that when there is a difference in the apprehensions, there is a difference in the modes of functioning (*vṛtti*), not a difference in the possessor of those modes (*vṛttimat*).
Furthermore, because the apprehension of distinct objects is one.
Or, approaching the matter from another angle, we say: if a distinct apprehension is postulated for each respective object—

in cases such as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), sublation (*bādha*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), duality (*dvitva*), and the negation of excellence (*atiśaya*)— then, likewise, there would be no single apprehension of a manifold form, such as "variegated," "spotted," or "multicolored."
That has been observed;
therefore, this is not a reason for momentariness.
Thus it remains established: cognition (*buddhi*) as ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) is not momentary.
Since the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of the three *guṇas*, when a particular *guṇa* reaches its preponderance, a corresponding transformation of its form arises.
It is asked: upon the preponderance of which *guṇa* does what kind of transformed form arise in the intellect?
To this it is said:
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—
this is the form characterized by sattva.

Although there is a distinction between dharma and the others, the singular number is employed here because the intention is to express their non-difference as being "the intellect" (buddhi) in this respect.

This is what is meant: when *rajas* and *tamas* have been brought under control and the *sattva* residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes predominant, then [the intellect] takes the form of virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Among these, virtue is said to be that portion of *sattva* situated in the intellect which has become a latent disposition (*āśaya*) through the performance of actions prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
That virtue, moreover, is of two kinds.
The first [type of discipline] brings about the enjoyment of desired bodies, senses, and objects in realms beginning with that of Brahmā, and serves as an auxiliary to knowledge and other virtues.
The other [type] is the means for performing rites such as the Agnihotra oblation and the means for practicing restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
Among these, the five restraints (yama) are non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from guile, and celibacy.

Freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food, and vigilance—these are the five observances (*niyamas*). By performing these without violation, the quality of *sattva* becomes established as the underlying disposition for crossing over in such a manner;
it brings about the nourishment of the forms of knowledge and the other [virtues].
This constitutes the first stage, which serves as a ladder to both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*);
established in this, the ascetic becomes fit for the performance of the subsequent stages.
Knowledge is twofold: that characterized by the perception of sound and other sense objects, and that characterized by the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.
In that regard, the means of knowledge characterized by the perception of sound and so forth consists of direct perception, inference, and scripture.

Furthermore, the means of knowledge characterized by the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* is twofold: that which is innate (*apūrva*) and that which arises from practice (*abhyāsaja*).
Of these two, the innate is defined as "reflection (*ūha*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), and study (*adhyayana*)" (YS 1.49).
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) fall under the category of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).

Furthermore, that which is born of cultivation—attained subsequent to the conquest [of the afflictions] preceded by dispassion—is peaceful, stainless, stable, and serves as the antidote to all existence and non-existence.
As the Master will say:
Thus, from the practice of reality, there arises the absolute, pure, and exclusive knowledge that "I am not, nothing is mine, and I do not exist," which is free from error.
Detachment (*virāga*), however, is the clarity of the intellect produced by the practice of knowledge, serving as the antidote to passion (*rāga*).
For him, however, there are four stages characterized by effort (*yatamāna*), withdrawal (*vyatireka*), one-pointedness of the senses (*ekendriya-vaśīkāra*), and mastery (*vaśīkāra*).
Among these, the exertion and enthusiasm directed toward the ripening of the impurities (*kaṣāya*) characterized by the longing for sense objects is designated as "effort" (*yatamāna*).
For a practitioner established in this stage is called a "striving ascetic" (*yatamānaka*).
But when some of the faculties have matured, that is the "notion of distinction" (*vyatireka-saṃjñā*);
for then the ascetic's matured faculties become distinguished from those that are not yet matured—this is the meaning.

However, when one whose all faculties are fully matured has the afflictions (*kaṣāya*) remaining only in the state of mere volition (*saṃkalpa-mātra*), then that is the "notion of a single faculty" (*ekendriya-saṃjñā*).
For the ascetic who has desisted from all desire for the objects of the senses, that single sense characterized as the mind then becomes fully matured.
Even for one who remains in a state of mere conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), this maturity is termed "mastery" (*vaśīkāra*).

For this ascetic, having cut off at the root of conceptualization the mirage of sense-objects, possesses mastery over both the engagement and withdrawal of the senses and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
One-pointed and finding delight in the One, having transcended the stage of ignorance,
he becomes immediately contiguous with the supreme Brahman.
Thus, having understood this fourfold stage of detachment, the ascetic should strive to practice it.

The means for that [attainment] consists of the renunciation of perceived and scripturally revealed objects, which has been taught and will also be described among the forms of contentment; by unifying these and making each successive stage of reality the object of his cognition, he should remain indifferent toward the preceding stage of reality. Sovereignty is characterized by the absence of obstruction.
Furthermore, that which is eightfold— namely, *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*—
among these, *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, and *laghimā*...
Gravity is a specific quality of the elements; from the intellect (buddhi), however, [arise] attainment and so forth. Thus, these fourfold forms of the Great One (mahat) are of the nature of sattva.
He asked: "Then what is the nature of the other quality? It is said:
"The quality of darkness (tāmasa) is the opposite of this."
This [ignorance] is perverted with respect to this dharma and so forth, having the nature of *sattva* and its like; the meaning is that it is *tāmasa*, produced by an excess of *tamas*.
Here, it has been stated that *dharma* is a constituent part of *sattva* perfected through the intention (*āśaya*) resulting from the performance of what is enjoined by the scriptures.

And *adharma* is a constituent part of *tamas* situated in the intellect (*buddhi*), which has attained the state of intention through the performance of obligatory action (*nitya-karma*) enjoined by the scriptures.
And that [ignorance] is also of two kinds: that which brings about the experience of undesirable bodies, senses, and objects, and that which obstructs right knowledge (*khyāti*).

Just as knowledge is twofold—characterized by the perception of sound and so forth, and characterized by the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*—so too ignorance should be described as its opposite.

Just as detachment has four stages, so too does passion have four stages beginning with *yatamāna* (striving); and just as there is eightfold sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the rest, so too is there eightfold lack of sovereignty. Such is this form of *mahat* characterized by *tamas*.

Furthermore, that preeminent form of *tamas*, which serves as the cause for unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the like, is taught by the teachers to be "impurity" (*aśuddhi*), having attained a state of virtual oneness with *rajas* due to their lack of mutual opposition.
The nature of *sattva* is illumination (*prakāśa*).

From these two [statements], the first is the position of the five substrates (*pañcādhikaraṇapakṣa*): just as in the case of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), there is the descent of the impelling portions of knowledge—both internal and external—upon the internal organ, which resembles a dry riverbed for both natural and modified cognitions; likewise, there is the persistence of non-cognition (*apratyaya*) produced by the state consisting of *sāttvika* stability.
That is rejected.
For what reason?
Because it is precisely impurity that, having become exceedingly active, must be turned back, while purity, having reached its culmination, must be set in motion.
Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*) has been explained as having eight forms.
Now we shall explain that *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) which was mentioned immediately prior.
He said: "If that is so, then let this first be stated: what is the definition of this ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)?
It is replied:
"Ego-sense is self-conceit (abhimāna)."
That cognition which arises in the agent, consisting of the self-reflection "I am," is indeed the ego (ahaṃkāra), which is a distinct principle from the Great One (mahat).
Why? Because it has the nature of determining all objects.
But for this [consciousness], [the manifestation] arises from the self-reflection of its own self;
it is not, however, a different object.

Why? Because we accept the non-difference between the material cause and its modification. Indeed, it has already been established at length that, for us, the modification is not an entity distinct from the material cause.
And that [Mahat] is grosser than the Great One (mahat) because of its association with the notion of form.
Why?
Because it possesses differentiation, like time and other such entities.

And because it is a transformation (*vikāra*) of the Great One (*mahat*), which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), this [ego-principle] also consists of the three qualities. Why? Because the nature of the cause is observed in its effect, as in the case of threads and cloth.
Those states inherent in it, namely *sattva* and the others, are designated by the teachers with the terms "transformative" (*vaikārika*), "fiery" (*taijasa*), and "elemental" (*bhūtādi*).
And so the Śāstra says: "From this Great Self (mahadātman), these three selves are produced—characterized as the Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi forms of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra).
'I' alone is their common characteristic;
however, in the activity of the qualities (guṇas), there is a specific characteristic."

He asks: "What, then, is the manifestation of qualities (*guṇapravṛtti*) through which there occurs a specific cognition of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which is of a single form consisting of the notion of 'I' (*asmipratyaya*)?
It is said:
"From that [unmanifest], this twofold creation proceeds."
It is of two kinds: characterized by the sense organs and characterized by the subtle elements. This is called the function of the *guṇas*.
Why? Because it is their effect.
For creation is indeed the effect of the activity of the *guṇas*. Indeed, in the world, we observe the metaphorical treatment of cause as effect;
for example, one says, "He eats rice."
He says: It was previously stated that the group of sixteen arises from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
now, however, it is further stated that from it two kinds of creation proceed.
Therefore, this is improper due to the contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
It is said: No, because it was intended in a general sense.
For when non-difference was intended, we taught that creation is of two kinds by defining it according to the nature of cause and effect;
however, when difference is intended—
The eleven consisting of the sense organs and the five consisting of the subtle elements.
This belongs to the senses, thus it is "sensual" (*aindriya*); its measure is eleven, thus it is "elevenfold" (*ekādaśaka*). The same should be said regarding the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
This creation belongs to the subtle elements—sound, touch, and so forth—thus it is the "subtle-elemental" (*tānmātra*) creation.
And "pañcaka" means that which has five as its measure; thus it is called *pañcaka*.
He will explain later the names, characteristics, and purposes of these sixteen transformations (*vikāra*).
This activity of the qualities (*guṇa*) has been explained.
In that [ahaṅkāra], there occurs the grasping of specific distinctions through the notion of "I"—namely, "I am in sound," "I am in touch," "I am in form," "I am in taste," and "I am in smell.
[The opponent] says: [This is merely] a different designation for the constituents such as *sattva* within *ahaṅkāra*, because [the latter] would otherwise be purposeless.
As for this [claim] that within the ego (ahaṃkāra), other designations—namely vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi—are initiated for the sake of sentient beings and so forth, that should not be stated.
Why? Because it is purposeless.

For there is no purpose whatsoever in assigning different names to the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest when they are situated within a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*), because that would merely result in a proliferation of designations. If, however, this [distinction] is insisted upon as being a distinct principle, [then...]
One attains an abundance of conceptualization,
or rather, the expression of a purpose;
for specific efforts do not arise without a cause.
Alternatively, the purpose must be stated: for what reason is this different designation applied to the *ahaṅkāra*?
Why? Because it is not logical that specific efforts should be accidental.
It is replied: No, because it is the cause of specific effects.

For it is not the case that a different designation is initiated for the commencement of the principles (tattva) from the qualities (guṇa) characterized as the Great One (mahat) and so forth, which possess manifold forms.

However, egoity (ahaṃkāra) is the material cause (prakṛti) of the two stages—the sense organs and the subtle elements—which abound in *sattva* and *tamas* respectively; it is for this purpose that the teachers exert such special effort.

If it is argued that there would be an over-extension to the "Great One" (mahat) because of the admission of specific qualities such as virtue (*dharma*) and so forth, we say no, because [the definition] has been specified.

It has been specified that "the commencement of another principle" [is meant], but qualities (*dharma*) and so forth are not another principle; therefore, there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the Great [Principle].
If it is argued that this is incorrect because no specific qualification is stated, it might be as follows:
But what is the distinction here by which *dharma* and so forth are not a separate reality (*tattvāntara*), whereas the ear and so forth are?
And this is not so; why?
Because the term is applied metaphorically to the mere function;
for it is only to the mere function that the attributes such as *dharma* are metaphorically attributed to the Great Principle (*mahat*).
And thus it is also stated in another treatise: "Dharma is the function of illumination."

However, the distinction between these two is that while a specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*) produced by a function (*vṛtti*) is not a different principle (*tattvāntara*) from that which possesses the function;
therefore, it is correct to say that [the function] is the cause of a specific effect. // 24 // Kārikā 25:
He says: "If this is so, then it must be stated that the activity of this specific effect proceeds from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) bearing such-and-such a name.
It is replied:
"The group of eleven, characterized by the quality of sattva, proceeds from the modified (vaikṛta) ego-sense."
The term "creation" (sarga) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].
The meaning is that the eleven organs, abounding in *sattva*, proceed—that is, they are produced—from the modified (*vaikṛta*) ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*).
And the understanding of them as "organs" follows simply from their being designated as "the eleven."

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word] in the preceding sūtra, the word "organ" (*indriya*) is not mentioned again. He asks: furthermore, what qualities does the creation consisting of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*) possess?
And from what ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) does it proceed?
It is said:
from the source of the elements (bhūtādi), which is the ego-sense characterized by tamas (tāmasa), [proceeds] the subtle elements (tanmātra).

From the *bhūtādi*—that is, from the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) known as *bhūtādi*, which has *tamas* as its predominant quality—the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) proceeds. Indeed, the creation of the subtle elements arises from the ego called *bhūtādi*, which is abundant in *tamas*.
In this context, because the term "subtle element" (*tanmātra*) is already included [in the compound], the specific number is not explicitly stated.
He says: [If so,] the specification of the particular nature [of each] would be purposeless.

It was stated previously that the names "Vaikārika" and so forth are applied to sattva and the other guṇas when they abide in the state of the ego (ahaṅkāra). Therefore, if sattva is expressed by the word "Vaikārika," then when it is said that "the elevenfold creation of the senses proceeds from the Vaikārikas," it is understood that this [creation] is sāttvika.

When it is stated that "from the *bhūta-ādi* [comes] the *tanmātra*," it is understood that this is *tāmasa*. Why? Because there is no possibility that a creation characterized by an abundance of *sattva* could arise from *tamas*, nor that one characterized by an abundance of *tamas* could arise from *sattva*. It is replied: No, because this would imply what is not established [in common experience].
For the purpose of making this very point understood, it is done here:
how is it known that *sattva* is expressed by the word "Vaikārika" and *tamas* by the word "Bhūtādi"?
Regarding the term *rajastaijasa*:
for this technical (*tāntrikī*) convention has an unfamiliar meaning; since it is not established, it is not understood.
He says: "The designation *taijasa* is purposeless."
It is said: No;
both [sound and touch] arise from the fiery element.
This is because of its capacity for both.
This would indeed be so if it lacked the capacity for causal efficiency;
however, it follows that from this luminous [element], both of these—designated as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*)—proceed.

How so? For when the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*) functions as the sense organs, then, because it is devoid of activity, it requires the *taijasa* [ego] as its activator, and the *bhūtādi* [ego] as its differentiator.
Why? Because their differentiation occurs through that very [activity].
Just as fire thrown into fire becomes fire alone,
or water thrown into water becomes water alone, so too does one being produce a distinction within another being, depending upon the contact with other qualities.

However, through association with *tamas*, which is characterized by the primary elements (*bhūta*), [the *ahaṃkāra*] becomes differentiated; and being assisted by *rajas*, which consists of activity (*kriyātmaka*) and is of the nature of light (*taijasa*), it assumes the state of the eleven organs.

Likewise, *tamas*, characterized by the primary elements, proceeding from the *ahaṃkāra* in the form of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), requires the *taijasa* for the sake of activity, and the *vaikārika* as its cause of differentiation.
Why? Because it is to be connected with the phrase: "because of its differentiation by that very [element].
And the scripture says this: "When this Vaikārika [ego] is about to create, this Bhūtādi [ego], being supported by the Taijasa [ego], thus rushes toward the Vaikārika.
Likewise, when that Bhūtādi is about to create, this Bhūtādi, being supported by the Taijasa, overcomes that [Vaikārika] Bhūtādi."
By this reasoning, the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) has been explained as that from which both [the eleven organs and the five tanmātras] are produced from the *taijasa* (fiery) type.
[Objection: It was previously stated that the group of eleven organs proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (modified) *ahaṃkāra*.
Because you state them by way of their general category, we do not understand [your specific meaning].
Therefore, it must be stated: which sense faculties (*indriya*) are intended by you?
It is replied: sense faculties are of two kinds.
The sense organs and the organs of action. Among them,
the sense organs are known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
The ears, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose—these are "karṇa-tvak-cakṣus-rasana-nāsikā.
"Ākhyā" means designation or communication;
those things which have these words as their designations are "karṇa-tvak-cakṣus-rasana-nāsikākhyāni."
The analysis is performed using the dual number due to the distinction of their bases.
These are to be understood as the sense-faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). They are the sense-faculties of the intellect; thus, they are "cognitive sense-faculties" (*buddhīndriya*).
But what, then, is the function of these [senses] with respect to the intellect?
It is said: they serve as the gateway for the apprehension of objects such as sound.
Why? Because the intellect does not operate externally.
Since the internal organ has no outward activity, it is not capable of directly apprehending objects such as sound and the like.
Therefore, it requires another cause characterized by the ear and other senses, which is capable of directly illuminating external objects;
through that channel, its apprehension of objects occurs.
Therefore, it is rightly said that the sense organs (buddhīndriya) are so called because they serve as the gateways for the intellect’s apprehension of external objects.
He asks: "But what, then, are the organs of action (karmendriya)?
It is said: "Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals are called the organs of action. (ISk 26)
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these are speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ.
These they call the organs of action (karmendriya);
that is, the sense-faculties whose purpose is action are the organs of action.
What, then, is action? It is speech and so forth, as will be described later.
Those which perform this [action] are the organs of action.
He asks: How is it known that the sense-faculties (indriya) are entities distinct from their bases (adhiṣṭhāna), and not merely the bases themselves?
It is said: The sense-faculties are separate from their bases.
Because a specific capacity is perceived.

Just as, from the perception of a specific capacity characterized by the determination of objects—which is impossible for the body—one infers that cognition (*buddhi*) is a distinct entity; so too, from the perception of a specific capacity characterized by the apprehension of objects—which is impossible for the locus [of the body]—the sense organ (*indriya*) is inferred to be a distinct entity.
He said: No, because the impossibility is not established.
That the mere substratum cannot apprehend an object, while for something else it can, is a claim that is unproven in both respects.
It is said: this is not unestablished, because that [capacity] is impossible in things of a similar class.

Since other elemental things, such as jars and the like, lack the capacity to grasp objects—despite the fact that such capacity is not denied in the case of the modifications of the *ahaṃkāra*—it should not be inferred that this capacity is denied of the sense organs.
Thus [it is said]. And this is incorrect. Why? Because it would result in a distinction of potencies (*śaktibheda*).
The *vaikārika* is the *sattva* aspect of the *ahaṃkāra*, which is of the nature of luminosity;
from its specific power, the sense organs (*indriya*) arise.
From the efficacy of *tamas*, characterized as the *bhūtādi*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise for the other [aspect].
Because earth and the other elements possess a single nature,
this concentration is therefore "unequal" (asama).
By this, their being composed of primary elements (bhautikatva) is refuted.
He asks: How is it known that there are many sense-faculties, rather than there being only one single sense-faculty—like the mind—which, having multiple bases, could apprehend all objects?
It is said in reply: No, because that would entail the consequence of simultaneous engagement and non-engagement.

If there were only one sense-faculty, like the mind (*manas*), it would have multiple bases for all objects; or else, upon the apprehension of a single object, there would be the apprehension of all objects.
However, a distinction in apprehension is observed; therefore, the sense-faculties are not one.
If it should be thought that the sense-faculties are composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*) because benefit and injury are seen to affect them by means of derivative matter (*bhautika*):
In this world, it is observed that material objects such as jars undergo benefit and injury through material means such as clay, staffs, wheels, strings, water, and hammers.
If the sense organs were not material, they would not be benefited by material applications such as medicinal ointments, nor would they be injured by dust and the like.
And this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is inconclusive (*anekāntāt*).
For example, by means of the physical organs such as the mouth, assistance characterized by perception, retention, and memory is rendered to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
And there is injury [to it] by stones and the like;
yet it does not possess the nature of being derived from the primary elements (bhautika).
The same would apply to the sense faculty as well.

If it is argued that there is a perception of modification because of the manifestation of specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), then the following view may be held: the specific quality of odor belonging to earth is manifested by the sense of smell; that of taste belonging to water by the sense of taste;
and the fiery quality of form by the sense of sight.
The tactile quality belonging to air is perceived by the skin;
the auditory quality belonging to space is perceived by the ear.
Furthermore, it is observed that whatever element manifests the specific quality of another is seen to be a modification of that element.
For example, it is like saying that a lamp possesses luminosity because it manifests visible forms.
But this is untenable. Why? Because it leads to an undesirable consequence.
For one who maintains that water possesses modifications manifested by its specific qualities, it follows that water must be of an earthy nature because it is the cause for the manifestation of odor.
If this is not accepted, then the reason is not conclusive.
In this regard, that which was stated—that the sense organs are elemental because they manifest specific qualities—is incorrect. [26] [The opponent] says:
It was previously established that the eleven sense organs arise from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
Now, the ten faculties—five of cognition and five of action—are being set forth.
To this objection that "this [list] is deficient in categories," it is replied:
it may indeed be so.
If this were all there is to the stage of the senses, what then? [The answer is:
"In this context, the mind is that which forms volitions."
In this section on the faculties (*indriya-parvan*), the mind (*manas*) is to be understood by you as follows:
we state its definition to be "that which forms volitional constructions" (*saṃkalpaka*).
Volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), desire (*icchā*), thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth, are synonymous terms.
It is called the "volitional" because it forms volitions;
this is the defining characteristic of the mind.
Therefore, the existence of this [mind], though not perceived through direct perception, is determined.
Why? Because that [volition] is impossible for the other sense organs, whether taken individually or collectively.
For, having set aside the mind, would you postulate volition for the other sense organs individually or collectively? And what follows from this?
Therefore, volition does not first arise from the sense faculties individually.
What is the reason?
Because their objects are not fixed.
For the objects of the ear and the other [senses], such as sound and so forth, are restricted;
whereas volition has unrestricted objects.
Furthermore, this is because [volition] has the three times as its object.
The functioning of the ear and other senses has the present as its object, whereas volition (*saṃkalpa*) has the three times as its object;
therefore, [the self] is neither distinct from them nor identical with them collectively,
because it would follow that such [volition] would be absent in those who are deaf and so forth.
If it should be thought that volition (*saṃkalpa*) is the function of all the sense organs, like the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth—
just as the vital breath and the rest are functions of all the sense organs, and there is no absence of them when any one of the organs is impaired— then [we reply]: [this is not so].
Thus, volition (*saṃkalpa*) would consist of the functioning of all the sense-faculties together, and it would not exist if even one of them were deficient; however,
this is untenable because [the definition] has been specified as particular.
The functioning of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is devoid of objects, whereas conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) has objects such as sound; thus it is distinguished.

Therefore, since conceptualization is impossible for the sense organs whether they are individually or collectively considered, it is established that this [conceptualization] is the mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the mind (*manas*).
He said: "That must be determined, because of the twofold nature of the faculties;
for two kinds of faculties were taught previously."
In this regard, the mind (manas) must also be determined as to whether it is a faculty of cognition (buddhīndriya) or a faculty of action (karmendriya).
It is said:
that faculty is designated in both ways.
The particle *ca* is read in the sense of "also" (*hy-arthe*).
The meaning is that this faculty is of both kinds;
the mind (*manas*) is not only a faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), but also a faculty of action (*karmendriya*).

If it be argued that this is untenable due to the absence of a restrictive cause (*niyamahetu*), it might further be asked: what here is the restrictive cause by which, despite the lack of distinction in their status as sense-faculties (*indriyatva*), it is accepted that the mind alone possesses the capacity for both types of movement,
while others do not?
It is said:
Therefore, that [consciousness] has the three internal times as its object and functions in both ways.
Because its object pertains to the three times;
here, that whose operation as an instrument extends internally across the three times is "active in both ways," such as the intellect (*buddhi*).
Because it does not directly intend objects and because its objects include the past, the future, and the present, the mind has the three periods of time as its object.
Therefore, it is established that its activity is twofold. // 27 //
In the *Yuktidīpikā*, the commentary on the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*, the sixth chapter [ends]. The section concerning the instruments (*karaṇaparva*) has been fully understood.
*Kārikā* 28:
The section concerning the instruments has been fully understood.
Now, its functions both individually and collectively must be explained.
Since both are being designated, the individual function is stated first,
not the collective function.
What is the reason?
Because it constitutes a supplement to the present topic.
For this discussion concerning the existence of the ear and the other [senses] has been introduced here.
And it has been stated that their existence [is established] because a specific capacity is perceived;
now, this specific capacity is said by us to function distributively.
Therefore, we shall enumerate it.
He said: "If this is so, then let it be stated for what purpose that instrument functions, or what its characteristic is?
It is replied: regarding that which was asked—'for what purpose does it function?'—we say this:

The function (*vṛtti*) of the five [senses] with respect to visible forms and so forth is held to be mere observation. With respect to visible forms and so forth— namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are divided into their own respective particulars— the activity (*vyāpāra*) of the five, consisting of hearing, touching, seeing, tasting, and smelling, is called their function.

In that context, regarding the enumeration of the instruments (karaṇa), since the sense organ of hearing is listed first, there is no purpose for skipping over its specific object; therefore, it should have been stated simply as "of the five [senses] with respect to sound and so forth.
The previous reading, however, is a scribal error.
Furthermore, as for what was asked—"What is its definition?"—we reply: it is held to be mere preliminary observation (ālocanamātra).
"Observation" (*ālocana*) and "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) are not different in meaning.
The word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding any qualification (*viśeṣa*).
For example, when it is said, "In this village, mere alms-food (*bhaikṣamātra*) is obtained," it is understood that there is no other qualification.
When it is said, "The boy studies only the Chandogas," it is understood that he does not study anything else;
likewise, when it is asserted that the function (*vṛtti*) of the sense organs is intended to be mere observation (*ālocana*), it is understood that there is no other specific [function].
What, then, is established by this?
What has been stated by other teachers—that the knowledge of generalities belongs to the sense organs and the knowledge of particulars belongs to the intellect—is thereby refuted.
[The opponent] asks: "But what is the fault in this view, such that it is refuted?
It is said in reply: Since the general and the particular are mutually dependent, there is no contradiction within a single entity; therefore, the conceptualization of one or the other is useless.

If, indeed, there were no cognition of the universal by means of the sense organ, then—given that the universal depends on the particular and the particular depends on the universal—the cognition of the particular would not be precluded wherever there is a cognition of the universal; thus, both would belong to the sense organ.
Consequently, the postulation of an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) would be purposeless.

Or rather, what contradiction could there be between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which possesses specific objects, and [the external object] in its general form? Since both are possible therein, the sense organs would be rendered useless.
Therefore, the sense organ is not a means of cognition (*apratyaya*).
For if the sense organ were a means of cognition, then—just as the internal organ, which possesses cognition, has unrestricted objects—the sense organ would likewise have unrestricted objects.
The same would apply to this [sense-faculty] as well, yet that is not the case;
therefore, the sense-faculty is not a condition (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of its existence transcending time.

If the sense organ were possessed of a cognition, then, just as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which possesses cognition has objects belonging to the three periods of time, this [sense organ] would likewise have them;
but that is not the case.
Therefore, the sense organ is devoid of cognition.
Furthermore, it is because no such memory is observed.
If the sense organ were the causal condition, then just as the internal organ—which possesses conditions—undergoes the production of its initial form, the same would occur here;
however, that is not the case.
Therefore, it is established that the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is not a [sufficient] condition.
It is replied: No, because it would entail the consequence of requiring another cause.
If the sense-faculty were an illuminator like a lamp, then just as one seeks another instrument for the objects such as jars that have been illuminated by it, so too would it be in this case.
And this is not accepted;
therefore, the sense organ is not an illuminator like a lamp.

If it should be thought that [the objection] is incorrect because of the existence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [then we reply]: there exists another cause characterized as the intellect (*buddhi*) which perceives the object illuminated by the sense organ, just as a lamp [illuminates].
Therefore, this is merely a restatement of the opponent's position, not a refutation;
however, that is not the case.
Why? Because it would follow that either the lamp or the sense organ would not be employed.
Since both the sense organ and the lamp are illuminators, it follows that one or the other would fail to be employed.
Why? Because there is no capacity for those performing a single function to act simultaneously.
Furthermore:
because of the abandonment of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

For one who asserts that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) directly perceives external objects illuminated by the sense organs like a lamp, the very existence of the internal organ is lost. Therefore, the capacity of the internal organ is untenable.
If it is argued that this capacity belongs to the person (puruṣa), we say no, because it would follow that the instruments (karana) are rendered useless.
For one who maintains that the person (*puruṣa*) is capable of directly apprehending objects, it would follow that the sense organs (*karaṇa*) are useless.
Therefore, it is correct that the sense organ is the apprehender (*grāhaka*), and not an illuminator like a lamp.
He says: Let it be granted, then, that the activity of the sense organ is merely an apprehension (*grahaṇamātra*) and is non-cognitive (*apratyaya*).
Is there no distinction between the apprehension, the cognition, and the manifestation?
It is said: through contact with the object, the modification of the sense organ assumes the form of that object; this is "apprehension" (*grahaṇa*).

Likewise, following the pattern of the object and the modification of the sense organ, there arises the determinate cognition (*niścaya*), such as "this is a cow," "this is white," or "it is running"; this is "cognition" (*pratyaya*).
Likewise, when there is contact with an object, the modification (*vṛtti*) of the auditory and other senses acquires that same form; this is its "presentness.

However, from the experience of the apprehension, an impression (*saṃskāra*) is deposited, and memory preceded by that [impression] arises; thus, the cognition has objects belonging to the three times. This is the distinction between these two. External light, however, does not assume the form of the object.
However, due to the processing [of the object], the earthy shadow— which acts as an intermediary— becomes fit for the manifestation of jars and the like,
serving to assist the eye;
or, according to others, it serves both the eye and its object.
Therefore, it is established that the lamp and so forth are illuminators,
the ear and so forth are perceivers, and the internal organ is the instrument of determination.
Now, what is the function of the organs of action? It is said: the Naiyāyikas, however, state as follows—"The sense organs—nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear—are derived from the elements.

By the phrase "from the elements," it is established that the definition of the sense organs as the apprehension of their respective objects is possible only if they have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*), and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the causes of those sense organs are the elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
From these five, respectively, arise the five sense faculties: the nose, tongue, eye, body, and ear.

Regarding the statement "having the primary elements as their nature" (*bhūtaprakṛtitva*), when explained as having the primary elements as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this applies to all five. However, "having the primary elements as their cause" (*bhūtakāraṇatva*) applies in the same way to the other four.
As for the ear, however, its status as a sense organ must be somehow justified through conventional usage by intending it to be a portion of space delimited by the ear-canal.

Thus, since the sense organs, being composed of the elements (*bhautika*), are capable of perceiving their respective objects, their definition as such is established; therefore, it is said that they "arise from the elements."
This, however, is not accepted by the teachers of Sāṃkhya.
For thus the elders of the Sāṃkhya school have said: "The sense-faculties, being derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), are capable of accomplishing their object, and not otherwise.
For indeed, an instrument, by virtue of being an instrument, acts by reaching its object."
Furthermore, how could material sense organs reach objects located at a distance?

However, for those [organs] derived from *ahaṃkāra*, because they are all-pervasive, it is easy to explain their capacity to reach [the object], since the modification (*vṛtti*)—consisting of the transformation into the form of the object—is not distinct from the possessor of that modification (*vṛttimat*). Moreover, their being derived from *ahaṃkāra* accounts for their grasping qualities (*guṇa*) that are both large and minute.
Not if they were composed of the elements (*bhautika*).
For if they were composed of the elements, the instrument would grasp an object only in its own dimension.
He asks: "Then what is the function (*vṛtti*) of the organs of action (*karmendriya*)?"
It is said:
speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the five [elements].
The functions of speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals should be understood respectively as speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure.
Regarding this, "speech" (vāc) is so called because one speaks by means of it.
Therefore, that collection of phonemes capable of conveying meaning—characterized as words, sentences, verses, and treatises—is the object of the organ of speech, and nothing else.
"Ādāna" means that by which something is taken up (*ādīyate*). The prefix *āṅ* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).

Consequently, whatever constitutes the entirety of grasping—such as washing, wiping, touching, reciting, hurling, crafts, physical exercise, and so forth—that alone is the "object of the senses" (*indriyārtha*), and nothing else.
Viharaṇa is a distinguished kind of taking (haraṇa).

Therefore, that which consists of walking on even or uneven ground, ascending and descending, turning around, dancing, physical exercise, and so forth—that alone is the object of the sense-faculties, and nothing else.
Likewise, utsarga is an excellent kind of emission (sarga).
It is nothing other than that.
Therefore, the emission of that which has been transformed by what was eaten and drunk, following the path of the correct stream, is the sense-object (*indriyārtha*) and nothing else.
Thus, bliss (*ānanda*) is bliss by pervading [all].

And therefore, that alone which is characterized by the production of the eye [of consciousness] through uncommon joy is the object of the sense-organ (indriyārtha), and nothing else. [Objection: It was previously stated that the function of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) has not yet been described.
Since it follows the order of creation, the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*) ought to be described first.
What is the reason?
For in this way, the order of creation is maintained.
Or rather, the purpose for the difference in sequence must be stated.
It is replied: No, because it is preceded by the functioning of the sense organs;
for the internal organ has as its activator the cognition [arising from] the functioning of the sense organs.
And so he will say: "Whether it be seen or unseen, the activity of the triad is preceded by that" (ISk 30).
Therefore, the Teacher provides that instruction prior [to the discussion of the creation sequence].
[The opponent] says: That is impossible.
Because pride (*abhimāna*) is mentioned first in the treatise (*śāstra*).
For the treatise says this: "O friend, what indeed is the designation for that which enters into the youth situated in the mother's womb?
[The answer is: "This is the noble consciousness (*saṃvit*) of 'I am' (*asmi*)."
Likewise, simultaneously with the manifestation of the arrangement of cause and effect, one awakens to the realization, "I am the body of majesty.
For even those [mental states] that have proceeded forth become unmanifest as mere "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra).
And the scripture is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) should have been mentioned first.
It is replied: because it is intended [to be mentioned] for the purpose of indicating that [the self].
This is true; at the very moment the arrangement of cause and effect is accomplished, this majestic consciousness "I am" arises in relation to each substrate (upadhi).
However, the cognition of objects such as sound is produced by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and has the ear and other sense organs as its instrumental cause;
this is what is intended by the word "preceding" (pūrva).
And it is not logical to designate the effect while bypassing its instrumental cause.
Alternatively, we should not have asked this at all, namely, that a description of the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) should be provided.
What is the reason? Because the specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) constitutes the function of the triad.
*Svalakṣaṇya* is simply *svalakṣaṇa*;
it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) used in the sense of the base word itself.
However, the state of being "other" (*anyabhāva*) arises because the word for time intervenes.

Just as it is impossible to describe the essential nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*) because of their subtlety, and for this reason only their function (*vṛtti*) is taught by way of definition;
so too, because the ear and the other senses are subtle, their definition cannot be stated, and thus only their function is mentioned, not their definition.
And this very thing constitutes their defining characteristic:
that which is capable of perceiving sound is the ear;
the same should be stated for the others as well.
The definition of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*) has been stated as "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth.

By declaring that very [definition] to be their "function" (*vṛtti*), and by stating the definition of the ears and other [senses], he makes known the non-difference between the function and that which possesses the function (*vṛttimān*).
Otherwise, just as ascertainment and so forth are the definitions [of the internal organs], it would be said that for the five [senses], the mere perception of form and so forth is their definition.
But it is not the function (*vṛtti*).
Just as with the ear and other senses, determination (*vyavasāya*) and so forth are called the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest,
but they are not their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the fact that the teaching is otherwise serves as an indicator that there is a difference between the function and that which possesses the function; thus has the instrumental function (*karaṇavṛtti*) been explained.
This very [function] is "uncommon" (*asāmānya*).
The word "this" (*sā*) refers back to the previously mentioned function.
By the pronoun "this" (eṣā), he points directly to that very same [entity] which has been drawn back by the relative pronoun;

by the word "it exists" (bhavati), which will be stated later, he makes known its possession of that property through the manifestation of another attribute; and by the term "non-common" (asāmānya), he explains its specific characteristic.
"Common" means "shared"; it does not mean "not common. What is intended is that it is restricted to each respective instrument.

This function, beginning with determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth, which has been enumerated as belonging to the section on the instruments (*karaṇaparvan*), is specific to each individual instrument when they are considered separately.

Consequently, the non-confusion of the essential natures of these [instruments], such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest—which are indicated by their status as causes for specific effects—is established.

[The opponent] says: Since the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are mutually dependent, the universal is also expressed by the mention of the particular; therefore, when it is stated that "the function of the instruments, beginning with determination, is particular," it follows by implication that—
"Since there is also a common mode of occurrence,
that too must be explained. It is said in reply:
The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.
This common function of the organs is the "common function of the organs" (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*).
Those whose first is *prāṇa* are the "prāṇa-first ones" (*prāṇādyāḥ*),
namely the five— *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*— which are to be understood as the collective function of all the organs.
"In the Vedāntas as well, it is said that *prāṇa* is accompanied by all of these.
[The opponent] says: "This is incorrect.
Why? Because it is logically impossible for a substratum (*dharmin*) to exist within another substratum."
The word "function" (*vṛtti*) denotes an operation.
And it is not possible for one property to be the operation of another property.
It is replied: No, because the cause is metaphorically designated as the effect.
This is true:
it is impossible to conceive of one substratum existing as the occurrence of another substratum.
However, the air, being impelled by the operation of the common instrument [of speech], attains the status of its effect because it is directed toward that [operation].
In that regard, having applied the metaphorical designation "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) to the wind that performs functions such as breathing, it is said: "The winds are five, beginning with *prāṇa*.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because their impulsion is not established, one might ask:
how is it known that this activity belongs to the wind impelled by something else, and not to an independent wind?
It is said: [The difference] does not arise from itself, because it is impossible for that [difference] to be non-distinct from it.
This distinct action of the wind must either be accidental or arise from itself.
Or because it is distinct from the activity of the instruments (*karaṇa*).
What follows from this? First, [the motion] is established by its own nature (*svataḥ*).

Why? Because of the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) [of the argument] everywhere; for if the movement of air through the directions were admitted as being inherent (*svābhāvika*), then such movement would be possible everywhere.
Consequently, the occurrence of falling obliquely and so forth would be destroyed, and not otherwise.
Why? Because it is not observed.
For the capacity of earth and the other elements to impel wind is not observed anywhere. If it is argued that this is seen in bellows and the like, we say no, because those have other causes.
In this case as well, since Caitra’s activity is perceived, one must necessarily admit that another cause is being perceived.
If you say it is the self (*ātman*), no; for action [in the self] has been refuted.
This has already been established previously: the self is devoid of action.
And the impelling of that which is devoid of action is not tenable. Nor can it be without a cause, because specific natures do not arise spontaneously.
Therefore, that which is caused by it is the activity of the entire set of instruments (karaṇas).
And this wind, being one alone, becomes designated by various names due to its specific movements through different locations,
just as the single Devadatta is called a "cook" or a "reaper" in certain contexts.
That is incorrect. Why? Because it is contradictory for there to be a simultaneous mutual intensification;
for it is indeed accepted that each subsequent wind is stronger than each preceding one.
This [simultaneous occurrence] is not possible for a single person at one time.
Therefore, it is established that there are five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.
What, then, is the defining characteristic of these [vital airs], beginning with prāṇa?

It is said: the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth are of two kinds—those with internal functions and those with external functions. Among these, it is called *prāṇa* because it moves forward (*pragamana*) and because it flows out through the mouth and nose (*praṇati*).

That wind which moves through the mouth and nose is designated as the internal functional wind called *prāṇa*. Whatever is known as "inclination" (*praṇati*) among beings— for example, "this army is inclined," or "this tree is inclined"— [is also that wind].
He is devoted to the Dharma, he is devoted to the goal, he is devoted to desire.
This [state] is inclined toward knowledge;
or else, in those who are its opposite, this is the outward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
It occurs only with respect to living beings.
Indeed, this becomes manifest here,
such as in one overwhelmed by great suffering, or separated from a great kinsman,
or like a bull of the Surabhi breed that has been reunited [with its herd].

Or, it is so called because of its perception of a buffalo that has descended to a watering place, and because of its downward movement. This internal wind, which moves downward while drawing up the essence, the bodily constituents, semen, urine, feces, flatus, menstrual blood, and the fetus, is designated as the *apāna* (downward-moving wind).

Furthermore, as for that which is called "departure" (*apakramaṇa*) among living beings—such as saying, "This person has departed from virtue and so forth, or from their opposites"—this is indeed an external function of the *apāna*.
This occurs specifically within the domain of the *apāna*.
And why is this [function] more powerful than the upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*)?
For this [speech] restrains and holds back that vital breath (prāṇa) which is moving upward, keeping it right here below;
thus it becomes manifest in this case.
It is just as when one is stepping over a centipede that is writhing near a well or near a pit.
It is called *samāna* because it abides in the heart and because it exists together [with the other vital breaths].

That which abides in the heart between the *prāṇa* and *apāna* is the internal function of the *samāna* wind; and furthermore, "existing together" refers to the state among beings of delighting in pairs, such as, for example, "together in servitude."

"I shall sacrifice together with them, I shall practice austerity together with them, and I shall live together with my wife, sons, kinsmen, and friends; this is the conduct of those who are outsiders.
Thus he becomes one whose sphere of activity is the same as theirs.
This [breath] is indeed more powerful than the prāṇa and apāna;
for it, being situated in the middle, controls these two, the prāṇa and apāna, as they move upward and downward,
and restrains them right there in the middle.
And this very [nature] becomes manifest here,
just as in the case of a dog whose strength has been exhausted,
or an ox that has carried its load.
Or, like that of a ewe tormented by heat, it causes the body to crack and break apart bit by bit.

At the end of life, having released the inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) of all living beings, he casts off the body, moving it unevenly like two horses whose traces have been unloosed—one upward and the other downward.
And because it ascends to the head and elevates the self, it is called *udāna*.

That internal wind which, having transcended the locations of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna* breaths, takes up the essence and the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and ascends to the head, and then, being struck back and turned downward, becomes the cause for the manifestation of sound— characterized by phonemes, words, sentences, verses, and texts— due to the specificities of the vocal organs (*sthāna*), articulations (*karaṇa*), and secondary efforts (*anupradāna*), is called the *udāna*.

Furthermore, whatever is called self-exaltation among living beings— for instance, thinking "I am superior to one who is inferior," or "I am equal to one who is my equal," or "I am superior to one who is my equal"— [is also a conceit].
He is either equal to one who is superior,
or superior to one who is superior;
in such a case, there may be pride regarding his form, but he is one who has attained true knowledge.

For example, when there is a great difference [in qualities], one thinks, "I am only slightly different," or "I possess qualities" when compared to one who lacks them; this is the operation of external exaltation (*udāna*).
This indeed occurs only with respect to the object of exaltation;
it is certainly more powerful than the former [types of pride].
How so? For he leads these—namely, the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth—which exist above, below, and in between, upward alone; he elevates them upward.
And he becomes manifest here for one who sees, for example, cold water being sprinkled, or a sword that has been unsheathed and raised.
And because it pervades the body and is absolutely inseparable from it, it is called *vyāna*.

That which, pervading the body from the hair to the nails, effects the distribution of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) such as the nutrient fluid (*rasa*), the arrangement of the elements such as earth, the throbbing of the vital points (*marman*), and the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—that is the internal function of *vyāna*.
Furthermore, there is a certain absolute inseparability among beings, such as when a devoted wife follows her husband even in death.
"May this very person be my husband even in another life," [one thinks] regarding dharma and its opposites; thus, this external object alone has power over the pervasive [vitality].
And this is the most powerful of all.
How so? For when the body-staff is pervaded by this, there occurs a state of equilibrium among the vital breaths and other factors that have been brought under its control.
This very [vital air], existing as an inseparable concomitant of living beings at the time of death, becomes manifest.
For example: "Alas! My feet have become cold; the ankles, shanks, thighs, hips, belly, chest, and throat [are cold]; there is only a rattling sound in his throat"—this is the external *vyāna*.

Thus, these five winds, beginning with *prāṇa*, have been explained as indicated by their specific locations and functions; the common function of the organs (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*) is their impeller. And this is called "effort" (*prayatna*) in other systems (*tantrāntara*). Furthermore, that [effort], which persists due to the force of the cultivation of impressions (*saṃskāra-bhāvanā*) such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, constitutes life. As it has been said:
The function of all the internal organs is like that of a lamp;
it is non-luminous, of the nature of activity, the life-force, and the sustainer of the body.
As long as that [vital breath] remains unobstructed, it overcomes the wind;
as long as it is not enveloped by the qualities such as dharma and so forth, the human being lives, for it is characterized by an abundance of rajas.
And here, by the force of the mention of the "functioning of the general organs," there are the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa;
the sense organs constitute the sixth;
and the action organs constitute the seventh.
"Pūraṣṭama" (the eighth stage of *pūra*). The term "pūri" refers to the consciousness (*saṃvit*) situated in the state of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*).
For it says therein: "In that [state]..."
Since the effect, which resides within consciousness and the ego-sense, fulfills the cause, it is therefore called *pūrī* (the fulfiller),
appearing as the eighth [tattva] for the enjoyer.
And that consciousness, which resides in the ego, is perceived by the *puruṣa* as residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone;
for it will be stated: "These specific qualities of the *guṇas*, being like lamps, are distinct from one another."
Having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, they deliver it to the intellect.
Since the intellect accomplishes every experience for the Puruṣa,
therefore it alone is called "the full" (pūr).
And the treatise says this: "The five winds are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
the sixth is the mind;
the seventh is the nose; and the eighth is speech."
By the mention of speech, the category of the organs of action is included;
by the mention of the mind, the category of the organs of cognition is included.

Thus, this group of eight, beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is transformative (*vaikārika*) in nature, serves as a constant pillar-like support for every limb of the *kṣetrajña*—the witness of the body composed of the qualities (*guṇa*)—as it assumes its physical form.
It is uncuttable, indivisible, unburnable, indestructible, and unshakable;
whereas external material things, which are impermanent and comparable to grass, clay, or stones, are subject to accumulation.
He asks: from what, then, does this activity of the vital breaths and so forth proceed?
It is said: that [rajas] arises from the wombs of karma.

For when rajas has fallen away from the Great One (mahat) and become modified, there are five wombs of karma corresponding to the egg: steadfastness (dhṛti), faith (śraddhā), happiness (sukhā), the desire to know (vividiṣā), and the lack of desire to know (avividiṣā). And it is said:
"He who has fallen from the Great One but has not yet attained the characteristic of knowledge..."
Activity [is the cause], because it is the source of knowledge; that source is like a hen's egg.
Their characteristics, objects, true nature, and endowment with qualities are as follows.
Among these, the characteristic is first: fortitude (*dhṛti*) is non-deviation from one's resolve.
Faith (*śraddhā*) is the state of being a seed consisting in the sense of necessity regarding tasks prescribed in the scriptures, without aiming for any reward.
For the mental application (*ābhoga*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is characterized by the desire for the fruits of what is seen or heard, is pleasure. The desire to know is *vividiṣā*;
the cessation of that is *avividiṣā*.

In this regard, when a living being—whether following its habitual conduct in auspicious or inauspicious actions, and whether desirous of knowledge or not—discards the body, it enters that very same womb of karma (*karmayoni*). Having entered it, it brings that very [womb] to fruition.
This, then, is the true nature of the characteristics [of rebirth]. And it is said:
He who does not fail to keep his promise regarding speech, action, and resolve—
he who is steadfast in that and true to his pledge— this indeed is the characteristic of fortitude.
Freedom from envy, celibacy, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
austerity, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and purity— these are recorded as the characteristics of faith.
But he who, seeking happiness, pursues knowledge, ritual action, or austerities,
and is constantly devoted to expiation— he indeed abides in happiness.

Duality, unity, and separateness; the eternal, the conscious, and the unconscious; the subtle; the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkārya), and the theory that it does not (asatkārya)—these are what ought to be investigated by one desiring knowledge.
Like one who has drunk poison and fallen asleep in a state of intoxication, this lack of desire for knowledge is the constant source for those who meditate;
it is declared to be the natural course of existence that brings about the destruction of both the body and the instruments of action.
Furthermore, the true nature of the objects is as follows: fortitude has all things as its object;
faith has the stages of life (āśrama) as its object;
and pleasure has both the perceptible and the scriptural as its object.
The desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has the manifest as its object; the absence of the desire to know (*avividiṣā*) has the unmanifest as its object.
Furthermore, the conjunction of the qualities (*guṇasamanvaya*) is a fortitude (*dhṛti*) abounding in *rajas* and *tamas*.

Faith (*śraddhā*) is characterized by an abundance of *sattva* and *rajas*; pleasure (*sukha*) is characterized by an abundance of *sattva* and *tamas*; and the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is characterized by an abundance of *rajas*.

"Desire for knowledge is characterized by an abundance of *tamas*. And it has been stated that he who knows the true nature of the five wombs— their definitions, their objects, their reality, and their composition of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*)— him indeed I consider a supreme bull among men.
Thus have the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the sources (yoni) been described.
Having understood these two, one should follow the correct path.

However, because of the cessation of the state of being governed by the means of passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and dharma, the internal functioning of the vital breaths here is irreversible, owing to its being free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhika).
The external application, however, should be employed by taking the path and the non-path as its object.
How so? It is said: first, the inclination toward the vital breath must be directed solely toward objects such as the Dharma;
for from that, there arises an increase in one's being (*sattva*).
And from the increase of *sattva*, there is the attainment of the forms of progressively higher levels of cognition.

However, the departure from the objects of *apāna* is the very removal [of the mind] from objects such as *dharma*; for in this way, there is the diminution of *tamas* which takes the form of the objects of phenomenal manifestation (*khyāti*).
Consequently, there is the attainment of the forms of progressively higher levels of cognition.
Likewise, one should act in accordance with the nature of sentient beings and their companionship regarding common objects;
for the scripture says: "One should always delight in sentient beings and form unions with sentient beings.
However, self-exaltation is a matter for generosity.
Having abandoned the final form of the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-parvan*), one should eliminate it through its antidotes.
One should cultivate the absolute inseparability of the object of the pervasive wind (*vyāna*) within the very object of knowledge.
One should take up only the seed-nature of reality (*dharmatā-bījatā*) of the four wombs (*yoni*).
One should also cultivate a lack of desire for those things that cause undesirable results.

Thus, being inclined toward the Dharma and other virtues, having turned away from their opposites, delighting in sentient beings, with pride eliminated, and established in knowledge, one who possesses a pure source of birth will before long attain supreme Brahman.
And it is said:
Having properly established the external movement of the vital breath upon the right path, the wise one,
with the impurities of mental distraction ceased, certainly attains the immortal state.

Having established the five wombs as having dharma and so forth as their causal signs, one should proceed once they are fully ripened; having cultivated them, one should not go back to that state below.

Thus has been explained the function of the instruments, both individually and collectively. [Sūtra 29] [The opponent] asks: Is this function of the fourfold instrument with respect to each object, such as color-form and so forth, simultaneous or successive?
If it is asked, "Whence comes this doubt? it is because [the phenomenon] is observed in both ways.
Here, the simultaneous operation of [cognitions] directed toward a single object is observed;
for example, in the case of the eyes or the mind with respect to the lunar disc.
And it proceeds gradually, just as in the case of honey, water, and milk in a jar;
furthermore, the four sense organs have a single object as their domain.
Therefore, we have a doubt: does its activity occur simultaneously, like that of the eye and the mind?
Or is it like honey and so forth, occurring in a gradual sequence?
It is replied: Let it be stated first according to what is observed;
what do you consider to be logical in this matter?
"If you will teach it correctly, what is the point of persistence? We shall accept that very thing.
If this is so, therefore, our view is that there is a simultaneous operation of the fourfold [cognition].
The word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction, meaning "simultaneously indeed.
For the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the sensory organs (*buddhīndriya*) occupy the same location.
In that case, it cannot be said that—given the presence of capacity and the connection with an object—the activity occurs for one and not for another.
Furthermore:
because no sequence is perceived in cases such as the thundering of clouds.

For if the operation of the ear and other senses, along with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), toward external objects were indeed sequential, then a sequence would likewise be perceived even in instances such as the hearing of the thundering of clouds or the sight of a black snake.
But it is not so perceived;
therefore, the fourfold operation occurs simultaneously with respect to the external object.
To this it is replied: regarding what was stated—that the operation of the ear and the other senses and that of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) occur at the same time—we say:
This is incorrect.
What is the reason? Because for us...
And its sequence has been specified;
the word "its" (tasya) connects with all four [of the preceding items],
and the word "and" (ca) serves to emphasize.
The meaning is "only gradually.
For it is only gradually that the external and internal organs' functions converge upon a single object.

As for what was stated—that if there were a real connection of capacities among things occupying the same location, the absence of such function would be untenable—[that objection is addressed as follows].
To this we reply: this would be like the case of the eye and the skin.

Just as, when the eye and the skin occupy the same location and there is a possibility of contact with their respective objects, only the touch residing in dust, smoke, sunlight, and so forth is perceived, and not the color;
so it would be here as well. Therefore:
Thus, the operation of the four [senses] occurs respectively with respect to both the perceived and the unperceived;
furthermore, by the term "unperceived," there is here the inclusion of objects that are past, future, or obstructed.
In that regard, the past is of two kinds:
that which has its object perceived and that which has its object unperceived.
Here too, it is the recognition of that which has its object perceived which is intended.
Memory has as its object that which has not been perceived;
it arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*), from scripture (*āgama*), or spontaneously.
And so it has also been stated by Vṛṣagaṇavīra: "However, knowledge of objects that are future or obstructed [from perception] arises from a logical mark and from scripture. And he says:
Perceptual knowledge is said to arise from the contact between the sense organs and their objects;
that same [knowledge], when it has become supersensuous through repeated cultivation, is memory.

That very same cognition, which depends upon mental cultivation, when it arises again at a later time with respect to that very same object together with the sense faculty, is called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
In that case, there is no doubt that the sequence does not exist for each [perception].

Furthermore, regarding what was said—that because a sequence is not perceived in cases such as seeing a cloud, hearing thunder, and spotting a snake, the four [faculties] function simultaneously—we reply: this too is incorrect.
Why? Because:
The functioning of the triad is preceded by that.

To begin with, the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*) do not possess the capacity to directly apprehend external objects; for if they did, it would follow that the internal organs are unnecessary and that the ears and other sense organs are redundant.
Furthermore, it would entail the absurd consequence that the state of being a door and a doorway would be mutually obstructed.

Therefore, the sense organs, such as the ear, must necessarily have a prior connection with their objects, even in cases such as the thundering of clouds; subsequently, however, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) encounters that [connection]. Thus, there is a sequence here as well.

In this regard, what was stated—that in cases such as the thundering of clouds, there is a simultaneous operation of the fourfold [internal organs] despite the absence of a sequential order—is incorrect.
However, others have demonstrated a different interpretation:

namely, that "of the fourfold" refers to the four internal organs—the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—together with one external organ, either the ear or the eye; such is the meaning.
Regarding this, the former teachers have taught that its operation is simultaneous with respect to what is seen— that is, the present— whereas the Teacher [Vasubandhu] maintains it is successive;
furthermore, with respect to what is unseen— the past and so forth— it is indeed successive, occurring only in a gradual sequence.
For the activity of the triad of internal organs is preceded by that [perception], being preceded by the external sense organs;

since a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is exactly as the experience was, and memory is exactly as the mental impression was, in this way, the activity is preceded by the external sense organs. // 30 //
Kārikā 31:
It is asked: "Furthermore, does the operation of these instruments occur with a restriction to their own respective objects, or rather by way of transgression?
It is replied: "Has it not already been stated that the operation of the five [senses] toward form and so forth is held to be mere observation (ālocana-mātra)? (ISk 28)
Having said this, the Teacher concluded by teaching: "This very [perception] is unique.
Since that is the case, you have a doubt.
Why? It is said: This is indeed true.
Nevertheless, a doubt arises.
Why? Because when an object is perceived by one sense organ, we observe a longing for another sense organ.
Here, when the form of a mango, pomegranate, or other fruit is perceived by the eye, which is one sense organ, a longing and an inclination toward another sense organ—namely the tongue—is observed.
If, therefore, the sense-faculties were restricted to their own respective objects,
then their apprehension of their own objects would not depend upon the perception of the objects of other instruments or upon association with them;
yet such dependence does exist.
Therefore, the doubt is justified. In this regard, what now is your position?
It is said: even here, there is no confusion on the part of the sense faculties regarding the apprehension of their own respective objects. What then?
Each [organ] adopts its own respective mode of activity, which is caused by the mutual intentions [of the others];
for the purpose of the Person alone is the cause, and no instrument is set in motion by anything else.
Whatever function is assigned to a particular instrument— such as the apprehension of sound by the ear,
the apprehension of form by the eye, and so forth— they engage in that very function; the meaning is that they take hold of it with the desire to grasp their own respective objects.

"Mutual intention" (*parasparākūtam*) means the intention (*ākūtam*) of one another; "intention" (*ākūtam*) signifies purpose (*abhiprāyaḥ*) or underlying motive (*abhisandhiḥ*). Mutual intention is the cause for this practice.
This [speech] has as its cause the mutual intention of others;
it receives its designation from that [intention], considering that mutual intention is the cause of the practice [of speaking].
It is just like "curd-pumpkin" or "fever."

This is what is meant: when a form such as a mango or a pomegranate has been perceived by the eye, then the gustatory faculty—having become aware of the activity of the eye whose object has already been grasped—undergoes a transformation characterized by eagerness due to its desire to seize its own object;
having become aware of the activity of the gustatory faculty, the feet begin to move toward it and the hands begin to grasp it, until that object is brought within the range of the gustatory faculty.
Then the gustatory faculty operates upon its own object;
the same should be stated for the others as well.

He says: if that is so, then it follows that when there is the experience of the operation of another sense-faculty, there would be the consequence of it being a cognition produced by a sense-organ (*akṣapratyaya*).
