If, then, the activity of one sense organ is perceived by another sense organ, it follows that this [perceiving organ] must possess a causal condition (*pratyaya*). Alternatively, if the sense organs were devoid of causal conditions, there would be a mutual perception of their respective intentions.
In that case, it should not be said [that there is no such thing].
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a mutual relationship of door and doorway:
if one sense-organ, having perceived the activity of another sense-organ, were to desire its own object.
It has been argued that it follows that one [sense] would possess the status of a door (dvāritva) for the other, and vice versa;
thus, it is improper to say that the senses perceive each other's intentions.
To this it is replied: No, because this is said figuratively (upacārāt).
We have already taught that the sense organ is not itself a source of cognition.

What then? Having come into contact with an object that is a concomitant of its own object—the cloth—and which has become the domain of another sense organ, the sense organ, by its very nature, becomes expectant toward its own object, because a transformation [of it] is observed upon the presence of that [other object].
In this regard, there is no fault, as it is stated thus by applying the term "cognition" figuratively.
Furthermore:
because its manifestation occurs in the same manner as the manifestation of the conditions for the parts of material objects.
Just as immediately following the clarity of the intellect, there occurs the clarity of the material components such as the mouth, eyes, and so forth,
yet these do not possess the status of being causal conditions,
so it would be here as well.
Nor does it possess conditions;
by this, the relationship of door and doorkeeper is refuted,
or [it is refuted] because of the capacity of the mind as its basis.

Alternatively, "mutual intention" (*parasparākūtam*) refers to an intention directed toward one another; just as a person whose object is water is called a "water-person" (*jalapuruṣaḥ*). "Intention" (*ākūtam*) means desire, volition, or the mind.
This is its cause; thus, this [cognition] has mutual intention as its cause.
This is what is meant:

just as when a certain sense faculty is engaged with an object, having apprehended the entire object through that [faculty], it desires another object associated with it, and another sense faculty functions—
It becomes established.

Then, by means of a mind possessed of longing, the sense faculty undergoes a transformation. Thus it is also stated in another treatise: "Whichever sense-object the mind contemplates for the sake of attainment, an eagerness and an engagement toward that very object arise."
This has been stated: that each [sense-faculty] engages its own respective object through an activity caused by mutual intention.
Does one sense-faculty, having presided over the activity of the mind, set it forth toward its own object—just as Caitra might employ an axe and so forth?
It is said: no.
Rather, through contact with the mind—which is assisted by the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) of its own object—the sense organ itself perceives its own object.
Why? Because the capacity for such application is not established.
For the capacity of the mind to apply the sense organ is not established in the same way that Caitra’s capacity to apply an axe or similar tools is established.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the mind is the impeller of the sense organ.
If it should be thought that it is *rajas* [that impels it], since *rajas* possesses the capacity for the application of other sense organs; [we reply: no.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that because the capacity for application is unestablished, the mind is not the mover of the sense organs.
And why is this [claim] incorrect?
Because there is no distinction.

For in that case, since there is indeed *rajas* even in another sense-organ (*indriya*), its activity would be unobstructed by that very cause which is its own nature; what then is the use of postulating a mind (*manas*)?
Furthermore, it is because no other instrument (*karaṇa*) is logically possible.
For Caitra performs the employment of axes and other tools by means of another instrument;
however, there is no other instrument for the mind, so the cases are not the same.
If it is argued that it is like the hand, we say no, because [the hand] depends upon the activity of Caitra.
For even that [activity] proceeds in dependence upon Caitra’s operation, not of its own accord;
moreover, because activity is observed to exist apart from it [the agent].
For that whose activity depends on another instigator never occurs independently.
However, there is indeed the operation of the sense organ toward the thundering of clouds and the like even apart from mental volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Therefore, the mind is not the instrument (*kāraka*) for another sense organ.

And if it is not an instrument, then just as with the primary qualities (*guṇas*), it is established here as well that the purpose of the Person (*puruṣārtha*) alone is the cause, and that the instrument is not caused by anything else. // 31 //
[The opponent] says: Because there is disagreement among teachers regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*),
that [instrument] must be determined.
Regarding the instruments (karaṇa), there is a disagreement among the teachers:
the Vārṣagaṇas hold that they are elevenfold,
while the Tantrikas, such as Pañcādhikaraṇa and others, hold that they are tenfold.
Patañjali [states that the instrument] is of twelve kinds. Therefore, it must be stated how many kinds of instruments you intend. It is said in reply:
The instrument (*karaṇa*) is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, retaining, and manifesting.
The five organs of action, the five organs of cognition, mind (*manas*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—all these constitute the instruments useful for the purposes of the *puruṣa*.
Why? Because if they were not useful for the purposes of the *puruṣa*, it would follow that their existence as distinct principles (*tattva*) would be untenable.

If it were as the Vārṣagaṇas claim— that the Great Principle (mahat) is imperceptible within the mere mark (liṅgamātra), being distinguished by the characteristics of cause and effect, both specific and general—
then it would be a separate reality (tattvāntara).
But that cannot be so, because it would be purposeless.
He says: "True; even though it consists merely of a state of imbalance among the *guṇas* characterized as *pradhāna*, this will still be a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*).
Why? Because from a state of equilibrium (*sāmya*), an imbalance (*vaiṣamya*) arises as a different designation.
But this is incorrect.
Why? Because it would lead to an infinite regress of principles (*tattvānavasthā*).

For if it were conceived in this way, that which lies between the *pradhāna* and the *mahat* would also, due to its nature as action, be a further designation for that which is devoid of action; thus, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of distinct principles.
Or, if [this were] accepted, there would be a contradiction regarding the time of action for the *mahat* and the other principles.

Therefore, either the existence of further principles is untenable or there would be an infinite regress; thus, one must necessarily accept that the instruments are of thirteen kinds, as in our own position.
And therein, it is our own thesis alone that appears to be faultless.
Therefore, it is established that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is of thirteen kinds.
[The opponent] says: This designation "instrument" contains within it the relationship between an action and its agent. How so? Because that by which something is done is the instrument.

In this regard, it must be stated: what is the action (*kriyā*), and what is that which is performed such that, in relation to it, the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors possess the status of instruments (*karaṇa*)?
It is said: regarding the question "What is the action?", we reply that what is intended here is that which brings about [the result], and not like a staff or similar objects.
What then? It performs the functions of grasping, maintaining, and illuminating. Among these, the organs of action perform grasping, because they possess the capacity to acquire objects.
The organs of perception perform the function of retention,
because when an object is present, the activity of the ear and the other senses assumes the form of that object.
The internal organ performs the function of illumination.
This is due to the power of determination (*niścaya*).

Another says: the organs of action (*karmendriya*) perform the function of grasping (*āharaṇa*), while the mind (*manas*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) perform the function of sustaining (*dhāraṇa*).
The organs of perception are illumination and the intellect;
it is with this intention that the status of the intellect and the others as instruments is stated.
As for what was asked—“What is the effect?”—it is said:
And its effect is tenfold, tenfold; thus there are five specific [evolutes] and five non-specific [evolutes].
That too receives the designation "effect" for this very reason.
It is to be brought forth, maintained, and revealed.
Therefore, it must be brought forth, maintained, and proclaimed;
for this reason it is said to be "that which is to be done" (*kārya*), not because it is something to be produced (*nirvartya*). // 32 //
Regarding these thirteen kinds of instruments (*karaṇa*), which one is the thirteenth?
It is said: intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*). Therefore...
The internal organ is threefold;
why? Because it does not itself intend toward objects, and because the apprehension of objects occurs through the channels of the ear and the other senses.
If it should be thought that the understanding of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is incorrect because the statement was made without distinction— namely, that "the internal organ is threefold"—
then how is it to be understood that the intention here was to include the intellect, ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*)?
But why not others?
It is said: No, because there is no justification for the reason that would cause a deviation from the primary number.
For there is no reason for the cognition of one who would deviate from the number [of categories] beginning with intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, only those [five] are to be understood [as sense organs], just as in the injunction: "One should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds for Spring.

If it be argued that this is incorrect because it would entail the consequence that the ear is an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the following might be said: having mentioned intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṃkāra*), he then states: "The sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyāṇi*) are called the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose."
Therefore, it would follow that the ear is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This is untenable.
Why? Because the mind (*manas*) is mentioned separately.
For this very reason, the Teacher, having taken this into account, has separately stated that the mind (*manas*) is an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*): "That sense organ is designated in two ways;
it is internal and its object pertains to the three times" (ISk 27).
Therefore, it is established that the internal organs are threefold, namely, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the others.
The external is tenfold:
the five sense organs and the five organs of action—this external is declared by the teachers to be of ten types.
[An objector] says: the statement that "the external is tenfold" is redundant.
Because of the cognition by elimination (*pariśeṣabuddhi*):
when it is stated that "the internal organ is threefold," it is understood from that very elimination that "the external [organs] are tenfold.
Therefore, the mention of that [external division] is redundant.
It is said: No, because it has the sense of "object.
The Teacher begins [this section] with the thought, "I shall state that the triad is called the 'object'";
for if this were not done, it would not be known what that "object" of the triad is.
He says: "Even so, since the apprehension [of the object] is established by the mention of 'object' (*viṣaya*), the separate mention of 'external' (*bāhya*) is redundant.
It is replied: This must necessarily be stated for the sake of establishing the state of being an object;
in that regard, whether it is placed as a remainder or stated according to the original order, there is no difference.
Alternatively, this is not undertaken for the purpose of establishing the designation "external"; rather, it is for the sake of restriction.
How so? So that the external, consisting of the tenfold grasping of objects such as sound and the rest, may indeed be designated as the "object" (viṣaya) for all three [of the senses].
Let it not be that [the external] consists of the internal vital breaths and so forth;
rather, the external is indeed tenfold.
The meaning is that the external is the object of differentiation.
However, since there is no distinction for that which consists of the vital breaths and so forth, there is no fault;
this is what is called the "object" of these three.

For the three— characterized by intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*)— the functions of the sense organs and the organs of action, having grasped their respective objects, attain the status of being called "objects" because, through contact, they become the cause for the manifestation of the forms of those objects;
likewise, the mind and the ego are also [objects] of the intellect.

The intellect (*buddhi*), however, because it consists of the nature of ascertainment (*niścaya*) and is independent of other instruments, presents every object—superimposed in the form of an ascertainment—to the *puruṣa* for the sake of its engagement.

In that regard, since the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) assume the same form as the objects when sound and so forth are present, and lose that form when those objects are removed, the intellect acts by reaching its object (*prāpyakāri*).
It concerns external objects belonging to the present time.

However, due to the proximity of the functioning of the sense organs toward their appropriated objects, the internal instrument [the mind] pertains to the three periods of time by virtue of the causal conditions of memory, which are produced by the instillation of latent impressions (saṃskāra) in the form of those objects. Kārikā 34:
He said: It was stated without distinction that the function (*vṛtti*) of the ear and the other senses toward sound and the other objects is mere perception (*ālocanamātra*).

In that regard, should it be understood exactly as such, or is there a specific distinction among the objects of the senses? Furthermore, it was stated that its effect is tenfold, characterized both by distinction (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) and by non-distinction (*aviśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
In this regard, by which instrument is which object apprehended?
It is said:
the sense organs have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific; of these, five are the sense organs of cognition.

Among those aforementioned faculties, the five sensory organs (buddhīndriya) beginning with the ear have as their objects both the specific (viśeṣa) and the non-specific (aviśeṣa), depending on the difference in the perceiver.

In that regard, the faculties of the gods, due to the excellence of their merit (dharma), are so pure that they perceive even the non-specific, let alone the specific; and so too it is for yogins who have attained excellence.
But for those such as ourselves, there is indeed a distinction [in perception] because they are enveloped by darkness.
He asks: "Is there also a difference in the apprehension of the organs of action due to a difference in the perceivers?
It is said: "No."

Rather, for all beings, speech has sound as its object. When the vocal organs— the palate and other regions of the mouth— are struck by the vital air (vāyu), the production of modifications of sound in the form of phonemes, words, sentences, verses, and books is common to all living beings without distinction.
He asks: "Then how are the other organs of action?
It is said:
"The remaining ones also have five objects. (ISk 34)

The hands, feet, anus, and genitals, however, transform their forms—which consist of the aggregates of sound, touch, taste, color, and smell—through their functions characterized by grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure.

[The opponent] says: "If it is accepted as a rule that the five objects alone are non-specific (aviśeṣa), then it follows that the actions of grasping and so forth would be impossible when there is only a single sense organ.
It is replied: No, because this is intended to negate such a restrictive rule.

Lest it be understood that the restriction to their own respective objects applies to the organs of action (*karmendriya*) just as it does to the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of negating such a restriction.

It is precisely for this reason that the Teacher employed the word "also" (*api*). Furthermore, it is used for the sake of possibility: that these [organs of action] may have five objects, and even more so, that they may have four or three objects.
He asks: How is this understood—that the sense organs have specific and non-specific objects as their domain, and not non-existent objects?
It is said: because the non-existence of specific objects is not established.
To begin with, particularities are perceived through direct perception;
therefore, it is impossible to assert their non-existence.
Furthermore, even if this were the case, this very [perception] would be an irreproachable means of direct perception that establishes the probandum.
This [cognition] is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), like the cognition of a mirage and so forth, which has external objects as its domain.
And this is incorrect.
Why? Because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is untenable.

Everything must be accepted as unreal, for there is nothing whatsoever that is a direct perception (pratyakṣa) in the sense of ultimate reality; even that which might appear to be so would merely be a semblance of direct perception (pratyakṣābhāsa).
This conceptual construction (vikalpa) has already been explained.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that this is mere cognition.
Furthermore,
[it is so] because it would entail the consequence of erroneous perception.
For one who desires the non-existence of existing things by means of unreal objects such as mirages and dreams, there would likewise follow the consequence of erroneous perception.
For instance, regarding illusory cities (*gandharvanagara*) and the like, at times one person sees that very object as a cow, while another sees it as an elephant.
Sometimes [one sees] a banner;
and in a dream, the sight of cows, men, horses, oxen, rivers, trees, and so forth—belonging to those who have fallen into a single form—is seen in memory as a reversal [of reality].
Likewise, [there is the experience] of entering a herd of elephants through a window.
Furthermore, the rejoining of severed limbs, traveling through the sky, and the acquisition of a kingdom without a lord or a cause—
these would also occur in other cases [of mere illusion],
yet they do not.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that entities are non-existent like a mirage or a dream; otherwise, causal efficiency would not occur.
Just as in a dream, bathing, anointing, eating, drinking, clothing, and covering are seen to be fruitless, [so too would all things be].
The same would apply here as well.

If it is argued that it is like the emission of semen, this might be so: just as the emission of semen is preceded by the union of two [persons], yet it occurs even in the absence of that [union] during a dream.
If it were argued that "the other [factors] would be likewise," that is incorrect,
because they have passion and so forth as their causes.
For it occurs even for one who is awake without the union of the two;
therefore, it is for the sake of pleasing the mind.
If it should be argued that "it is like [the experience] of a hungry ghost (preta)," and that this is my correct understanding:
Just as for hungry ghosts there is causal efficiency through non-existent rivers of pus and so forth,
and by the wardens of hell there is infliction of harm,
so it might be in this case as well.
That is incorrect, because it is unestablished;
for it is not established that this is non-existent.
Furthermore, because the imperceptible is sublated by the perceptible,
and since the perceptible is stronger in this case, the rejection of the imperceptible by means of it is logical;
yet you reject the perceptible by means of the imperceptible.
Therefore, it is illogical that non-existent things, like the guardians of hell and so forth, possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

If it is argued that their non-existence follows from a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*), this may be so: if the guardians of hell were to exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), they too would have to experience suffering.
Because there is no difference in their possessing form, yet there is no sublation of them;
therefore, this is an illusion.
This is incorrect.
Why? Because of the diversity of the power of karma.

First of all, it is directly perceived that the manifold cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is differentiated by various distinctions in the powers of speech, intellect, physical nature, food, and movement, all of which have karma as their cause.

It is impossible to examine it with precision because of its profundity; how much less, then, could the intellects of people like us determine the diverse nature of the maturation of karmas whose effects are not directly perceptible and which lie beyond the scope of logical reasoning?
Therefore, this is merely a product of imagination;
furthermore, there would be no occurrence of merit or demerit.
Just as in a dream, acts such as killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, or sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached bear no fruit.
The same would apply in other cases as well, since there is no difference in their non-existence.
If it is argued that there is a distinction due to the impairment caused by torpor (*middha*), we say no, because there is still no difference.

Since non-existence is equal [in all cases], the claim that there is injury in some instances but not in others is merely a matter of personal whim. If this were so, then earth and the other elements would not be non-existent. If they are not non-existent, then it is logical that it was correctly taught: "The five sense organs have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific. (34)
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Śrī Yuktidīpikā*. Now we shall explain the relationship between the door-keeper and the door among these [faculties].
*Kārikā* 35:
Now we shall explain the relationship between the door-keeper and the door among these [faculties].
In this context, the external instrument is the door, and the internal instrument is the one who passes through the door.

An objection is raised: this is incorrect because there is no distinction between instruments; for the status of being an instrument is no different for the internal organs and the sense organs alike.
In this regard, what is the reason for saying that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the gatekeeper and the senses are the gates?
It is said:
Since the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), penetrates every object,
therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates.
That which exists together with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the intellect accompanied by the internal organ;
the meaning is that the intellect is conjoined with both the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and the mind (manas).
Here, although the intellect is already established by the mention of the "internal organ" itself, the intellect is mentioned again for the purpose of indicating its preeminence.
For it occurs that even when a principal element is included within a general category, it is taught separately; for example:
"Vyāsa went to that forest region together with the great seers (*maharṣi*).
Here, although Vyāsa is included within the mention of "great seers," he is mentioned separately due to his preeminence.
Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organs (*sāntaḥkaraṇā*), penetrates every object;

by the power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it takes as its objects—within its own functioning—all specific and non-specific qualities such as sound, whether they are near, distant, or concealed.
This is what is meant: the door is one whose objects are unrestricted.
The gates have fixed locations.

For example, just as the gates of a palace— eastern, northern, southern, and western— are restricted to their respective directions such that the eastern gate never becomes the northern, southern, or western, so too it is with the other gates.
In that case, just as [the senses] are unrestricted and proceed through doors situated in all directions, so too here, the ear and the other [senses] are restricted to their own respective objects.

However, the intellect (*buddhi*), accompanied by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), penetrates every object. Therefore, because its objects are unrestricted, it is logical that the threefold instrument is the "door-keeper" (*dvārin*), while the remaining ones are the "doors" (*dvārāṇi*). // 35 //
Kārikā 36: These specific qualities, which are like lamps and mutually distinct, having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect.
By the word "these," he connects the triad consisting of any one of the senses beginning with hearing, as well as the mind and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
By the phrase "resembling a lamp," he explains the similarity in their function as illuminators for the stage of the instruments (*karaṇaparvan*);
just as a lamp is an illuminator, so too is the instrument.
Because, if that [cognition] were active, the manifestation of the object would be untenable.
By the phrase "mutually distinct," he invokes the previously mentioned separate functioning;
for by that [separate functioning], their distinctness is inferred.
This is due to the distinctions of observation (*ālocana*), conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), and self-identification (*abhimāna*).

By the phrase "particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāḥ*), [the author] indicates that the *sattva* and other [qualities] undergo transformation into the state of being that [consciousness], directed toward the cognition of the *puruṣa*.

"The entire purpose of the *puruṣa*" refers to the effects characterized as the specific and the non-specific; having manifested them as they occur through their roles as the object to be grasped, the sustainer, and the illuminator, and having made them conformable to their own functions, [the qualities] experience them through the operation upon the objects.
The meaning is that it renders [the object] non-subject to that [consciousness].
However, sometimes the intellect itself [perceives] what has been grasped by the external organs through conceptualization and self-identification.
But in every case, this is the meaning of the treatise: the intellect determines the object as it has been apprehended by whichever organ [it may be].

And by that [intellect], having assumed the form of determination (*adhyavasāya*), the power of consciousness (*cetanā-śakti*) is assisted. There is no connection of the Person (*puruṣa*) with any other instrument. Consequently, because there is a plurality of gatekeepers [the internal organs], there is no occurrence of the faults [attributed to the Person] such as being the agent of the internal organ, the agency of the Person, or the confusion arising from the independence and aggregation of those specific perceptions. // 36 // Kārikā 37: [The intellect, though a single entity, performs its functions through its various powers, just as a single person acts through his various faculties. Just as a single person, though one, performs different actions through his various faculties—such as seeing, hearing, and so forth—so too does the intellect, though a single entity, perform its respective functions through its various powers, such as ascertainment (*niścaya*), memory (*smṛti*), and so on. Therefore, it is not contradictory for the intellect to be both manifold and unitary. Furthermore, since the intellect is the instrument of the Person, it is the intellect that undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*), not the Person; thus, the Person remains eternally unchanging. This is established by the fact that the intellect, being composed of the three qualities (*guṇa*), undergoes modification, whereas the Person, being devoid of qualities, does not. Thus, the intellect, while being a single principle, is designated by various names according to its specific functions. // 37 //

He asks: What, then, is the reason here, such that—despite there being no difference in their status as gateways—the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind (*manas*) project the objects onto the intellect (*buddhi*), rather than these two having a direct connection with the *puruṣa*?
It is said:
Because the intellect accomplishes every experience for the sake of the *puruṣa*.
For the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and the mind (manas) lack the nature of certainty,
because they consist merely of volition and self-conceit.
Furthermore, if the connection of the Puruṣa were with an instrument whose function is indeterminate, that connection would be purposeless;
or else, this [Puruṣa] itself would become the agent of determination.
Consequently, because it would be the cause of an unmixed determination, this [Puruṣa] too would possess an unmixed nature.
All of this has already been answered: for cognition (*buddhi*) is indeed of the nature of determination.
Therefore, an object that falls within its range, being perceived by the *puruṣa* through mere proximity, is not able to subvert his state of indifference;
nor, indeed, does it follow that [the *puruṣa*'s existence] is rendered purposeless.
All this has been stated because the intellect accomplishes everything for the sake of the individual's experience.
[The opponent] says: Even so, the object characterized by sound and the rest is the subject under discussion, and all of that is presented by the intellect.
In that regard, there is also another object characterized as the distinction between Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Thus they have said:
"The beginning of experience is the perception of sound and so forth; the end is the perception of the Guṇas and Puruṣa."
Therefore, it must be stated that another instrument (karaṇa) is required for the sake of accomplishing that [cognition].
It is replied: it need not be stated.
For what reason? Because:
And that very [discrimination] further distinguishes the subtle difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa.

For this reason— that is, because that very intellect (buddhi), being overwhelmed by darkness (tamas) which has reached its ultimate limit, determines the qualities (guṇas)— which are the constituent nature of the sattvic attributes such as dharma and so forth, which are modifications, dependent, neither benefactors nor beneficiaries, insentient, and characterized by association— to be the Self, and thus presents them to the Puruṣa.

And he, following the cognitive determination of the intellect which is colored by the latent impressions of the habitual practice of false knowledge, perceives it exactly as it is presented to him because its objects have been shown to him. But when, through the practice of virtue (*dharma*) and other qualities, there arises an influx of the nature of *tamas* and a subsequent pre-eminence of the qualities of *sattva*, then the mental modification (*vṛtti*) turns away from false cognitions. [He realizes: "The conscious principle (*cetana*) is neither a product nor a constituent of primordial matter (*prakṛti*); it is independent, neither benefited nor benefiting, and its nature is non-conjunction."
Then, [the intellect] forms a pure determination that the qualities (*guṇas*) are the opposite [of the Self].
And the Puruṣa, because its activity is induced by another, likewise conforms to that [determination].

This distinction between the qualities and the Puruṣa—since both possess the nature of certainty—is subtle, profound, and difficult to discern, even though there exists the aforementioned difference in their attributes.

And therefore, by relying upon that which is subtle— the mere intellect (*buddhi*)— there occurs the [distinction] between the grasped and the grasper within the undifferentiated power of consciousness (*cetanā-śakti*). The stage of the instruments (*karaṇa-parva*) has been explained.
Now the section on the "task" (kārya) must be discussed. Its summary (uddeśa) was provided previously: "The task is tenfold; there are five distinctions.
We shall now provide its detailed explanation (nirdeśa).
He said: "If that is so, then let this first be explained: what are the specificities (viśeṣas), and what are the non-specificities (aviśeṣas)?
It is replied:
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are the non-specific (aviśeṣa).
It was previously stated that these five subtle elements arise from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
they are indeed the non-specific.
What, then, are those subtle elements? They are said to be the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, and the subtle element of form.
[These are] the subtle element of taste and the subtle element of smell. But how, then, are they called "subtle elements" (tanmātra)?
It is said: because no specific qualities of a similar kind are possible;

for even though other [sounds] do not differ in their sound-genus (*śabda-jāti*), there are no specific qualities therein such as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), nasalized (*anunāsika*), and so forth. Therefore, it is the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*).
In this way, softness, hardness, and so forth [arise] from the subtle element of touch;
in this way, white, black, and so forth [arise] from the subtle element of form;
in this way, sweet, sour, and so forth [arise] from the subtle element of taste.
In the same way, fragrant odors and so forth exist in the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*).

Therefore, in these [subtle elements], there is only the generality (*sāmānya*) of each respective quality, not its particularity (*viśeṣa*); thus, these are called "non-particulars" (*aviśeṣa*) among the subtle elements.
He asked: "What, then, are the specific qualities?
It is said: "Indeed, from those five [elements], there are five [qualities]."
These specific elements are said to arise; therein, from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), space (ākāśa) arises.
From the subtle element of touch arises air; from the subtle element of form arises fire;
from the subtle element of taste arise the waters.
From the subtle element of smell arises earth;

although it would have been sufficient to say "from those [subtle elements] arise the gross elements," the inclusion of the phrase "five from five" is for the purpose of indicating that their production occurs in equal numbers.
By this, it is established that each specific gross element arises from each respective subtle element.

Consequently, the view held by other teachers—that from the *tanmātras*, which possess a single characteristic each, successive specific elements (*viśeṣas*) are produced through mutual interpenetration—is thereby refuted.
Rather, even without the interpenetration of the *tanmātras*, there is the production of successive elemental specificities from the elements that increase by one [quality] each.
In this regard, from the *tanmātra* of sound, which has sound as its quality, space (*ākāśa*) arises with a single quality.
From the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), which has the qualities of sound and touch, air arises with two qualities;
from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra), which has the qualities of sound, touch, and form, fire arises with three qualities;
and from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), which has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste, water arises with four qualities.
From the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), which possesses sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, earth arises as having five qualities.
And herein, the touch of wind is cold, that of water [is cold], and that of fire is hot.
The temperature of earth is neither hot nor cold;
and the color of fire and water is bright white,
while that of earth is black.
The taste of water is sweet;
that of earth is common [to all tastes]. Smell, however, belongs exclusively to earth, yet it is perceived in other elements due to the penetration of its constituent parts.
These are the properties of earth and the other elements;
there are also others that mutually assist one another.
As to what these are, he says:

Its form is white, its quality is roughness, its function is obstruction, and it is characterized by stability; its particular state is persistence, its color is black, and its shadow is dark; it is the source of all objects of enjoyment.
Thus are the qualities of those earthly beings, as well as others superior to them;
understand those qualities which pervade water, fire, air, and space.
Viscosity, subtlety, luster, whiteness, softness, weight, coldness,
protection, purity, and continuity are the qualities of water.
Fire moves upward, is a burner, a cooker, light, and radiant;
its destruction and its brilliance are characteristics of light that distinguish it from the two preceding elements.
Moving horizontally, purity, projection, impelling, strength,
roughness, lack of shadow, and coolness— these are the various qualities of wind.
Sarvatogati, Avyūha, and Viṣkambha—
these three should be known as space-like phenomena that oppose the previously mentioned phenomena.
Whatever common effect belongs to those things when combined—such as cows and the like—is distinct from their individual properties; of this there is no doubt.
In that regard, the earth benefits the world and other primary elements through its qualities such as shape (*ākāra*) and so forth.
First, by means of shape, the formation of the shapes of cows, jars, and the like occurs; and due to its heaviness (*gaurava*), these things maintain their stability.
Due to its dryness (*raukṣya*), there is the cohesion of water and the clarity of living beings.
*Varaṇa* is the warding off of what is undesirable;
*vṛtti* is the stability of living beings and other elements;
and *sthiti* is the support provided by the presence of the mother and other factors.
From differentiation comes the production of jars and the like; from arrangement comes the configuration of parts;
and from receptivity comes the state of being fit for enjoyment.
Because it possesses a dark shadow, its function as the shadow of the perfection of night is established;
because it is fit for the enjoyment of all, it bestows favor upon all beings.
In this way, assistance is rendered to the world and to other elements through moisture and the rest.
Through its moisture, it provides the remedy for wind, the pacification of fire, and the cohesion of earth;
through its subtlety, it effects penetration;
and through its whiteness, it originates from the moon.
Because of its softness, bathing and immersion are performed as a single action; because of its hardness, it causes the bending down of rigid things.
Because of its weight and continuity, it flows for the sake of favoring living beings;
because of its coolness, it counteracts heat.
From protection comes the pacification of horrors among the subjects;
from purity comes the accumulation of merit through the rules of purification and the absence of imperceptible injury;
and from progeny comes the collection of material wealth.

Likewise, by means of their purely functional properties such as upward motion and so forth, fire benefits both the world and other primary elements. Through its upward motion, it accomplishes cooking and illumination; and through its nature as a purifier, it effects the cleansing of substances.
From its burning nature arises alkalinity;
the heat of the ether serves as a remedy for cold and for the production of sound.
From its cooking nature arises the sweating of what is to be sweated, the digestion of food, and the functional capacity for action of the constituent parts of earth.
Likewise, there is an internal and external transformation;
due to its lightness, it overcomes the combustible elements such as chyle, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, marrow, and semen;
and due to its luminosity, it illuminates other substances.
Because it destroys what has been burnt and ripened, fire provides enjoyment;
through its fiery nature, it protects living beings.
Likewise, by means of qualities such as blowing horizontally, the wind provides benefit to the world and to other elements.
From its horizontal movement, there is the diffusion of vision and the carrying away of odors;
because of its purity, it wafts away putrid substances;
and through attraction and propulsion, it first elevates the waters of Dharma.
There is the arrangement of the bodily constituents (dhātus), such as the nutrient fluid (rasa) and the rest,
as well as the fanning of the fire and the striking against the space;
and there is the equalization of all these through force.
From its roughness comes desiccation;
from its lack of shadow comes the establishment of day and night;
and from its coldness comes the counteraction of heat.
Likewise, space benefits the world and other primary elements through its various qualities, such as omnipresence (*sarvatogati*).
Because of its omnipresence, it is called "single-hearing" (*ekaśruti*), since it is heard equally from all directions.
Through non-obstruction (*avyūha*) and non-expansion (*viṣkambha*), it provides space for all things; thus have earth and the other elements been described.
"These are called the distinctions.
He asks: But how are these called distinctions?
Because—
They are peaceful, terrible, and deluded.

Among these, those that are peaceful are so because, through their association with specific conditioned qualities (*saṃskāra*), qualities such as serenity arise in their presence; those that are fierce are so because they are the cause of qualities such as cruelty;
and those that are deluded are so because they are the cause of qualities such as obscuration.
Furthermore, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are called "non-specific" (*aviśeṣa*) because they are neither peaceful, nor terrible, nor deluded.
Thus, these aforementioned non-specific [elements] become specific (*viśeṣa*) in many ways for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the Puruṣa.
Why? Because the purpose of the Puruṣa cannot be accomplished if these remain in a single state. // 38 //
[The opponent] says: This has been stated too generally; therefore, we do not understand it.
Consequently, it must be explained how the particularizations are established.
It is said:
the subtle [elements], those born of mother and father, and those that are abundant—these are the three kinds of specific [elements].
Among them, the so-called "subtle" refers to the eightfold vital breath (*prāṇa*) which, dependent on activity, transmigrates.
Those born from mother and father are of two kinds:
the womb-born and the egg-born.
For them, the "sheaths" (kośa) refer to the sheaths consisting of hair, blood, flesh, bone, sinew, and semen.
In that regard, hair, blood, and flesh originate from the mother;
bone, sinew, and semen originate from the father.
Furthermore, others explain eight sheaths (kośa) consisting of what is eaten and drunk.
But how do these possess the nature of a sheath?
Because they have the capacity to envelop.
Just as a silkworm, enveloped by its cocoon, is rendered powerless; so too are these [defilements].

Thus, the subtle body, together with the vital breaths and enveloped by these [gross elements], being dependent, accumulates various karmas. Furthermore, there are numerous beings born from sprouts and those born from sweat; thus, by means of these three types [of birth], the threefold creation of beings—characterized as divine, human, and animal—is commenced.
Among these, the fourfold body of the gods arises through the favor of *pradhāna*.
As in the case of the Supreme Rishi and Viriñca;
as from their respective attainments in the case of the sons of Brahmā and the sons of those sons;
and from mother and father, as in the case of the sons of Aditi and Kaśyapa.
Alternatively, it may arise solely from the father, as in the case of Vasiṣṭha born from Mitra and Varuṇa;
however, for human beings, birth is generally from a womb,
though due to a particular excellence of merit and power, it may occur otherwise for some.
As in the case of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Kṛpī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others;
and even among those of animal birth, there are four types:
the womb-born, such as cattle and so forth, and the egg-born, such as birds.
The birth of grass and similar plants is known as *udbhijja* (sprouting), while that of small creatures is recorded as *svedaja* (sweat-born).
Thus, the three kinds of distinctions have been explained. Regarding this, some are fixed and some are unfixed; thus he asks: "Which, then, among these are fixed, and which are unfixed?"
For them, those [beings] born of parents cease to exist, while the subtle ones remain constant.
The subtle [elements] are eternal from the beginning of creation until its dissolution; those born of mother and father cease [to exist].
This continues with the phrase "along with the gross [elements].
However, some maintain that by the inclusion of the term "gross," only external specificities are intended.
The reason for not including those born from sprouts and those born from sweat is that they are not [explicitly] mentioned there;
therefore, the statement that "they are abundant in both ways" is faultless.
An objection is raised: the mention of the "subtle" beings is unnecessary because they are not well-known.
Since those born of parents are numerous, their inclusion is appropriate;
however, the subtle ones are unestablished. Therefore, it must be explained how these [subtle beings] arise or even exist.

It is said: In a previous creation, for beings born from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), due to the excellence of the quality of goodness (*sattva*), offspring or whatever else was desired manifested through the mind alone, even without sexual union;
indeed, upon beholding what was pleasing with the eye, one considered oneself to have achieved one's purpose.
When that too had ceased, the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) arose.
Having addressed living beings, they bring about whatever they desire;
this continues even today—as the conch-bearer supports his offspring by his trumpeting.
Furthermore, by speaking kindly, one experiences great joy.
When that [power] had been exhausted, there arose the perfection of the hand (*hastasiddhi*). By merely touching a hand, they would bring about whatever object was desired.
This very thing continues even today: that upon seeing a beloved after a long time, joy arises by touching them on the hand.
When this [desire] was exhausted, the accomplishment of embrace occurred;
for through embracing, living beings obtain their desired object.
This very principle continues even today: that by embracing what is dear, one attains fulfillment.
When that [state] had been exhausted, the establishment of pairs began;
man and woman, having united, produced offspring, and the grasping of possessions arose, such as "this is mine" and "this is mine.
It is precisely at this juncture that saṃsāra is described.
In this regard, there is a disagreement among the teachers.
According to Pañcādhikaraṇa, first, the *vaivarta* body, permeated by the instruments (*karaṇa*), enters the semen and blood at the time of the union of the mother and father;
and through that entry, it develops through the stages of the *kalala* and so forth.

Having emerged from the mother's womb with its constituent parts fully developed and having acquired the capacity for perception, it remains under the influence of those *dharma* and *adharma* which were performed during the time of experiencing the six types of success (*ṣaṭsiddhi*).
It remains there until the body falls due to the exhaustion of that [karma].
If the instrument (*karaṇa*) is conditioned by *dharma*, then it reaches the celestial regions with the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*).
By the reverse of that, however, one reaches a place of torment or the animal womb; through a mixture of both, one attains human birth.

Thus, this subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*), which is capable of sustaining and transporting the senses, is eternal and is constantly enveloped by and discarded from the perishable external [gross body].

According to Patañjali, however, there is a subtle body which, at the time of the attainment of powers (*siddhi*), first leads the senses to the place of the seed; having brought the instruments (*karaṇa*) either to the celestial realm or to a place of torment by the force of the latent impressions (*āśaya*) produced therein, it returns. And for one whose impressions are thus disposed, another [subtle body] arises by the force of karma, which leads the senses to the place of the seed; that too ceases.
Upon the fall of the body, another arises;
thus there are many bodies.
However, according to Vindhyavāsin, because the sense organs are all-pervasive, birth occurs through their functioning at the location of the seed.
The abandonment of that [body] is death;
therefore, there is no subtle body.
Consequently, the position is that saṃsāra is without distinction.
This is the origin of the subtle body.
(39) [The opponent] asks: "Since there are thus many teachers with differing conclusions, what is your own position?"

It is said in reply: As for what Patañjali stated—that the subtle body ceases and another arises again—that is not accepted by us on the basis of the statement, "their subtle [components] are fixed. Therefore, that which has arisen previously is unattached, fixed, and consists of the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the subtle elements.
The subtle body (liṅga), permeated by latent dispositions (bhāva), transmigrates without experiencing [objects].

In this context, by the phrase "arisen previously," he states that the *liṅga*—beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements—is eternal from the time of non-creation until dissolution.
By the phrase "unattached," he explains its penetration into hidden and stable seeds;
for the *liṅga* is never obstructed anywhere.
Rather, it enters even seeds such as lice-eggs;
it enters even by piercing through a jujube fruit.
By the word "certainly," he asserts the fixed determination for each individual person.
"For the Great One (mahat) is common [to all] because it is primordial matter (prakṛti)"—this is the position of the Vārṣagaṇas.

By the phrase "beginning with the Great One," he includes the eightfold vital breaths (*prāṇāṣṭaka*): the five [subtle elements] whose essence is prior [to the gross elements], as well as the five winds beginning with *prāṇa*.
By the expression "up to the subtle," he indicates the exclusion of any other ontological principles (*tattva*).
"It is only this much and nothing more than this" means that it describes [the self] as wandering through transmigrations; and consequently,
because it is not all-pervading, the entry into and abandonment of seeds become well-established.
"Devoid of experience" means it makes room for another body;
for if the subtle body were admitted to possess the capacity for experience, there would be the undesirable consequence that no other body could arise due to a lack of space.
By the phrase "perfumed by dispositions," he indicates the inclusion of the eightfold dispositions.

In this world, the eightfold vital force (*prāṇāṣṭaka*), permeated by the attributes such as *dharma* and so forth which take the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), remains established within the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*)—which has as its sole fruit the capacity for staying and moving—unimpeded everywhere due to their power. Since it transmigrates through luminous beings, animals, and ghosts, and since the purpose is accomplished by that very [subtle body], the postulation of other bodies is useless; therefore, there are not many bodies.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated— that because of the pervasiveness of the senses, their abiding in their own nature is the attainment of function (*vṛtti-lābha*), and the cessation of function (*vṛtti-nirodha*) is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—
this is incorrect.
Why? Because omnipresence is not established.
For no one accepts that the sense organs are omnipresent.
What is the reason?
Because it would follow that there would be constant perception,
and because it would follow that there would be simultaneous perception.
For if the instruments (kāraṇa) and the person (puruṣa) were all-pervasive (vibhu), it would follow that there would be constant perception.
Because there would be no obstruction to objects,

it follows that all specific objects would be perceived simultaneously due to the lack of distinction in their reaching [the sense organ]; furthermore, it would follow that even obstructed objects could be apprehended.
Because [the self] is present everywhere, it would follow that there is no distinction between near and distant objects, nor between perception, inference, and scripture.
If it is argued that this distinction arises from a specific mode of functioning (*vṛtti*), we say no, because there is no reason for such a distinction.
No reason has been stated for the claim that there is a specific functioning of all-pervading [entities] here;

therefore, the all-pervasiveness of the instruments is not established. Consequently, [the mind] is manifold according to its substratum, just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or other such support.
In the same way, the subtle body (liṅga) does not remain without a support, being devoid of the specific elements (viśeṣas).
For just as a painting has no existence without a wall,

or as a shadow does not exist without a post, a person, or the like, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*) does not abide without specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), being without support. Therefore, it is established that saṃsāra possesses specific qualities.
He said: "If that which possesses specific characteristics were perceived as a body upon reaching the location of the seed of saṃsāra, it would not be so;
therefore, this is illogical."
It is said: No, because it has been specified.
That body is specified as being subtle;
therefore, its non-perception is not without a cause.
He says: "Because of the connection with a subtle body, there would be the consequence of being a lord (Īśvara) as before;
therefore, it is incorrect that its non-perception is caused by that.
It is replied: No, because of the lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntāt).

For example, just as small creatures possess subtle bodies and lightness, yet they do not possess lordship (īśvaratva), so it would be for all living beings. Now, if it is thought that even a gross body is not perceived due to the lack of a perceptible connection— just as in the cases of hungry ghosts, collyrium, magical powers, garlands, and so forth— [then the following applies].
That too is untenable because it is inconclusive;
for example, the connection of the body with the sense organs when they are not being perceived.
Nor is it a case of non-perception, for this same [non-perception] might occur in the case of Piśācas and the like;
furthermore, if there were conformity with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), it would result from the conceit of possessing sovereign power.
And the sovereignty intended belongs to one who conforms to the determination [of will] by means of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth,
but not to one for whom these are established by their very nature.
Otherwise, even ants and the like would possess sovereignty because of their ability to travel through the air.
He said: No, because it would follow that a body could not arise.
For if a subtle body were produced, then the capacity for another body in those two [the intellect and the self] whose purpose has already been fulfilled would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is incorrect that transmigratory existence possesses specific distinctions.
It is said: No, because that is not accepted.
The body of transformation is not caused by merit and demerit;
rather, it is functional (ādhikārika), and thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, the existence of multiple bodies is not admitted;
therefore, this is merely a criticism of an alternative position.
Moreover, it is because the transformation of the entire substrate (āśaya) has not been asserted.
If one were to know the transformation of the entire disposition (*āśaya*), then it would be thus reproachable that a single part [of it] does not undergo transformation;
therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
If it is argued that the manifestation of a portion of the disposition is illogical because of the persistence of the causal sign (*nimitta*):

It might be thought: here, a distinction in the manifestation of intention is observed due to the specific difference in the smallness or greatness of causal conditions, as for example in the cases of wind and so forth, or anger and so forth;
and this time of death is the causal condition for the manifestation of the fruit.
And this [transformation] is undifferentiated;
therefore, the transformation of a portion of the intention (āśaya) is untenable.
This, moreover, is incorrect.
Why? Because it is conditional (*naimittikatvāt*).
The completion of the enjoyment of the fruit of previously performed karma, and the transformation for the sake of experiencing the fruit of present karma, are the conditions (*nimitta*) for death.
But it is not the case that death undergoes transformation. Furthermore, there would be an absence of another body;
for one who desires the manifestation of the entire latent disposition (āśaya), the absence of another body follows due to the absence of any other cause.
If it is argued that [the result] occurs there [in the intermediate state], we say no; because that is impossible once the stages such as the *kalala* have perished.

For, although the entry of the seed and the production of the instrument (the body) were accomplished by those two [volitions] performed there, if that very body perishes during the stage of the *kalala* and so forth, then since the latent disposition (*āśaya*) performed there is impossible, it would follow that another body could not arise.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of another body for stationary beings (*sthāvara*).

Since the latent disposition (*āśaya*) has already fulfilled its purpose in initiating the stationary body, and since it is impossible for that disposition to take up a new substratum in the form of a stationary body, it follows that such a being would lack further transmigration.
Therefore, it is logically established that this subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), produced at the beginning of creation for the sake of the person's goal, undergoes transmigration.
"And as long as that purpose of the Person (puruṣārtha) is not fully accomplished, so long does it remain. // 41 // It is said:

If it is admitted that the manifestation of the subtle body (liṅga) occurs for the sake of the Person's purpose, then that purpose must be brought to completion immediately thereafter; there should not, however, be a repeated state of coming and going through the conditions of gods, humans, and animals.
"It must be performed.
It is said in reply:
"This [cycle] is motivated by the aim of human beings (puruṣārtha), proceeding through the connection of causes and their effects."
Due to its connection with the pervasive power of primordial nature (prakṛti), the subtle body (liṅga) assumes various forms like an actor.

Although the *liṅga* arises for the sake of accomplishing the goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*), nevertheless, because all three— sattva, rajas, and tamas— are predominant, when sattva is overwhelmed by rajas and tamas, it is impelled by them and hears that which brings about the experience of the body, the sense organs, and their objects, both as causes and effects.

For example: "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice," or "One conquers the realm of Yama by means of the Agniṣṭoma. In these cases, out of a desire for the fruit, one brings forth the womb and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and undertakes the ritual action.
Furthermore, due to the diversity of the functions of the *guṇas*, even one who exerts effort performs actions that are defiled by mind, speech, and body.

Consequently, through the pervasive power of *prakṛti*, the subtle body (*liṅga*), although possessing a single nature, assumes various forms—such as those of gods, humans, animals, or pretas—presented by their respective causes; it does so like an actor, because of its similarity in both assuming and discarding specific physical forms.
As for the pervasiveness of all three *guṇas*, it is observed that they mutually suppress one another when in a state of equilibrium.
Therefore, saṃsāra has existence as its cause;
liberation results from the non-appropriation of that cause.
// 42 // Kārikā 43:
He said: "In this context, you speak of 'entities' (bhāva), yet we do not comprehend the meaning of this term.
Therefore, it must be explained: what, then, are these entities?"
It is said: the entities (bhāva) are dharma and so forth;
namely, dharma is knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, while adharma is ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty—these are the entities.
Regarding these, there is a disagreement among the teachers.
Regarding the fivefold basis (*adhikaraṇa*), knowledge is first of two kinds: innate (*prākṛtika*) and acquired (*vaikṛtika*).
Innate knowledge is threefold: simultaneous with the principles (*tattva*), innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), and produced by moisture (*ābhiṣyandika*).
Among these, that which is simultaneous with the principles occurs when the Great Principle (*mahat*), though composite, becomes the cognition of the Great Principle through its own essential nature.
However, for that which has already arisen through cause and effect, there is both the innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) and the induced (*ābhiṣyandika*).
The innate is that which is accomplished simultaneously with the formation of the aggregate,
such as the primordial knowledge of the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*).
The *ābhiṣyandika* [type of cloud] arises from another cause for one who has already accomplished his task;
the *vaikṛta* [cloud], however, is of two kinds: *svavaikṛta* and *paravaikṛta*.
The *svavaikṛta* is the *tāraka* [cloud].
The transformations of others are the intermediate accomplishments. And it is said:
"The *vaivarta* is equal to the *tattva*; therein, the second would be the *abhiṣyandika*.
The third is the *vaikṛta*; this is declared to be the *ṣāṭkauśika*."
But here, because there is no distinction in its arising together with sentient beings, he describes it as innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) without differentiation:
"And the transformed (*vaikṛta*) is also of two kinds; therein, the *tāraka* is self-transformed (*svavaikṛta*).
The other-transformed (*paravaikṛta*) may be of seven kinds, as indicated by 'one's own *tāraka*' and so forth."

Thus, just as it is with knowledge, so it is with dharma and the other [faculties]. However, according to Vindhyavāsin, there is no innate [knowledge] that is equal to reality; rather, it is simply of the nature of accomplishment (siddhi).

In this regard, even for the Supreme Sage (paramarṣi), knowledge is produced only after the manifestation, collection, and arrangement [of the world] have occurred; for he will attain it through the instruction of a teacher. Thus it is said: "The established cause effects the favor of that which is caused by it;
it does not produce something previously non-existent."
Thus, this is established through the relationship between the cause (nimitta) and its effect (naimittika).
In this regard, the distinction is that while the supreme seer possesses keen insight, for others it is obscured.

However, the Teacher has stated that for all beings alike, there is no difference regarding the "stars" and so forth; he said: "The dispositions (bhāvas) are of three kinds: innate (sāṃsiddhika), natural (prākṛtika), and acquired (vaikṛtika)."
In this context, by the mention of the "innate" (sāṃsiddhika), he refutes [the existence of the other types] as being simultaneous with the principles (tattva);
that is, such [other types] do not exist at all.
How so? For if it were otherwise, the non-production of further principles, as well as their combination and manifestation, would be purposeless.

Since the cognition has arisen in the great [elements] and is perceived in those very same [elements], what is the meaning of "combination" (*saṃghāta*)? Likewise, the inference (*ūha*) of a seer (*ṛṣi*) is not tenable,
because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
For there is no obstacle whatsoever to the arising of his cognition at the same time as the arrangement of cause and effect;
it does not wait for another moment because its nature is not obstructed by wickedness or the like.
Therefore, his cognition is produced simultaneously with the cause and the effect, like the light of a lamp; thus, it is innate (sāṃsiddhika).
But for others, because the sentient being lacks acuity, it occurs suddenly after some time due to the natural overflowing [of the latent tendencies],
like the sight of a black snake;
that is the innate [nature].
The modified [power], however, is of two kinds, as previously stated.
Just as the knowledge of the Supreme Sage is innate, so too is the sovereignty of one possessing a body of greatness;
likewise is the dharma of Bhṛgu and others.
The dispassion of Sanaka and others;
the unrighteousness of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and so forth;
and the lack of sovereignty among humans and animals born at the time of the destruction of the six supernatural powers.
Passion and ignorance belong to those other than the supreme sages;
however, for ordinary people, it is as follows: just as detachment arose in Bhagadāsuri because his spiritual attainment was produced through his veneration of the supreme sage.

Impurity departed due to its opposition; once that was destroyed, a stream of purity from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) set in, by which he was favored. Thus, having developed the desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) because of the assault of the threefold suffering, he went forth as a renunciant.
Likewise, through contact with Maheśvara, Nandin attained sovereignty.
In the case of Nahuṣa, dharma arose from contact with Agastya, and so forth;
however, the transformed states (*vaikṛtā bhāvāḥ*) belong to those such as ourselves.
Thus, because the Teacher [Patañjali] adopts all three types of states, not everything arises from himself alone, as is the case with Patañjali.

Not everything [is derived] from another, as in the case of the five substrates (*adhikaraṇa*). Rather, there is a great transcendence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), whereas from itself there is little modification (*vikṛti*). Thus, both innate states and qualities such as *dharma* are both primordial (*prākṛtika*) and modified (*vaikṛta*).
Just as these [faculties] are observed to reside in the instruments, so too do those beginning with the *kalala* reside in the effects.
By mentioning the *kalala* and so forth, he refers to bodies as being of exactly three kinds.
Their diversity of form within the fourteen-fold cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) is threefold.
Among these, first, the innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) belongs to those who do not undergo retrogression, such as the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and so on.
Furthermore, there is a distinction produced by birth, such as the whiteness of swans and the variegated plumage of partridges, peacocks, and the like.
This is the natural state resulting from the identification with the body; for he has such an identification, thinking: "Ah, I shall create sons who will perform my work."
Those who will know me and the Supreme—
one creates such a world as he contemplates, which arises from Pradhāna;
just as, for example, in the case of Maheśvara’s creation of ten million Rudras.
The modified [transformations], however, are the *kalala* and so forth;
as it is stated in the science of medicine (*bhiṣagveda*): "Having drunk milk, a pregnant woman gives birth to a fair-skinned son.
These states have been explained.
Due to the manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*) of these, there occurs the specific movement of the *liṅga* (the subtle body), which is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
// 43 // [Kārikā 44] It is asked: By the performance of which state (*bhāva*), what specific movement of the *liṅga* is accomplished?
It is said:
"Going upwards by means of the Dharma has been explained;
[now] the Dharma [itself] is explained."
From the practice of that [dharma], birth occurs in the eightfold divine realm;
descent to lower states occurs through unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Unrighteousness has also been explained.
Following that, there is birth in the animal realm, which consists of five types of divisions.
It is said: there is no arising in a single specific level, because of the distinctions among the destinies.

If it were restricted that things have specific levels (*bhūmi*) as their cause, then within a single level, the states of inferior, middling, and superior—consisting of birth, form, intrinsic nature, benefit, and harm—would not be possible. It is said in reply: "In that case, the specific level is not being restricted by this [term]; rather, the word 'upward' (*ūrdhva*) signifies 'superior' (*utkṛṣṭa*)."
Through dharma, there is upward movement among gods, humans, and animals, resulting in an excellent birth; likewise, through adharma, there is downward movement, resulting in an inferior birth;
and through knowledge, there is liberation.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction:
liberation is through knowledge alone, and not by means of any other state of being.
That which has been stated by other teachers—that isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *puruṣa* results from dispassion (*vairāgya*), or from both knowledge and dispassion—is thereby refuted.

[The opponent] asks: "If, however, it is admitted that the isolation of the *puruṣa* results from dispassion, what fault would there be in that case? It is replied: "It is not possible to maintain such a position."
Why? Because it is not an antidote to the cause of saṃsāra.
If the conjunction of Pradhāna and Puruṣa were caused by passion (rāga), then it would follow that their separation would occur through dispassion (vairāgya), which is its antidote;
but this is not the case.
Why? Because the manifestation of the body and the organs is produced by their conjunction;
for passion arises only after the arrangement of the body and the organs has taken place.
Therefore, it cannot be maintained that this [passion] is the cause of the production of the body and the organs.
However, for one who holds the position that liberation results from knowledge, it follows that bondage results from its opposite, ignorance;
yet this [ignorance] does not exist even prior to the production of the body and the instruments of action.
Therefore, liberation does not arise from dispassion;
for this very reason, there is no liberation through both knowledge and dispassion,
because the two causes cannot coexist.
Therefore, it is well said: liberation occurs through knowledge alone;
bondage is held to arise from its opposite.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the inversion of knowledge (*jñāna-viparyaya*).

From that, bondage becomes threefold: the bondage of nature (*prakṛti-bandha*), the bondage of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*), and the bondage of transformation (*vaikārika-bandha*). // 44 // Kārikā 45:
He asks: from what cause does bondage to prakṛti arise?
It is said:
dissolution into prakṛti results from dispassion (vairāgya).
Through dispassion, one undergoes dissolution into the eight primordial natures;
this is called the "bondage of nature" (prakṛtibandha). It is asked: if dissolution into nature results from dispassion, then what is this straightforward dispassion toward nature?
Prakṛti is another [entity], consisting of the three guṇas,
being both the cause and the effect.
It is characterized as being either in the state of cause and effect, not in the state of cause and effect, insentient, and dependent;
the other, the Puruṣa, is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Neither effect, nor cause,
nor both effect and cause.
The opposite of that is the conscious [self], which is independent; therefore, there would be dissolution back into primordial nature (prakṛti), and from that, the consequence of no liberation.
It is said: the term "by way of reversal" (viparyayāt) carries over;
we shall connect it here.

Furthermore, that which is the opposite—namely, detachment (*vairāgya*) falling under the category of contentment (*tuṣṭi*), consisting of the conceit of superiority regarding *prakṛti* and the rest—is precisely from that [conceit] that absorption into *prakṛti* (*prakṛtilaya*) occurs, and not from anything else.
Alternatively, even here, liberation arises from that very knowledge of otherness regarding *prakṛti*, and not from detachment.
Why? Because it has been stated that [detachment] is not an antidote to the seed of worldly existence (*bhavabīja*).
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of liberation for one who is still immersed in the water;
for his cognition of diversity is equal [to that of the other],
since the fault of attachment has been eliminated.
And this is not accepted.
Therefore, it is correct that "dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛtilaya) results from dispassion.
He asks: "Then, from what does bondage through sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇābandha) arise?"
It is said:
transmigration arises from passionate attachment (*rāga*).
This desire for objects that are either perceived or heard of is what constitutes attachment.
In that regard, due to attachment to perceived objects, one performs karma that brings about the attainment of them,
and consequently, one is reborn there.
Due to a longing for objects heard of through tradition, one engages in such acts as the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
And from that, rebirth in heaven and other realms occurs;
this is the bondage of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*).

Through the gateway of longing for objects seen and heard of in the scriptures, one engages in the actions that bring those about; yet, due to the diversity of the functions of the *guṇas*, one also performs actions that produce undesirable results.
Thus, whatever birth occurs in the human realm or other destinies, all of it arises from passion (*rāga*).
[The opponent] says: "The inclusion of *rajas* (passion) is redundant, because passion is preceded by that [*rajas*].
For passion has *rajas* as its very cause."
In that regard, one might say that it should simply be stated that "saṃsāra is due to passion (rāga)," and thus the inclusion of the term "rajas" (passion/energy) is redundant.
It is replied: No, because it serves as a qualification of the object.
This is stated for the purpose of making known the point that attachment toward sense objects is the cause of saṃsāra;

otherwise, even the sattvic attachment of an ascetic to the performance of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), meditation, and so forth, or his attachment to the sacred teachings, would also lead to saṃsāra. [The power of] sovereignty is the absence of obstruction.

When the eightfold sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā*, which was previously taught, arises as unimpededness within its respective domains, attachment to that is the *vaikārika* (transformative) bondage. [The opponent] says: "If threefold bondage is brought about by three causes, namely dispassion and so forth, then the statement that 'bondage arises from ignorance' is incorrect."
"Since ignorance (*ajñāna*) is indeed a distinct state of being (*bhāvāntara*), it must therefore have a distinct result.
It is said in reply: "No, because it is the root cause.
For ignorance is the root of whatever result belongs to those states of being that are devoid of knowledge."
Because all [results] have that as their cause;
for the dispassion of a knower (*jñānin*) is not sufficient for dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*).

Likewise, since other [causes] are not observed in the case of the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*) and others, it is illogical for a diverse effect to arise from a single cause; therefore, dispassion and the rest are postulated as distinct and non-common causes.
Since ignorance is common [to all], there is no fault whatsoever;
from the opposite [of knowledge], its opposite [ignorance] arises.
Due to the lack of mastery over the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā*, there occurs the opposite of non-obstruction, namely obstruction.
Thus, by depending on this eightfold arrangement of *dharma* and the other qualities, an eightfold set of effects arises.
In this way, both the creation of the principles (*tattva-sarga*) and the creation of entities (*bhāva-sarga*) have been explained.
And this is conceived as the form of the manifest and its activity;
now we shall explain the result. // 45 //
Thus ends the eighth daily lesson and the third chapter in the *Yuktidīpikā*.
[The author] asks: What, then, is that fruit?
It is said:
This creation of conditions, which is termed error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment—that is the fruit; such is the completion of the sentence.
The word "this" (eṣa) is stated for the purpose of bringing to mind that which is about to be described.

"Pratyayasarga" means that *pratyaya* is a synonym for *padārtha* (category) and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic); thus, the creation of *pratyayas* is the *pratyayasarga*, meaning the creation of categories or the creation of characteristics.

Alternatively, *pratyaya* is synonymous with *buddhi*, *niścaya*, and *adhyavasāya*. Since this creation arises from that [intellect], it is called the "creation of the intellect" (*pratyayasarga*), meaning the effect of the intellect or the activity of the intellect. Or else, the creation preceded by the intellect is the "creation of the intellect."
It has been stated that [the creation] is preceded by intelligence.
How so? For the scripture says thus: "The creation, beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), is preceded by intelligence.
But once his body and organs had arisen, he who possessed a body of majesty, beholding himself alone, reflected: 'Alas! I shall create sons who will perform my work.'"
As he was thinking, "May those who shall know me as both the higher and the lower [Brahman] appear," five principal streams of gods manifested before him.
When they had arisen, he did not find satisfaction.
