Then twenty-eight others were born who flowed crosswise;
his mind did not rest even upon them.
Then nine other gods appeared who flowed upward.
Even when they had arisen, he did not consider himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Then eight others arose who were directed downwards;
thus, from that meditation of Brahmā, this creation of the intellect (pratyayasarga) was produced.
"It consists of that which is called error (viparyaya), that which is called incapacity (aśakti), that which is called contentment (tuṣṭi), and that which is called attainment (siddhi).
Among these, the designation of what is not beneficial as being beneficial is error;
the lack of capacity due to deficiency is incapacity."
Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is satisfaction with less than what one intended to achieve.
Success (*siddhi*) is the accomplishment of what one desired.
For example, if one engaged in [the pursuit of] Dharma and Artha were to abandon the *agniṣṭoma* and other such rites and instead engage in confusion (*saṃkara*), that would be a failure for him.
Incapacity is the lack of ability due to a deficiency in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Contentment is satisfaction with merely the initial undertaking.
Success is the performance of the entire remainder of the ritual action.
The same should be applied to the objects and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding these four types of specific results, such as the "inversion" (viparyaya) and the rest, which have been described:
through the suppression caused by the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas), there are fifty subdivisions of them.
The inequality of the *guṇas* is *guṇavaiṣamya*.
The meaning of *guṇavaiṣamya* is the connection with the states of predominance and subordination. From the inequality of the *guṇas* comes conflict; thus, it is *guṇavaiṣamyavimarda*.
Through the alternation of conditions, there is a mutual transformation of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Based on that, these conditions have fifty varieties. (46) [Verse 47]
How so? It is said:
there are five varieties of error, namely, tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra.

In that regard, the first misconception (*viparyaya*), which is called *tamas*, consists of the conceit of superiority in one who is engaged in what is not beneficial, while regarding a lower object as superior.
It is the grasping of a self in material forms such as the head, hands, and so forth—thinking, "I am he who has broad shoulders, white teeth, copper-colored eyes, and long arms.

Likewise, [it is the grasping of a self] in those characterized by hearing, touching, tasting, smelling, speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, sexual pleasure, volition, ego-conceit, and determination.

The misconception that arises from the very first moment of activity—such as the notions "I am the hearer" or "I am the seer" regarding the functions of the instruments—is called the most inferior delusion (*moha*).

Why, then, is this said to be inferior? Because one who previously desires to perceive [the Self] as distinct from the body and the senses, failing to apprehend it due to its subtlety, might either adopt a non-existent means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that has the form of the elements as imagined by others, or imagine such a thing himself; thus, this [delusion] does not stray far from the path [of inquiry].

But this [ego] conceives the notion "I" with respect to the various forms of effects and instruments—such as arising, persisting, and perishing—which are apprehended through perception and other means;
therefore, it is inferior to the former. Furthermore, the attachment "this is mine" regarding external objects is said to be inferior even to that [ego].

Since the prior [self] is not perceptible to the embodied being, or because the activity of the self is no different from the activity of the instruments, one might think that the self performs the functions of the body and instruments; yet it is possible that this person, due to the influence of distinct causes, forms, locations, natures, and purposes, as well as benefits and harms, births, continuities, and destructions—
regarding such things as mother, father, son, brother, grandson, wife, cattle, gold, clothing, and shelter— views them suddenly as the self.
Therefore, it is inferior to the former.
Anger is the fourth perversion; being inferior to the former, it is designated as *tāmisra*.
But how is this one inferior to the former?
It is said: the former [verse] permits the negation of attachment.

When, upon separation from external objects, someone associated with the virtuous says to him: "Establishing [the mind] in the Buddha, let this be reflected upon for as long as this life lasts; if there has ever been anyone who was not previously separated from what is dear, therefore a wise person should not form an attachment to external objects which come and go."
Then he replies, "It is true; it is so.
However, because the time of separation is imminent, it is impossible to stabilize his understanding.
Furthermore, one who is possessed by anger and whose intellect is perverted by the crocodile imagined by his own conceptualization cannot be turned back even by punishment.
Therefore, it is inferior to the former.
The fifth perversion, the despair of death, is called "Andhatāmistra" (Blinding Darkness) because it is inferior to the former.
But how is it said to be inferior to the former? Because the former, being obstructed by attachment (*abhiniveśa*), [seeks] a remedy at least to the end...
Even one who gazes with the eyes of a tongue does not yet begin [to act];
for among the cycle of existence, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, no one has ever devised a remedy for destruction— the downfall which is most certainly determined by its own causes.
Therefore, one should not grieve over death as something unavoidable, thinking that what follows is inferior to what preceded it.
These are the five types of misconceptions (*viparyaya*).
Furthermore, there is incapacity due to the impairment of the sense organs.
It continues that there are twenty-eight varieties.
Among these, the impairment of the external organs, together with the mind, is of eleven kinds.
The deficiency of intellect is of seventeen kinds;
these are the varieties of incapacity.
Contentment is ninefold, and accomplishment is eightfold.
Thus, through the agitation caused by the inequality of the *guṇas*, there are fifty varieties of this fourfold creation of conditions (*pratyayasarga*).
In detail, however, the objects of experience number one hundred thousand, or rather, the characteristics are infinite.
How so? It is said:
because the eightfold division of *tamas* consists of those five varieties of error (*viparyaya*) that have been explained; therein lies the eightfold division of *tamas*.
How so? Because one who has proceeded by relying on the supreme consciousness (paravijñāna) grasps at the conceit of supremacy regarding the eight lower natures (prakṛtis).
And what of delusion (moha)? It has an eightfold division.
By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that there is the notion of "I" with respect to the eightfold capacity of the body and its instruments, such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
Great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is tenfold:
it is this intense attachment of "mine" toward the tenfold family circle, characterized by mother, father, brother, sister, wife, son, daughter, teacher, friend, and benefactor.
Others say it refers to visible objects or to those heard through tradition, such as sound and so forth.
This tenfold great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is enumerated;
the darkness (*tāmisra*) is eighteenfold.
When one is obstructed in the eightfold capacity for action and instrument, or in the tenfold family, or regarding sense objects,
that state of being overwhelmed is likewise the "Andhatāmisra" (blinding darkness).
The term "likewise" (tathā) serves to extend the general rule. Regarding the statement "blindness (andhatāmisra) is indeed eighteenfold":

how so? This too consists of the dejection resulting from the eightfold capacity for action and the instruments [of perception], as well as the tenfold family [circumstances] of one who has fallen away from [worldly] enjoyment.
Thus, these five varieties of error have been characterized according to their specific characteristics and their particular objects.

Furthermore, within the eight primal natures (*prakṛti*), because of the distinctions in the conceit of "otherness" regarding the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—whether combined, isolated, transformed, dispersed, or aggregated—each primal nature has fifteen varieties.
For this very reason, those eight become one hundred and twenty-five.
Just as it is for one engaged in liberation, so it is regarding those who desire the Dharma;
when a single category of object is enumerated in detail, it results in infinite divisions.
This which has been done by the Teacher is merely an illustration.
In this same manner, [the definition] should be applied to other characteristics such as incapacity (*aśakti*) and so forth.
Thus, this ignorance (*avidyā*), consisting of five sections and accompanied by its manifold elaborations (*saprapañca*), has been explained.
Immediately following that, we shall explain the various divisions of incapacity (*aśakti*) which were listed next. 48.
[Kārikā 49] He says: "This which has been stated is overly extensive; it does not remain in our minds.
Therefore, setting aside the statement of the divisions as expressed through negation (*viparyaya*), it must be explained: how is there a twenty-eight-fold division of incapacity (*aśakti*)?"
It is said:

"The incapacitation of the eleven faculties, together with the incapacitation of the intellect, is designated as 'incapacity' (aśakti). The 'incapacitations of the faculties' (indriyavadhāḥ) are the impairments of the faculties."

Due to the conjunction with their respective objects of refinement, when *tamas* has reached its peak, it overpowers the *sattva* whose nature is perception; consequently, there is a lack of engagement with one's own objects. This is as follows:
deafness, blindness, loss of smell, muteness, and dullness; insanity, hoarseness, lameness, impotence, upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), and lameness.
In that regard, deafness is of the ear,
blindness is of the eye,
and lack of smell is of the nose.
Muteness of speech, numbness of the tongue,
and madness of the mind.
A deformity of the chest is a defect of the skin;
a deformity of the hand is a defect of the hand; impotence is a defect of the generative organ.
The obstruction of the downward wind (udāvarta) in the anus and lameness in the feet— thus there are eleven impairments of the sense organs.
Others, however, [state]:
There are seventeen types of destruction of the intellect due to the inversion of contentment and attainment.
In that context, the satisfactions (tuṣṭi) beginning with "nature" (prakṛti) will be explained;
their error (viparyaya) is twofold:
for one who is undisciplined, there is a failure to engage in that stage through the practice of yoga.
Furthermore, for one who has attained proficiency, because they have not yet fully realized the higher stages, there is a perception of the preceding stage as being insecure;
or, for one who knows the self, this applies to all stages.
Among those [perceptions], that which is prior is intended to signify the state of incapacity.
That which is intermediate is relative.

How so? For one who abides on the stage of *tanmātra* is satisfied by not conquering the stages of *asmitā* and the rest, yet is successful in transcending the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). Likewise, one whose form of *asmitā* has been conquered is satisfied in relation to the stages of *mahat* and the rest.
It is established in relation to the preceding stage.
Thus, the state of the Great One (*mahat*) is [established] in relation to primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and in relation to what precedes it;
the state of primordial matter is [established] in relation to the person (*puruṣa*) and in relation to what precedes it.
One who knows the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and the person (puruṣa) is indeed already perfected.
Therefore, for one who is unenlightened, there are nine misconceptions regarding water and so forth, such as taking water to be non-water;
and by way of the reversal of the stars and so forth, there are eight misconceptions regarding the stars and so forth.
This incapacity (*aśakti*) indeed has twenty-eight divisions.

Contentment (*tuṣṭi*), however, is generally one— consisting of cessation through being satisfied with a proximate object or with less than the wealth one desires— but it is infinite with respect to each specific object.

"Contented with a hundred, [or] with a thousand," and so forth. In the treatise (*śāstra*), however, there are nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*) because they possess means (*upāyavat*), characterized by verbal determination regarding the attainment or departure of external and internal pleasure, pain, and delusion. (49) *Kārikā* 50: The nine obstacles (*paripantha*) are: doubt (*saṃśaya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*ālasya*), attachment to objects (*viṣayāsakti*), lack of detachment (*anaiṣkarmya*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), instability (*anavasthiti*), and lack of faith in the teacher (*aguruśraddhatva*).
Among these, four are internal;
they are known as nature, material cause, time, and fortune.

Regarding "internal": for the yogin who desires to perceive the distinction between the body and the embodied self, that which is established as the notion of a self in what is not-self is indeed internal accomplishment (*siddhi*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), satisfaction (*santoṣa*), or security (*kṣema*)—this is the meaning.
These are designated by the term "nature" (*prakṛti*).

When, through repeated discriminative discernments, one has realized Pradhāna and understands that the transformations beginning with Mahat are preceded by it; and when, because of the infinity of these modifications,

one determines that it is impossible for the entire nature of Pradhāna to undergo transformation into the state of Mahat and the rest— thereby concluding that only a single part of it is neither the material cause nor the modification [but rather] the experiencer and non-agent— one attains the cessation of attachment and aversion.
This immediate satisfaction is called *ambhas*.

Why? Because the immeasurable *pradhāna*-tattva shines forth as the seed of the world through its transformation into states such as the *mahat* and so on, due to the filling of even a deficient portion of the Self itself.

Furthermore, because there exists another portion characterized by both [subjective and objective] qualities—the experiencer—which is distinct from that [deficient portion], it remains unwithdrawn even when [the world] is thoroughly cleansed.
Because the manifold variety of forms is never cut off;
and thus the scripture says: "The term 'water' refers specifically to the collection of the qualities (guṇa) and their marks (liṅga).
And the qualities are sattva, rajas, and tamas.
And here the *liṅga* (the subtle causal body), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), is present.
Because this *pradhāna* shines forth immeasurably and is perceived as immeasurable, it is called *ambhas*.

Having indeed conquered that stage characterized by *pradhāna*, and having seen through its power that it is not empty [of anything else], the yogi, considering there to be no other distinct entity apart from it, [rests] upon that very stage.
He grasps at it as being absolute liberation (kaivalya).
When the body is broken, he goes to dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti), and from there he returns once again.
And in that [state], the other seven causes beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) should be understood as being similarly suppressed.
Just as there is no consciousness in the Puruṣa for the follower of Pradhāna, so it is for the others regarding the subsequent principles:
for the one whose cause is the Great Principle, [suppression occurs] in Pradhāna; for the one whose cause is the I-principle (asmitā), in the Great Principle.
In the *ahaṃkāra*, these [qualities] have the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as their cause;
and, as before, certain portions of them are the enjoyers.

Furthermore, here too, one should understand that due to the distinctions among the *sattva* and other qualities—whether combined or isolated, transformed or separate, individual or collective—the divisions resulting from the delimitation by ignorance (*avidyā*) are infinite.
He said: There is no difference between contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), because their defining characteristics are identical.
Contentment is the notion of selfhood regarding the eight primal natures (*prakṛti*);
and that very same thing is designated as "darkness" (*tamas*) in the section on ignorance.
"Therefore, there is a confusion of categories.
To this it is replied: No, because of the distinction in cognition.

When instruction is given regarding the Puruṣa in whom Tamas predominates, one who desires to ascertain the nature of that cognition would become firmly convinced that between those two, the Pradhāna alone is superior, not the Puruṣa.

But what is the highest satisfaction? Relying on this, one who has set out [on the path] does not even care to discern other categories of reality, due to finding contentment in the mere knowledge of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, because of the specific nature of abandonment:
for the deeply rooted grasping at a self in that which is non-self must be abandoned through cultivation subsequent to the attainment of knowledge.
Because of its abundance of *tamas*, it is designated as "darkness" (*tamas*);
however, that which is delicate and abundant in *sattva* is "contentment" (*tuṣṭi*), characterized by a longing for vision.
Furthermore, this is due to the mastery over the principles (*tattva*).

For the yogin who has conquered a stage (*bhūmi*), the engagement with another stage—due to being mastered by its majesty—is "contentment" (*tuṣṭi*); for the other, however, it is merely attachment. This is the distinction between the two.
Therefore, there is no confusion of categories; thus has been explained contentment known as "nature" (*prakṛti*).

However, even though the capacity of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) exists, it is not possible for entities to arise without depending on their respective material causes (*upādāna*), because if there were no distinction in primordial matter, it would follow that everything could arise at all times. Furthermore,

for one who accepts that this entire universe is merely the activity of primordial matter, since there is no distinction [in that matter], it would follow that a cow could arise from a human, or a human from a buffalo.
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence that there is no distinction between classes;

for one who accepts that this entire universe is the activity of primordial nature (prakṛti), there could be no differentiation of classes, because there is no distinction in that [primordial nature].
However, it is observed that the arising of entities follows from their material cause (*upādāna*);
therefore, it is logical to conceive of that alone as the cause.

Furthermore, by means of this insight—that the "enjoyer" is simply a particular aspect of the material cause itself consisting of the nature of cause and effect—one attains the cessation of attachment and aversion.
That second contentment is called "water" (salila). But why is it "water"? Because when there is a cause for grasping, modification dissolves (līyate) therein.
And having established this, the scripture says: "When one says 'water, water,' it refers only to the occurrence of a transformative accident; when that [accident] exists, the world dissolves.

Indeed, this yogi, having failed to conquer the earthly [element], perceives the world as non-empty through its greatness and, imagining there to be no other category of entity, takes that very state to be isolation (*kaivalya*).

When the body is destroyed, it dissolves into the elements such as earth, and from that state it returns once more. Furthermore, even when the capacity for the material cause (*upādāna*) exists, the manifestation of entities does not occur by that alone; rather, there is a dependence upon time even for those whose means (*sādhana*) are present—for instance, a sprout [emerges] from a seed due to a specific point in time.
From the sprout comes the stalk, from the stalk the stem, from the stem the flower, and so forth.
Otherwise, by the mere presence of the causal conditions (*upādāna*), these specific states would manifest in a single moment;
furthermore, it would follow that they arise at the wrong time,
which is not accepted.
Furthermore, because that [other cause] is not mentioned;
and because we observe among living beings the natural arrangements of their dispositions, food, and activities according to the seasons,
therefore that [time] alone is the cause.
And because one perceives that a portion of this [nature] is the enjoyer, which exists neither as cause nor as effect, one attains the cessation of attachment and aversion;
that is the third contentment, designated as "the flood" (ogha).
But why is this time called "the flood"?
Because it carries everything along like a torrent of water;
just as a torrent of water carries away grass, wood, stones, or living beings— whatever is in contact with its own form— and carries them all along,
so too does this time [carry one] from the womb to childhood.
From childhood to youth, from youth to old age, and from old age [to death].
From old age comes death;
likewise, from the seed comes the root, and from the root the sprout—thus it proceeds. And so it is said:
"On the very first night that a person enters the womb..."
Having set out for that state, he goes on without turning back.
Therefore, because it shares the common characteristic of being a flood (*ogha*), time is called a "flood.
This yogi, having conquered time and believing that there are no other distinct entities, considers that very state to be absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
And upon the dissolution of the body, he enters into time.
And consequently, it returns again.
However, even when the efficacy of time exists, the production of entities depends upon fortune.
Why? Because they do not manifest even when that [time] is present.
Even though the capacity of the causal factors (*sādhana*) exists, the production of some things occurs at a particular time while that of others does not;
therefore, there must be another cause upon which the production and non-production of entities depend.
Furthermore, [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that rising from one's seat could never occur.

For one who maintains that the fruit arises solely from time, there would be no engagement in the specific ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures—such as ablutions, vows, fasting, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so forth.
Why? Because they would be purposeless.
Yet such engagement does exist; therefore, the production of entities is not caused by time alone.
Furthermore, because it conforms to that [past action]:
indeed, even when there is no difference in nature, material cause, or time, differences in results are observed due to differences in fortune;
therefore, the latent predisposition (*saṃskāra*) alone is the cause.
And because one perceives that a single part of this [nature] is the enjoyer, which exists neither as the material cause nor as its modification, one attains the cessation of attachment and aversion.
This is the fourth contentment, called *vṛṣṭi* (rain).
But why is it called *vṛṣṭi*?
Because it nourishes all sentient beings: for just as even withered grasses, creepers, and the like are restored to life upon receiving rain,
in the very same way, the restoration of all living beings occurs through the transformation of their fortune.

Therefore, because of this similarity to rain, contentment called fortune (*bhāgya*) is designated as "rain. The scripture also says: "The term 'rain, rain' refers to the descent of prosperity; for that, like rain, nourishes everything."

Indeed, this yogi, having mastered his fortunes and seeing the world as not empty by virtue of their power, considers other objects to be non-existent and grasps that very state as absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
He merges into that very state upon the dissolution of the body,
and from there he returns once more.
He said: There is no comprehension of time and destiny, because of a lack of thorough knowledge of their designations.
It has been stated previously that for the yogin whose nature is primordial matter (prakṛti), the eight primordial matters are the objects.
Furthermore, for that which consists of appropriation (*upādāna*), the great elements such as earth and so forth are [the cause], whereas time (*kāla*) and destiny (*bhāgya*) are not stated to be so.
Therefore, it must be explained: to which reality (*tattva*) does this designation belong?
It is said: No, because it has already been stated. This was previously demonstrated: there is no such category of entity as "time. What then? The designation "time" applies to actions.
And it has been established that these are the functions of the instruments;
nor is there any function other than that which belongs to the possessor of the function.
Therefore, one who maintains the thesis that consciousness is caused [by something else] is [refuting] Time as the cause.
As for the designation "destiny" (bhāgya), it refers to merit and demerit (dharma-adharma);
and it has been previously stated that these two are qualities of the intellect (buddhi).
Therefore, one who asserts destiny is a proponent of the intellect as the conscious principle.
[The author] replies: No, because it is a different form of contentment (*tuṣṭi*).
Since the Great Principle (*mahat*) is primordial, it was already included within the contentment called "Nature" (*prakṛti*).
Now, it is argued that conceiving of this [state] as a distinct form of contentment is not entirely appropriate.
To this it is replied: "In that case, it would be greatly diminished from being the object of the previous contentment.

Having conceptualized the activity consisting of the functioning of the instruments of action—which is illuminated by the possessor of that activity—he speaks of its temporal nature with respect to that [activity].
Furthermore, the form of the "Great" (mahat), such as dharma and so forth, is distinct from the Great; thus one is "fortunate" (bhāgyavān) because of this fortune (bhāgya).
Alternatively, this external time is indicated as the cause of karma.
In that regard, it should be understood that the proponents of Sāṅkhya—who assert that there is the grasping of other entities whose nature is imagined by their own intellects—have been refuted.

Another says: "The proponents of primordial nature (prakṛti) as consciousness, who maintain that [the world] arises from the primary state, from the latent dispositions (āśaya), from material causes (upādāna), from time, and from destiny, and who assert the existence of the Great One (mahat), the I-principle (ahaṃkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātra).
This is incorrect because it is unestablished;
for primordial natures characterized by the Great One, the I-principle, and the subtle elements are not known to exist as material causes, time, or destiny.
Therefore, this too is incorrect. Thus, these four internal contentments and five external ones arising from the cessation of sense objects—nine contentments have been declared. (ISk 50)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

For a yogin who has not yet mastered the investigation of the self, the cessation of the fault of attachment resulting from merely perceiving the defects in sense-objects is external contentment (*bāhya-tuṣṭi*). In that regard, when he perceives the defect in acquisition, [he reflects]: "Not everyone possesses noble birth; therefore, one who desires [objects] must necessarily engage in the acquisition of sense-objects."
It was stated previously that because these things lack intrinsic nature (*asvābhāvikatva*), they can only exist in certain circumstances.
Furthermore, because they are subject to their opposites,
even the acquisition of objects through acceptance and other means— which might otherwise be conceived as an inherent state— is improper.
Why? Because there are adversaries.

Even so, since no one is without an adversary to acquire objects, one must necessarily strive to counteract them. And if, while striving, one were to destroy that adversary, there would be a contradiction with the scripture because of performing an act of self-benefit through the injury of another. For it says:
One should not inflict upon another that which is disagreeable to oneself;
this is the Dharma in brief, while anything other than this proceeds from desire.
Furthermore, it is said:
Whatever purpose arises through the injury of living beings must be abandoned by those who are indifferent to it, for it causes harm in other worlds.
Therefore, because beings and so forth are merely aggregates, like a jar or similar objects,
one should fully understand the instability of bodies from Brahmā downwards.
Truth is kindled by the virtuous; happiness is as flickering as a torch of straw.
It must not be cast down by the very firm miseries arising from other bodies.
Furthermore, if this [person] is struck down by adversaries,
then for him there is an absence of objects.
And seeing that for one who has set out for the sake of pleasure, there is mostly only suffering, he attains equanimity.
That fifth contentment is called *sutāra*.
Why, then, is it called *sutāra*? Because by means of this method, they cross over the perilous straits of sense objects easily; thus, it is *sutāra*.
But when the yogi, having attained the aforementioned defects through his noble birth or through objects acquired with effort, points out the defect of protection—how so?
Because there is no distinction between the state of being the enjoyer and the enjoyed, sense-objects are common to all living beings;
therefore, their protection must be maintained.
And if, while operating upon that [object], it were to obstruct another [cognition], then the previously mentioned fault would follow;
if, however, it obstructs itself,
there would be an absence of an object.
And for one who is engaged day and night with a one-pointed mind for the sake of happiness, there is mostly only suffering; from this insight, one attains equanimity.
That is the sixth contentment, which is designated as "Supāra" (the Good Crossing).
But why is it called "Supāra"?
"By means of this, they go happily to the further shore of the ocean of sense-objects.
But when, despite the previous fault,

or due to the employment of means such as the settlement of villages, cities, and market towns, the practitioner who has secured the protection of his sense-objects introduces the fault of decay— how so?
That very substance which embodied beings, out of delusion, desire to enjoy becomes the cause of their dissatisfaction precisely because of its perishable nature.
The objects of the senses, which seekers of sense-pleasures acquire with effort and guard so carefully,
vanish even as they look on, like bubbles upon the water.
There is no being whatsoever in this world, whether stationary or moving,
whose destruction is not observed through either direct perception or inference.
Therefore, a wise person should strive with effort to turn away the notion of "mine" from those things subject to destruction, such as sons, wives, and houses, in which people are deeply attached.
From this insight, one attains equanimity;
that is the seventh contentment, called *sunetra*. But why is it called *sunetra*?
It is called *sunetra* because by means of it one leads the self to the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
However, when the previous defects are present, he introduces the defect of attachment (*prasaṅga*).
How so? For those whose senses have attained their objects, the cessation of the desire for them is that happiness.
And there is suffering due to the desire to grasp sense objects;
even their acquisition leads to a lack of peace and requires skill in their enjoyment. For it has been said:
"When a subject pursues sense objects in a continuous stream..."
Then his intention toward this very [state] proceeds all the more.
For this reason as well, a man should not seek to pacify the submarine fire by indulging the senses; rather, he should withdraw them from their objects.
Therefore, having fully understood that the contact of the senses with their objects is incapable of being turned back, one should move about with a mind free from attachment.
From this insight, one attains equanimity; this is the eighth contentment, called *sumārīca*.
Why is it called *sumārīca*?
Because the root *arca*, meaning "to worship," [implies] that for the yogin who has desisted from attachment to sense objects, there occurs a beautiful state (*sumarcitam*) of abiding.
But when he introduces the fault of violence among the previously mentioned faults, how so? Because the enjoyment of sense-objects is impossible without harming other beings.
For what is called "enjoyment" is indeed the consumption of what is pleasing to the mind.
Service to women, vehicles such as horses, elephants, and men, and so forth— in these matters,
one who desires to partake of pleasant food must necessarily cause the slaughter of their constituent parts, namely cows, goats, sheep, oxen, women, men, and the like.
Alternatively, if there were no harm [caused by desire], it would follow that objects of sense do not arise;

for one who indulges with a woman, there would be no [sense of] other women, nor of mothers, fathers, brothers, and so forth, whereas otherwise [such feelings exist] in the case of horses and the like.
Therefore, one who desires enjoyment must necessarily cause injury to others, or else one who has laid aside the rod of punishment must renounce the enjoyment of sense objects. And it is said:
"In whatever measure the objects of the embodied beings increase, in that very same measure the injury to their own limbs increases."
Therefore, not wishing to cause bodily pain to other living beings,
one should live in contentment alone, having renounced all possessions.
For one who speaks the truth, who is tranquil, and who desires nothing from any living being,
knowledge that reaches the end of the darkness of existence arises before long.
From this insight, one attains equanimity; that is the ninth contentment, designated as "supreme fearlessness.
How so? For among all fears for living beings, the fear of violence is indeed supreme; therefore, because of its disappearance, it is called "supreme fearlessness."
He said: "But even in the two forms of contentment characterized by acquisition and preservation, there are the faults of harming others; and these have been pointed out in this [treatise] as well.
In that case, how is the distinction between these two to be understood?"
It is said: No, because the objects [of concern] differ.

In that [previous] case, it was stated that for those who are intent upon the acquisition and preservation of sense-objects, one must necessarily carry out the destruction of adversaries by those seeking such objects;

however, here what is intended is that for those very same people, the enjoyment of sense-objects is impossible without harming them [the adversaries], even while engaged in their acquisition and preservation.
Therefore, this [classification] is unconfused; thus, the nine objects beginning with water have been explained as the causes for the cessation of attachment and aversion.
For yogins devoid of knowledge, these attain the designation of "contentments" (*tuṣṭi*).
However, for those possessing knowledge, they are established as the very stages of dispassion (*vairāgya*) upon their respective levels of reality (*tattva*). // 50 //
[The opponent] says: It was previously stated that accomplishment is eightfold; let that now be explained. It is replied:
Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three types of removal of suffering, and the acquisition of a friend.
There are also the eight perfections (*siddhis*).

Among them, *ūha* (reasoning) is as follows: when one realizes a desired object solely through the power of inquiry, apart from perception, inference, and scripture, that first perfection is designated as *tāraka*; it is called *tāraka* because it carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.

But when one, being hindered in self-realization, realizes it through the instruction of a teacher, that is the second accomplishment, designated as "easily crossing" (*sutāra*). How so? Because by this means one easily crosses over the straits of existence even in the present. But when one is incapable of realizing it even through the instruction of another and accomplishes it through study, that is the third accomplishment, designated as "causing to cross" (*tārayanta*).
Because this very act of delivering remains unceased even to this day and possesses a vast scope, it is designated as "delivering" (*tārayantam*).
These three [scriptures] enable living beings down to the level of the *brāhmaṇas* to attain their intended goals by means of the methods of practice.
And it is said: "The seers were those who had directly realized the Dharma."

They taught the mantras by oral instruction to others who had not personally realized the Dharma; and others, weary of such oral instruction, committed this book—the Veda and the Vedāṅgas—to memory for the purpose of grasping the *bilma*.
*Bilma* means illumination; it refers to a specific convention stated for the sake of correct manifestation.
To counteract the obstacles to these means of accomplishment, there is the threefold destruction of suffering.

The three sufferings are those that are internal and so forth. Among them, having eliminated the obstacles to the success of internal factors such as [imbalances of] wind and so on through the application of medical treatments according to the *Āyurveda*, one accomplishes [the goal] by means of any one of the first three; this is the fourth [means].
Success (*siddhi*) is designated as "joy" (*pramoda*). Why? Because living beings rejoice when they are freed from disease.

When, however, one overcomes through conciliation (*sāma*) or other means consistent with the duties of an ascetic—any one of the three previously mentioned—the obstacles to success caused by external factors such as humans and so forth, [then that is joy].
That fifth accomplishment is called "The Joyful" (*pramuditam*). Why? Because one who is undisturbed is indeed joyful.

When, however, having warded off by means of his own duty the divine pairs of opposites such as cold and so forth which are adverse to accomplishment, he achieves [the goal] through any one of the three previously mentioned [means], [then that is the Joyful accomplishment].
That sixth perfection is called "Delight" (*modanā*).
Why? Because living beings rejoice when they are not afflicted by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).
As for "Attaining Friends": it is when, having encountered a virtuous friend who has realized the truth, one attains the cessation of doubt.
This seventh accomplishment is designated as "Ram yak a.
For in the world, contact with good friends is delightful; thus, from the naming of that [delight], it is called "Ram yak a" (the Delightful).

Regarding generosity: when one overcomes misfortune through generosity and accomplishes any one of the three previously mentioned [perfections], that eighth accomplishment is called "Ever-Joyful" (*sadāpramudita*). For one who is ever-joyful becomes fortunate; therefore, the cessation of misfortune is "Ever-Joyful."
Thus, these eight accomplishments (*siddhi*) have been explained.
Since one accomplishes the desired object by relying upon them, one who wishes to ascend the path transmitted by the ancient teachers should be inclined toward it.
He asks: what, then, is the reason here, given that there is no difference in their being human goals (*puruṣārtha*), that one experiences the qualities as the cause of all accomplishments?
It is said:
Because prior to accomplishment, there is a threefold restraint.
Having accepted the generality of the capacity for understanding the probandum (*sādhya*), he says "because of its establishment" (*siddheḥ*).

The former [type of person] is characterized by error, incapacity, and complacency; it is called a "restraint" (*aṅkuśa*) because it functions like a goad (*aṅkuśa*) due to the commonality of turning back [the mind].
Although the stream of success proceeds eternally from Pradhāna, its non-operation among all living beings occurs due to the obstructions of error, incapacity, and contentment.
First, with respect to error, this is the case among immobile beings;
for they are primarily characterized by the nature of error.
Due to incapacity, one is reborn among animals;
for they are those whose nature is characterized by the flow toward the animal realm.
Due to contentment, one is reborn among the gods.
For those who flow upwards have contentment as their essence,
whereas humans flow downwards and have accomplishment as their essence;
therefore, only they engage in the practices beginning with the *tāraka*.

Because there is a fixed relationship of primary and subordinate factors among the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, [the means] are obstructed by error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and contentment (*tuṣṭi*); thus, success (*siddhi*) does not occur for everyone at all times.
Therefore, it is said that "prior to success, the threefold restraint exists.
And just as error, incapacity, and contentment are the adversaries of success, [so too are their opposites].
In this way, accomplishment (*siddhi*) also [removes] error and the rest;
for once it has arisen, it causes all these to cease.
How so? Non-erroneous knowledge removes error regarding the past, future, and present, whether [objects] are near or distant.

Because there is no obstruction for the person—who is distinct from the transformations of *prakṛti*—whether toward objects perceivable by the senses or those beyond the senses, one sees that the person lacks power [over them]; thus, contentment arises in all stages.
In this way, these channels, beginning with *prāṇa*, as well as the sources of action (*karmayoni*), have been explained.
By establishing these [beings] upon the path, one attains in no long time the supreme accomplishment characterized by absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). And it is said:
"By correctly directing those of various origins along with their measures onto the right path, and because the streams are purified, one should proceed with a mind free from attachment. (51)
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Yuktidīpikā*.
Now, regarding what was previously stated: "Creation is produced by conjunction" (*kārikā* 21).
Thus that has been explained.
Here, however, there is currently a disagreement among the teachers (*ācārya*) because phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth do not arise in the absence of a body.
Furthermore, since there can be no other cause for the absence of dharma and so forth in the body, both of these are beginningless.
Therefore, this creation is of a single uniform nature; just as it is at present, so too was it in past and will it be in future reaches of time.
To this, the Teacher says: "This is not so."

What then? Prior to the activity of the *pradhāna*, there is no possibility of *dharma* and *adharma*, because they are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect is a modification of the *pradhāna*.

Therefore, with a view toward an object characterized by the perception of sound and so forth, as well as the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*, the *sattva* and other *guṇas* abide as the Great One (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, and the gross elements, for the sake of the Supreme Sage (*paramarṣi*), Hiraṇyagarbha, and others.
They produce the body.

However, following the dissolution of the six perfections (*ṣaṭsiddhi*) at the end of time, the wheel of saṃsāra proceeds, conforming to the activity of *rajas* and *tamas* due to the diversity of the suppression of the *guṇas*.
Without the objective entities (*bhāvas*), the subtle body (*liṅga*) does not exist.
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "it remains established in the state of a god, a human, or an animal.
There is no accomplishment of existence without a characteristic mark (*liṅga*);
here, "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) is intended to mean "production" (*niṣpatti*).
From that, the two-fold creation proceeds: that which is called the Linga and that which is called Bhāva.
Thus, this [creation] consists of that which is called "mark" (liṅga) and that which is called "existence" (bhāva), occurring after the period of the dissolution of the six perfections.
Immediately following the qualities (guṇas), however, is that characterized by office (adhikāra).
Therefore, creation is twofold: characterized by office and called existence.

However, for those who maintain that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), as well as the body, stand in a reciprocal relationship of cause and effect, it has already been refuted that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is their cause.

Furthermore, as for those Sāṃkhyas who say, "The activity of *pradhāna* occurs by virtue of the influence of merit and demerit," for them the postulation of one or the other [of these two] is purposeless.

How so? If, first of all, this merit alone (adhi-kāra) is sufficient for the primary cause to proceed, what is the use of virtue and vice (dharma-adharma)? Or, if on the other hand, merit is incapable of bringing about the primary cause's activity without [the assistance of] virtue and vice;
Even so, by what authority? Because the capacity for activity belongs to those two alone.
Therefore, creation is twofold, caused by both authority and material nature.

In this regard, just as this body—which is undivided—becomes divided for the sake of activities characterized by virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*), and thus possesses the differentiation of hands and so forth; likewise, the creation of *sattva* (the unevolved nature), though undivided, must be capable of those activities characterized by virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. // 52 // Kārikā 53: [The following verse follows: "Just as a single seed produces many fruits, and from those fruits other seeds arise, so too from the Unmanifest (Avyakta) proceed many effects, and from those effects other effects arise. [This is the full verse.]
The divine [realm] consists of eight varieties, that of the animals is fivefold,
and the human is of one kind; because it has these eight varieties, it is called "the eightfold."
"Eightfold" means consisting of eight varieties; namely: Brahmā, Prajāpati, Indra, the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.
Furthermore, the animal realm (*tairyagyona*) is fivefold: domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings.
And the human state is of one kind, because there is no arising from another birth.
He asks: Is this alone the variety of the creation of beings, or is there another?
It is said: there is another alternative [classification] due to the internal division of sub-groups within these very same categories.
Is this one, or is there yet another?
It is said: there is another alternative due to the internal division of sub-groups within these very same categories. And this...
In brief, creation consists of the derivative elements.
What? The remainder of the sentence is "has been taught.
In that regard, there is a division among the gods into the Sādhyas, Maruts, Rudras, and so forth;
and among animals, a division into domestic, wild, and so forth.

Furthermore, if the division of human beings—based on the distinctions of Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—and the division of plants were to be described in detail, it would result in an infinite enumeration. Therefore, the creation of the elements is taught here in summary. (53)
It is said: this statement of another alternative is due to a difference in the stream [of discourse].
A threefold classification of beings is taught—namely, those born of gods, humans, and animals;
yet four streams have been mentioned.
Therefore, another classification must be stated.
It is said: No, because of the capacity for the inclusion of the qualities of the dharmas.
Those with an abundance of *sattva* are those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*); those with an abundance of *rajas* are those who flow downwards (*arvāksrotas*).
Those who are dominated by darkness (*tamas*) are the *tiryaksrotas* (those with horizontal currents) and the *mukhyasrotas* (those with downward currents).
Therefore, these two are taught without distinction.
[An objector] says: "The addition of the *asuras* and others must be made."
Since they are not included among the others, should they not be taught without distinction, rather than being categorized as divine, human, or animal?
It is said: No, for they are subsumed within those already mentioned.
To begin with, the Asuras are included within the very station of Indra.
Because they were formerly gods;
for the asuras were indeed former gods. Furthermore, because they hold the position of Indra in turn.
It is heard that Dhanvin and others attained the status of Indra in turn;
likewise, the Yakṣas [attain it] among the Rākṣasas because they are of one form;
and the Kinnaras and Vidyādharas [attain it] among the Gandharvas.

Because they share similar dispositions; and because the *pretas* share a commonality with the *pitṛs* as lords. Therefore, the creation of beings consists of exactly three categories, and this is as follows:
"Above, it is vast with sentient beings.
By the word "above," he refers to the eight celestial abodes;
therein, this creation is vast with sentient beings.
From the Piśācas [the power] of the Rakṣasas,
from the Rakṣasas that of the Nāgas, and from the Nāgas that of the Gandharvas.
From the Gandharvas [to] the Pitṛs;
from the Pitṛs [to] the Tridaśas;
from them [to] the Prajāpatis.
From them also comes Brahmā;
thus, the inclusion of the term "vast" (viśāla) is justified.
However, the creation rooted in darkness (tamas) is vast from its very foundation.
But from the very root, creation is characterized by an abundance of tamas;
for the darkness of wild animals is more intense than that of domestic cattle, and that of birds is more intense than that of wild animals.
From birds come the reptiles; from reptiles, the stationary beings.
In the midst [of these] is the one in whom passion (rajas) predominates.

In the realms inferior to those of the gods and animals, as the sattva and tamas decrease, so too does the rajas increase. Since humans occupy the middle ground between these two, it is there that the rajas reaches its highest intensity.
Because it has the nature of accomplishment for those whose stream of consciousness flows downward and because of their extreme engagement in ritual action;
and just as there is an abundance of *rajas* among humans, so too is there an abundance of *sattva* in the station of Brahmā, and an abundance of *tamas* among immobile beings.
Indeed,
this [world] extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

The creation, which has been explained as having fourteen divisions and three types of conceptualization, functions as the object for the increase or decrease of the qualities such as *sattva*. Herein, the conscious *puruṣa* undergoes the suffering caused by old age and death.
It is produced by old age, produced by death, and produced by both old age and death.

In that regard, first, that which is produced by old age is as follows: the state of having limbs trembling with wrinkles, and the inability to engage in activities such as walking about without the aid of a staff.
Incapacity of all the sense faculties to enjoy their respective objects, severe coughing and labored breathing, and eyes clouded with tears.
The instability of the ten teeth, discoloration, looseness, impediment in speech, dullness of memory, and so forth.

Death-induced [change] also consists in the cessation of the mutual assistance that occurs while earth and the other elements remain in the state of a body— namely, their functioning through distinct natures, their cohesion, their structural arrangement, and their providing space—

and in the impairment of the sense faculties' bases, resulting in the non-perception of existing sounds, tangibles, forms, tastes, and odors, the perception of those that do not exist, the perception of objects in an unreal form, or the perception of all objects in a manner contrary to reality;
for example, on the full moon night, the perception of a crescent moon in the southern sky, of ghosts and the like, or of a white sky, and so forth.

Likewise, one who has developed various kinds of diseases arising from the imbalance of wind and other humors, whose functions of all the sense organs are failing, whose limbs have collapsed, whose eyes are copper-colored, yellow, and clouded with tears, and who is overcome by dizziness, burning sensations, labored breathing, and so forth; whose vital joints are failing within, and who looks toward the quarters for water; who finds no protector even in the worlds including those of Brahmā; and whose intellect is being impaired by the instruments of the self through the long-matured grasping at a self due to passion and other afflictions—even when [the objects] are very faint...

The suffering caused by death— consisting of the loss of memory while recollecting one's beloved people and oneself, the falling away from the tenfold family circle, which is inevitable for all beings, causes supreme agitation, is uncomprehended, unavoidable, and occurs at an uncertain time— is designated by the Great Beings, such as the Supreme Sages, by the term "blinding darkness" (andhatāmisra).

Furthermore, since this suffering—which consists of the stages of the principles (tattvas) characterized by primordial matter (pradhāna), the Great One (mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, and the gross elements—is devoid of consciousness, it is the Spirit (puruṣa) alone who perceives it through his connection with the power of consciousness.
Having considered this, the Teacher stated: "In this regard, the conscious Spirit undergoes the suffering caused by old age and death.
[The opponent] says: "An addition must be made for that which is caused by birth."
For just as old age and death cause intense agitation for oneself, so too does birth.

Thus, while in the mother’s womb, his body enveloped by the placenta and drenched in impurities, within that vessel of the embryo which is like a mere wound, his limbs are tormented by the lack of any possibility of comfort; experiencing suffering in the dwelling of the womb, he is oppressed by the mother’s food and other such things.

Later, having emerged through the opening between two bones that had closed up, his body drenched with urine, blood, and fetal fluids, he was tormented by the external wind and by hands that felt like blades of grass as they touched him; unable to describe the suffering existing within himself which is only personally experienced,
he was [ignored] by those with firm limbs and accumulated afflictions who, due to their own commonality of pleasure and pain, possessed only conceptual notions of pleasure and pain regarding others.
Being driven [in the cycle of existence], one experiences the suffering of birth;
therefore, that too must be explained.
It is said in reply: No, because it is not all-pervasive.
Suffering produced by birth occurs only for humans and animals, not for the gods.
Why? Because their bodies manifest in a mere instant, like a flash of lightning. However, that which is produced by old age and death does not cease even for them.
Therefore, because of its preeminence, only this has been taught and not the other.
He says: there is no possibility of including the other [realms], because they are equal;
for indeed, neither old age nor death is heard of in the celestial abodes.
Therefore, because those two are not all-pervasive, there would follow the consequence that they too are not apprehended.
It is said in reply: No, because of the statement regarding memory.
"It decays by means of this" is what is meant by *jarā*; thus, it is said to be decay (*kṣaya*).
And that [condition] occurs even in the realm of the gods.
Why? For it is said thus:
"The adherence of dust to the limbs, discoloration, and the withering of flowers."
For living beings who are about to fall from the world of the gods, [this] arises.
The body of Śakra and others perishes upon hearing of their illness;

for thus it is said: "The *sāman* belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ was employed; even though Indra was exhausted, all beings were unable to put him to sleep, but he caused him to sleep by means of this *sāman* belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Likewise, Vāyu devoured Prajāpati.
Furthermore, due to the curse of Dakṣa, there was a waning of Soma.
Likewise: "Prajāpati indeed gave his daughters, the constellations, to King Soma; he dwelt only with Rohiṇī."
When they looked back for them, however, they had gone;
therefore, not finding her own [children], she went again.
As they followed after them, she asked for them once more.
He did not give them back to him.
She said, "Dwell briefly with all of them together, and then I will give them back to you.
He dwelt with Rohiṇī alone; while he was in that state of falsehood, consumption seized him.
Soma, the King, is indeed the moon; when the King was seized by consumption (*yakṣman*), that was the origin of royal consumption (*rājayakṣma*).
He withered away like a blade of grass. He then sought refuge with Prajāpati.
He said, "Dwell equally among all [the constellations], and then I shall release you from this.
Therefore, the moon dwells equally among all the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

On the night of the new moon (amāvāsyā), they sacrifice to him with a sacrificial pap (caru) for the Viśvedevas, thinking, "The consumption by evil spirits (yakṣma) has not released him," and so forth.

Therefore, even in the celestial realm (*devabhūmi*), there is suffering caused by old age, as well as suffering caused by death due to migrating to another realm after being born there; Yayāti serves as an example of this. As stated in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa*: "There were indeed fifteen hundred gods; they diminished because of their offense against Brahman."
Then thirty-three gods remained; this is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Of the fifteen hundred uterine brothers, thirty-three gods remained;
the rest were consumed."
"In the Śvetāraṇya forest, suffering was inflicted upon Antaka by Rudra;
this is either merely an illustration,
or rather, it is simply one example among many sufferings."
Alternatively, it should be stated that there is an elision of the word "etc.
(ādi); what is intended as the illustrative example is precisely that which is produced by aging and death, and not some other form of suffering.

Why? Because even there, the elision of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is mentioned as a mere illustration; it is stated thus because it can be inferred by implication, not because it is the locus of all suffering.
For the common locus of all sufferings is that which is produced by old age and death.
How so? Because it is a cause of distress even for one's kinsmen and friends;
it is not caused by birth, since [birth] is a source of great joy for relatives.
And because in this world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, no one transcends the suffering caused by old age and death—
as long as the subtle body (*liṅga*) has not ceased— therefore, in brief, [existence] is suffering.
Because even a mere fragment of pleasure is pervaded by that [suffering];
as long as this mark does not cease, there must necessarily be suffering, since through the power of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), one is reborn in another world in turn. And thus it has been said:
For he experiences pleasure, pain, or doubt there and there in turn;
if it is asked how pleasure can be pervaded by pain, it is because impurity increases progressively up to the level of Brahmā.
And because that [existence] has suffering as its root;
for it is heard that Prajāpati suffered from an eye disease,
and Indra was afflicted by desire.
Due to Gautama’s contempt, Rambhā underwent the state of being stone because of his curse;
due to the exhaustion from the snake-sacrifice, the Nāgas [suffered]; and due to Yaska’s curse, Vaiśravaṇa underwent the state of being an elephant.

Because Jaratkāru was pulled from the pit of the ancestors (*pitṛ-garta*), and because Piśācas are driven away by the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and auspicious rites, and because human and animal beings are generally the very locus of suffering through direct perception;

therefore, there is no place in *saṃsāra* where one, together with the *liṅga*, would not encounter suffering. For this very reason, one must strive in such a way that the *liṅga* itself is utterly eradicated.
For from that [cessation], there is the absolute pacification of all sufferings.
However, the inclusion of "pleasure" (in the definition of suffering) is for the purpose of providing scope for pleasure and delusion;
otherwise, it would be admitted that these two simply do not exist within saṃsāra. (55)
Having thus described the creation exactly as it is, he concludes by saying:
"In this way, this process— consisting of the principles, the elements, and the objects of existence— proceeds as both nature and its transformations."
For the sake of the liberation of each individual soul, the undertaking for the sake of others is like that for one's own sake.
By the use of the particle *iti*, he indicates the conclusion of the section.
Although it has already been stated as "this" (*eṣa*), it is required again for the purpose of referring back [to what precedes].
That which is produced by primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is "produced by primordial nature" (*prakṛtikṛta*).
By this, for the sake of completing the statement, the existence of the Pradhāna is established through both the positive (vīta) and negative (avīta) arguments;
it also implies the refutation of atoms and other such causes.
This [existence] is produced by Primordial Matter alone, not by atoms and the like.
The phrase "it proceeds" expresses a continuity of action.
It has not already proceeded, nor will it proceed; rather, it simply proceeds, through its manifestation as infinite bodies and so forth, and by means of mutual assistance.
This action never takes on the form of having already occurred or yet to occur.
Rather, it has a present form,
as when one says, "the rivers flow" or "the mountains stand."
He provides a restatement of the meaning of what was said regarding "that which is called reality, the elements, and existence":

that which is called "reality" consists of the Great Principle (mahat) and the others; that which is called "existence" consists of space (vyoman) and the others. Liberation for each individual person is "liberation for every person" (pratipuruṣavimokṣa).

"For that purpose" means for the sake of the liberation of each individual self (*puruṣa*). The meaning is: for the sake of rendering all power—which is bound to the office of all selves—free from further desire. Thus, the undertaking is for the sake of others as if it were for one's own sake.
By way of the relationship between cause and effect:
therein, first, the status of being an object for the sense faculties with respect to the effects such as sound is like [their own] respective objects;
and the eagerness of the sense faculties, which do not reach their objects, is—inferable from the modification of their bases—like [their own] respective objects.

The instruments—the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—attain the state of being gateways to objects through their functions of volition (*saṃkalpa*), self-identification (*abhimāna*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, the mind and ego have as their sphere of activity their own respective operations, which are withdrawn into the intellect. The intellect, in turn, possesses the qualities of being calm, fierce, or deluded, as well as the agency of determination. And the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* qualities mutually assist one another through their characteristics of illumination, activity, and restraint.
And this is not for its own sake,
because all of this is insentient;
rather, this undertaking is solely for the sake of another.
"Because it is a composite.
He says: That which was stated—that this undertaking is for the sake of the liberation of each individual—is incorrect, because there is a contradiction with the Teacher's position.

The Paurika, a teacher of the Sāṃkhya school, maintains that a distinct primary matter (pradhāna) exists for each individual soul to produce bodies and other effects; and when the primary matter belonging to those of great majesty initiates activity, the others do so as well, and upon its cessation, theirs also cease.
How then can a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) be accepted without being refuted?
It is replied: No, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
First of all, it cannot be ascertained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself.
Because the primary causes (pradhāna) are beyond the senses,
there is no unambiguous mark (liṅga) [of their existence],
and authoritative persons (āpta) have not declared them; therefore, we consider that this is not so.
Furthermore, because the purpose is accomplished by one alone,
and because it is immeasurable, this single primary cause is sufficient for the production of the bodies of all persons;
therefore, the postulation of anything else is useless.
If it is thought that [the world] is finite, then [it is argued]: no, for the primary cause (pradhāna) is not finite, as that would entail the consequence of annihilation.
Even so, its annihilation would follow as in the case of milk;
and thus there would be the undesirable consequence of the annihilation of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of an infinite regress.

The possession of multiple bodies by a single Lord or yogi through the application of his will is untenable because it implies limitation. Alternatively, if a separate primal matter (*pradhāna*) is postulated for each body, there would be an infinite regress of primal matters.
Since it is accepted that the cause consists of a limited body, the postulation of anything else is useless;
consequently, there is only a single *pradhāna*.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that there is a *pradhāna* for each individual person.

Regarding what was stated—that when the primary activity of the Great Self (māhātmyaśarīra) proceeds, the others proceed, and upon its cessation they cease—we reply: No, because there is no excellence (atiśaya).

Just as the individual knowers (kṣetrajñas) do not act as mutual instigators due to their being beyond all measure (niratiśayatva), so too it would follow that these [guṇas] could not constitute the Pradhāna if they possessed such excellence, owing to the resulting inequality (vaiṣamya).
Therefore, it is logical that a single primordial nature (prakṛti) operates for the sake of the liberation of each individual person. Objection:
That is untenable because [primordial nature] is insentient (acetana).

In this world, it is never observed that insentient things such as jars act with a specific purpose in mind. If this primordial nature (prakṛti) is likewise insentient, then its activity directed toward the goal of the Puruṣa is not logically possible.
If, however, such activity does occur, then it follows that sentience must belong to it.
Regarding this, as for what was stated—that the activity of *prakṛti* is for the sake of the liberation of each individual—this is incorrect.
It is replied: No, because it is established by means of an analogy;
just as the activity of insentient milk is for the purpose of the growth of the calf.
The primordial matter (pradhāna) proceeds in such a manner for the sake of the liberation of the person (puruṣa).
Just as insentient milk functions with the aim of nourishing the calf, so too does the Pradhāna function with the aim of the liberation of the Puruṣa;
yet it would not possess consciousness.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatva*), the thought might be:
"Is this yet to be proven—whether the activity [of milk] is directed toward the growth of the calf, or not?
Therefore, the example is incorrect because it is yet to be proven."
And this is incorrect.
Why? Because it is absent when that is absent, and present when that is present.
Where there is no growth of the calf, there the flow of milk is not observed.
Where something exists, there it is perceived;
if something occurs when another is present, the activity of the former is seen to be for the sake of the latter,
as, for example, that of the potter with respect to the jar.
And this is our intended meaning: namely, that [the effect] exists for the sake of that [cause]. Therefore, there is no need for the proof to rely on an illustrative example.
If it is argued that because [the cause] is said to possess non-existence [of the effect], this contradicts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), we say no.
Because it is a synonym for manifestation (*vyakti*). For that [Great Principle] is indeed a synonym for manifestation, according to the authority of both scripture and the world.
Regarding scripture, "the Great" is merely existence (*sattāmātra*), meaning it is mere manifestation.
In the world as well, one says, "There is no water in this well";
it does not mean that there is no water at all in the well, nor that it is not manifest.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*).
If it is argued that [the example] is unestablished because it is impelled by the unseen (adṛṣṭa),
and if you think that milk flows forth impelled by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) for the sake of the calf's growth,
that too is incorrect.
Why? Because the defect is the same.
Dharma and Adharma, being insentient, cause milk to flow at the time of its increase and cause it to cease at its conclusion;
therefore, even if this [theory] is postulated in such a manner, the defect remains equal.
If it is argued that this is due to the impulsion of God— that is, if the thought should arise that God causes the milk to flow there for the sake of the calf, and not of its own accord—
that is incorrect.
Why? Because of its prohibition.
The activity of the Lord has been previously refuted;
therefore, this too is untenable.

If the illustration is established in this way, then for the followers of Vārṣagaṇya, the illustration is as follows: just as the insentient bodies of women and men function toward one another by aiming at each other, so too does the Pradhāna.
He asks: how is it understood that the connection of the Puruṣa with the manifested [world] produced for his sake is not merely due to proximity?
If it is argued that [the Puruṣa is like] a monk, it is said: No, because that would entail the impossibility of liberation (anapavarga).
For one who maintains that the experience of the Puruṣa occurs through mere proximity, there could be no possibility of liberation, since that proximity is eternal.
Therefore, this is incorrect.

If it should be thought: "The activity of causes and effects toward one who does not instigate them is illogical"—[we reply: the monk Kṛṣṇa and others do not instigate [the activity] of those [causes], and thus there is no activity of them toward him; likewise, the *puruṣa* does not instigate the activity of the causes and effects.
Therefore, the claim that their activity toward him is likewise illogical is for this very reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For a calf is not the instigator of the milk’s flow, yet the milk flows toward it. Thus, it is correct that the activity of *prakṛti* is for the sake of the liberation of the Person (*puruṣa*), and there is no consequence of [the Person] possessing consciousness. // 57 //
[Kārikā 58] He says: No, because it would follow that there is no activity.

If the activity of *pradhāna* is for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *puruṣa*, then since isolation is already established in the absence of that [activity], it follows that there would be no activity at all.
Now, if the Pradhāna operates toward the Puruṣa alone, then its operation is not for his sake.
Just as people engage in activities for the sake of satisfying their curiosity,
so too does the Unmanifest operate for the sake of the Puruṣa’s liberation.

This has already been explained: because the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa possess the powers of the object-to-be-seen and the seer respectively, and because either one would be purposeless in the absence of the other, they both have a mutual eagerness toward their connection. Furthermore, just as the activity of people in the world—even when aimed at cessation—is observed to be for the sake of ending their eagerness, so too is the activity of the Pradhāna for the sake of its own cessation. If it is argued that it acts for the sake of ending the eagerness of the powers of the seen and the seer, then since its purpose would be fulfilled in one instance, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-activity in others. To this, [the reply] may be as follows:
If the *pradhāna* were to cease after having manifested itself to a single *puruṣa*, then the cessation of the longing for the powers of the seen (*dṛśya*) and the seer (*darśana*) would occur.
// 58 // Furthermore, this [argument] that there would be a lack of activity is also untenable.
Why? Because of the force of another example. What is it like?
It is said:
Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after displaying herself to the audience,
so does primordial nature (prakṛti) cease after manifesting itself to the person (puruṣa).
In that context, the assembly of people who possess cognitions of various colors and natures and who seek to observe them is called a "theater" (*raṅga*).
And the dance performed by the dancer for their gratification serves the purpose of many men.
Or, if someone here were to ask: "Why does this [cognition] not cease even when seen by the dance instructor or the actors?"
How so?
Because her purpose remains unfulfilled.

Thus, how can Prakṛti—having set out for the sake of rendering desireless all Puruṣas who possess longing through the connection between cause and effect—be one whose purpose is fulfilled by the cessation of longing in a single Puruṣa?
Could it be so?

Therefore, it is not logical that the cessation of *prakṛti* occurs for a single person after having manifested the Self. And in this regard— [commentary on kārikās 60–63 lost] —@-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Kārikā 64:
The Puruṣa is the witness of the activity of cause and effect.

Therefore, those things which are elemental—such as the head, hands, and so forth—and those which are derived from the ego (ahaṃkāra)—such as hearing and so forth, speaking and so forth, as well as volition, self-conceit, and determination—are excluded [from being the Puruṣa] because their characteristics are contrary [to his]; thus, "I am not," nor am I the eight primal natures (prakṛtis).

Thus, for the ascetic whose mind is one-pointed through the practice of the principles (*tattva*) in this manner, by repeated practice— even with respect to the single principle of egoism (*asmitā*)— there arises, by way of negating the distinctions of imagined objects,
the realization "I am not," "nothing is mine," and "I do not exist," without remainder,
until the grasping of the antidote reaches the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Due to the absence of error,

upon the cessation of this stage of ignorance consisting of the five streams, there arises a knowledge that is peaceful, stable, the antidote to the attachment to all states of existence, free from doubt, non-erroneous, pure, and absolute, belonging to the principle of consciousness (buddhitattva) which has been nourished by the Dharma and other virtues.
He said: "Pure" and "exclusive" [are used];
the non-mentioning of either one is because there is no difference in meaning.
Since that which is pure is the very same as that which is exclusive, because there is no difference in meaning, it is possible to leave one or the other unspoken.
It is said: because it is the cause for the cessation of the forms of other qualities.

Since it involves the grasping of the attributes of *rajas* and *tamas*, [the knowledge] is pure—that is, distinct from doubt and error—and it is "exclusive" (*kevala*) in that it is truly unprecedented (*apūrva*) regarding the full comprehension of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). // 64 //
[The opponent] says: It follows that the body must fall at that very same moment.
It is said that while abiding in existence, the body has ignorance as its cause.
Thus it is stated: "The body has ignorance as its cause;
yet this one perceives multiplicity."
When the causes for [the arising of] phenomena and so forth have ceased,
he remains with his body sustained by the force of conditioned formations, like the spinning of a wheel.
The qualities such as merit (*dharma*) acquired in another body are not yet the cause;

for although they have reached the intellect (*buddhi*), the purpose has not yet been fulfilled, and thus the intellect remains in its primary state (*pradhāna*). At that time, this [soul] who perceives diversity remains [in bondage] due to the power of that latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
What is the illustration?
The body is maintained like the whirling of a wheel.

For example, the whirling of a potter’s wheel is a motion capable of producing a jar or similar object, brought about by the specific effort of the potter using a stick; "like the whirling of a wheel" means it is similar to that.
Just as the spinning of a wheel is for the sake of a jar;
once the jar has been produced, the wheel's spinning is the activity suitable for the completion of the jar and so forth.
"Like the spinning of a wheel" means it is similar to that.

Just as the spinning of a wheel for the purpose of making a pot does not cease even when the pot is finished— due to the persistence of prior momentum— and yet it does not remain there once that [momentum] has ceased, so too the body, though intended for the sake of right vision, does not cease even upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, owing to the force of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
And it is not the case that, because [the suffering] has ceased at that time, one remains even when the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) have been exhausted.
// 67 // But when, upon the exhaustion of the formative forces, there is the dissolution of the body which is their cause, from that...
