When the dissolution of the body has occurred, dharma and adharma, having fulfilled their purpose, dissolve into their cause, which is characterized by the intellect (buddhi).
Furthermore, that constituent element of the [five] elements which initiates the formation of the body dissolves into all the elements within the subtle elements (tanmātras).
The sense organs and the subtle elements [dissolve] into the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra);
the ego-principle dissolves into the intellect (buddhi), and the intellect into the unmanifest (avyakta).
This is the sequence of the principles; having emerged from the Pradhāna for the sake of that purpose, it returns to dissolution once that purpose is fulfilled and the Pradhāna is no longer active.
Prakṛti also fashions bodies for him according to the requirements of his purpose throughout various successions of births;
and this noble one has accomplished his purpose.
Therefore, because his purpose has been fulfilled, there occurs the cessation of Prakṛti.
One attains absolute liberation— beyond the senses, imperceptible, light, omnipresent, praiseworthy, uncreated, pure, inexhaustible, unsurpassed,
exclusive, ultimate, and fearless.
This state is explained by the Buddhists as liberation (*apavarga*), characterized by *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This is the supreme Brahman—eternal, stainless, and fearless—in which all qualities and attributes undergo total dissolution.
Having attained this, one becomes liberated from all exertions and all bonds, freed from passion and hatred that have been active since beginningless time.

For this purpose, Brahmins—having abandoned their attachment to beloved sons, wives, wealth, and kin—devote themselves to the service of their gurus and subject their bodies to exhaustion in the forests. How indeed may absolute and final liberation (*kaivalya*) be attained? The Teacher has brought the treatise to its conclusion precisely where its exposition began. // 68 // Kārikā 69: The means for attaining that [liberation] have been stated; now, the means for attaining that [means] must be explained. These are: non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*). Among these, non-violence is the primary one, because it is the cause of the attainment of all virtues. It is said: "Non-violence is the highest dharma; from non-violence arises truth. Therefore, non-violence is the foremost. Truthfulness is the speaking of what is beneficial and pleasant. Non-stealing is the non-appropriation of what belongs to others. Celibacy is the restraint of the sexual organ. Non-possessiveness is the absence of attachment to external objects. These are the five great vows (*mahāvratas*). Furthermore, there are the five minor vows (*aṇuvratas*): non-injury to mobile beings, truthfulness with respect to the immobile, non-stealing regarding small items, celibacy limited to one's own wife, and non-possessiveness limited by a specific amount. There are also the three guṇavratas: dig-vrata (the vow of limiting movement to certain directions), deśa-vrata (the vow of limiting movement to a specific area), and anartha-danda-vrata (the vow of avoiding useless injury). And the four śikṣāvratas: sāmāyika (periodic meditation and renunciation), proṣadhopavāsa (fasting on specific days), bhogopabhoga-parimāṇa (limiting the consumption of food and luxuries), and atithi-saṃvibhāga (sharing with guests). By practicing these eleven vows through the twelve types of conduct, one attains liberation. The twelve types of conduct are: equanimity (*sāmāyika*), reverence (*vandana*), repentance (*pratikramaṇa*), expiation (*kāyotsarga*), renunciation (*pratyākhyāna*), right faith (*darśana*), right knowledge (*jñāna*), right conduct (*cāritra*), austerity (*tapas*), self-restraint (*saṃyama*), truthfulness (*satya*), and non-stealing (*asteya*). Through the practice of these, the soul becomes free from the eight karmas and attains the state of the liberated ones. Thus ends the exposition of the means to liberation. // 69 //
He asks: "For what purpose, then, was this treatise composed, or by whom was it previously revealed?
It is said in response: Regarding that which was asked—"for what purpose"—this [treatise] is for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

How indeed might liberation be attained by living beings who have fallen under the influence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from ignorance? It is for this purpose that this treatise has been explained.
As for the question "by whom [was it taught]?", it is said:
"It was declared as a secret by the Supreme Sage."
"Secret" (guhya) means that which is to be concealed;
"esoteric" (rahasya) means that which is not to be studied even with respect by those of unrefined self who are not established in the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).

The Supreme Seer (paramarṣi), the Blessed One, the Sage Kapila, was the first-born of the universe, his physical body permeated by the innate perfections of dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

This was correctly explained by that sage Kapila; it was rightly explained because of his capacity for verbal exposition resulting from his long-standing cultivation of the stream of knowledge (*vidyāsrotas*). This might be so.
How is this secret?
It is said: how could this not be a secret?
Even by those born at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), such as Sanaka, Sanātana, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and others, [the nature] of impermanent things...
And wherein the stability, arising, and dissolution of all beings are contemplated.

In this regard, persistence [of primordial nature] is indicated by the description of the results of the manifestation of form; its origination is likewise shown by the sequence beginning with "from primordial nature comes the Great One" (*mahat*);
and its dissolution is indicated by the statement, "the manifold variety [returns to] non-distinction. This occurs because the eagerness of primordial nature and the spirit (*puruṣa*) does not cease.
The persistence and arising of both the power of seeing and the power of the object seen are dependent upon one another;
and so it has been said:
"The purpose of the Puruṣa is perception, and likewise the purpose of Pradhāna is isolation."
"The union of both is like that of the lame and the blind; from that [union] proceeds creation" (ISk 21).
"Dissolution occurs when the body is destroyed, because the *pradhāna* has fulfilled its purpose and thus ceases its activity" (ISk 68).

Alternatively, since the momentary destruction of stability is refuted, there is no destruction of this [world] at other times; therefore, origination results from transformation, not from the manifestation of what was previously non-existent, nor from causelessness, as that is impossible.
Dissolution also occurs due to another cause, or rather by the very nature of things, for all manifested entities—that is to say, even for those possessing production.
And in this way, the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat) are also included.
[The opponent] says: "In that case, the Person (puruṣa) and so forth are excluded."
Or how is the word "bhūta" (real) used?
It is said: because it serves to negate what is false (vitatha).
Whatever is not false is "bhūta," and here the stability and other [characteristics] of all such things are being described.
Because there is no distinction in the refutation of arising and destruction.
Even so, it would follow that the arising and dissolution of the person (puruṣa) and other such entities would also occur.
What is the reason?
"Because there is no distinction," it is said: a qualification applies only where [such a distinction] is possible;
in this case, however, stability alone belongs to the person (puruṣa) and the others.
But we shall understand that for the others, however, there are stability, origination, and dissolution.
(69) [The opponent] asks: For what purpose, then, was this treatise revealed by the Supreme Sage?
It is said:
out of compassion, the Sage gave this most pure and supreme [teaching] to Āsuri;
therein, it is "pure" (pavitra) because of its purifying nature (pāvana).
It is supreme because it is capable of exhausting all suffering.
Other purifiers, such as the Adhamarṣaṇa and the Gaṅgā, wash away only a single portion [of impurity].
Therefore, the Sage, out of compassion, bestowed this very [text] upon Āsuri.
He said: The act of giving would be accidental, because causes such as *dharma* and so forth are untenable.
First of all, it is not tenable that the Supreme Sage gave the treatise for the sake of *dharma*.
Because of non-attachment to the fruit;
nor for the sake of wealth or desire,
since that would result in the disciples undergoing unnecessary hardship.
It is not for the sake of liberation,
because that is attained through innate knowledge (*sāṃsiddhika-jñāna*) alone.
Therefore, since no other purpose is possible, it follows by elimination that the Teacher bestowed this treasure of the scriptures spontaneously.
It is said: not without cause, but rather out of compassion he bestowed [the teaching].
Having perceived Āsuri being tormented by sufferings—internal, celestial, and elemental—and having [perceived] within himself the capacity for knowledge, [he gave it].
Having fully understood that suffering does not arise when there is no conjunction between the cause and the effect, and considering the qualities of his disciples— thinking,

"How might the Āsuri also attain equanimity regarding pleasure and pain through the application of knowledge, just as it has come to me, and by means of that, how might other persons likewise [attain it]?"— the Blessed One, the Supreme Sage, out of compassion, proclaimed this treatise.
And just as the Supreme Rishi [taught] to Āsuri,
so too did Āsuri [teach] to his ten sons.
And by him, Pañcaśikha, the tantra was made manifold.
It has been handed down by many, such as Janaka, Vasiṣṭha, and others.

However, because this scripture was first promulgated in the presence of the Blessed One, its lineage cannot be fully recounted even in hundreds of thousands of years, unlike other scriptures. Kārikā 71:

In brief, however, there are two [traditions]: that which has come down through the lineage of disciples beginning with Āhārīta, Vāddhalika, Airātapaurika, Ārṣabheśvara, the five authorities (pañcādhikaraṇa), Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka, and others;
and the treatise composed by the venerable Īśvarakṛṣṇa as an aid.

In the textual compositions of the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*), because they did not take into account the relative weight of brevity versus detail, they provided excessive explanations that were pregnant with Eastern-style commentaries; thus, the bulk of the work increased. Since the lifespan of living beings today is so short, it is already difficult to master such works merely by reading them, let alone through hearing and practice.

As it has been said: "Knowledge becomes properly applied in four ways: at the time of its transmission (*āgama*), at the time of its study (*svādhyāya*), and at the time of its practical application (*prayoga*)."
In that case, his lifespan would have been exhausted at the very moment of his arrival, and consequently, the treatise would be rendered useless. Therefore,

so that even those of dull intellect might achieve success in its swift comprehension, retention, and application, Īśvarakṛṣṇa— out of compassion for his disciples— has condensed the statements from the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* by removing the intervening narratives and verses and has composed this work in *Āryā* meters.
It was condensed into seventy [verses] by Āryamati,
who is devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having correctly understood the established tenet.

And how is it that he, though possessing the knowledge of the perfectly established doctrine, has condensed the reality of the categories of Sāṃkhya—which could be described in many hundreds of thousands of treatises—into an unbroken whole by means of the *Saptati* of the Teacher?
And it is said:
"The seventy topics that are in [this work] are indeed the topics of the entire *Ṣaṣṭitantra*."
They are devoid of narratives and also free from the arguments of opponents.

Since the categories such as *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* have been accepted, taught, and praised by the teachers beginning with Nārāyaṇa, Manu, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, and Dvaipāyana, [this work was composed] by the venerable Īśvarakṛṣṇa— whose essential intellect is skilled in defining the nature of these categories— in order to adorn the noble path through its natural renown and its fruit, which is prosperity (*ṛddhi*).

Having placed the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) before him in accordance with the scriptures taught by the supreme sages and others, he has conducted an investigation through the lens of reasoning;
and in this work, not even the slightest trace of fault exists, just as there is no flaw whatsoever in a mass of pure gold. // 72 //
And it is said:
"The moonlight of knowledge, fallen from the moon-like Sage for the purpose of pacifying the darkness of ignorance, is obscured by the turbid clouds of the waters of the [false] traditions."
Thus, let this *Yuktidīpikā*, which dispels the darkness of false views and illuminates creation, be upheld by the wise who are free from confusion.
Even speech that is clear in meaning and sweet does not shine in the presence of a fool;
though it contains fire within, the radiance of the sun becomes lukewarm when surrounded by frost at the onset of winter.
Since the virtuous, by their own power, lead others toward even a slight excellence or nobility,
let this labor of mine serve as a mere object for the gracious consideration of the wise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter and the eleventh daily lesson in the Yuktidīpikā, the commentary on the Sāṃkhyasaptati.
This is the work of the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
